PHYS-L17 Cardiac circuit

27 learning questions · of 61
Learning questions 27

Two pumps in series

L1Learning
Why must right and left ventricular output be equal in the steady state?
  1. A. They are in parallel: each side pumps half the cardiac output
  2. B. They are in series: the left side always pumps twice what the right side pumps
  3. C. They are in series: whatever the right side pumps, the left side must pump
AnswerC. They are in series: whatever the right side pumps, the left side must pump
WhyThe ventricles are in series: every millilitre the right ventricle ejects must come round to the left, so their outputs are equal.
Explanation

Cardiac output is the volume one ventricle pumps per minute (about 5 L/min). Because the right ventricle's output is the left ventricle's input, the two outputs must match over anything longer than a few beats; otherwise blood would pile up on one side.

  • In parallel, half each is wrong: each ventricle pumps the whole cardiac output, one through the lungs and one through the body.
  • Left pumps twice the right confuses pressure with flow: the left generates about five times the pressure, but the same flow.

In reality a little bronchial venous blood drains straight into the left heart, so left output is about 2% higher; exams treat the two as equal.

Slides (2)
L2Learning
While the right ventricle ejects blood into the pulmonary artery, what is the left ventricle doing?
  1. A. Filling from the left atrium through the open mitral valve
  2. B. Receiving extra blood as the left atrium contracts
  3. C. Contracting and ejecting blood into the aorta
AnswerC. Contracting and ejecting blood into the aorta
WhyBoth ventricles contract at the same time: while the right ejects into the pulmonary artery, the left ejects into the aorta.
Explanation

'In series' describes the path of the blood, not the timing of the beats. One conduction system depolarizes both ventricles together, so right and left ventricular systole coincide and both semilunar valves are open during the same ejection phase (the pulmonic valve opens a little earlier and shuts a little later than the aortic, which is why the second heart sound can split).

  • Filling through an open mitral valve happens in diastole, when the right ventricle is filling through the tricuspid valve too.
  • Left atrial contraction (the atrial kick) tops up the ventricle at the very end of diastole, just before the ventricles contract; the right atrium contracts at the same moment.
Slides (1)
L3Learning
What fraction of the cardiac output passes through each heart chamber and through the lungs every minute?
  1. A. 100%
  2. B. 50%
  3. C. 25%
AnswerA. 100%
WhyThe circuit is one series loop, so 100% of the cardiac output passes through each chamber and through the lungs every minute.
Explanation

The left ventricle's output is shared out among the systemic organs, but on the way back every stream reunites in the venae cavae and passes, in full, through the right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary veins and left heart. The lungs are the only organ that receives the whole cardiac output.

  • 50% treats the two sides as parallel halves.
  • 25% is the share of a single systemic bed (kidneys, gut or skeletal muscle), not of a chamber.
Slides (2)
L4LearningHigh yield
In the steady state, how does cardiac output compare with venous return?
  1. A. Cardiac output is greater than venous return
  2. B. Venous return is greater than cardiac output
  3. C. Cardiac output equals venous return
AnswerC. Cardiac output equals venous return
WhyIn the steady state cardiac output = venous return: the heart can only pump out what comes back to it.
Explanation

In a closed loop, flow out of the heart must equal flow back into it, or blood would pile up in the heart or drain out of the veins. The Frank-Starling mechanism keeps them matched beat by beat: more venous return stretches the ventricle and raises stroke volume.

  • Cardiac output greater than venous return would empty the veins and heart within minutes.
  • Venous return greater would distend the heart and veins more and more.

The two can differ for a few beats during a change (standing up, a sudden haemorrhage), not in the steady state.

Slides (2)
L5Learning
If the right ventricle pumped slightly less than the left ventricle for many beats, where would blood accumulate?
  1. A. In the pulmonary veins → raised pulmonary capillary pressure and lung oedema
  2. B. In the systemic veins → raised venous pressure and leg oedema
  3. C. Nowhere: the lungs would absorb the difference indefinitely
AnswerB. In the systemic veins → raised venous pressure and leg oedema
WhyBlood piles up upstream of the weaker pump: a lagging right ventricle backs blood into the systemic veins, raising venous and capillary pressure → oedema.
Explanation

Because the pumps are in series, even a tiny mismatch adds up: 1 mL per beat at 70 beats/min shifts 70 mL per minute from one circuit to the other. Blood collects in the circuit that feeds the weak side. The right ventricle is fed by the systemic veins, so they congest: raised jugular venous pressure, an enlarged liver and leg oedema.

  • Pulmonary congestion follows when the left ventricle lags, because the left ventricle is fed by the pulmonary veins.
  • The lungs hold only a small blood volume and cannot absorb a sustained difference; it ends up as congestion.
Slides (1)

One full lap: chambers, valves, vessels

L6LearningHigh yield
Trace one full lap of the circulation, starting at the right atrium.
  1. A. Right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonic valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → organs → veins → vena cava → right atrium
  2. B. Right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonic valve → pulmonary vein → lungs → pulmonary artery → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → organs → veins → vena cava → right atrium
  3. C. Right atrium → mitral valve → right ventricle → pulmonic valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → tricuspid valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → organs → veins → vena cava → right atrium
AnswerA. Right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonic valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → organs → veins → vena cava → right atrium
WhyEach side has an atrioventricular then a semilunar valve (tricuspid → pulmonic, mitral → aortic); the pulmonary artery leaves the heart, the pulmonary vein returns.
Explanation

Two rules generate the whole lap:

  • Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, whatever its oxygen content. So the pulmonary artery leaves the right ventricle and the pulmonary veins enter the left atrium. The choice that sends blood from the right ventricle into the pulmonary vein breaks this rule.
  • Each side has an atrioventricular valve, then a semilunar valve: tricuspid then pulmonic on the right, mitral then aortic on the left. The choice with the mitral valve on the right and the tricuspid on the left swaps the two atrioventricular valves.

Hook: 'try before you buy': the tricuspid is met before the bicuspid (mitral).

Slides (3)
L7LearningHigh yield
Which vessel carries oxygen-poor blood away from the heart?
  1. A. Pulmonary artery
  2. B. Pulmonary vein
  3. C. Aorta
AnswerA. Pulmonary artery
WhyThe pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs: arteries are named by direction of flow, not by oxygen content.
Explanation

'Artery' means a vessel carrying blood away from the heart. In the systemic circuit that blood is oxygenated, but the right ventricle pumps returned venous blood to the lungs, so the pulmonary artery is the artery with oxygen-poor blood, and the pulmonary veins are the veins with oxygen-rich blood.

  • The pulmonary vein carries oxygen-rich blood toward the heart, into the left atrium.
  • The aorta carries oxygen-rich blood away from the left ventricle.
Slides (2)
L8LearningHigh yield
A drug is injected into a vein of the left leg. Which capillary bed does it reach first?
  1. A. Coronary capillaries
  2. B. Pulmonary capillaries
  3. C. Liver capillaries (first-pass)
AnswerB. Pulmonary capillaries
WhyLeg venous blood returns through the vena cava to the right heart, which pumps it straight to the lungs: the pulmonary capillaries come first.
Explanation

Path: leg vein → inferior vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonic valve → pulmonary artery → pulmonary capillaries → pulmonary veins → left heart → aorta → systemic organs. Anything entering a systemic vein meets the lung capillaries before any systemic organ; it is also why a leg-vein clot lodges in the lung as a pulmonary embolus.

  • Coronary capillaries are the first systemic bed off the aorta, reached only after the lungs and the left heart.
  • Liver first-pass applies to drugs absorbed from the gut, which drain through the portal vein to the liver; a leg vein does not.
Slides (2)

Right vs left: pressure and wall

L9Learning
Typical pulmonary artery pressure?
  1. A. About 25/0 mmHg (mean 8)
  2. B. About 25/8 mmHg (mean 15)
  3. C. About 40/15 mmHg (mean 25)
AnswerB. About 25/8 mmHg (mean 15)
WhyPulmonary artery pressure is about 25/8 mmHg, mean 15: roughly a sixth to a seventh of aortic pressure.
Explanation

The right ventricle ejects into a short, wide, very compliant, low-resistance bed, so a systolic pressure of about 25 mmHg is enough. Diastolic pressure stays near 8 because the pulmonic valve closes and blood keeps draining slowly into the lungs.

  • 25/0 (mean 8) is roughly the right ventricle's own pressure: the ventricle relaxes to near zero, but the artery beyond the closed pulmonic valve does not.
  • 40/15 (mean 25) is in the range of pulmonary hypertension (mean above about 20–25 mmHg), not normal.
Slides (3)
L10Learning
Both sides pump the same flow. How do left-side pressures compare with right-side pressures?
  1. A. Peak ventricular pressure about 2× (120 vs 60)
    Mean outflow-artery pressure about 3× (aorta 100 vs pulmonary artery 35)
  2. B. Peak ventricular pressure about 5× (120 vs 25)
    Mean outflow-artery pressure about 7× (aorta 100 vs pulmonary artery 15)
  3. C. Peak ventricular pressure about 10× (120 vs 12)
    Mean outflow-artery pressure about 20× (aorta 100 vs pulmonary artery 5)
AnswerB. Peak ventricular pressure about 5× (120 vs 25)
Mean outflow-artery pressure about 7× (aorta 100 vs pulmonary artery 15)
WhyLeft-side pressures are about 5× higher at peak (120 vs 25 mmHg) and about 7× higher on average (aorta 100 vs pulmonary artery 15).
Explanation

Same flow, very different pressure. Because resistance = pressure difference ÷ flow and the two flows are equal, the pressure ratio is essentially the resistance ratio of the two circuits.

  • 2× / 3× would need a right ventricular peak of about 60 mmHg, which happens only in pulmonary hypertension.
  • 10× / 20× would put mean pulmonary artery pressure at 5, below the pulmonary capillaries (10) and veins (8) it feeds, so blood could not flow forward.
Slides (2)
L11Learning
Both ventricles pump the same flow. Why must the left ventricle generate far more pressure?
  1. A. The systemic circuit has about ten times the resistance of the pulmonary circuit
  2. B. The systemic circuit carries more flow than the pulmonary circuit
  3. C. The pulmonary circuit has about ten times the resistance of the systemic circuit
AnswerA. The systemic circuit has about ten times the resistance of the pulmonary circuit
WhyPressure = flow × resistance. With equal flow, the systemic circuit's roughly tenfold higher resistance demands a much higher driving pressure.
Explanation

Rearranging Q = ΔP/R gives ΔP = Q × R. With the same cardiac output through both circuits, the circuit with the higher resistance needs the higher driving pressure. The systemic tree is long, with many narrow, muscular arterioles; the pulmonary tree is short, wide and thin-walled. Picture a short garden hose versus a mile of narrow pipe fed by the same tap.

  • More systemic flow is wrong: the circuits are in series, so their flows are equal.
  • Pulmonary resistance ten times higher reverses the relationship; it would make the right ventricle the high-pressure pump.
Slides (2)

Mean pressure at each level

L12Learning
What pressure pattern do both the systemic and pulmonary circuits share?
  1. A. Lowest leaving the ventricle → highest arriving back at an atrium
  2. B. Highest leaving the ventricle → lowest arriving back at an atrium
  3. C. Highest in the capillaries → lowest in the arteries and veins
AnswerB. Highest leaving the ventricle → lowest arriving back at an atrium
WhyIn both circuits pressure is highest leaving the ventricle and falls step by step to its lowest at the receiving atrium; that gradient drives the flow.
Explanation

Blood flows from high to low pressure, and each segment's resistance uses up some of the pressure. Systemic: aorta 100 → arterioles 50 → capillaries 20 → vena cava 4 → right atrium 0–2. Pulmonary: pulmonary artery 15 → capillaries 10 → pulmonary vein 8 → left atrium 2–5. The pulmonary circuit follows the same pattern at about a sixth of the pressure.

  • Lowest leaving the ventricle reverses the gradient; blood would flow backward.
  • Highest in the capillaries is wrong: capillaries lie downstream of the arteries and arterioles, so their pressure is lower.
Slides (3)
L13Learning
Mean pressure in the main veins: vena cava vs pulmonary vein?
  1. A. Vena cava 8 mmHg
    Pulmonary vein 4 mmHg
  2. B. Vena cava 4 mmHg
    Pulmonary vein 15 mmHg
  3. C. Vena cava 4 mmHg
    Pulmonary vein 8 mmHg
AnswerC. Vena cava 4 mmHg
Pulmonary vein 8 mmHg
WhyMean pressure is about 4 mmHg in the vena cava and 8 mmHg in the pulmonary vein: here the pulmonary value is the higher one.
Explanation

Each main vein sits just above the atrium it drains into: vena cava 4 → right atrium 0–2; pulmonary vein 8 → left atrium 2–5. Because the left atrium runs at a higher pressure than the right, the pulmonary vein must too, even though the rest of the pulmonary circuit is lower than its systemic counterpart. This is the classic trap in the table.

  • Vena cava 8, pulmonary vein 4 swaps the pair.
  • Pulmonary vein 15 is the mean pulmonary artery pressure, upstream of the lung capillaries (10).
Slides (3)
L14Learning
Left atrial pressure is hard to measure directly. What is used clinically to estimate it?
  1. A. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
  2. B. Mean pulmonary artery pressure
  3. C. Central venous pressure
AnswerA. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
WhyPulmonary capillary wedge pressure, read from a catheter wedged in a small pulmonary artery branch, approximates left atrial pressure.
Explanation

What it is: a balloon-tipped pulmonary artery (Swan–Ganz) catheter is passed from a systemic vein through the right atrium and right ventricle into the pulmonary artery. Inflating the balloon wedges it in a small branch and stops flow there.

Why it reads the left atrium: with no flow there is no pressure drop along the still column of blood from the catheter tip through the capillaries and pulmonary veins, so the tip senses pulmonary venous ≈ left atrial pressure (and, with a normal mitral valve, left ventricular filling pressure). Normal is a few mmHg (2–5 in the table; clinical references accept up to about 12).

  • Mean pulmonary artery pressure (~15), read with the balloon down, lies upstream of the pulmonary resistance, so it runs higher.
  • Central venous pressure, read in the vena cava or right atrium, reflects right heart filling.
Slides (3)
L15LearningHigh yield
After a heart attack, a papillary muscle anchoring the mitral valve ruptures. The patient becomes short of breath with crackles at the lung bases. What causes the lung finding?
  1. A. ↑ Right atrial and systemic venous pressure → fluid filters into the lungs
  2. B. ↑ Left atrial and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure → fluid filters into the lungs
  3. C. ↓ Pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure → the alveoli collapse
AnswerB. ↑ Left atrial and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure → fluid filters into the lungs
WhyA leaking mitral valve sends blood back into the left atrium each systole, raising left atrial → pulmonary vein → pulmonary capillary pressure, which drives fluid into the lungs.
Explanation

Papillary muscles and chordae tendineae stop the mitral cusps from turning inside out into the atrium when the ventricle contracts. If one ruptures, the valve suddenly leaks (acute mitral regurgitation): part of each stroke volume goes backward into the left atrium, and left atrial pressure rises sharply. That pressure is transmitted upstream through the pulmonary veins to the pulmonary capillaries; higher capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid into the interstitium and alveoli (pulmonary oedema → crackles).

  • Raised right atrial and systemic venous pressure causes leg oedema and liver congestion, not lung fluid.
  • Falling capillary pressure would draw fluid out of the lungs, not into them.
Slides (3)

Resistance: TPR vs PVR

L16Learning
For pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), what is the pressure difference (ΔP)?
  1. A. Mean pulmonary artery pressure − right atrial pressure
  2. B. Mean pulmonary artery pressure − left atrial pressure
  3. C. Mean arterial pressure (MAP) − left atrial pressure
AnswerB. Mean pulmonary artery pressure − left atrial pressure
WhyPulmonary vascular resistance spans the lungs, so ΔP = mean pulmonary artery pressure − left atrial pressure.
Explanation

The pulmonary circuit starts where the right ventricle ejects (pulmonary artery, mean about 15) and ends where blood enters the left atrium (2–5, estimated from the wedge pressure). The flow through it is the whole cardiac output.

  • Pulmonary artery − right atrial pressure uses the systemic circuit's end point; the right atrium is not downstream of the lungs.
  • MAP − left atrial pressure starts in the wrong circuit.

Rule for both: ΔP = pressure where blood enters the circuit − pressure where it leaves.

Slides (2)
L17Learning
Calculate TPR: MAP 96 mmHg, right atrial pressure 2 mmHg, cardiac output 5,229 mL/min.
  1. A. (96 − 2) / 5,229 ≈ 0.018 mmHg/mL per min
  2. B. (96 − 2) / 5,229 ≈ 0.18 mmHg/mL per min
  3. C. (96 + 2) / 5,229 ≈ 0.019 mmHg/mL per min
AnswerA. (96 − 2) / 5,229 ≈ 0.018 mmHg/mL per min
WhyTPR = (MAP − right atrial pressure) ÷ cardiac output = 94 ÷ 5,229 ≈ 0.018 mmHg/mL per min.
Explanation

Step by step: ΔP = 96 − 2 = 94 mmHg; 94 ÷ 5,229 mL/min = 0.0180 mmHg per mL/min.

  • 0.18 slips a decimal place: 94 ÷ 5,229 must be under 0.02, because 5,229 × 0.02 ≈ 105.
  • (96 + 2) adds the downstream pressure instead of subtracting it; ΔP is always upstream minus downstream.

Sanity check: 100 mmHg ÷ 5,000 mL/min = 0.02, so TPR must come out just under 0.02.

Slides (2)
L18Learning
What do you need to calculate the resistance of a single organ?
  1. A. Mean arterial pressure − right atrial pressure and the cardiac output
  2. B. That organ's own arterial − venous pressure and its own blood flow
  3. C. That organ's own arterial pressure alone and the cardiac output
AnswerB. That organ's own arterial − venous pressure and its own blood flow
WhyOrgan resistance = (that organ's arterial − venous pressure) ÷ that organ's own blood flow.
Explanation

R = ΔP/Q works for any segment, but both terms must belong to that segment. For the kidney, ΔP is renal artery pressure − renal vein pressure and Q is renal blood flow (about a quarter of the cardiac output).

  • MAP − right atrial pressure with cardiac output gives TPR, the whole systemic circuit.
  • Arterial pressure alone ignores the outflow pressure, and the cardiac output is the wrong flow: the organ receives only its share.
Slides (2)

Vessel numbers, area and volume

L19LearningHigh yield
Which vessels have the largest total cross-sectional area, and about how large?
  1. A. Arterioles: about 2,500 cm² (vs a few cm² for the aorta)
  2. B. Aorta: about 2,500 cm² (vs a few cm² for the capillaries)
  3. C. Capillaries: about 2,500 cm² (vs a few cm² for the aorta)
AnswerC. Capillaries: about 2,500 cm² (vs a few cm² for the aorta)
WhyCapillaries have by far the largest total cross-sectional area, about 2,500 cm², against a few cm² for the aorta.
Explanation

Total cross-sectional area is the sum of the areas of all vessels at one level. One capillary is tiny, but 1010 of them add up to several hundred times the aorta's area. Since velocity = flow ÷ area and the same cardiac output crosses every level, blood moves slowest in the capillaries, which leaves time for exchange.

  • Arterioles are far fewer (107) and total well under 100 cm².
  • Aorta 2,500 reverses the picture: the single aorta has the smallest total area and the fastest blood.
Slides (3)
L20Learning
Which vessels are called the capacitance vessels, and why?
  1. A. Veins: high compliance lets them hold most of the blood at low pressure
  2. B. Arteries: high compliance lets them hold most of the blood at low pressure
  3. C. Arterioles: high resistance lets them hold most of the blood at low pressure
AnswerA. Veins: high compliance lets them hold most of the blood at low pressure
WhyVeins are the capacitance vessels: their high compliance lets them store most of the blood at low pressure.
Explanation

Capacitance (compliance) = volume ÷ pressure (C = V/P). A vein's thin wall stretches easily, so added volume barely raises its pressure. The veins therefore act as a reservoir that can be squeezed (venoconstriction) to push blood toward the heart when needed, as in haemorrhage or exercise.

  • Arteries are stiffer (less compliant) and hold a small, high-pressure (stressed) volume.
  • Arterioles are the resistance vessels: they set the pressure drop and the distribution of flow but hold little blood.
Slides (3)

Organ shares of cardiac output

L21Learning
How are the systemic organs arranged relative to the aorta, and what follows for their flows?
  1. A. In series → their separate flows add up to the whole cardiac output
  2. B. In series → each organ receives the whole cardiac output in turn
  3. C. In parallel → their separate flows add up to the whole cardiac output
AnswerC. In parallel → their separate flows add up to the whole cardiac output
WhyThe organs branch off the aorta in parallel, so each takes a fraction of the flow and the fractions add up to the cardiac output.
Explanation

Each systemic organ gets its own artery from the aorta and drains into the venae cavae, so blood passes through only one organ per lap (apart from portal arrangements such as gut → liver). Flow into a junction equals flow out of it (Kirchhoff's rule), so the organ flows sum to 100% of the cardiac output. In parallel, each organ sees roughly aortic pressure at its inlet and can change its own flow by changing its arteriolar resistance.

  • Series, flows add up is wrong: in series every element carries the same flow.
  • Series, each receives the whole output describes the two hearts and the lungs, not the systemic organs.
Slides (3)
L22LearningHigh yield
Which three organ systems each receive about a quarter of the resting cardiac output?
  1. A. Kidneys, brain, coronary circulation
  2. B. Kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, skeletal muscle
  3. C. Skin, skeletal muscle, gastrointestinal tract
AnswerB. Kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, skeletal muscle
WhyThe kidneys, gastrointestinal tract and skeletal muscle each receive about 25% of the resting cardiac output.
Explanation
BedResting share
Kidneys25%
Gastrointestinal25%
Skeletal muscle25%
Brain15%
Coronary5%
Skin5%
  • Kidneys, brain, coronary: the brain gets 15% and the coronaries only 5%.
  • Skin, skeletal muscle, gut: the skin gets only 5% at rest.

Hook: 25-25-25, 15, 5-5.

Slides (2)
L23Learning
Which organ receives the most blood flow per gram of tissue at rest?
  1. A. Brain: about 2% of body weight, about 15% of the output
  2. B. Heart: under 1% of body weight, about 5% of the output
  3. C. Kidneys: under 1% of body weight, about 25% of the output
AnswerC. Kidneys: under 1% of body weight, about 25% of the output
WhyThe kidneys are under 1% of body weight yet receive about 25% of the output: the highest flow per gram of the major organs.
Explanation

Flow per gram = organ flow ÷ organ mass. Kidneys: about 0.3 kg receiving about 1.25 L/min, roughly 4 mL/min per gram. Brain: about 1.4 kg receiving 0.75 L/min, about 0.5 mL/min per gram. Heart: about 0.3 kg receiving 0.25 L/min, under 1 mL/min per gram.

  • Brain: a large share, but spread over a large mass.
  • Heart: a small mass, but only 5% of the output.
Slides (1)
L24Learning
Why do the kidneys take so much of the cardiac output?
  1. A. Their tubules extract almost all the oxygen delivered to them
  2. B. Their flow serves filtration of the plasma, not their own metabolism
  3. C. They store a large reserve of blood for haemorrhage
AnswerB. Their flow serves filtration of the plasma, not their own metabolism
WhyRenal flow serves filtration of the plasma, not the kidneys' own metabolism, so it far exceeds their O2 needs.
Explanation

The kidneys filter about a fifth of the plasma reaching them; to clear wastes and regulate volume and electrolytes they need a very high throughput. Their O2 extraction is therefore low, and renal venous blood is still rich in O2.

  • Near-total O2 extraction describes the heart, the opposite pattern.
  • A blood reservoir is the role of the veins, not the kidneys.
Slides (1)

Oxygen extraction and redistribution

L25Learning
When myocardial oxygen demand rises, how does the heart mainly get more oxygen?
  1. A. By increasing the fraction of O2 it extracts from each unit of blood
  2. B. By increasing coronary blood flow (metabolic vasodilation)
  3. C. By drawing on O2 stored on myoglobin
AnswerB. By increasing coronary blood flow (metabolic vasodilation)
WhyExtraction is already near-maximal, so the heart meets higher demand mainly by increasing coronary blood flow through metabolic vasodilation.
Explanation

O2 delivered = flow × arterial O2 content; O2 used = delivered × extraction. With extraction near its ceiling, flow is the only big lever left. Working myocardium releases vasodilator metabolites (adenosine, hypoxia, CO2, H⁺, K⁺) that dilate the coronary arterioles, so coronary flow rises in step with cardiac work.

  • Raising extraction is a main reserve of skeletal muscle, not of the heart.
  • Myoglobin stores only a few seconds' worth of O2; it cannot cover a sustained rise in demand.
Slides (2)
L26LearningHigh yield
During strenuous exercise, how do skeletal and cardiac muscle get a larger share of the cardiac output?
  1. A. Cardiac output rises and arteriolar resistance changes bed by bed (muscle dilates, gut and kidney constrict)
  2. B. Cardiac output rises while every organ keeps the same percentage share
  3. C. The compliance of the vessels to muscle rises, so they hold more blood
AnswerA. Cardiac output rises and arteriolar resistance changes bed by bed (muscle dilates, gut and kidney constrict)
WhyCardiac output rises and arteriolar resistance changes selectively: muscle arterioles dilate while gut and kidney arterioles constrict.
Explanation

Flow to any organ = arterial pressure ÷ that organ's resistance. Because the organs are in parallel, the body can redistribute output by changing arteriolar resistance bed by bed: vasodilator metabolites open the exercising-muscle and coronary arterioles, while sympathetic constriction narrows the splanchnic and renal arterioles. At the same time cardiac output rises several-fold.

  • Raising output with fixed percentages would not change the muscle share, yet the share does rise.
  • Compliance sets how much blood a vessel holds at a given pressure, not how much flows through it.
Slides (3)
L27Learning
During strenuous exercise, how does absolute blood flow (mL/min) change in these beds?
  1. A. Skeletal muscle ↑↑
    Coronary ↑
    Brain ↓ sharply
  2. B. Skeletal muscle ↑↑
    Coronary ↑
    Gut and kidney ↓
  3. C. Skeletal muscle ↑ slightly
    Coronary ↓
    Gut and kidney ↑↑
AnswerB. Skeletal muscle ↑↑
Coronary ↑
Gut and kidney ↓
WhyIn strenuous exercise flow rises hugely in skeletal muscle, rises in the coronaries and falls in the gut and kidneys; brain flow stays about constant.
Explanation

Muscle flow can rise more than tenfold through metabolic vasodilation; coronary flow rises with cardiac work; gut and kidney flows fall through sympathetic vasoconstriction. Brain flow is autoregulated and stays roughly constant, so only its percentage falls as the total rises. Skin flow rises later as body temperature climbs.

  • Brain ↓ sharply is wrong in absolute terms; a sharp fall in brain flow would cause fainting.
  • Muscle ↑ slightly, coronary ↓, gut and kidney ↑↑ reverses every direction.
Slides (2)

PHYS-L18/19 Peripheral fluid dynamics 1 & 2

60 learning questions · of 129
Learning questions 60

Lecture 18 · Ohm's law: pressure difference drives flow

L1Learning
What drives blood flow through a vessel?
  1. A. The absolute pressure at its inflow end
  2. B. The average pressure inside the vessel
  3. C. The pressure difference between its two ends
AnswerC. The pressure difference between its two ends
WhyBlood moves only down a pressure gradient (ΔP), from higher to lower pressure; a pressure level on its own moves nothing.
Explanation

Flow (Q) is driven by the pressure difference between the two ends of a vessel, ΔP = Pin − Pout, and opposed by resistance: Q = ΔP / R. Blood always flows from the higher-pressure end to the lower-pressure end.

  • The absolute pressure at the inflow end says nothing about flow by itself: 100 mmHg at the start gives no flow if the far end is also at 100 mmHg.
  • The average pressure inside the vessel is also a level, not a gradient. A vessel can sit at high pressure with no flow at all.

Exam tip: when a stem gives pressures, subtract downstream from upstream before doing anything else.

Slides (2)
L2LearningHigh yield
Which equation is Ohm's law for blood flow?
  1. A. Q = R / ΔP
  2. B. Q = ΔP × R
  3. C. Q = ΔP / R
AnswerC. Q = ΔP / R
WhyFlow = pressure difference ÷ resistance: flow rises in proportion to ΔP and falls in proportion to R.
Explanation

Q = blood flow (mL/min), ΔP = pressure difference between the two ends (mmHg), R = resistance (mmHg per mL/min). It is the same relationship as current = voltage ÷ resistance in an electric circuit.

  • Flow is directly proportional to ΔP and inversely proportional to R.
  • Q = R / ΔP would make flow rise as the gradient falls.
  • Q = ΔP × R would make a narrower, higher-resistance vessel carry more flow.

Rearranged: R = ΔP / Q and ΔP = Q × R. The units of resistance follow from the first form: mmHg per mL/min.

Slides (3)
L3LearningHigh yield
Applied to the whole systemic circulation, Ohm's law becomes which equation?
  1. A. CO = MAP × TPR
  2. B. MAP = CO × TPR
  3. C. MAP = CO / TPR
AnswerB. MAP = CO × TPR
WhyFor the whole systemic circuit, ΔP ≈ mean arterial pressure, Q = cardiac output and R = total peripheral resistance: MAP = CO × TPR.
Explanation

Rearranging Q = ΔP / R gives ΔP = Q × R. Across the systemic circulation, the flow is the cardiac output (CO), the resistance is the total peripheral resistance (TPR) of all the parallel beds, and the pressure difference is mean arterial pressure (MAP) minus right atrial pressure, which is about MAP.

  • CO = MAP × TPR would make output rise when resistance rises; in fact output falls if MAP is unchanged.
  • MAP = CO / TPR would make constriction of the arterioles lower blood pressure, the opposite of what happens.

This one equation explains every blood-pressure drug: lower CO or lower TPR to lower MAP.

Slides (3)
L4LearningHigh yield
Renal artery pressure is 120 mmHg, renal vein pressure 20 mmHg and renal blood flow 400 mL/min. What is the renal vascular resistance?
  1. A. 0.30 mmHg per mL/min
  2. B. 4.0 mmHg per mL/min
  3. C. 0.25 mmHg per mL/min
AnswerC. 0.25 mmHg per mL/min
WhyR = ΔP / Q = (120 − 20) mmHg ÷ 400 mL/min = 0.25 mmHg per mL/min.
Explanation

To find one organ's resistance, use that organ's own pressure difference (artery minus vein) and its own flow: R = ΔP / Q = 100 / 400 = 0.25 mmHg per mL/min.

  • 0.30 uses the arterial pressure alone (120 / 400) and forgets to subtract the venous pressure.
  • 4.0 divides flow by pressure difference (400 / 100), which gives conductance, the reciprocal of resistance, and has the wrong units.

Units check: resistance is always pressure over flow, mmHg per mL/min.

Slides (2)

Lecture 18 · Poiseuille: what sets resistance

L5LearningHigh yield
Which is the Poiseuille equation for resistance?
  1. A. R = 8ηl / πr2
  2. B. R = πr4 / 8ηl
  3. C. R = 8ηl / πr4
AnswerC. R = 8ηl / πr4
WhyR = 8ηl / πr4: viscosity and length on top (resistance rises with them), radius to the fourth power underneath.
Explanation

η (eta) = blood viscosity, l = vessel length, r = vessel radius. Resistance is directly proportional to viscosity and length and inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius.

  • r2 in the denominator is the cross-sectional area term from the velocity equation (A = πr2), not Poiseuille.
  • πr4 / 8ηl is the formula turned upside down; that expression is conductance, so a wider vessel would have more resistance.

Combined with Q = ΔP/R it gives Poiseuille's law for flow: Q = ΔP·πr4 / 8ηl.

Slides (3)
L6Learning
Polycythaemia vs severe anaemia: effect on blood viscosity and vascular resistance?
  1. A. Polycythaemia: viscosity ↓ → resistance ↓
    Anaemia: viscosity ↑ → resistance ↑
  2. B. Polycythaemia: viscosity ↑ → resistance ↓
    Anaemia: viscosity ↓ → resistance ↑
  3. C. Polycythaemia: viscosity ↑ → resistance ↑
    Anaemia: viscosity ↓ → resistance ↓
AnswerC. Polycythaemia: viscosity ↑ → resistance ↑
Anaemia: viscosity ↓ → resistance ↓
WhyViscosity follows the haematocrit, and resistance follows viscosity (R ∝ η): more red cells → thicker blood → higher resistance.
Explanation

Polycythaemia (too many red cells) raises viscosity; Poiseuille puts η in the numerator, so resistance rises and the heart must work harder for the same flow. Severe anaemia does the reverse: thinner blood, lower resistance, and (with the raised cardiac output of anaemia) faster flow.

  • The reversed pairing gets the haematocrit–viscosity link backwards.
  • The mixed pairing gets viscosity right but breaks R ∝ η: higher viscosity cannot lower resistance.

The same viscosity changes also move the Reynolds number in opposite directions (see the turbulence section).

Slides (2)

Lecture 18 · Radius changes in numbers

L7LearningHigh yield
A vessel's radius is halved while the pressure difference across it stays the same. What happens to its flow?
  1. A. Falls to one quarter
  2. B. Falls to one half
  3. C. Falls to one sixteenth
AnswerC. Falls to one sixteenth
WhyResistance rises 16-fold, and at a constant ΔP flow is inversely proportional to resistance (Q = ΔP/R), so flow falls to 1/16.
Explanation

Combine Poiseuille and Ohm: Q = ΔP·πr4 / 8ηl. With ΔP, η and l fixed, flow is proportional to r4, so a halved radius leaves (½)4 = 1/16 of the flow. A 50% narrowing of a renal artery, for example, cuts its flow to 1/16 if the pressure gradient does not rise.

  • One quarter uses r2 (area) instead of r4.
  • One half treats radius linearly.
Slides (3)
L8Learning
Plaque reduces a vessel's radius to 90% of normal. By about how much must the pressure difference rise to keep flow the same?
  1. A. About 1.5-fold
  2. B. About 1.1-fold
  3. C. About 1.2-fold
AnswerA. About 1.5-fold
WhyResistance rises by 1/0.94 = 1/0.66 ≈ 1.5-fold, so ΔP = Q × R must rise 1.5-fold to hold flow constant.
Explanation

0.94 = 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 ≈ 0.66. Resistance therefore rises to 1/0.66 ≈ 1.52 times normal, and to keep Q the same the pressure gradient must rise by the same factor. A mere 10% loss of radius needs about 50% more driving pressure.

  • About 1.1-fold (1/0.9) treats radius linearly.
  • About 1.2-fold (1/0.81) squares the radius instead of raising it to the fourth power.
Slides (2)
L9Learning
A hypotensive patient needs fluid as fast as possible. Which intravenous cannula gives the highest flow at the same pressure?
  1. A. Long (7 cm) and wide (2 mm radius)
  2. B. Short (5 cm) and wide (2 mm radius)
  3. C. Short (5 cm) and narrow (1 mm radius)
AnswerB. Short (5 cm) and wide (2 mm radius)
WhyFlow ∝ r4/l: the widest and shortest tube has the lowest resistance, and radius matters far more than length.
Explanation

By Poiseuille, the 2 mm tube has 24 = 16 times less resistance than the 1 mm tube of the same length; shortening from 7 to 5 cm lowers resistance further, to 5/7 of the long tube's. So the short, wide cannula wins.

  • Long and wide has the right radius but 40% more length, so 40% more resistance.
  • Short and narrow saves a little length but loses 16-fold on radius.

This is why trauma teams ask for "two large-bore IVs".

Slides (2)

Lecture 18 · Arterioles: the resistance vessels

L10LearningHigh yield
Which vessels are the main resistance vessels of the circulation?
  1. A. Arterioles: the small muscular vessels just before the capillaries
  2. B. Capillaries: the thin exchange vessels between arterioles and venules
  3. C. Large arteries: the elastic vessels leaving the heart
AnswerA. Arterioles: the small muscular vessels just before the capillaries
WhyThe arterioles have the highest resistance in the vasculature, so they are the site of the largest pressure drop and of flow control.
Explanation

Arterioles are narrow and have a thick wall of smooth muscle with a rich sympathetic nerve supply. Their small radius gives them high resistance, and because their smooth muscle can contract or relax, that resistance can be changed quickly. Together they make up most of the total peripheral resistance.

  • Capillaries are individually narrower, but there are about 1010 of them in parallel, so their combined resistance is lower; they also have no smooth muscle to adjust.
  • Large arteries are wide (low resistance); mean pressure barely falls along them.
Slides (2)
L11LearningHigh yield
How is the blood flow to an individual organ mainly adjusted?
  1. A. By changing the cardiac output
  2. B. By changing the diameter of that organ's arterioles
  3. C. By changing the blood viscosity
AnswerB. By changing the diameter of that organ's arterioles
WhyEach organ sets its own flow by changing the radius of its arterioles: a small change in radius changes resistance (R ∝ 1/r4) and flow enormously.
Explanation

The organs are supplied in parallel from the aorta at about the same arterial pressure. The share of cardiac output each one gets therefore depends on its own resistance relative to the others, and that resistance is set by arteriolar diameter (sympathetic tone, circulating hormones and local metabolites).

  • Changing cardiac output changes the total flow available to all organs together; it cannot send more blood to one bed and less to another.
  • Changing viscosity would affect every bed equally, and the body does not regulate haematocrit minute to minute.
Slides (1)
L12LearningHigh yield
The arterioles feeding one skeletal-muscle bed constrict. What happens in that bed's capillaries?
  1. A. Capillary flow ↑
    Capillary hydrostatic pressure ↓
  2. B. Capillary flow ↓
    Capillary hydrostatic pressure ↑
  3. C. Capillary flow ↓
    Capillary hydrostatic pressure ↓
AnswerC. Capillary flow ↓
Capillary hydrostatic pressure ↓
WhyConstriction raises arteriolar resistance, so less flow gets through and more pressure is lost across the arteriole, leaving lower pressure in the capillaries.
Explanation

In a series chain, ΔP = Q × R for each segment. Raising the arteriole's resistance makes it consume a bigger share of the pressure drop, so the pressure arriving at the capillaries (capillary hydrostatic pressure) falls, and flow through the bed falls too. With lower capillary hydrostatic pressure, filtration and interstitial volume also fall; dilation does the reverse.

  • Flow ↓ but capillary pressure ↑ is the classic trap: pressure rises upstream of a constriction, not downstream of it.
  • Flow ↑ is impossible when the resistance in its path rises.
Slides (1)

Lecture 18 · Alpha-1 and beta-2 receptors on arterioles

L13LearningHigh yield
Alpha-1 receptors on arterioles: effect, and where they dominate?
  1. A. Constriction
    Skin, splanchnic (gut) and renal arterioles
  2. B. Constriction
    Skeletal muscle arterioles only
  3. C. Dilation
    Skin, splanchnic (gut) and renal arterioles
AnswerA. Constriction
Skin, splanchnic (gut) and renal arterioles
Whyα1 receptors cause vasoconstriction and dominate the arterioles of the skin, gut (splanchnic) and kidney; activating them raises resistance and TPR.
Explanation

α1 receptors are excitatory on vascular smooth muscle. They are the main receptors on arterioles of the skin, the splanchnic (gut, spleen) circulation and the kidney, so sympathetic activation shunts blood away from those beds. Activating α1 raises total peripheral resistance and blood pressure; blocking it does the reverse.

  • Skeletal muscle only is wrong twice over: α1 is widespread, and skeletal muscle is the bed known for its additional β2 receptors.
  • Dilation is the β2 effect, not α1.
Slides (3)
L14LearningHigh yield
A selective α1 agonist acts on skin arterioles. Which signalling chain produces its effect?
  1. A. Gq → IP3 → ↓ intracellular Ca2+ → relaxation
  2. B. Gs → ↑ cAMP → ↑ intracellular Ca2+ → contraction
  3. C. Gq → IP3 → ↑ intracellular Ca2+ → contraction
AnswerC. Gq → IP3 → ↑ intracellular Ca2+ → contraction
Whyα1 is a Gq receptor: phospholipase C → IP3 → Ca2+ release → smooth-muscle contraction → vasoconstriction and ↑ resistance.
Explanation

Gq activates phospholipase C, which splits membrane phospholipid into IP3 and diacylglycerol. IP3 releases Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum; Ca2+–calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase, and the smooth muscle contracts. In the skin that means vasoconstriction, higher resistance and less flow.

  • Gs → cAMP is the β2 pathway, and in vascular smooth muscle cAMP relaxes rather than contracts.
  • IP3 → ↓ Ca2+ reverses what IP3 does; it raises cytosolic Ca2+.
Slides (3)
L15LearningHigh yield
During exercise, epinephrine acts on β2 receptors of skeletal-muscle arterioles. Which mechanism directly causes the vasodilation?
  1. A. Gs → ↑ cAMP → protein kinase A → inhibition of myosin light-chain kinase
  2. B. Gq → IP3 → ↑ intracellular Ca2+ → relaxation
  3. C. Gi → ↓ cAMP → activation of myosin light-chain kinase
AnswerA. Gs → ↑ cAMP → protein kinase A → inhibition of myosin light-chain kinase
Whyβ2 is a Gs receptor: ↑ cAMP → protein kinase A → inhibits myosin light-chain kinase → less cross-bridge cycling → smooth-muscle relaxation.
Explanation

Smooth muscle contracts when myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK) phosphorylates myosin. β2 → Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A, which phosphorylates and inhibits MLCK, so the arteriole relaxes, its radius widens and resistance falls.

  • Gq → IP3 → ↑ Ca2+ is the α1 pathway, and it produces contraction, not relaxation.
  • Gi → ↓ cAMP → MLCK activation is the reverse of the β2 mechanism and would favour contraction.
Slides (3)
L16Learning
A surge of circulating epinephrine (fight or flight) redistributes blood flow how?
  1. A. Away from skeletal muscle → towards skin and gut
  2. B. Away from skin and gut → towards skeletal muscle
  3. C. Away from every bed equally, since all arterioles constrict
AnswerB. Away from skin and gut → towards skeletal muscle
WhyThe receptor map does it: α1 constricts skin and gut arterioles while β2 dilates skeletal-muscle arterioles, so blood shifts to muscle.
Explanation

Because the organs are in parallel, lowering resistance in one bed and raising it in others redirects cardiac output towards the low-resistance bed. Epinephrine constricts α1-dominated beds (skin, splanchnic, kidney) and dilates β2-bearing skeletal-muscle arterioles, sending blood to the muscles needed to fight or run.

  • Towards skin and gut reverses the receptor distribution.
  • All arterioles constrict equally ignores the β2 receptors of skeletal muscle; equal constriction everywhere would raise pressure but not redistribute flow.
Slides (3)

Lecture 18 · Resistances in series and in parallel

L17LearningHigh yield
Within an organ, blood passes artery → arteriole → capillary → venule → vein. How do these resistances combine?
  1. A. 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + … + 1/R5
  2. B. Rtotal = R1 × R2 × R3 × R4 × R5
  3. C. Rtotal = R1 + R2 + R3 + R4 + R5
AnswerC. Rtotal = R1 + R2 + R3 + R4 + R5
WhyThe vessels inside an organ are in series, one after another, so their resistances simply add.
Explanation

In series, all the blood must pass through every segment in turn, so each segment's resistance adds to the whole. The arteriole is the largest single term in the sum.

  • Adding reciprocals is the rule for resistances in parallel, such as the organs branching off the aorta.
  • Multiplying resistances is not a rule for either arrangement.

Hook: series = sum; parallel = reciprocals.

Slides (3)
L18LearningHigh yield
In vessels arranged in series, how do flow and pressure behave from one segment to the next?
  1. A. Flow: the same at every level
    Pressure: the same at every level
  2. B. Flow: falls across each segment
    Pressure: the same at every level
  3. C. Flow: the same at every level
    Pressure: falls across each segment
AnswerC. Flow: the same at every level
Pressure: falls across each segment
WhyIn series, the same flow passes every level, and pressure falls across each segment in proportion to its resistance (ΔP = Q × R).
Explanation

Blood cannot accumulate or disappear between segments, so the flow through the artery, arterioles, capillaries, venules and veins of a bed is the same. Each segment uses up part of the driving pressure: the higher its resistance, the bigger its share of the pressure drop.

  • Flow falling across each segment would mean blood was being lost along the way.
  • Pressure the same at every level describes the start of each parallel branch, not a series chain; with no pressure fall there would be no flow.
Slides (2)
L19LearningHigh yield
How do resistances in parallel combine?
  1. A. 1/Rtotal = R1 + R2 + … + R6
  2. B. 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + … + 1/R6
  3. C. Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + … + 1/R6
AnswerB. 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + … + 1/R6
WhyIn parallel, the reciprocals add: 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + …
Explanation

Each branch offers its own path, and the reciprocal of resistance (conductance) measures how easily blood passes. Conductances add in parallel, so the total conductance is the sum of the branch conductances, and Rtotal is the reciprocal of that sum.

  • 1/Rtotal = sum of R mixes the two sides of the formula.
  • Rtotal = sum of 1/R forgets to take the reciprocal at the end; it gives a conductance, not a resistance.
Slides (2)
L20LearningHigh yield
What does adding another parallel path do to total resistance, and why?
  1. A. Always raises it: blood has to supply another bed
  2. B. Always lowers it: blood has another way through
  3. C. Leaves it unchanged: pressure is shared equally
AnswerB. Always lowers it: blood has another way through
WhyEvery added parallel branch adds conductance, so total resistance always falls; the same is true as the aorta branches into more and more vessels.
Explanation

Adding a branch adds a 1/R term to the sum, which can only increase 1/Rtotal. This is why total resistance falls when the aorta divides into many arteries, and why opening more capillaries in exercising muscle lowers that bed's resistance.

  • Always raises it is series reasoning: in parallel, a new bed is an extra route, not an extra obstacle.
  • Unchanged is wrong because pressure at the branch points stays the same, but flow now has more paths.
Slides (2)
L21Learning
Two parallel branches share the same pressure difference. Branch Y has resistance 3 and branch Z resistance 6. What fraction of the total flow goes through Y?
  1. A. One third
  2. B. Two thirds
  3. C. One half
AnswerB. Two thirds
WhyAt the same ΔP, flow is inversely proportional to resistance: Y (resistance 3) carries twice Z's flow, so 2 of every 3 parts go through Y.
Explanation

Q = ΔP/R in each branch with the same ΔP, so QY : QZ = RZ : RY = 6 : 3 = 2 : 1. Of 3 parts of total flow, Y carries 2 (two thirds) and Z carries 1 (one third). The total flow entering the junction equals the sum of the branch flows.

  • One third gives Y the share in proportion to its resistance, the wrong way round.
  • One half would need equal resistances.

The same logic sets each organ's share of cardiac output: its resistance relative to the others.

Slides (2)
L22Learning
Why does the parallel arrangement of the systemic organs matter?
  1. A. Each organ's resistance adds to the next → one organ's constriction lowers flow everywhere
  2. B. Each organ gets the same flow → controls its own pressure independently through its venous tone
  3. C. Each organ gets about the same driving pressure → controls its own flow independently through its arterioles
AnswerC. Each organ gets about the same driving pressure → controls its own flow independently through its arterioles
WhyEvery parallel bed starts at about aortic pressure, so each organ can set its own flow by changing its own arteriolar resistance without starving the others.
Explanation

Because all the branches leave the aorta, they share the same inflow pressure; there is no meaningful pressure loss between the aorta and the major arteries. Each organ's flow is then its own ΔP divided by its own resistance. When muscle arterioles dilate in exercise, muscle flow rises while brain flow, set by brain resistance, is protected. The fraction of cardiac output each organ receives depends on its resistance relative to the total.

  • Same flow is the series rule, and venous tone does not set organ flow.
  • Resistances adding is again series reasoning.
Slides (1)

Lecture 18 · Velocity versus flow

L23LearningHigh yield
Which formula gives the velocity of blood flow?
  1. A. v = Q / A
  2. B. v = A / Q
  3. C. v = Q × A
AnswerA. v = Q / A
Whyv = Q / A: velocity equals flow divided by total cross-sectional area; for a given flow, the bigger the area, the slower the blood.
Explanation

Q = flow (cm3/min = mL/min), A = total cross-sectional area (cm2), so v comes out in cm/min. For a single round vessel A = πr2.

  • A / Q would make blood speed up as the area widened.
  • Q × A gives cm5/min, which is not a velocity.
Slides (2)
L24Learning
A cardiac output of 5,229 mL/min passes through an aorta 20 mm across (area 3.14 cm2). What is the velocity in the aorta?
  1. A. About 16,420 cm/min
  2. B. About 1,665 cm/min
  3. C. About 166 cm/min
AnswerB. About 1,665 cm/min
Whyv = Q/A = 5,229 cm3/min ÷ 3.14 cm2 ≈ 1,665 cm/min (about 28 cm/s).
Explanation

1 mL = 1 cm3, so dividing cm3/min by cm2 gives cm/min. All of the cardiac output squeezes through one vessel of small area, which makes the aorta the fastest-flowing part of the circulation.

  • 16,420 cm/min multiplies flow by area (5,229 × 3.14) instead of dividing.
  • 166 cm/min is a decimal slip (a factor of 10 too small).
Slides (2)
L25LearningHigh yield
Where does blood move slowest, and why?
  1. A. Capillaries: highest resistance in each single vessel
  2. B. Capillaries: largest total cross-sectional area
  3. C. Aorta: smallest total cross-sectional area
AnswerB. Capillaries: largest total cross-sectional area
WhyThe same flow passes every series level, so velocity (v = Q/A) is lowest where the total cross-sectional area is largest: the capillaries.
Explanation

Each capillary is tiny, but there are about 1010 of them side by side, giving a total area of about 2,500 cm2. The whole cardiac output spread over that area moves very slowly.

  • Highest resistance per vessel is a true-sounding distractor, but resistance sets the pressure drop, not velocity; and the arterioles, not the capillaries, are the highest-resistance segment.
  • Aorta has the smallest total area and therefore the fastest flow.
Slides (3)
L26Learning
Blood leaves the capillaries and converges into venules, veins and finally the venae cavae. What happens to its velocity, and why?
  1. A. Keeps falling: the veins hold most of the blood volume
  2. B. Stays at the capillary value: venous pressure is low
  3. C. Rises again: total cross-sectional area shrinks as vessels merge
AnswerC. Rises again: total cross-sectional area shrinks as vessels merge
WhyAs vessels merge, total cross-sectional area falls (veins about 300 cm², venae cavae a few cm²), so by v = Q/A velocity rises again toward the heart.
Explanation

Velocity depends on the total cross-sectional area at each level, and the same cardiac output passes every level in series. Past the capillaries (about 2,500 cm²) the vessels converge: venules join into veins (about 300 cm² in total on the lecture graph) and the veins into the two venae cavae (a few cm²). Area shrinks, so v = Q/A climbs again. It stays somewhat below aortic velocity, because the two venae cavae together are wider than the aorta.

  • Keeps falling confuses blood volume with area: the veins hold about 65% of the blood because they are long and compliant, but their total area is far below the capillaries'.
  • Stays at the capillary value confuses pressure with velocity: venous pressure is low, but velocity is set by flow and area, not by pressure.
Slides (2)
L27LearningHigh yield
Why is the slow velocity of blood in the capillaries useful?
  1. A. It gives time for exchange of gases and nutrients
  2. B. It keeps capillary pressure high enough for filtration
  3. C. It prevents rupture of the thin capillary wall
AnswerA. It gives time for exchange of gases and nutrients
WhySlow capillary flow gives blood time for exchange of O2, CO2, nutrients and wastes across the thin capillary wall.
Explanation

The capillaries are the exchange vessels: a single layer of endothelium with a huge total surface area. Slow transit (roughly a second or two through each capillary) lets diffusion approach equilibrium before the blood leaves.

  • Keeping pressure high for filtration confuses velocity with pressure; capillary hydrostatic pressure is set by the resistances upstream and downstream, not by velocity.
  • Preventing rupture is not the purpose; wall stress depends on pressure and radius (Laplace), not on velocity.
Slides (2)

Lecture 18 · Laminar vs turbulent flow: the Reynolds number

L28Learning
In turbulent flow, what happens to the blood streams, and what does it cost?
  1. A. They line up in parallel layers moving only forward → energy saved, silence
  2. B. They break into eddies that mix sideways as well as forward → energy wasted, noise
  3. C. They break into eddies that mix sideways as well as forward → lower resistance, silence
AnswerB. They break into eddies that mix sideways as well as forward → energy wasted, noise
WhyTurbulent flow has eddies with radial as well as axial movement; it wastes energy (more pressure is needed for the same flow) and produces sound.
Explanation

Because some of the pressure energy goes into swirling motion rather than forward flow, turbulence needs a larger pressure difference to drive the same flow, and the vibrations it sets up are heard as murmurs and bruits.

  • Parallel layers moving forward describes laminar flow.
  • Lower resistance and silence gets both consequences backwards: turbulence raises the effective resistance and is noisy.
Slides (2)
L29LearningHigh yield
Which is the Reynolds number?
  1. A. NR = ηdv / ρ
  2. B. NR = ρdv / η
  3. C. NR = ρη / dv
AnswerB. NR = ρdv / η
WhyNR = ρdv / η: density × diameter × velocity, divided by viscosity. The higher it is, the more likely flow is turbulent.
Explanation

ρ (rho) = density of blood, d = vessel diameter, v = velocity of flow, η (eta) = viscosity of blood. NR is dimensionless. Values above about 2,000 make turbulence increasingly likely; below that, flow is laminar.

  • ηdv / ρ swaps density and viscosity; viscosity belongs in the denominator because thick blood damps eddies.
  • ρη / dv puts velocity in the denominator, which would make faster flow less turbulent.

Hook: "thick blood (η) keeps it calm"; it is the only term underneath.

Slides (2)
L30LearningHigh yield
A vessel narrows while the same flow is forced through it. What happens to its Reynolds number?
  1. A. Falls: diameter sits in the numerator of ρdv/η
  2. B. Rises: velocity increases with 1/d2, outweighing the smaller d
  3. C. Unchanged: the smaller diameter and the faster velocity cancel
AnswerB. Rises: velocity increases with 1/d2, outweighing the smaller d
WhyAt constant flow, v = Q/A rises as 1/d2, so NR ∝ d × v ∝ 1/d: narrowing raises the Reynolds number.
Explanation

The trap: d is in the numerator, so a smaller d looks as if it should lower NR. But velocity also depends on diameter: halving the diameter quarters the area and quadruples velocity. NR then changes by ½ × 4 = 2, a doubling. This is why stenoses, thrombi and atherosclerotic plaques cause turbulence.

  • Falls forgets that velocity changes with the square of the diameter.
  • Unchanged assumes d and v change by the same factor; v changes by the square.
Slides (2)
L31LearningHigh yield
How does anaemia produce a flow murmur?
  1. A. ↑ Viscosity and ↓ velocity → ↓ Reynolds number
  2. B. ↓ Viscosity and ↑ velocity → ↑ Reynolds number
  3. C. ↓ Viscosity and ↓ velocity → ↑ Reynolds number
AnswerB. ↓ Viscosity and ↑ velocity → ↑ Reynolds number
WhyLow haematocrit lowers viscosity, and the compensatory rise in cardiac output raises velocity: both increase NR = ρdv/η, so flow becomes turbulent.
Explanation

Anaemia means fewer red cells, so blood is thinner (η falls, and η is the denominator). The body also raises cardiac output to keep O2 delivery up, so blood moves faster (v rises, in the numerator). The Reynolds number climbs from both sides, and a soft "flow murmur" can be heard without any valve disease.

  • ↑ Viscosity describes polycythaemia, which lowers NR.
  • ↓ Velocity is wrong: cardiac output and velocity rise in anaemia.
Slides (3)
L32Learning
Why can you hear Korotkoff sounds while measuring blood pressure with a cuff?
  1. A. The cuff partly occludes the vein → venous pooling → sound
  2. B. The cuff fully occludes the artery → laminar flow resumes → sound
  3. C. The cuff partly occludes the artery → turbulent flow → sound
AnswerC. The cuff partly occludes the artery → turbulent flow → sound
WhyBetween systolic and diastolic pressure the cuff partly compresses the brachial artery; blood jets through the narrowed segment at high velocity and becomes turbulent, which is audible.
Explanation

Above systolic pressure the artery is closed and there is no flow, so no sound. As the cuff pressure falls below systolic, blood squirts through a narrowed lumen each beat: high velocity, high Reynolds number, turbulence, Korotkoff sounds. Once cuff pressure falls below diastolic, the artery stays open, flow is laminar again and the sounds disappear.

  • Full occlusion means no flow, so silence, and laminar flow is silent anyway.
  • Venous pooling makes no sound; the sounds come from the artery.
Slides (2)
L33Learning
An arteriole's radius halves while the pressure difference, viscosity and length stay constant. What happens to its resistance, its flow and its Reynolds number?
  1. A. Resistance ↑ 16-fold
    Flow ↓ 16-fold
    Reynolds number ↓ 8-fold
  2. B. Resistance ↑ 16-fold
    Flow ↓ 16-fold
    Reynolds number ↑ 8-fold
  3. C. Resistance ↑ 4-fold
    Flow ↓ 4-fold
    Reynolds number ↑ 2-fold
AnswerA. Resistance ↑ 16-fold
Flow ↓ 16-fold
Reynolds number ↓ 8-fold
WhyAt a constant ΔP, flow falls 16-fold; velocity (Q/A) falls 16 ÷ 4 = 4-fold and diameter halves, so NR ∝ d·v falls 8-fold.
Explanation

Work it step by step:

  • Resistance: 1/(½)4 = 16-fold rise.
  • Flow: Q = ΔP/R with ΔP fixed → 1/16.
  • Velocity: v = Q/A = (1/16)/(1/4) = 1/4.
  • Reynolds number: d × v = ½ × ¼ = 1/8 → 8-fold fall.

This differs from a stenosis, where the same flow is forced through the narrowing (flow held constant) and NR rises. Here the arteriole constricts at a fixed pressure difference, so flow collapses and the blood slows. The "NR ↑ 8-fold" option makes exactly that mix-up; the "4-fold" option squares the radius instead of raising it to the fourth power.

Slides (1)

Lecture 18 · Velocity profile and shear

L34LearningHigh yield
Where is shear highest and where is it lowest in a vessel?
  1. A. Highest in the centre; lowest at the wall
  2. B. Highest at the wall; lowest in the centre
  3. C. Highest halfway between wall and centre; equal elsewhere
AnswerB. Highest at the wall; lowest in the centre
WhyShear is highest at the wall, where blood slides past the motionless outer layer, and lowest in the centre, where neighbouring layers move at similar speeds.
Explanation

The parabolic profile is steepest near the wall (velocity climbs from zero quickly) and flat at the centre (the peak). Shear tracks how steeply velocity changes from layer to layer, so it is greatest at the wall and almost zero in the middle, even though velocity itself is highest in the middle.

  • Highest in the centre confuses shear with velocity.
  • Highest halfway has no basis in the parabolic profile.
Slides (3)
L35Learning
How does shear affect blood viscosity, and where is viscosity therefore lowest?
  1. A. Breaks up red-cell aggregates → lowers viscosity → lowest in the centre
  2. B. Packs red cells together → raises viscosity → lowest in the centre
  3. C. Breaks up red-cell aggregates → lowers viscosity → lowest near the wall
AnswerC. Breaks up red-cell aggregates → lowers viscosity → lowest near the wall
WhyShear breaks up red-cell aggregates, lowering viscosity; since shear is highest at the wall, viscosity is lowest near the wall.
Explanation

Red cells tend to stick together in stacks when blood moves slowly and evenly, which thickens it. Where layers slide fast past each other, the aggregates are pulled apart. At the wall, where shear is highest, aggregation and viscosity are lowest; in the centre, where shear is low, red cells aggregate more.

  • Packs red cells together reverses the effect of shear.
  • Lowest in the centre places the low viscosity where shear is lowest; it follows high shear, at the wall.
Slides (3)

Lecture 19 · What compliance is

L36Learning
The same volume is added to a compliant vessel and to a stiff vessel. What happens to the pressure in each?
  1. A. Compliant: pressure jumps
    Stiff: pressure barely rises
  2. B. Both: pressure rises by the same amount, because the volume is the same
  3. C. Compliant: pressure barely rises
    Stiff: pressure jumps
AnswerC. Compliant: pressure barely rises
Stiff: pressure jumps
WhyA compliant wall stretches to make room, so pressure barely rises; a stiff wall cannot, so the same volume makes pressure jump (ΔP = ΔV/C).
Explanation

Rearranging C = ΔV/ΔP gives ΔP = ΔV/C: for a fixed added volume, the pressure rise is inversely proportional to compliance.

  • The swapped pair gets the inverse relationship backwards.
  • An equal rise would need equal compliances; volume alone does not set the pressure.

This one line carries the lesson: veins (high C) hold a lot of blood at low pressure; arteries (low C) turn each stroke volume into a pressure pulse; stiff aged arteries make that pulse bigger.

Slides (2)
L37LearningHigh yield
How is compliance related to elasticity (elastance)?
  1. A. Direct: the stiffer, more elastic wall has the higher compliance
  2. B. Inverse: the stiffer, more elastic wall has the lower compliance
  3. C. Inverse: the floppier, less elastic wall has the lower compliance
AnswerB. Inverse: the stiffer, more elastic wall has the lower compliance
WhyElastance is the tendency to resist stretch and recoil; the more of it a wall has, the less it distends per mmHg, so compliance is its inverse.
Explanation

In physiology elastance (elasticity) means stiffness: ΔP/ΔV, the pressure needed to push in each extra mL. Compliance is ΔV/ΔP, so the two are reciprocals. Arteries have high elastance and low compliance; veins have low elastance and high compliance.

  • Direct confuses everyday ‘elastic’ (stretchy) with the physiological term, which means resisting stretch and springing back hard.
  • The floppier wall with lower compliance keeps the inverse wording but reverses the direction: a floppy wall is the most compliant.
Slides (3)
L38LearningHigh yield
A drug relaxes vascular smooth muscle (an α1 blocker or a β2 agonist). What happens to the compliance of the vessels it relaxes?
  1. A. Falls: the dilated vessel is already stretched and takes less volume per mmHg
  2. B. Unchanged: compliance is set only by the elastin and collagen in the wall
  3. C. Rises: the relaxed wall stretches more for each mmHg
AnswerC. Rises: the relaxed wall stretches more for each mmHg
WhySmooth-muscle tone stiffens the wall: relaxing it raises compliance (more volume per mmHg), and constricting it lowers compliance.
Explanation

α1 stimulation (Gq → IP3 → Ca2+) contracts vascular smooth muscle; α1 blockade or β2 stimulation (Gs → cAMP) relaxes it. A relaxed wall is more distensible, so the vessel holds more volume at any pressure. The fall in pressure that follows is the result of the higher compliance, not its cause. In reverse, venoconstriction lowers venous compliance and squeezes blood toward the heart.

  • Falls: it is constriction, not dilation, that lowers compliance.
  • Unchanged: elastin and collagen set the passive stiffness, but active smooth-muscle tone adds to it.
Slides (1)

Lecture 19 · Veins vs arteries, and ageing

L39LearningHigh yield
Why can the veins hold most of the blood volume at very low pressure?
  1. A. They are highly elastic: their walls resist stretch
  2. B. They have thick muscular walls that hold the volume in
  3. C. They are highly compliant: their walls stretch easily
AnswerC. They are highly compliant: their walls stretch easily
WhyVeins are the most compliant vessels, so they take up a large volume with little rise in pressure; they hold about 60–65% of the blood.
Explanation

Thin walls with little elastic tissue and a wide lumen let veins expand as blood enters, so they act as the circulation's capacitance (reservoir) vessels: about 60–65% of the blood volume sits in them at a few mmHg.

  • Highly elastic walls resist stretch: that describes arteries, which hold a small volume at high pressure.
  • Thick muscular walls belong to the arterioles, the resistance vessels; veins are thin-walled.

Picture it: an artery is a bicycle inner tube (stiff, holds pressure); a vein is a plastic shopping bag (floppy, holds volume at almost no pressure).

Slides (3)
L40Learning
Roughly how much more compliant is the venous system than the arterial system?
  1. A. About 2×
  2. B. About 200×
  3. C. About 20×
AnswerC. About 20×
WhyVenous compliance is about 20 times arterial compliance: the same pressure rise stores roughly twenty times more volume in the veins.
Explanation

On the volume–pressure graph the vein line is far steeper than the artery line. Quantitatively, each vein is about 8 times as distensible as its matching artery, and the venous system holds about 3 times the volume, so venous compliance is roughly 20–25 times arterial compliance (an arterial:venous ratio of about 1:20).

  • 2× would make veins and arteries similar reservoirs; in fact the veins hold most of the blood at a small fraction of arterial pressure.
  • 200× overshoots by an order of magnitude.
Slides (1)
L41Learning
Why do arteries lose compliance with age?
  1. A. Collagen in the wall is replaced by elastin, which recoils harder
  2. B. Elastin in the wall is replaced by collagen, which stretches less
  3. C. Smooth muscle in the wall relaxes, so the wall resists stretch
AnswerB. Elastin in the wall is replaced by collagen, which stretches less
WhyWith age elastin fibres are replaced by collagen, which is far less stretchy, so the wall distends less per mmHg: compliance ↓, elastance ↑.
Explanation

The stretch of the arterial wall comes mainly from elastin, which extends easily and recoils. Collagen is a stiff, high-tensile fibre that limits stretch. Over decades elastin fragments while collagen (and calcium) accumulates, so the aorta and large arteries become stiff tubes. By C = V/P, each stroke volume then produces a higher pressure.

  • The swap the other way (collagen → elastin) would make arteries more compliant.
  • Relaxed smooth muscle raises compliance; age-related stiffening is a structural change in the wall fibres.
Slides (2)
L42Learning
Thirty years ago a man's arterial compliance was 1.75 mL/mmHg with a stroke volume of 70 mL. Today his blood pressure is 170/70 mmHg with the same stroke volume. What is his arterial compliance now?
  1. A. 0.41 mL/mmHg
  2. B. 0.7 mL/mmHg
  3. C. 1.0 mL/mmHg
AnswerB. 0.7 mL/mmHg
WhyCompliance = ΔV/ΔP = stroke volume ÷ pulse pressure = 70 mL ÷ (170 − 70) mmHg = 0.7 mL/mmHg: it has fallen as his arteries stiffened.
Explanation

Each beat adds one stroke volume (ΔV) to the arteries and lifts their pressure from diastolic to systolic, so ΔP is the pulse pressure: 170 − 70 = 100 mmHg, and C = 70/100 = 0.7 mL/mmHg. Thirty years ago the same 70 mL gave a pulse pressure of 70/1.75 = 40 mmHg (for example 120/80); stiffening has more than doubled it.

  • 0.41 divides by the systolic pressure (70/170) instead of the change in pressure.
  • 1.0 divides by the diastolic pressure (70/70).

Stroke volume ÷ pulse pressure is a bedside estimate: it ignores the blood that runs off through the arterioles during ejection.

Slides (1)

Lecture 19 · Systolic, diastolic, pulse and mean arterial pressure

L43Learning
How does the aorta turn the heart's intermittent ejection into continuous flow at the tissues?
  1. A. Balloons in systole, storing part of the stroke volume → recoils in diastole and keeps pushing
  2. B. Stays rigid throughout, passing each stroke volume straight on → valves smooth the flow
  3. C. Balloons in diastole, storing venous return → recoils in systole and adds to ejection
AnswerA. Balloons in systole, storing part of the stroke volume → recoils in diastole and keeps pushing
WhyThe compliant aorta stretches in systole, storing part of each stroke volume, then recoils in diastole, pushing that blood on so tissue flow never stops.
Explanation

This is the windkessel (elastic reservoir) effect. Only part of the stroke volume runs off through the arterioles during ejection; the rest stretches the large arteries. Their elastic recoil during diastole drives it onward, which is why arterial pressure falls only to about 80 mmHg between beats rather than to zero.

  • A rigid aorta would pass flow only during ejection; valves stop backflow but cannot smooth flow.
  • The aorta never receives venous return; it fills only when the left ventricle ejects in systole.
Slides (2)
L44LearningHigh yield
Pulse pressure is set by which two factors?
  1. A. Heart rate and blood viscosity
  2. B. Stroke volume and venous compliance
  3. C. Stroke volume and arterial compliance
AnswerC. Stroke volume and arterial compliance
WhyPulse pressure ≈ stroke volume ÷ arterial compliance: it widens when stroke volume rises or when the arteries stiffen, and narrows when stroke volume falls.
Explanation

Each beat pushes one stroke volume (ΔV) into the arterial tree; how far that lifts pressure depends on how compliant the arteries are (ΔP = ΔV/C).

  • Wide: ↑ stroke volume (exercise, aortic regurgitation) or ↓ arterial compliance (ageing, arteriosclerosis).
  • Narrow: ↓ stroke volume (aortic stenosis, haemorrhage, heart failure).

Venous compliance governs where the blood volume is stored, not the arterial swing. Viscosity affects resistance and so mean pressure, not the pulse.

Slides (1)
L45Learning
A paced heart is switched from 60 to 100 beats/min. Stroke volume falls from 80 to 48 mL, so cardiac output (4.8 L/min) and mean arterial pressure stay the same. What happens to the arterial pressures?
  1. A. Systolic ↓, diastolic ↑, pulse pressure ↓
  2. B. Systolic ↑, diastolic ↓, pulse pressure ↑
  3. C. Systolic ↓, diastolic ↓, pulse pressure unchanged
AnswerA. Systolic ↓, diastolic ↑, pulse pressure ↓
WhyThe smaller stroke volume lifts pressure less each beat (systolic ↓), and shorter diastoles leave less run-off time (diastolic ↑), so pulse pressure narrows.
Explanation

Mean arterial pressure = cardiac output × total peripheral resistance, and neither changed, so MAP is unchanged. What changes is the shape of the swing around it: each beat adds only 48 mL (smaller rise, lower peak), and the next beat arrives before pressure has fallen as far (higher trough).

  • Systolic ↑ / diastolic ↓ is the pattern of a bigger stroke volume (as in aortic regurgitation).
  • Both ↓ would lower the mean, which the unchanged CO × TPR rules out.
Slides (1)
L46LearningHigh yield
Formula for mean arterial pressure?
  1. A. MAP = diastolic + ⅔ pulse pressure
  2. B. MAP = diastolic + ⅓ systolic pressure
  3. C. MAP = diastolic + ⅓ pulse pressure
AnswerC. MAP = diastolic + ⅓ pulse pressure
WhyMAP = diastolic + ⅓ pulse pressure: for 120/80, 80 + 40/3 ≈ 93 mmHg.
Explanation

Start from the floor (diastolic) and add one third of the swing (pulse pressure), because only about a third of each cycle is spent in systole.

  • Diastolic + ⅔ pulse pressure weights the average toward systole: 80 + 27 = 107 for 120/80, too high.
  • Diastolic + ⅓ systolic adds a third of the whole systolic pressure instead of a third of the swing: 80 + 40 = 120, as high as systolic itself.
Slides (2)
L47LearningHigh yield
Why does mean arterial pressure sit closer to diastolic than to systolic pressure?
  1. A. About two thirds of each cycle is spent in diastole
  2. B. About two thirds of each cycle is spent in systole
  3. C. The arteries are less compliant than the veins
AnswerA. About two thirds of each cycle is spent in diastole
WhyAt rest about two thirds of each cycle is diastole, so arterial pressure spends most of its time near the diastolic value and the time average is pulled toward it.
Explanation

At 70 beats/min a cycle lasts about 0.85 s, of which ventricular ejection takes roughly a third. When the heart rate rises, diastole shortens more than systole, so MAP moves toward the midpoint and the ⅓ rule becomes less accurate.

  • Two thirds in systole reverses the timing; it would pull MAP toward the systolic value.
  • Arterial compliance sets the size of the pulse, not where the time average falls within it.
Slides (3)

Lecture 19 · Stiff arteries: ageing and arteriosclerosis

L48LearningHigh yield
Stiff aorta (ageing or arteriosclerosis): systolic, diastolic and pulse pressure?
  1. A. Systolic normal
    Diastolic ↑
    Pulse pressure narrow
  2. B. Systolic ↑
    Diastolic ↑
    Pulse pressure unchanged
  3. C. Systolic ↑
    Diastolic normal or ↓
    Pulse pressure wide
AnswerC. Systolic ↑
Diastolic normal or ↓
Pulse pressure wide
WhyA stiff aorta turns each stroke volume into a bigger pressure rise (systolic ↑) but recoils less in diastole (diastolic normal or ↓), so pulse pressure widens.
Explanation

This is the isolated systolic hypertension of older people: for example 160/80 instead of 120/80. With compliance down, the same stroke volume gives a bigger ΔP (ΔP = ΔV/C). The textbook figure keeps diastolic at 80; clinically it is normal or slightly low because less blood is stored for diastolic recoil.

  • Systolic normal, diastolic ↑ is the opposite of what stiffness does to the swing.
  • Both ↑ with pulse pressure unchanged describes a parallel upward shift, as with raised resistance alone, not a loss of compliance.
Slides (3)
L49LearningHigh yield
Arteriosclerosis: effect on systolic, pulse and mean arterial pressure?
  1. A. All fall
  2. B. Only systolic rises; pulse and mean pressure are unchanged
  3. C. All rise
AnswerC. All rise
WhyIn arteriosclerosis ↓ compliance makes each stroke volume raise pressure more: systolic, pulse and mean pressure all rise.
Explanation

The stiff arteries convert the same stroke volume into a taller pressure peak, so systolic and pulse pressure rise, and the higher peak lifts the time average (mean) as well. Plaque narrowing the vessels adds resistance, which also pushes mean pressure up.

  • All fall is the pattern of aortic stenosis, where stroke volume falls.
  • Only systolic is impossible: if systolic rises while diastolic does not, pulse pressure must rise too.
Slides (3)

Lecture 19 · Aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation

L50LearningHigh yield
Aortic stenosis: effect on systolic, pulse and mean arterial pressure?
  1. A. Only pulse pressure falls
  2. B. All fall
  3. C. All rise
AnswerB. All fall
WhyWith a smaller stroke volume entering the aorta, systolic, pulse and mean pressure all fall: the opposite pattern to arteriosclerosis.
Explanation

Less volume per beat means a smaller rise above diastolic (systolic and pulse pressure ↓), and the lower peak drags the time average (mean) down.

  • Only pulse pressure cannot fall alone here: with diastolic roughly unchanged, a smaller pulse pressure means a lower systolic pressure too.
  • All rise is the arteriosclerosis pattern.

Pair to remember: arteriosclerosis ↑↑↑, aortic stenosis ↓↓↓.

Slides (3)
L51Learning
Aortic stenosis: effect on the pressure the left ventricle must generate?
  1. A. ↑ (higher afterload) to eject through the narrowed valve
  2. B. ↑ (higher preload) to fill through the narrowed valve
  3. C. ↓ (lower afterload) as the narrowed valve slows ejection
AnswerA. ↑ (higher afterload) to eject through the narrowed valve
WhyThe left ventricle must generate a pressure well above aortic pressure to force blood through the narrow valve: afterload rises even though aortic pressure falls.
Explanation

Afterload is the pressure the ventricle works against during ejection. With a stenotic valve a large systolic gradient opens between the left ventricle and the aorta, so ventricular systolic pressure rises, ejection is impaired, end-systolic volume rises and stroke volume falls. Over time the ventricle thickens (concentric hypertrophy).

  • Preload is the filling (end-diastolic) volume; the ventricle fills through the mitral valve, not the aortic valve.
  • Lower afterload reverses it: the narrow outlet is an obstacle, not a relief.
Slides (3)
L52Learning
Aortic regurgitation: what happens to diastolic pressure, and why?
  1. A. Rises: the leaky valve lets ejected blood pool in the aorta
  2. B. Unchanged: the leak only affects systolic pressure
  3. C. Falls: blood runs back through the leaky valve into the relaxed ventricle
AnswerC. Falls: blood runs back through the leaky valve into the relaxed ventricle
WhyIn aortic regurgitation the valve fails to close, so in diastole blood runs back into the relaxed ventricle as well as forward: arterial pressure falls further, diastolic ↓.
Explanation

Normally the closed aortic valve leaves the arterioles as the only exit during diastole. With an incompetent valve the arteries empty in two directions, so pressure decays faster and lower between beats.

  • Rises: no blood ‘pools’; the leak is a second outlet, which can only lower pressure.
