  • Unchanged: the leak happens during diastole, so diastolic pressure is the value it hits hardest.
Slides (3)
L53Learning
Aortic regurgitation: what happens to stroke volume and systolic pressure, and why?
  1. A. Both rise: the ventricle ejects the regurgitated blood again with the next beat
  2. B. Stroke volume falls, systolic rises: the aorta stiffens to compensate
  3. C. Stroke volume rises, systolic falls: the extra blood leaks back before reaching the arteries
AnswerA. Both rise: the ventricle ejects the regurgitated blood again with the next beat
WhyThe blood that leaked back adds to normal filling, so end-diastolic volume and (by Frank–Starling) stroke volume rise, and the bigger ejection drives systolic pressure up.
Explanation

The left ventricle fills from the left atrium and from the aorta. The larger end-diastolic volume stretches the fibres, they contract more forcefully, and a large total stroke volume (forward plus regurgitant) is ejected into the aorta, raising systolic pressure.

  • Stroke volume falls is the aortic stenosis pattern; the aorta does not stiffen in response.
  • Systolic falls confuses the timing: the leak happens in diastole, after the bigger ejection has already raised systolic pressure.
Slides (3)
L54Learning
A patient has an early diastolic murmur along the left sternal border and a blood pressure of 170/60 mmHg. Which lesion fits?
  1. A. Aortic stenosis
  2. B. Aortic regurgitation
  3. C. Arteriosclerosis without valve disease
AnswerB. Aortic regurgitation
WhyA diastolic murmur with a wide pulse pressure and low diastolic pressure is aortic regurgitation: blood leaks from the aorta back into the left ventricle during diastole.
Explanation

The incompetent aortic valve lets blood flow backward in diastole, which is both the cause of the murmur (turbulent backflow, heard in diastole) and of the low diastolic pressure. The extra filling raises stroke volume and systolic pressure.

  • Aortic stenosis gives a systolic murmur (turbulent forward flow through the narrow valve) and a narrow pulse pressure.
  • Arteriosclerosis can widen the pulse pressure by raising systolic pressure, but it causes no diastolic murmur.
Slides (2)
L55Learning
Why do arteriolar vasodilators help in aortic regurgitation?
  1. A. They lower aortic pressure, so less blood leaks back and more flows forward
  2. B. They raise aortic diastolic pressure, which presses the leaky valve shut
  3. C. They dilate the veins, raising venous return and stroke volume
AnswerA. They lower aortic pressure, so less blood leaks back and more flows forward
WhyArteriolar dilation lowers afterload (aortic pressure), so less blood is driven back across the leaky valve in diastole and more of each stroke volume flows forward to the tissues.
Explanation

The arterioles are where systemic resistance can be changed. Lowering that resistance gives ejected blood an easier forward path, and the lower aortic pressure shrinks the diastolic gradient that drives blood back into the ventricle.

  • Raising aortic diastolic pressure would increase the backward gradient and the leak; a valve that cannot close is not sealed by more pressure.
  • Arteriolar dilators act on the resistance side, not the veins; more venous filling would only add to the volume overload.
Slides (1)

Lecture 19 · The pressure profile

L56Learning
What does a pressure profile along the vasculature tell you?
  1. A. Where flow is fastest: the steep drop marks the exchange vessels
  2. B. Where compliance is highest: the steep drop marks the capacitance vessels
  3. C. Where resistance is highest: the steep drop marks the resistance vessels
AnswerC. Where resistance is highest: the steep drop marks the resistance vessels
WhyAlong vessels in series the flow is the same at every level, so a steep pressure drop marks a segment of high resistance: the resistance vessels (arterioles).
Explanation

Reading the profile is Ohm's law in a picture: flat line = low resistance (large arteries), steep slope = high resistance (arterioles), low flat tail = the low-pressure venous reservoir.

  • Fastest flow (highest velocity) is in the aorta, where the pressure line is flat; the exchange vessels (capillaries) are where velocity is slowest.
  • The capacitance vessels (veins) sit on the low, flat end of the profile, not on the steep drop.
Slides (2)
L57LearningHigh yield
Compared with the aorta, what are systolic and pulse pressure in the large downstream arteries?
  1. A. Both lower, because the pulse is already being damped
  2. B. Both higher, even though mean pressure is slightly lower
  3. C. Both the same, because no pressure is lost in large arteries
AnswerB. Both higher, even though mean pressure is slightly lower
WhyMoving out from the aorta into the large arteries the pulse grows: systolic and pulse pressure are higher downstream, while mean pressure falls only slightly.
Explanation

On the pressure profile the pulsations are taller in the large arteries than in the aorta. Pressure waves reflected from branch points add to the outgoing wave, and the downstream arteries are narrower and stiffer. So systolic pressure is higher in, for example, the renal or femoral artery than in the aorta. The pulse is then damped in the small arteries and arterioles and has almost gone by the capillaries.

  • Both lower describes what happens further on, in the small arteries and arterioles.
  • Both the same ignores wave reflection; it is the mean that barely changes.
Slides (2)

Lecture 19 · Unstressed and stressed volume

L58LearningHigh yield
What is stressed volume, and why does it matter?
  1. A. Volume above the unstressed volume: it is simply held and generates no pressure
  2. B. Volume held before the wall stretches: it alone drives blood back to the heart
  3. C. Volume above the unstressed volume: it stretches the walls and creates the pressure that drives blood back to the heart
AnswerC. Volume above the unstressed volume: it stretches the walls and creates the pressure that drives blood back to the heart
WhyStressed volume is the blood above the unstressed volume: it stretches vessel walls, so it alone produces pressure, including the filling pressure that drives venous return.
Explanation

Only blood that stretches the walls is pressurised. The stressed volume therefore sets the mean filling pressure of the circulation, which pushes blood back toward the right atrium. Raise the stressed volume (transfusion, or venoconstriction) and venous return rises.

  • Blood that is ‘simply held’ without pressure is the unstressed volume.
  • The volume held before the wall stretches is unstressed and generates no driving pressure.
Slides (2)
L59LearningHigh yield
Which vessels hold mainly the stressed volume, and which mainly the unstressed volume?
  1. A. Arteries: stressed (small volume, high pressure)
    Veins: unstressed (large volume, low pressure)
  2. B. Veins: stressed (large volume, low pressure)
    Arteries: unstressed (small volume, high pressure)
  3. C. Arterioles: stressed (small volume, high pressure)
    Capillaries: unstressed (large volume, low pressure)
AnswerA. Arteries: stressed (small volume, high pressure)
Veins: unstressed (large volume, low pressure)
WhyThe compliant veins hold the large unstressed volume at low pressure; the stiff arteries hold the small stressed volume at high pressure.
Explanation

This follows from compliance. Veins stretch easily, so they hold about 60–65% of the blood with little pressure: the unstressed reservoir. Arteries are stiff, so their smaller volume is under high pressure: the stressed volume. (Both kinds of volume exist in every vessel; the labels describe where each dominates.)

  • The swap contradicts itself: high pressure goes with stressed volume, and it is the arteries that are high-pressure.
  • Arterioles and capillaries hold only a small share of the blood (capillaries about 5–7%); they are resistance and exchange vessels, not the stores.
Slides (2)
L60LearningHigh yield
What does sympathetic venoconstriction do to the blood in the veins?
  1. A. Converts unstressed volume → stressed volume (adds no blood)
  2. B. Converts unstressed volume → stressed volume (adds new blood)
  3. C. Converts stressed volume → unstressed volume (adds no blood)
AnswerA. Converts unstressed volume → stressed volume (adds no blood)
WhyVenoconstriction lowers venous compliance and unstressed volume, shifting that blood into stressed volume: filling pressure and venous return rise with no blood added.
Explanation

Squeezing the venous reservoir lets the same total blood volume generate more filling pressure, so more blood returns to the heart and cardiac output can rise. In effect the body gives itself a transfusion from its own veins within seconds. It is part of the response to exercise and to haemorrhage. Expect it as the answer to ‘what raised venous return without adding volume’.

  • Adds new blood: constriction only moves existing blood from one category to the other; total volume is unchanged.
  • Stressed → unstressed is what venodilation does (for example nitrates), lowering filling pressure.
Slides (3)

PHYS-L20/21 Cardiac electrophysiology & EKG (+ clinical cases)

81 learning questions · of 174
Learning questions 81

Conduction pathway

L1Learning
Why can the heart beat without any nerve telling it to?
  1. A. Circulating catecholamines trigger each beat; the adrenal medulla sets the rate
  2. B. It contains cells that depolarise on their own; the fastest of them sets the rate
  3. C. Resting vagal tone triggers each beat; the vagus nerve sets the rate
AnswerB. It contains cells that depolarise on their own; the fastest of them sets the rate
WhyThe heart has its own pacemaker cells that depolarise spontaneously (automaticity); nerves and hormones only speed up or slow down a rhythm the heart makes itself.
Explanation

Automaticity is the ability of a cell to reach threshold and fire without any outside stimulus. Nodal tissue does this because its resting potential is not stable: it drifts upward every cycle until it fires. The cell that drifts fastest, normally the sinoatrial (SA) node, sets the rate for the whole heart. A transplanted heart, which has no nerves, still beats.

  • Catecholamines from the adrenal medulla only raise the rate of a beat that already exists; they do not start it.
  • Vagal tone is a brake: it slows the SA node. Cutting the vagus makes the heart beat faster, not stop.
Slides (2)
L2LearningHigh yield
What is the main job of the conducting cells (nodes, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibres)?
  1. A. Start and spread the impulse, and also generate most of the contractile force
  2. B. Generate most of the contractile force, while the working cells spread the impulse
  3. C. Start and spread the impulse; they add little contractile force
AnswerC. Start and spread the impulse; they add little contractile force
WhyThe heart has two cell types: conducting cells start and spread the action potential, and working (contractile) cells of the atria and ventricles generate the force.
Explanation

Conducting cells are specialised myocytes with few myofibrils. Their job is electrical: the nodes generate the impulse and set its timing, and the His–Purkinje system carries it quickly to every part of the ventricles. The working cells (atrial and ventricular myocytes) are packed with contractile proteins and do the pumping.

  • Saying conducting cells also generate most of the force is the classic false statement: their contribution to force is negligible.
  • The swapped version reverses the roles: working cells do pass the impulse cell to cell through gap junctions, but they are not the specialised conduction system.
Slides (2)
L3LearningHigh yield
What is the normal conduction pathway of the cardiac impulse?
  1. A. SA node → internodal tracts (atria) → atrioventricular (AV) node → Purkinje fibres → right and left bundle branches → bundle of His
  2. B. SA node → internodal tracts (atria) → bundle of His → atrioventricular (AV) node → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres
  3. C. SA node → internodal tracts (atria) → atrioventricular (AV) node → bundle of His → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres
AnswerC. SA node → internodal tracts (atria) → atrioventricular (AV) node → bundle of His → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres
WhyThe impulse runs SA node → internodal tracts → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres → ventricular muscle.
Explanation

The sinoatrial (SA) node fires; the impulse crosses both atria (internodal tracts, Bachmann's bundle) to the atrioventricular (AV) node. The AV node and its continuation, the bundle of His, are the only normal electrical bridge through the fibrous ring between atria and ventricles. The bundle of His carries it into the interventricular septum, where it splits into the right and left bundle branches, which end in the Purkinje network under the endocardium.

  • Putting the bundle of His before the AV node swaps the two: the His bundle is the continuation of the node.
  • Putting Purkinje fibres before the bundle branches reverses the end of the path: Purkinje fibres are the terminal branches.

Hook: "the further down, the slower it goes" refers to the intrinsic rates along this same path.

Slides (3)
L4Learning
Which pathway carries the impulse from the right atrium to the left atrium?
  1. A. The posterior internodal tract
  2. B. The middle internodal tract
  3. C. Bachmann’s bundle
AnswerC. Bachmann’s bundle
WhyBachmann's bundle, a branch of the anterior internodal tract, crosses the roof of the atria and carries the impulse from the right to the left atrium.
Explanation

From the SA node, three internodal tracts (anterior, middle and posterior) run through the right atrial wall to the AV node. The anterior tract gives off Bachmann's bundle, which crosses to the left atrium, so both atria depolarise almost together and contract as one.

  • The posterior and middle internodal tracts run from the SA node to the AV node; they stay on the right side and do not supply the left atrium.
Slides (2)
L5LearningHigh yield
Why does the AV-node delay matter?
  1. A. Lets the ventricles finish relaxing before the atria contract
  2. B. Lets the atria finish emptying into the ventricles before the ventricles contract
  3. C. Lets the SA node repolarise before the ventricles contract
AnswerB. Lets the atria finish emptying into the ventricles before the ventricles contract
WhyThe AV delay gives the atria time to finish contracting and fill the ventricles, so the ventricles do not contract while only partly full.
Explanation

If the atria and ventricles were activated together, the atria would squeeze against AV valves already being closed by ventricular pressure, and the atrial kick would be lost. Holding the impulse in the AV node lets atrial systole top up the ventricles first. The AV node also limits how many atrial impulses reach the ventricles, which protects them in fast atrial rhythms.

  • The ventricles are already relaxed when the atria contract; the delay does not exist for ventricular relaxation.
  • The SA node repolarises on its own schedule; the AV delay has nothing to do with it.
Slides (3)
L6Learning
Why do the Purkinje fibres conduct so fast?
  1. A. So the ventricle contracts from base to apex in a slow ripple
  2. B. So the AV node has time to repolarise before the next beat
  3. C. So the whole ventricle contracts almost at once, not in a ripple
AnswerC. So the whole ventricle contracts almost at once, not in a ripple
WhyThe fast Purkinje network (2–4 m/s) spreads the impulse through both ventricles almost at once, so they contract as one coordinated unit and eject efficiently.
Explanation

If the impulse spread only muscle cell to muscle cell, the far parts of the ventricle would contract well after the near parts and much of the force would be wasted. The Purkinje fibres are the fastest tissue in the heart and deliver the impulse to the whole endocardium within a few hundredths of a second, so the ventricles squeeze together.

  • A slow ripple is exactly what the Purkinje system prevents; slow muscle-to-muscle spread is what widens the QRS in bundle-branch block or ventricular beats.
  • The AV node recovers on its own; Purkinje speed is about the ventricles, not the node.
Slides (2)

Working-cell action potential

L7LearningHigh yield
Why does a working muscle cell rest near the potassium equilibrium potential?
  1. A. Its resting potassium channels are all closed, so potassium is trapped inside the cell
  2. B. Its resting sodium channels are ungated (always open), so sodium dominates the resting membrane
  3. C. Its resting potassium channels are ungated (always open), so potassium dominates the resting membrane
AnswerC. Its resting potassium channels are ungated (always open), so potassium dominates the resting membrane
WhyAt rest the ungated potassium channels (inward rectifier, IK1) are open, so potassium conductance dominates and the membrane sits near EK.
Explanation

The membrane potential moves towards the equilibrium potential of whichever ion it is most permeable to. Each ion's equilibrium potential comes from the Nernst equation, the balance between its concentration gradient and the electrical force. At rest, cardiac muscle has a high conductance to potassium through always-open inward-rectifier channels, so the resting potential sits close to EK (about −94 mV).

  • If potassium channels were closed, potassium could not set the potential at all.
  • Resting sodium conductance is very low; if sodium dominated, the cell would rest near +65 mV.
Slides (2)
L8LearningHigh yield
Which cells have the five-phase (fast, sodium-driven) action potential?
  1. A. Atrial, ventricular and SA-node cells
  2. B. Atrial, ventricular and Purkinje cells
  3. C. SA node, AV node and Purkinje cells
AnswerB. Atrial, ventricular and Purkinje cells
WhyAtrial muscle, ventricular muscle and Purkinje fibres have the fast action potential: sodium upstroke, plateau and stable rest (phases 0–4).
Explanation

The fast-response action potential has all five phases: 0 upstroke (fast sodium), 1 early dip, 2 plateau (calcium in, potassium out), 3 repolarisation and 4 stable rest. Purkinje fibres are conducting cells but share this shape (they have the longest one, about 300 ms).

  • The SA node (and the AV node) have the slow-response action potential: phases 4, 0 and 3 only, with a calcium upstroke and an unstable phase 4.
  • Putting the nodes with the Purkinje cells mixes the two families.
Slides (2)
L9LearningHigh yield
When is the working-cell upstroke steepest, and why?
  1. A. From a more negative resting potential: more calcium channels are ready to open
  2. B. From a more negative resting potential: more sodium channels are ready to open
  3. C. From a less negative resting potential: the cell is already closer to threshold
AnswerB. From a more negative resting potential: more sodium channels are ready to open
WhyThe rate of rise of the upstroke (dV/dt) is greatest when the resting potential is most negative, because the most sodium channels have reset and are available.
Explanation

Sodium channels recover from inactivation only when the membrane is well polarised. At −90 mV almost all of them are ready, so the upstroke is steep and large. If the resting potential is less negative (for example with high extracellular potassium), a share of the channels stays inactivated, so phase 0 is slower and smaller and conduction slows.

  • Being closer to threshold does not help: a partly depolarised cell has fewer usable sodium channels, so its upstroke is shallower.
  • The upstroke of working cells is carried by sodium, not calcium.
Slides (1)
L10LearningHigh yield
Phase 1 of the working-cell action potential: what happens?
  1. A. Brief dip: sodium channels reopen and a little calcium enters
  2. B. Brief dip: sodium channels inactivate and potassium leaves
  3. C. Brief dip: calcium channels close and chloride enters
AnswerB. Brief dip: sodium channels inactivate and potassium leaves
WhyPhase 1 is the small initial repolarisation (notch): the fast sodium channels inactivate while an outward potassium current flows.
Explanation

Right after the peak, the sodium current stops and a transient outward potassium current (Ito) brings the potential down a little, giving the notch before the plateau. The lecture calls these "ungated potassium channels"; textbooks name the current Ito, a voltage-gated transient outward current.

  • Sodium channels do not reopen here; they are inactivated and stay that way until repolarisation.
  • Calcium channels are just opening at this point (they make the plateau), not closing.
Slides (2)
L11LearningHigh yield
Phase 2 of the working-cell action potential: what happens and which current?
  1. A. Plateau: potassium out through inward rectifiers (IK1), balanced by sodium in
  2. B. Plateau: calcium in through T-type channels (ICa-T), balanced by chloride in
  3. C. Plateau: calcium in through L-type channels (ICa-L), balanced by potassium out
AnswerC. Plateau: calcium in through L-type channels (ICa-L), balanced by potassium out
WhyPhase 2 is the plateau: inward calcium through L-type channels roughly equals outward potassium current, so the potential stays near 0 mV.
Explanation

The plateau is the unique feature of the cardiac action potential. Slow L-type ("long-lasting") calcium channels open and positive charge entering holds the membrane up ("positive in keeps it up"), while slow delayed-rectifier potassium current (IKs) leaks positive charge out. With inward and outward currents nearly equal, the potential barely changes for 100–200 ms.

  • IK1 is the resting (phase 4) potassium current; it is largely shut during the plateau.
  • T-type calcium channels belong to late phase 4 of the SA node, not the working-cell plateau.
Slides (3)
L12LearningHigh yield
What does the calcium entering during the phase 2 plateau do?
  1. A. Triggers calcium uptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum → relaxation
  2. B. Triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum → contraction
  3. C. Triggers potassium channels to open → repolarisation
AnswerB. Triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum → contraction
WhyPlateau calcium is the trigger: it releases much more calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (calcium-induced calcium release), which starts contraction.
Explanation

The calcium that enters through L-type channels is small in amount but opens the ryanodine receptors of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which pour out stored calcium. That calcium binds troponin C and lets the myofilaments contract. Because the trigger comes in during the plateau, the electrical plateau and mechanical systole overlap.

  • Uptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by the SERCA pump causes relaxation; that happens after the calcium signal ends, not because of plateau entry.
  • Repolarisation starts when the calcium channels close and potassium current wins, not because calcium opens potassium channels.
Slides (3)
L13LearningHigh yield
Phase 3 of the working-cell action potential: what happens and which currents?
  1. A. Repolarisation: sodium channels shut and chloride in wins (ICl, with Ito)
  2. B. Repolarisation: calcium channels open and potassium in wins (IK1, with If)
  3. C. Repolarisation: calcium channels shut and potassium out wins (IKs, IKr, with IK1)
AnswerC. Repolarisation: calcium channels shut and potassium out wins (IKs, IKr, with IK1)
WhyIn phase 3 the calcium channels close and the big voltage-gated potassium channels carry positive charge out, so the cell repolarises.
Explanation

As the L-type calcium channels inactivate, inward current falls, while the delayed-rectifier potassium currents (IKs slow and IKr rapid) grow. Outward current now clearly exceeds inward current, and the potential falls back towards −90 mV. Near the end, the inward rectifier IK1 reopens and finishes the job.

  • Chloride plays no major role in phase 3, and sodium channels have been shut since phase 1.
  • Potassium flows out, not in; and calcium channels close in phase 3.
Slides (2)
L14Learning
What does the long plateau protect the heart against, and why?
  1. A. Summation: it lets successive twitches add together into a stronger beat
  2. B. Tetany: the cell cannot be re-excited until it is already relaxing
  3. C. Fibrillation: it lets each cell fire as often as it is stimulated
AnswerB. Tetany: the cell cannot be re-excited until it is already relaxing
WhyThe plateau keeps the cell depolarised and refractory almost until contraction is over, so a second stimulus cannot summate the beats into tetany.
Explanation

While the plateau lasts, the sodium channels stay inactivated, so the absolute refractory period covers phases 0, 1, 2 and most of 3, which is almost the whole twitch. A new action potential therefore cannot start until the muscle is relaxing. Skeletal muscle, with its 1–2 ms spike, can be restimulated during its twitch and tetanised; a tetanised heart would stop filling and pumping.

  • Summation is exactly what the plateau prevents.
  • Letting each cell fire as often as stimulated is the opposite of a long refractory period; short refractoriness is what favours fibrillation.
Slides (1)

Pacemaker cells

L15LearningHigh yield
What makes pacemaker cells automatic?
  1. A. A long plateau: calcium keeps them depolarised and firing continuously
  2. B. No stable resting potential: they drift up to threshold, fire and repeat
  3. C. A very negative stable resting potential: they fire whenever the vagus releases them
AnswerB. No stable resting potential: they drift up to threshold, fire and repeat
WhyPacemaker cells have an unstable phase 4: instead of resting, the potential drifts upward until it hits threshold, fires, and starts again.
Explanation

This spontaneous phase 4 depolarisation is automaticity. After each action potential the SA node repolarises to about −65 mV and immediately starts creeping up, driven by the inward funny current and then T-type calcium current, to threshold at about −45 mV. Changing the slope of that drift changes heart rate.

  • Pacemaker cells have no plateau; a sustained plateau would hold the cell refractory, not make it fire repeatedly.
  • A stable, very negative resting potential describes working muscle, which never fires without being stimulated; the vagus slows the node but does not trigger it.
Slides (2)
L16LearningHigh yield
What actually sets heart rate at the SA node?
  1. A. How long the cell takes to drift from −65 to −45 mV (phase 4)
  2. B. How long the cell stays at its 0 mV plateau (phase 2)
  3. C. How long the cell takes to repolarise from +10 to −65 mV (phase 3)
AnswerA. How long the cell takes to drift from −65 to −45 mV (phase 4)
WhyHeart rate is set by how long phase 4 takes to reach threshold: a steeper phase 4 means more beats per minute, a flatter one fewer.
Explanation

The upstroke and repolarisation of the SA node take roughly the same time every beat; the variable part of the cycle is the diastolic drift. Anything that steepens phase 4 (sympathetic stimulation, more funny current) shortens the interval between beats; anything that flattens it or starts it lower (acetylcholine) lengthens it. Hook: phase 4 is heart rate.

  • The SA node has no phase 2 plateau.
  • Phase 3 repolarisation changes little from beat to beat and is not the rate-setting step.
Slides (1)
L17LearningHigh yield
What current drives SA-node phase 4?
  1. A. Fast sodium current, INa: an inward sodium current
  2. B. Funny current, If: an inward sodium current
  3. C. Funny current, If: an outward potassium current
AnswerB. Funny current, If: an inward sodium current
WhyPhase 4 of the SA node is driven by the funny current (If), a slow inward sodium current that keeps depolarising the cell.
Explanation

Funny channels (HCN channels) are unusual: they open when the cell repolarises, the opposite of most voltage-gated channels, hence "funny". At the voltages of phase 4 they let sodium leak in, so the membrane creeps up from −65 mV towards threshold. cAMP opens them further, which is how sympathetic stimulation speeds the heart.

  • Fast sodium channels are mostly inactivated at the SA node's depolarised potentials, so they play no part in nodal phase 4 or the nodal upstroke.
  • An outward potassium current would hyperpolarise the cell; that is the vagal GK effect, not the funny current.
Slides (2)
L18LearningHigh yield
Why is the nodal upstroke slow, and why does the node conduct slowly?
  1. A. It has very few potassium channels to repolarise it
  2. B. Its upstroke is carried by sodium, not calcium
  3. C. Its upstroke is carried by calcium, not sodium
AnswerC. Its upstroke is carried by calcium, not sodium
WhyNodal phase 0 runs on slow L-type calcium current, which is small and slow to activate, so dV/dt is low and the impulse spreads slowly (0.01–0.03 m/s in the AV node).
Explanation

Conduction velocity depends on the size of the inward current during the upstroke. A fast sodium current gives a steep upstroke that quickly brings the next patch of membrane to threshold; a calcium current gives a gentle one that charges the neighbour slowly. This is why the AV node is the slowest tissue in the heart and creates the AV delay.

  • Fewer potassium channels would affect repolarisation and the resting level, not the speed of the upstroke.
  • "Carried by sodium" reverses the facts: sodium is the fast upstroke of working cells.
Slides (1)
L19LearningHigh yield
Which phases does a pacemaker-cell action potential have?
  1. A. All five, 0 to 4 (with a short plateau and a stable rest)
  2. B. Only 0, 1 and 2 (no repolarisation and no drift)
  3. C. Only 4, 0 and 3 (no phase 1 or 2, no plateau, no stable rest)
AnswerC. Only 4, 0 and 3 (no phase 1 or 2, no plateau, no stable rest)
WhyPacemaker cells use only phases 4, 0 and 3: drift up, calcium upstroke, potassium repolarisation. There is no phase 1 or 2.
Explanation
Phase 4Slow drift up: funny current (sodium in), then T-type calcium
Phase 0Upstroke: L-type calcium in
Phase 3Repolarisation: potassium out
  • Pacemaker cells have no plateau and no stable rest, so "all five phases" is wrong.
  • "0, 1 and 2" describes the start of the working-cell action potential; without phases 3 and 4 a cell could neither repolarise nor fire again.

Hook: "0, 3, 4" sounds like a quarterback's call, and it is the SA node.

Slides (2)
L20Learning
How do verapamil and diltiazem slow conduction through the AV node?
  1. A. They block fast sodium channels that carry the nodal upstroke
  2. B. They block funny channels that carry nodal phase 4
  3. C. They block L-type calcium channels that carry the nodal upstroke
AnswerC. They block L-type calcium channels that carry the nodal upstroke
WhyAV-nodal phase 0 runs on L-type calcium channels; verapamil and diltiazem block them, so the upstroke and conduction through the node slow and the PR interval lengthens.
Explanation

With less inward calcium current, the nodal upstroke is smaller and slower, conduction through the node slows and the node stays refractory longer. Fewer atrial impulses get through, which is how these drugs (with beta-blockers and digoxin) control the ventricular rate in rapid atrial fibrillation.

  • Nodal cells barely use fast sodium channels; sodium channel blockers act on working muscle and Purkinje fibres.
  • The funny channel is not blocked by calcium channel blockers (ivabradine is the funny-channel blocker).

Note: one lecture figure labels the AV nodal calcium channels as "not inhibited by calcium channel blockers". As drawn, the label is incorrect: the upstroke channels it points to are L-type and are blocked by verapamil and diltiazem, as the lecture itself says when it lists calcium channel blockers among the drugs that slow the AV node. (Only the T-type channels of late phase 4 escape ordinary calcium channel blockers.)

Slides (2)

Autonomic control of rate

L21Learning
Do alpha-1 receptors control the heart’s rate or conduction?
  1. A. Yes: alpha-1 is the heart’s main sympathetic receptor
  2. B. No: alpha-1 acts on vessels; the heart’s sympathetic receptor is beta-1
  3. C. No: alpha-1 acts on vessels; the heart’s sympathetic receptor is beta-2
AnswerB. No: alpha-1 acts on vessels; the heart’s sympathetic receptor is beta-1
Why"Alpha does not touch the heart": alpha-1 constricts blood vessels, while sympathetic effects on the heart go through beta-1.
Explanation

Rate, AV conduction and contractility all rise through beta-1. Alpha-1 receptors are on vascular smooth muscle (skin, kidney, spleen, gut) and raise blood pressure by vasoconstriction. An alpha-1 agonist such as phenylephrine therefore tends to lower heart rate indirectly, through the baroreceptor reflex, rather than raise it. (Myocardium has a few alpha-1 receptors with minor effects, which the course does not test.)

  • Alpha-1 is not the heart's main receptor.
  • Beta-2 dilates skeletal-muscle vessels and bronchi; the heart's receptor is beta-1.
Slides (2)
L22LearningHigh yield
What does beta-1 stimulation do inside the cardiac cell?
  1. A. Stimulates guanylyl cyclase → cyclic GMP (cGMP) up
  2. B. Inhibits adenylyl cyclase → cyclic AMP (cAMP) down
  3. C. Stimulates adenylyl cyclase → cyclic AMP (cAMP) up
AnswerC. Stimulates adenylyl cyclase → cyclic AMP (cAMP) up
WhyBeta-1 is coupled to Gs, which stimulates adenylyl cyclase and raises cAMP; cAMP and protein kinase A then increase the funny and calcium currents.
Explanation

In the SA node, cAMP binds the funny channels directly and protein kinase A phosphorylates L-type calcium channels, so phase 4 steepens and rate rises. In the AV node more calcium current speeds conduction; in the myocardium more calcium current (plus phospholamban phosphorylation) raises contractility.

  • Inhibiting adenylyl cyclase is the M2 (Gi) pathway, the opposite effect.
  • cGMP is the nitric oxide / natriuretic-peptide messenger in smooth muscle, not the beta-1 pathway.
Slides (3)
L23LearningHigh yield
What does M2 stimulation do inside the cardiac cell?
  1. A. Activates Gi → inhibits adenylyl cyclase → cAMP down
  2. B. Activates Gs → stimulates adenylyl cyclase → cAMP up
  3. C. Activates Gq → phospholipase C → IP3 up
AnswerA. Activates Gi → inhibits adenylyl cyclase → cAMP down
WhyM2 is coupled to Gi, which inhibits adenylyl cyclase and lowers cAMP; its βγ subunits also open acetylcholine-activated potassium channels.
Explanation

Less cAMP means less funny current and less calcium current, so phase 4 flattens and AV conduction slows. Separately, the G-protein βγ subunits open IK-ACh channels directly, without a second messenger, hyperpolarising the SA node. Both effects slow the heart.

  • Gs → cAMP up is the beta-1 pathway.
  • Gq → IP3 is the M1/M3 and alpha-1 pathway, used by smooth muscle and glands.
Slides (3)
L24LearningHigh yield
What do chronotropic, dromotropic and inotropic refer to?
  1. A. Chronotropic: heart rate
    Dromotropic: contractility
    Inotropic: AV conduction
  2. B. Chronotropic: heart rate
    Dromotropic: AV conduction
    Inotropic: contractility
  3. C. Chronotropic: contractility
    Dromotropic: heart rate
    Inotropic: AV conduction
AnswerB. Chronotropic: heart rate
Dromotropic: AV conduction
Inotropic: contractility
WhyChronotropic = heart rate, dromotropic = conduction velocity (mainly through the AV node), inotropic = contractility.
Explanation

Positive effects increase, negative effects decrease. Sympathetic stimulation is positively chronotropic, dromotropic and inotropic; parasympathetic stimulation is negatively chronotropic and dromotropic and negatively inotropic in the atria only.

  • Memory hooks: chronos = time (rate); dromos = a running track (conduction, as in hippodrome); ino = fibre (force of the muscle fibres).
Slides (1)
L25LearningHigh yield
A woman relaxes on the sofa with friends, eating popcorn. Which division, receptor, G protein and transmitter mainly set her heart rate?
  1. A. Sympathetic, beta-1, Gs, norepinephrine
  2. B. Parasympathetic, M2, Gs, acetylcholine
  3. C. Parasympathetic, M2, Gi, acetylcholine
AnswerC. Parasympathetic, M2, Gi, acetylcholine
WhyAt rest ("rest and digest") the parasympathetic system dominates the heart: acetylcholine on M2 receptors acting through Gi.
Explanation

The SA node on its own would fire at about 100 per minute (a denervated, transplanted heart beats about that fast). A normal resting rate of 60–80 per minute shows that a steady vagal brake is applied at rest. The lecture's summary: sympathetic = "stop eating and run away"; parasympathetic = "stop running and eat".

  • Sympathetic / beta-1 / norepinephrine dominates in fight-or-flight, not on the sofa.
  • M2 is coupled to Gi, not Gs.
Slides (2)
L26LearningHigh yield
How do sympathetic and vagal stimulation change the PR interval?
  1. A. Sympathetic shortens it
    Vagal lengthens it
  2. B. Sympathetic lengthens it
    Vagal shortens it
  3. C. Sympathetic shortens it
    Vagal leaves it unchanged
AnswerA. Sympathetic shortens it
Vagal lengthens it
WhyThe PR interval is mostly AV-nodal delay: sympathetic stimulation speeds the node and shortens PR; vagal stimulation slows the node and lengthens PR.
Explanation

Positive dromotropy (beta-1, more calcium current) means the impulse crosses the AV node faster, so the time from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS shrinks. Negative dromotropy (M2, less calcium current, more IK-ACh) lengthens it; strong vagal tone can even block some beats.

  • The second option reverses the two.
  • Vagal stimulation clearly does change PR: the AV node is richly supplied by the vagus.
Slides (2)
L27Learning
How does parasympathetic stimulation affect the vessels of skin, kidney, spleen and gut?
  1. A. Dilates them through muscarinic receptors
  2. B. Constricts them through alpha-1 receptors
  3. C. Constricts them through muscarinic receptors
AnswerA. Dilates them through muscarinic receptors
WhyThe lecture table shows parasympathetic (muscarinic) stimulation dilating the vessels of skin, kidney, spleen and gut, the opposite of sympathetic alpha-1 constriction.
Explanation

The lecture labels this receptor M2. Textbooks (including the Costanzo table shown in the TA session) place it on the endothelium as M3: acetylcholine makes endothelial cells release nitric oxide (endothelium-derived relaxing factor), which relaxes the smooth muscle. Most vessels have no parasympathetic nerves, so this effect is seen mainly with directly acting muscarinic drugs. For the exam: dilation, muscarinic.

  • Alpha-1 constriction is the sympathetic effect on the same vessels.
  • Muscarinic stimulation of vessels dilates (through nitric oxide); it does not constrict.
Slides (1)

Autonomic drugs and the heart

L28LearningHigh yield
How does atropine change the SA-node action potential?
  1. A. Muscarinic blocker: strengthens the vagal brake → phase 4 slower
  2. B. Muscarinic blocker: removes the vagal brake → phase 4 faster (shorter)
  3. C. Nicotinic blocker: removes ganglionic input → phase 4 flatter
AnswerB. Muscarinic blocker: removes the vagal brake → phase 4 faster (shorter)
WhyAtropine blocks muscarinic (M2) receptors, removing the resting vagal brake: phase 4 speeds up (shortens) and heart rate rises.
Explanation

At rest the vagus is constantly flattening phase 4 and hyperpolarising the node. Blocking M2 receptors with atropine takes away both effects, so the SA node drifts to threshold sooner. It also removes vagal slowing of the AV node, so AV conduction speeds up. This is why atropine treats symptomatic bradycardia and nerve-gas (cholinesterase-inhibitor) poisoning.

  • A blocker cannot strengthen the vagal brake; that is what a muscarinic agonist or a cholinesterase inhibitor does.
  • Atropine is muscarinic, not nicotinic; ganglion blockers are a different drug class.
Slides (3)
L29LearningHigh yield
Why can myasthenia gravis treatment (a cholinesterase inhibitor) cause bradycardia?
  1. A. Less acetylcholine at the heart → GK down → SA node depolarises → bradycardia
  2. B. More acetylcholine at the heart → GNa up → SA node depolarises → bradycardia
  3. C. More acetylcholine at the heart → GK up → SA node hyperpolarises → bradycardia
AnswerC. More acetylcholine at the heart → GK up → SA node hyperpolarises → bradycardia
WhyNeostigmine or pyridostigmine stops acetylcholine breakdown, so more acetylcholine reaches cardiac M2 receptors: GK opens, the SA node hyperpolarises and phase 4 flattens.
Explanation

The drug is given to boost acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, but it also boosts acetylcholine at the vagal endings on the heart. Opened acetylcholine-activated potassium channels let potassium leave, the SA node starts each cycle more negative, the funny current falls, and the rate drops; a pulse of 38 with syncope has been reported. An overdose can even cause asystole.

  • The drug raises acetylcholine; it does not lower it.
  • Acetylcholine raises potassium conductance, not sodium; sodium entry would speed the heart.
Slides (2)
L30Learning
A drug lowers heart rate but leaves ventricular contractility unchanged. How does it most likely act on the heart?
  1. A. Stimulates muscarinic M2 receptors
  2. B. Blocks beta-1 receptors
  3. C. Stimulates beta-1 receptors
AnswerA. Stimulates muscarinic M2 receptors
WhyM2 stimulation slows the SA node and AV node but lowers contractility only in the atria, so ventricular contractility is spared.
Explanation

The vagus barely supplies the ventricles, so a muscarinic (M2) agonist slows the heart and AV conduction (longer PR) without a direct effect on ventricular force. Expected side effects come from the other muscarinic receptors: bronchoconstriction, more secretions, gut cramps.

  • A beta-1 blocker slows the heart but also lowers ventricular contractility (negative inotropy), since beta-1 drives ventricular force.
  • Beta-1 stimulation raises both rate and contractility.
Slides (1)
L31Learning
A woman with a regular heart rate of 180/min drops to 75/min during gentle carotid sinus massage. How did the massage work?
  1. A. More vagal output → slower AV-node conduction and a longer AV-node refractory period
  2. B. Less vagal output → faster AV-node conduction and a shorter AV-node refractory period
  3. C. More vagal output → a longer refractory period in the ventricular muscle
AnswerA. More vagal output → slower AV-node conduction and a longer AV-node refractory period
WhyCarotid massage stretches the baroreceptors, which reflexly increases vagal output; acetylcholine slows AV-node conduction and lengthens its refractory period, breaking the tachycardia.
Explanation

Pressing on the carotid sinus mimics high blood pressure, so baroreceptor firing rises and the brainstem increases parasympathetic outflow. At the AV node, acetylcholine (M2) reduces the calcium current and opens IK-ACh: conduction slows and the node stays refractory longer. A regular narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia that uses the AV node in its circuit is interrupted.

  • Less vagal output is the reflex to low blood pressure, the opposite of what massage mimics.
  • The vagus has little effect on ventricular muscle; its target here is the AV node.
Slides (2)

Conduction velocity

L32LearningHigh yield
Rank cardiac conduction velocity, fastest to slowest.
  1. A. Atrial and ventricular muscle → Purkinje fibres → AV node
  2. B. Purkinje fibres → atrial and ventricular muscle → AV node
  3. C. Purkinje fibres → AV node → atrial and ventricular muscle
AnswerB. Purkinje fibres → atrial and ventricular muscle → AV node
WhyPurkinje fibres (2–4 m/s) are fastest, working muscle (about 1 m/s) is in between, and the AV node (0.01–0.03 m/s) is slowest.
Explanation

Both extremes are deliberate: the slow node buys time for the atrial kick, and the fast Purkinje network makes the ventricle contract as one unit. A research question may give raw numbers, for example 2.2, 1.1, 0.3 and 0.05 m/s: the slowest point (0.05) is the AV node, the site that gives the ventricles time to fill.

  • Working muscle is not faster than the Purkinje fibres.
  • The AV node is not faster than working muscle; it is the slowest of all.
Slides (2)
L33LearningHigh yield
What two things determine cardiac conduction velocity?
  1. A. Size of the outward potassium current during repolarisation
    Thickness of the ventricular wall
  2. B. Duration of the plateau phase
    Number of sympathetic fibres reaching the tissue
  3. C. Size of the inward current during the upstroke
    Cable properties (membrane and internal resistance)
AnswerC. Size of the inward current during the upstroke
Cable properties (membrane and internal resistance)
WhyConduction velocity depends on the size of the inward current during the upstroke and on the cable properties of the fibre (membrane and internal resistance).
Explanation

An action potential spreads because current from the depolarised patch flows ahead inside the fibre and brings the next patch to threshold. It goes faster when more current is generated (a big, fast upstroke) and when that current travels far along the inside of the fibre without leaking out (high membrane resistance, low internal resistance). The lecture's summary: high membrane resistance plus low internal resistance = "super fast".

  • The potassium current and the plateau shape repolarisation and refractoriness, not the speed of spread.
  • Wall thickness and nerve supply do not set velocity directly.
Slides (2)
L34LearningHigh yield
What keeps internal resistance low between cardiac cells?
  1. A. Desmosomes
  2. B. Gap junctions
  3. C. Fasciae adherentes
AnswerB. Gap junctions
WhyGap junctions in the intercalated discs connect neighbouring cells' cytoplasm, letting current pass directly so the myocardium acts as a functional syncytium.
Explanation

Gap junctions are channels (connexons) linking the interiors of adjacent myocytes. Ions, and so electrical current, pass through them with little resistance; the lecture calls them "wormholes". As a result an action potential started in one cell spreads to all of its neighbours, and the atria and ventricles each behave as one electrical unit.

  • Desmosomes and fasciae adherentes are the other parts of the intercalated disc; they hold cells together mechanically and anchor the filaments, but carry no current.
Slides (3)
L35Learning
What is the defect in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome?
  1. A. A damaged AV node lengthens the delay before the impulse reaches the ventricles
  2. B. An extra pathway lets the impulse reach the ventricles without the AV-node delay
  3. C. A slowed internodal tract delays the impulse before it reaches the AV node
AnswerB. An extra pathway lets the impulse reach the ventricles without the AV-node delay
WhyIn Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) connects atria to ventricles directly, bypassing the AV-node delay: a pre-excitation syndrome.
Explanation

Part of the ventricle is activated early through the extra pathway, before the impulse arriving through the AV node. Typical EKG clues are a short PR interval and a slurred upstroke of the QRS (delta wave). The pathway can also form a re-entry loop with the AV node and cause supraventricular tachycardia.

  • A damaged AV node with a longer delay is first-degree AV block, the opposite.
  • A slow internodal tract would delay, not speed, ventricular activation; Wolff-Parkinson-White is a too-fast problem.
Slides (2)
L36LearningHigh yield
An antiarrhythmic drug blocks many fast sodium channels. What does it do to ventricular muscle?
  1. A. Resting potential unchanged; upstroke slower; conduction slower
  2. B. Resting potential less negative; upstroke slower; conduction slower
  3. C. Resting potential unchanged; upstroke unchanged; conduction slower
AnswerA. Resting potential unchanged; upstroke slower; conduction slower
WhyBlocking fast sodium channels leaves the resting potential unchanged (it is set by potassium channels) but slows the upstroke, so conduction slows.
Explanation

The resting potential depends on the open inward-rectifier potassium channels, not on sodium channels, which are closed at rest. During phase 0, fewer available sodium channels mean a smaller inward current, a lower dV/dt and slower propagation. This is how class I drugs such as lidocaine and flecainide work. Nodal cells, whose upstroke is calcium, are affected far less.

  • A less negative resting potential is the effect of high extracellular potassium, not of a sodium channel blocker.
  • The upstroke cannot stay unchanged when its carrier current is blocked; the slower upstroke is the reason conduction slows.
Slides (1)

Refractory periods

L37Learning
Why is a cardiac cell refractory just after it depolarises?
  1. A. Depolarisation closes the fast sodium activation gates; while they stay closed, the cell is refractory
  2. B. Depolarisation closes the slower sodium inactivation gates; while they stay closed, the cell is refractory
  3. C. Depolarisation empties the sarcoplasmic reticulum; until it refills, the cell is refractory
AnswerB. Depolarisation closes the slower sodium inactivation gates; while they stay closed, the cell is refractory
WhyDepolarisation opens the sodium activation gates fast and shuts the inactivation gates more slowly; until repolarisation reopens the inactivation gates, the channel cannot conduct.
Explanation

Each fast sodium channel has two gates. At rest the activation gate is closed and the inactivation gate is open, so the channel is ready. Depolarisation (1) flings the activation gate open, giving the upstroke, and (2) a little later swings the inactivation gate shut. A channel with a closed inactivation gate cannot reopen whatever the stimulus. Only repolarisation resets the inactivation gate, so the cell stays refractory until it has repolarised.

  • Activation gates are the ones that open on depolarisation; they do not close to cause refractoriness.
  • Sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium governs contraction, not the ability to fire another action potential.
Slides (2)
L38LearningHigh yield
What does the absolute refractory period (ARP) of a ventricular cell span, and when does it end?
  1. A. Upstroke, plateau and most of repolarisation; ends once the membrane falls below about −50 mV
  2. B. Upstroke, plateau and all of repolarisation; ends only at the resting potential of about −90 mV
  3. C. Plateau and phase 4; ends when the cell drifts back up to threshold
AnswerA. Upstroke, plateau and most of repolarisation; ends once the membrane falls below about −50 mV
WhyThe ARP covers phase 0, phases 1–2 (plateau) and most of phase 3; it ends when repolarisation passes about −50 mV, as sodium channels start to recover.
Explanation

During the ARP so many sodium channels are inactivated that no stimulus, however large, can produce an action potential. Sodium channels recover in a voltage-dependent way as the membrane repolarises; once the potential passes roughly −50 mV enough have recovered for a strong stimulus to work, and the ARP gives way to the relative refractory period.

  • All of repolarisation, down to −90 mV, overstates it: the last part of phase 3 is the relative refractory period and then the supranormal period.
  • Plateau and phase 4 is wrong because the ARP begins with the upstroke, and in phase 4 a working cell is fully excitable.
Slides (3)
L39LearningHigh yield
What is the effective refractory period (ERP)?
  1. A. Slightly shorter than the ARP: a strong stimulus produces a normal, propagated action potential
  2. B. Slightly longer than the ARP: a strong stimulus may cause a local response, but no action potential that propagates
  3. C. The same as the ARP: no stimulus of any size produces even a local response
AnswerB. Slightly longer than the ARP: a strong stimulus may cause a local response, but no action potential that propagates
WhyThe ERP is the ARP plus the start of the relative refractory period: a strong stimulus may cause a small local response, but no conducted (propagated) action potential.
Explanation

Just after the ARP ends, a few sodium channels have recovered. A strong stimulus can then trigger a small, weak depolarisation in that cell, but it carries too little inward current to excite the neighbouring cells, so the impulse does not propagate. The ERP therefore includes the ARP and the first part of the relative refractory period; it is the period that actually protects the heart from extra conducted beats.

  • Slightly shorter than the ARP reverses the relationship: the ERP contains the ARP.
  • The same as the ARP ignores the local, non-propagated response that is possible at the end of the ERP.
Slides (2)
L40LearningHigh yield
What can fire a cardiac cell during the relative refractory period, and why?
  1. A. No stimulus at all, because the sodium channels are all still inactivated
  2. B. A stronger-than-normal stimulus, because some sodium channels have recovered
  3. C. A stronger-than-normal stimulus, because calcium channels have taken over the upstroke
AnswerB. A stronger-than-normal stimulus, because some sodium channels have recovered
WhyIn the relative refractory period some sodium channels have recovered, so a greater-than-normal stimulus can fire the cell; the action potential is smaller and slower.
Explanation

The relative refractory period follows the ARP, late in phase 3. Repolarisation has reset part of the sodium-channel population, so threshold can be reached, but only with more inward current than usual. Because fewer channels take part, the upstroke is slower and lower, so the impulse also conducts slowly.

  • No stimulus at all describes the absolute refractory period.
  • Calcium channels taking over is wrong: working-cell upstrokes stay sodium-driven; recovery of sodium channels is what makes firing possible again.
Slides (2)
L41LearningHigh yield
What is special about the supranormal period?
  1. A. The cell is more excitable than normal: a weaker-than-normal stimulus can fire it
  2. B. The cell is less excitable than normal: a stronger-than-normal stimulus is needed to fire it
  3. C. The cell cannot be fired: it is hyperpolarised below its resting potential
AnswerA. The cell is more excitable than normal: a weaker-than-normal stimulus can fire it
WhyIn the supranormal period the sodium channels have recovered while the membrane is still slightly depolarised, near threshold, so less inward current than normal fires the cell.
Explanation

The supranormal period comes right after the relative refractory period, at the very end of phase 3. Almost all sodium channels are available again, yet the membrane has not quite reached the resting potential and so sits a little closer to threshold. A smaller-than-normal stimulus is therefore enough: the cell is more excitable than normal.

  • A stronger-than-normal stimulus is needed in the relative refractory period, not the supranormal one.
  • Cannot be fired, hyperpolarised is wrong: working cardiac cells have no after-hyperpolarisation below rest, and the cell is easier, not harder, to fire.
Slides (2)
L42Learning
On the surface EKG, when is the ventricle in its relative refractory period?
  1. A. During the QRS complex and ST segment
  2. B. During the TP segment before the next P wave
  3. C. Near the end of the T wave
AnswerC. Near the end of the T wave
WhyThe ventricle is absolutely refractory from the QRS through the early T wave and relatively refractory near the end of the T wave, as it repolarises.
Explanation

The T wave records ventricular repolarisation (phase 3), the time when sodium channels recover. So the refractory periods map onto the EKG: absolute refractory period from the start of the QRS through the ST segment and the first part of the T wave; relative refractory period over the late T wave; the supranormal period just at its end. A stimulus landing on the late T wave meets partly recovered tissue, which is why an ill-timed extra beat there is dangerous.

  • QRS and ST segment: the ventricle is depolarised and on its plateau, so it is absolutely refractory.
  • TP segment: the ventricle is fully repolarised and normally excitable.
Slides (2)

Latent pacemakers

L43LearningHigh yield
Why does the SA node, rather than the other pacemaker cells, normally control heart rate?
  1. A. It has the fastest conduction velocity, so its impulse spreads first
  2. B. It has the steepest phase 4 depolarisation, so it reaches threshold first
  3. C. It has the fastest phase 0 upstroke, so its action potential is the largest
AnswerB. It has the steepest phase 4 depolarisation, so it reaches threshold first
WhyThe pacemaker with the steepest phase 4 reaches threshold first; the SA node's slope is steepest, so it fires fastest and sets the rate.
Explanation

All pacemaker cells drift upward during phase 4. The SA node drifts fastest, from about −65 mV to its threshold of about −45 mV, so it fires first, and its impulse then depolarises the slower latent pacemakers before they can fire on their own. "The SA node is the pacemaker because it IS FASTER than the others."

  • Fastest conduction velocity belongs to the Purkinje fibres (2–4 m/s); the nodes conduct slowly.
  • Fastest phase 0 belongs to working cells with sodium upstrokes; the nodal upstroke is a slow calcium upstroke.
Slides (3)
L44Learning
Why do the latent pacemakers not normally fire on their own?
  1. A. They have no automaticity until the SA node fails, which switches their funny channels on
  2. B. Vagal acetylcholine holds them hyperpolarised, because only the SA node receives sympathetic fibres
  3. C. Each SA-node impulse depolarises them before their slower phase 4 reaches threshold, resetting their cycle
AnswerC. Each SA-node impulse depolarises them before their slower phase 4 reaches threshold, resetting their cycle
WhyOverdrive suppression: the faster SA-node impulse fires the latent pacemakers first, so their own slower phase 4 never gets to threshold.
Explanation

A latent pacemaker's phase 4 is less steep than the SA node's. Each normal beat arrives from above and depolarises it before its own drift reaches threshold; after it repolarises, its 'clock' restarts from the bottom. Because the SA node always wins the race, the automaticity of the AV node, bundle of His and Purkinje fibres stays hidden. This is called overdrive suppression.

  • No automaticity until the SA node fails is wrong: their automaticity is always present, merely pre-empted.
  • Vagal hyperpolarisation is not the mechanism; the ventricular conduction system has little vagal supply, and both nodes receive both autonomic divisions.
Slides (2)
L45LearningHigh yield
Rank the heart's pacemakers by intrinsic rate, fastest to slowest.
  1. A. SA node → AV node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres
  2. B. SA node → Purkinje fibres → bundle of His → AV node
  3. C. AV node → SA node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres
AnswerA. SA node → AV node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres
WhyIntrinsic rate falls down the conduction system: SA node (60–100) → AV node (40–60) → bundle of His (about 40) → Purkinje fibres (20–30).
Explanation

"The further down, the slower it goes." The SA node fires fastest and therefore leads. If it fails, the next fastest site, the AV node, takes over; if that also fails, the bundle of His and finally the Purkinje fibres pace the ventricles, each more slowly.

  • Purkinje before His and AV node confuses conduction velocity (Purkinje fastest) with intrinsic firing rate (Purkinje slowest).
  • AV node first is wrong: the AV node is the first back-up, not the leader.

The exact numbers differ between slides (one figure gives AV node 45–50, His 40–45, Purkinje 35–40); the order never changes.

Slides (2)
L46LearningHigh yield
When does a latent pacemaker become an ectopic pacemaker that drives the heart?
  1. A. When the SA node is suppressed, or the latent site starts firing faster than the SA node
  2. B. When the SA node speeds up, so the latent sites are recruited to keep pace with it
  3. C. When the latent site slows down, so the SA node hands control over to it
AnswerA. When the SA node is suppressed, or the latent site starts firing faster than the SA node
WhyA latent site drives the heart (an ectopic pacemaker) only if the SA node fails or slows, or the latent site's own rate rises above the SA node's.
Explanation

Control always goes to whichever site reaches threshold first. Normally that is the SA node. Two things can change the winner: the SA node slows or stops (disease, ischaemia, drugs), letting a back-up escape; or a latent site becomes abnormally fast (for example an irritable Purkinje focus firing above 80 per minute) and overtakes the SA node. Either way the beat now starts outside the SA node, an ectopic focus.

  • SA node speeding up makes overdrive suppression stronger, not weaker.
  • Latent site slowing makes it even less likely to win the race.
Slides (1)
L47Learning
An EKG shows no P waves, but normal narrow QRS complexes and normal T waves at 45 per minute. Where is the pacemaker?
  1. A. SA node
  2. B. Purkinje fibres
  3. C. AV node
AnswerC. AV node
WhyNo P waves: the SA node is not leading. Narrow, normal QRS: the ventricles are activated through the His–Purkinje system. So the beat starts at the AV node.
Explanation

A rate of 45 matches the AV node (40–60). An impulse arising in the AV node travels down the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibres in the usual order, so the QRS and T waves look normal. The atria are not activated in the normal way from the SA node, so no normal P wave precedes the QRS (any retrograde atrial activation is often hidden in the QRS). This is a junctional (AV-nodal) escape rhythm.

  • SA node: a sinus beat always produces a P wave before each QRS.
  • Purkinje fibres: a beat starting low in the ventricle spreads muscle to muscle, giving wide, bizarre complexes at 20–30 per minute.
Slides (2)

EKG waves and intervals

L48Learning
What does the EKG record?
  1. A. The summed electrical activity of the whole heart, picked up from the skin
  2. B. The mechanical contraction of the heart, picked up from the skin as pressure
  3. C. The action potential of a single ventricular cell, picked up from the skin
AnswerA. The summed electrical activity of the whole heart, picked up from the skin
WhyThe electrocardiogram records, from skin electrodes, the sum of the voltage changes of millions of cardiac cells as waves of depolarisation and repolarisation sweep through the heart.
Explanation

Each EKG wave appears when a large mass of muscle depolarises or repolarises at once: atria → P wave, ventricles → QRS complex, ventricular repolarisation → T wave. Flat stretches mean either that nothing large is changing or that all cells are at the same potential (for example the ST segment, when the whole ventricle is on its plateau).

  • Mechanical contraction is not recorded: the EKG is electrical, and an organised EKG can even appear without effective contraction.
  • A single cell's action potential needs an intracellular electrode; a ventricular action potential spans the whole QT interval, but its shape is not what the EKG traces.
Slides (1)
L49Learning
On an EKG lead, what does a wave of depolarisation moving toward the positive electrode produce?
  1. A. A downward (negative) deflection
  2. B. An upward (positive) deflection
  3. C. No deflection, because only repolarisation is recorded
AnswerB. An upward (positive) deflection
WhyDepolarisation moving toward a lead's positive electrode gives an upward deflection; moving away gives a downward one.
Explanation

Each lead compares a positive electrode with a reference. Lead II runs from the right arm to the left leg, roughly parallel to the heart's main axis, so the atrial and ventricular depolarisation waves travel toward its positive electrode: P and R are upright. The small Q and S waves are the parts of ventricular depolarisation (the septum and the base) heading away from it.

  • A downward deflection is what depolarisation moving away from the positive electrode produces.
  • Only repolarisation recorded is wrong: both depolarisation (P, QRS) and repolarisation (T) are recorded.
Slides (2)
L50Learning
What is the difference between an EKG interval and an EKG segment?
  1. A. An interval is the flat stretch between two waves; a segment includes at least one wave
  2. B. An interval is measured in millivolts; a segment is measured in seconds
  3. C. An interval includes at least one wave; a segment is the flat stretch between two waves
AnswerC. An interval includes at least one wave; a segment is the flat stretch between two waves
WhyAn interval includes a wave (PR interval = P wave + PR segment); a segment is just the flat line between waves (PR segment, ST segment).
Explanation

The PR interval runs from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS, so it contains the P wave; the PR segment is only the flat part from the end of P to the start of QRS. Likewise the QT interval contains the QRS, ST segment and T wave, while the ST segment is only the flat line between the QRS and the T wave.

  • The reverse definition swaps the two terms.
  • Millivolts versus seconds is wrong: both intervals and segments are durations, read along the time axis.
Slides (2)
L51Learning
Why is there no visible EKG wave for atrial repolarisation?
  1. A. It is hidden in the QRS complex
  2. B. It is hidden in the T wave
  3. C. The atria do not repolarise
AnswerA. It is hidden in the QRS complex
WhyAtrial repolarisation happens at the same time as ventricular depolarisation, so its small signal is swamped by the much larger QRS complex.
Explanation

After the P wave the atria stay depolarised on their plateau while the impulse crosses the AV node; they repolarise just as the ventricles depolarise. The ventricles have far more muscle, so the QRS overwhelms the small atrial repolarisation wave.

  • Hidden in the T wave is wrong timing: the T wave is ventricular repolarisation, well after the atria have recovered.
  • Atria do not repolarise is impossible: they must repolarise to fire again on the next beat.
Slides (2)
L52LearningHigh yield
What does the PR interval span, and what does it contain?
  1. A. Start of P to end of QRS: atrial plus ventricular depolarisation (mostly the QRS)
  2. B. End of P to start of T: AV-node delay plus the ventricular plateau (mostly the plateau)
  3. C. Start of P to start of QRS: atrial depolarisation plus the AV-node delay (mostly the delay)
AnswerC. Start of P to start of QRS: atrial depolarisation plus the AV-node delay (mostly the delay)
WhyThe PR interval runs from the start of P to the start of QRS: atrial depolarisation + AV-nodal delay, the time for the impulse to reach the ventricles.
Explanation

The PR interval is the P wave (atrial depolarisation) plus the PR segment, during which the impulse crawls through the AV node (the slowest tissue, 0.01–0.03 m/s) and then through the bundle of His, bundle branches and Purkinje fibres. Most of that time is the AV-nodal delay. Normal: 0.12–0.20 s.

  • Start of P to end of QRS would add ventricular depolarisation; the PR interval stops where the QRS begins.
  • End of P to start of T mixes the PR segment with the ST segment; it is not a standard interval.
Slides (3)
L53Learning
What is the normal duration of the QRS complex?
  1. A. Under 0.20 s (typically 0.12–0.20 s)
  2. B. Under 0.12 s (typically 0.08–0.10 s)
  3. C. Under 0.44 s (typically 0.36–0.44 s)
AnswerB. Under 0.12 s (typically 0.08–0.10 s)
WhyA normal QRS lasts under 0.12 s (3 small boxes), typically 0.08–0.10 s; a wider QRS means slow, abnormal ventricular spread.
Explanation

The fast Purkinje network (2–4 m/s) delivers the impulse to the ventricular muscle almost simultaneously, so ventricular depolarisation is brief. If the beat starts in the ventricle, or a bundle branch is blocked, the impulse must creep muscle to muscle and the QRS widens beyond 0.12 s.

  • 0.12–0.20 s is the normal PR interval.
  • 0.36–0.44 s is about the QT interval, which includes depolarisation and repolarisation.
Slides (2)
L54LearningHigh yield
What does the ST segment represent?
  1. A. The whole ventricle repolarised at once, in phase 4
  2. B. The whole ventricle depolarised at once, on its plateau
  3. C. The whole atrium depolarised at once, on its plateau
AnswerB. The whole ventricle depolarised at once, on its plateau
WhyDuring the ST segment every ventricular cell is depolarised on its plateau (phase 2), so there is no voltage difference to record: the line is flat while the ventricles contract.
Explanation

The EKG records only differences in potential between regions of the heart. During the plateau all ventricular cells sit near 0 mV, with calcium inward current balancing potassium outward current, so the trace is isoelectric. Mechanically this is when the ventricles are contracting and emptying. Ischaemia shifts the segment: ST elevation in acute infarction, ST depression in ischaemia. One lecture figure labels the ST segment "ventricular repolarization": strictly it is the plateau (phase 2), the slow early part of repolarisation, while every ventricular cell is still depolarised.

  • Whole ventricle repolarised describes the TP segment, when the ventricles are relaxed and filling.
  • Atrial plateau falls in the PR segment, before the QRS.
Slides (3)
L55Learning
Why is the normal T wave upright, like the QRS, even though it records repolarisation?
  1. A. Repolarisation spreads in the same direction as depolarisation, so it is recorded the same way
  2. B. The T wave records atrial repolarisation, which always points the same way as the QRS
  3. C. Repolarisation spreads in the opposite direction to depolarisation: the last cells to depolarise repolarise first
AnswerC. Repolarisation spreads in the opposite direction to depolarisation: the last cells to depolarise repolarise first
WhyVentricular repolarisation travels in the reverse direction to depolarisation (outer wall first); a repolarisation wave moving away from the positive electrode gives an upward deflection.
Explanation

Depolarisation spreads from the inner (endocardial) to the outer (epicardial) wall, but the outer cells have shorter action potentials, so they repolarise first: repolarisation spreads outer to inner. A repolarisation wave is electrically the mirror of a depolarisation wave, so a repolarisation wave heading away from the positive electrode writes the same upward deflection as a depolarisation wave heading toward it. Two reversals make the T wave point the same way as the QRS.

  • Same direction would give an inverted T wave.
  • Atrial repolarisation is hidden in the QRS; the T wave is ventricular.
Slides (2)
L56LearningHigh yield
What does the QT interval span, and what does it contain?
  1. A. Start of QRS to end of T: the entire ventricular action potential (depolarisation and repolarisation)
  2. B. Start of P to end of QRS: atrial depolarisation and the AV-node delay
  3. C. End of T to the next P: ventricular relaxation and filling
AnswerA. Start of QRS to end of T: the entire ventricular action potential (depolarisation and repolarisation)
WhyThe QT interval runs from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave: ventricular depolarisation + plateau + repolarisation, the electrical systole of the ventricles.
Explanation

A single ventricular action potential matches the QT interval: phase 0 lines up with the QRS, the plateau with the ST segment and phase 3 with the T wave. Anything that lengthens the plateau or slows repolarisation (for example hypokalaemia or potassium-channel-blocking drugs) prolongs the QT interval, and a long, unstable plateau predisposes to dangerous ventricular arrhythmias.

  • Start of P to end of QRS is not a standard interval; the PR interval stops at the start of the QRS.
  • End of T to the next P is the TP segment, the electrical rest between beats.
Slides (3)

Heart rate from the strip

L57Learning
Where do the rate and the rhythm of an EKG strip come from?
  1. A. Rate: spacing of the beats (further apart = slower)
    Rhythm: their regularity, and whether each P has a QRS
  2. B. Rate: how tall the R waves are (taller = faster)
    Rhythm: how wide each QRS is
  3. C. Rate: how regular the R waves are
    Rhythm: how far apart the beats are (further apart = slower)
AnswerA. Rate: spacing of the beats (further apart = slower)
Rhythm: their regularity, and whether each P has a QRS
WhyRate comes from the spacing of the R waves; rhythm from their regularity and the P–QRS relationship (is there a P before every QRS, a QRS after every P?).
Explanation

The paper moves at a fixed speed, so the distance between consecutive R waves is the cycle length: the further apart, the slower the rate. Rhythm asks where the beats come from and whether they are orderly: regular spacing with an identical P before every QRS is sinus rhythm; irregular spacing with no P waves suggests atrial fibrillation; P waves that are not followed by QRS complexes suggest AV block.

  • R-wave height reflects the mass of muscle and the lead position, not the rate.
  • The swapped pairing gives regularity to rate and spacing to rhythm, the reverse of how they are read.
Slides (2)
L58Learning
How long is one large EKG box at standard paper speed (25 mm/s)?
  1. A. 0.04 s
  2. B. 0.20 s
  3. C. 1.0 s
AnswerB. 0.20 s
WhyOne large box (5 mm) is 0.20 s; it contains five small boxes of 0.04 s each, and five large boxes make 1 second.
Explanation

At 25 mm per second, 1 mm (one small box) = 0.04 s and 5 mm (one large box) = 0.20 s. So 300 large boxes pass in one minute (60 s ÷ 0.2 s), which is where the "300 ÷ number of large boxes" rule for heart rate comes from.

  • 0.04 s is one small box.
  • 1.0 s is five large boxes.
Slides (2)
L59LearningHigh yield
How is heart rate calculated from the R-to-R interval?
  1. A. Rate (per min) = 60 × R-to-R interval (s)
  2. B. Rate (per min) = 300 ÷ R-to-R interval (s)
  3. C. Rate (per min) = 60 ÷ R-to-R interval (s)
AnswerC. Rate (per min) = 60 ÷ R-to-R interval (s)
WhyThe R-to-R interval is the cycle length; beats per minute = 60 s ÷ cycle length in seconds (rate = 1 ÷ cycle length).
Explanation

If one beat takes 0.8 s, there are 60 ÷ 0.8 = 75 beats in a minute. A shorter cycle means a faster rate: R-to-R 0.4 s → 150 per minute; R-to-R 1.0 s → 60 per minute.

  • 60 × interval would make a longer cycle give a faster rate, which is backwards.
  • 300 ÷ is the shortcut for the number of large boxes between R waves, not for an interval in seconds.
Slides (1)
L60LearningHigh yield
Which heart rates go with R waves 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 large boxes apart?
  1. A. 300, 200, 150, 100, 75, 60 (then 50, 43)
  2. B. 300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50 (then 43, 37)
  3. C. 300, 150, 75, 60, 50, 43 (then 37, 33)
AnswerB. 300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50 (then 43, 37)
WhyThe 300-150-100-75-60-50 sequence (then 43, 37) is just 300 ÷ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (7, 8) large boxes.
Explanation

Find an R wave on a heavy line, then count the heavy lines to the next R wave, reciting 300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50, 43, 37. If it falls between two lines, the rate lies between those values (for example between the 75 and 60 lines → about 65).

  • 300, 200, 150… is not 300 ÷ n: two boxes give 150, not 200.
  • 300, 150, 75… skips the 100 for three boxes.
Slides (2)

Rhythm strips

L61Learning
Which set of features defines normal sinus rhythm?
  1. A. Rate 60–100; each impulse starts in the SA node; normal order SA node → AV node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres
  2. B. Rate 60–100; each impulse starts in the AV node; normal order AV node → SA node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres
  3. C. Rate 40–60; each impulse starts in the SA node; normal order SA node → bundle of His → AV node → Purkinje fibres
AnswerA. Rate 60–100; each impulse starts in the SA node; normal order SA node → AV node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres
WhyNormal sinus rhythm: a rate of 60–100, every beat from the SA node, and the normal conduction sequence (one P before every QRS, normal PR and QRS).
Explanation

On the strip this means regular R waves 3–5 large boxes apart, an identical upright P wave before every QRS, a PR interval of 0.12–0.20 s and a QRS under 0.12 s. Below 60 with everything else normal is sinus bradycardia; above 100 is sinus tachycardia.

  • Starting in the AV node is a junctional rhythm, not sinus; and the AV node never comes before the SA node in the normal order.
  • Rate 40–60 is the AV node's intrinsic rate (sinus bradycardia if from the SA node), and His before AV node is the wrong order.
Slides (2)
L62LearningHigh yield
A patient with long-standing hypertension develops a cardiomyopathy, and an EKG shows atrial fibrillation. Where is the defect?
  1. A. Internodal pathways: the SA node and atrial pathways no longer conduct in an orderly way
  2. B. AV node: impulses are blocked between the atria and the ventricles
  3. C. Purkinje fibres: the ventricular network no longer conducts in an orderly way
AnswerA. Internodal pathways: the SA node and atrial pathways no longer conduct in an orderly way
WhyIn atrial fibrillation the SA node and internodal pathways stop working in an orderly way: the atria fire chaotically, "a seizure of the heart".
Explanation

Long-standing hypertension stiffens and enlarges the atria (here with a cardiomyopathy), disrupting orderly atrial conduction. Instead of one wave from the SA node, many wavelets circulate through the atria at 350–650 per minute. The ventricles are still activated through the normal AV node and His–Purkinje system, so the QRS stays narrow.

  • AV node is not the defect; it is where treatment acts, filtering the chaotic atrial impulses to control the ventricular rate.
  • Purkinje fibres disorganised would mean ventricular fibrillation, with no QRS complexes at all.
Slides (2)
L63Learning
What are the EKG features of atrial fibrillation?
  1. A. Regular sawtooth waves, no PR interval, narrow QRS complexes at regular or variable intervals
  2. B. No P waves, no PR interval, wide QRS complexes at regular intervals
  3. C. No P waves (fibrillatory baseline), no PR interval, narrow QRS complexes at irregular intervals
AnswerC. No P waves (fibrillatory baseline), no PR interval, narrow QRS complexes at irregular intervals
WhyAtrial fibrillation: no P waves, a wavy fibrillatory baseline, no PR interval and narrow QRS complexes that are irregularly irregular.
Explanation

Chaotic atrial activity bombards the AV node at random, so the impulses that get through arrive at random intervals: the R-to-R spacing follows no pattern. Because conduction below the AV node is normal, the QRS stays narrow (under 0.12 s). The ventricular rate may be slow or rapid.

  • Regular sawtooth waves are atrial flutter.
  • Wide QRS at regular intervals with no P waves is ventricular tachycardia.

Hook: an irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm with no P waves is atrial fibrillation until proved otherwise.

Slides (3)
L64Learning
In atrial fibrillation, what determines the ventricular rate?
  1. A. The SA node, which keeps firing normally beneath the fibrillation
  2. B. How many of the chaotic atrial impulses the AV node lets through
  3. C. The Purkinje fibres, which take over as an escape pacemaker
AnswerB. How many of the chaotic atrial impulses the AV node lets through
WhyThe ventricles beat only when an atrial impulse gets through the AV node; the node's conduction and refractoriness set the ventricular rate.
Explanation
