Hundreds of atrial impulses reach the AV node each minute; many find it refractory and are blocked. Whatever gets through is conducted normally to the ventricles. A fast-conducting node gives rapid atrial fibrillation (over 100); drugs that slow the AV node (beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, digoxin) lower the rate.

  • The SA node is overwhelmed by the chaotic atrial activity; its impulses no longer organise the atria or ventricles.
  • Purkinje escape occurs only when no atrial impulse reaches the ventricles (complete block); in atrial fibrillation they get through all the time.
Slides (1)
L65Learning
What is the fastest way to convert atrial fibrillation back to sinus rhythm?
  1. A. Intravenous beta-blocker
  2. B. Intravenous digoxin
  3. C. Electrical cardioversion
AnswerC. Electrical cardioversion
WhyElectrical cardioversion depolarises the whole heart at once, stopping the chaotic atrial wavelets so the SA node can take over again.
Explanation

A shock makes every excitable cell refractory at the same moment, so the circulating wavelets have no recovered tissue to re-enter and die out. The SA node, with the steepest phase 4, then fires first and normal sinus rhythm returns: a fibrillatory strip turns into normal P–QRS–T beats immediately after the (synchronised) shock.

  • Beta-blockers and digoxin, even intravenously, slow the AV node; they control the ventricular rate but do not stop the fibrillation itself.

Long-standing atrial fibrillation also needs anticoagulation (for example warfarin), because blood stagnating in the quivering atria can clot and cause a stroke; warfarin does not change the rhythm.

Slides (2)
L66Learning
Why can a patient live for years with atrial fibrillation?
  1. A. The AV node converts the chaotic atrial impulses into a perfectly regular ventricular rhythm
  2. B. The ventricles also fibrillate, but slowly enough to keep pumping
  3. C. Atrial contraction adds only a small share (roughly 10–20%) of ventricular filling; most filling is passive
AnswerC. Atrial contraction adds only a small share (roughly 10–20%) of ventricular filling; most filling is passive
WhyMost ventricular filling is passive; losing the atrial kick costs only about 10–20% of filling, so cardiac output is largely preserved.
Explanation

The ventricles still contract normally, because the impulses that pass the AV node travel the normal His–Purkinje route. What is lost is the atrial "top-up" at the end of diastole. That matters more at fast rates and in stiff ventricles, but at rest most patients cope. The main long-term danger is blood stasis in the atria → clot → embolic stroke.

  • A perfectly regular ventricular rhythm is wrong: the hallmark of atrial fibrillation is an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm.
  • Ventricles fibrillating is ventricular fibrillation, which produces no cardiac output and kills within minutes.
Slides (1)
L67Learning
In atrial flutter, what are the ventricular rate and QRS like?
  1. A. Equal to the atrial rate, always regular; narrow QRS
  2. B. Under 60 per minute, always irregular; wide QRS
  3. C. Under 300 per minute, regular or variable; narrow QRS
AnswerC. Under 300 per minute, regular or variable; narrow QRS
WhyThe AV node passes only some flutter waves (for example every second, 2:1), so the ventricles run below 300, regular or variable, with a narrow QRS.
Explanation

The AV node cannot conduct 300 impulses per minute; its refractory period blocks some of them in a fixed or changing ratio (2:1 → about 150, 4:1 → about 75). Below the node conduction is normal, so the QRS is under 0.12 s.

  • Equal to the atrial rate would mean 1:1 conduction at 220–430, which the AV node normally prevents.
  • Under 60, irregular, wide fits a slow ventricular escape rhythm, not flutter.
Slides (2)
L68Learning
What are the EKG features of ventricular tachycardia?
  1. A. Fast, regular, wide complexes with no visible P waves
  2. B. Fast, irregular, narrow complexes with no visible P waves
  3. C. Slow, regular, wide complexes with more P waves than QRS complexes
AnswerA. Fast, regular, wide complexes with no visible P waves
WhyVentricular tachycardia: a fast, regular run of wide, bizarre QRS complexes with no visible P waves, because the beats start in the ventricle.
Explanation

An irritable ventricular (Purkinje) focus fires rapidly, often over 150 per minute, sometimes so wide and fast that the trace looks like a sine wave. The atria may still be beating, but their P waves are lost in the large ventricular complexes. Ventricular tachycardia can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation.

  • Fast, irregular, narrow complexes without P waves describes rapid atrial fibrillation.
  • Slow, regular, wide complexes with extra P waves describes complete heart block with a ventricular escape rhythm.
Slides (2)
L69Learning
What are the EKG features of ventricular fibrillation?
  1. A. No countable rate: chaotic, irregular waves with no recognisable QRS complexes
  2. B. No countable rate: a flat line with no electrical activity at all
  3. C. A fast, regular rate: sawtooth waves with narrow QRS complexes between them
AnswerA. No countable rate: chaotic, irregular waves with no recognisable QRS complexes
WhyVentricular fibrillation is chaotic ventricular electrical activity: irregular waves, no QRS complexes, no pumping; it is fatal within minutes unless defibrillated.
Explanation

Many re-entrant wavelets circulate through the ventricles, so different regions depolarise at random. The ventricles quiver instead of contracting, cardiac output falls to zero and the pulse disappears. Ventricular tachycardia can break down into it, as the arrow on the strip shows. Only an electrical shock that depolarises the whole heart at once can stop it.

  • A flat line is asystole, absence of all electrical activity.
  • Sawtooth waves with narrow QRS is atrial flutter, an atrial rhythm with normal ventricular conduction.
Slides (2)

Where conduction breaks: blocks, re-entry, ischaemia and potassium

L70Learning
If the AV delay is longer than normal but every atrial impulse still reaches the ventricles, what does the EKG show?
  1. A. A prolonged QT interval with a QRS after every P wave
  2. B. A prolonged PR interval with a QRS after every P wave
  3. C. A widened QRS complex with no P waves
AnswerB. A prolonged PR interval with a QRS after every P wave
WhySlow but successful AV conduction shows as a PR interval over 0.20 s, with every P still followed by a QRS: a first-degree heart block.
Explanation

Each impulse spends longer crossing the AV node, so the gap between the P wave and the QRS stretches, but none is lost. This is called first-degree heart block. Causes include high vagal tone, AV-nodal drugs (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin) and nodal disease. It usually causes no symptoms.

  • Prolonged QT reflects slowed ventricular repolarisation, not AV conduction.
  • Wide QRS with no P waves describes a ventricular rhythm, such as ventricular tachycardia or a ventricular escape rhythm.
Slides (2)
L71Learning
If some atrial impulses fail to pass the AV node, what does the EKG show?
  1. A. Sawtooth waves between narrow QRS complexes
  2. B. Wide QRS complexes with no P waves
  3. C. Some P waves that are not followed by a QRS complex
AnswerC. Some P waves that are not followed by a QRS complex
WhyA blocked P wave, a P wave with no QRS after it, means that atrial impulse never reached the ventricles: a second-degree heart block.
Explanation

The atria are depolarised normally (P wave), but the AV node fails to conduct that impulse, so the ventricles skip a beat. If every second impulse is blocked, two P waves precede each QRS (2:1 block). The ventricular rate falls, while the atrial rate stays normal.

  • Sawtooth waves between narrow QRS complexes are atrial flutter: here the AV node is protecting the ventricles by blocking some flutter waves, but the atrial waves are not normal P waves.
  • Wide QRS complexes with no P waves are a ventricular rhythm.
Slides (2)
L72Learning
If no atrial impulses at all get through the AV node or bundle of His, what happens?
  1. A. Atria and ventricles beat independently; a slow latent pacemaker drives the ventricles
  2. B. The ventricles stop completely, because no other cell can pace them
  3. C. The atria slow to match the ventricles, and both beat together at 40–60 per minute
AnswerA. Atria and ventricles beat independently; a slow latent pacemaker drives the ventricles
WhyComplete (third-degree) heart block: the atria follow the SA node and the ventricles follow a latent pacemaker below the block, each at its own rate (AV dissociation).
Explanation

With the connection cut, the P waves march on regularly at the sinus rate while separate, slower QRS complexes appear at their own regular rate, with no fixed relation between the two. The ventricles survive because the cells below the block have their own automaticity. The slow ventricular rate can cause dizziness and fainting; the treatment is an artificial pacemaker.

  • Ventricles stop completely ignores the latent pacemakers; asystole occurs only if they too fail.
  • Atria slowing to match is wrong: the SA node knows nothing of the block and keeps its own rate.
Slides (2)
L73Learning
An 80-year-old with AV conduction disease receives a pacemaker. Paced at 60 per minute: stroke volume 80 mL, cardiac output 4.8 L/min, total peripheral resistance (TPR) 20 mmHg·min/L. Paced at 100 per minute: stroke volume 48 mL, cardiac output 4.8 L/min, TPR 20. What is his mean arterial pressure (MAP) at each rate?
  1. A. 96 mmHg at both rates
  2. B. 96 mmHg at 60 per minute; higher at 100 per minute, because heart rate rose
  3. C. 96 mmHg at 60 per minute; lower at 100 per minute, because stroke volume fell
AnswerA. 96 mmHg at both rates
WhyMAP = cardiac output × TPR = 4.8 × 20 = 96 mmHg; neither cardiac output nor TPR changed, so MAP is the same at both rates.
Explanation

Mean arterial pressure depends only on how much blood enters the arteries per minute (cardiac output) and how hard it is to drain them (TPR). Raising the pacing rate from 60 to 100 per minute shortened filling time, so stroke volume fell from 80 to 48 mL; cardiac output (heart rate × stroke volume) stayed at 4.8 L/min. With TPR also unchanged, MAP is unchanged.

  • Higher at 100 per minute forgets that stroke volume fell in proportion: heart rate alone does not set pressure.
  • Lower at 100 per minute forgets that heart rate rose: it is the product, cardiac output, that counts.
Slides (1)
L74Learning
In the same paced patient, the rate is switched from 60 to 100 per minute with MAP unchanged. How do systolic, diastolic and pulse pressure change?
  1. A. Systolic ↑, diastolic ↓, pulse pressure ↑
  2. B. Systolic ↓, diastolic ↓, pulse pressure unchanged
  3. C. Systolic ↓, diastolic ↑, pulse pressure ↓
AnswerC. Systolic ↓, diastolic ↑, pulse pressure ↓
WhyA smaller stroke volume gives a smaller systolic rise (systolic ↓); shorter diastole leaves less time for runoff (diastolic ↑); so pulse pressure falls.
Explanation

Each beat now ejects 48 instead of 80 mL into the aorta, so arterial pressure rises less during systole. Between beats the arteries drain into the periphery; at 100 per minute the next beat arrives sooner, so pressure has less time to fall and diastolic pressure ends slightly higher. Systolic down and diastolic up, with the mean unchanged, means a narrower pulse pressure (systolic − diastolic).

  • Systolic ↑, diastolic ↓ is the pattern of a larger stroke volume and longer diastole, the opposite change.
  • Both ↓ would lower MAP, which the unchanged cardiac output and TPR rule out.
Slides (1)
L75Learning
What is re-entry?
  1. A. The wave returns to tissue it has already passed, finds it recovered and re-excites it, circling in a loop
  2. B. A wave of excitation meets tissue that stays refractory, is blocked and dies out, so a beat is dropped
  3. C. A latent pacemaker starts firing faster than the SA node and takes over the rhythm
AnswerA. The wave returns to tissue it has already passed, finds it recovered and re-excites it, circling in a loop
WhyIn re-entry an impulse travels around a loop and returns to tissue that is no longer refractory, re-exciting it again and again: the basis of the fast arrhythmias.
Explanation

Normally each wave dies out because every cell behind it is refractory. Re-entry needs a loop of tissue, a region of one-way block and slow enough conduction that, by the time the wave comes back round, the starting tissue has recovered. The wave then circles indefinitely, firing the heart at a fast rate: one large loop gives atrial flutter; many small wandering wavelets give fibrillation.

  • Meeting refractory tissue and dying out is how re-entry is normally prevented.
  • A latent pacemaker firing faster is an ectopic pacemaker (abnormal automaticity), a different mechanism.
Slides (1)
L76Learning
What property defends the heart against re-entry, and what does that mean for anti-arrhythmic drugs?
  1. A. A short refractory period; drugs that shorten refractoriness are anti-arrhythmic
  2. B. A high resting vagal tone; drugs that block muscarinic receptors are anti-arrhythmic
  3. C. A long refractory period; drugs that lengthen refractoriness are anti-arrhythmic
AnswerC. A long refractory period; drugs that lengthen refractoriness are anti-arrhythmic
WhyA long refractory period means a returning wave finds tissue still refractory and dies out; drugs that lengthen refractoriness therefore oppose re-entry.
Explanation

For re-entry to persist, the tissue ahead of the circulating wave must have recovered by the time the wave arrives. Lengthening the effective refractory period (for example by prolonging the plateau or slowing sodium-channel recovery) closes that gap, so the wave runs into refractory tissue and stops. This is why the long cardiac plateau is protective.

  • Shortening refractoriness does the opposite: a short atrial refractory period favours atrial fibrillation.
  • Blocking muscarinic receptors (atropine) only removes vagal slowing of the nodes; it is used for bradycardia, not to prevent re-entry.
Slides (1)
L77Learning
AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT) is caused by what?
  1. A. A re-entry circuit within the AV node region, giving a fast regular rhythm with narrow QRS complexes
  2. B. Many chaotic atrial foci, giving an irregularly irregular rhythm with no P waves
  3. C. A focus in the ventricles, giving a fast rhythm with wide QRS complexes
AnswerA. A re-entry circuit within the AV node region, giving a fast regular rhythm with narrow QRS complexes
WhyAVNRT is re-entry in and around the AV node: the impulse circles there and re-excites the ventricles through the normal pathway, so the tachycardia is regular with narrow QRS complexes.
Explanation

AVNRT is the textbook example of re-entry close to home: the AV node region has two pathways with different speeds and refractory periods, so an early impulse can travel down one and back up the other, circling repeatedly. Each lap sends an impulse down the His–Purkinje system, so the ventricles are activated normally (narrow QRS) at a fast, regular rate; it is a supraventricular tachycardia, sorted with the atrial rhythms on the lecture slide.

  • Many chaotic atrial foci with an irregularly irregular rhythm and no P waves is atrial fibrillation.
  • A ventricular focus with wide QRS complexes is ventricular tachycardia: the impulse spreads cell to cell outside the fast Purkinje system, so the QRS is wide.
Slides (1)
L78LearningHigh yield
A man with crushing chest pain radiating down his left arm is sweating and breathless. Which EKG finding indicates an acute myocardial infarction?
  1. A. ST-segment elevation
  2. B. QT-interval prolongation
  3. C. PR-interval shortening
AnswerA. ST-segment elevation
WhyAcute transmural injury shifts the normally flat ST segment upward (ST elevation, a STEMI), while the ventricle is on its plateau.
Explanation

Normally the whole ventricle sits at the same plateau voltage during the ST segment, so the line is flat. Injured, ischaemic muscle cannot hold a normal resting potential or plateau, so current flows between injured and healthy regions (the current of injury) and displaces the ST segment. Elevation signals acute full-thickness infarction; depression signals ischaemia (for example during a stress test).

  • QT prolongation reflects slowed repolarisation (for example hypokalaemia or drugs), not acute infarction.
  • A short PR interval means fast AV conduction or pre-excitation, unrelated to infarction.
Slides (2)
L79Learning
As plasma potassium rises to about 7 mmol/L, what is the first EKG change?
  1. A. Tall, peaked (tent-shaped) T waves
  2. B. Flattened T waves with prominent U waves
  3. C. ST-segment elevation with deep Q waves
AnswerA. Tall, peaked (tent-shaped) T waves
WhyEarly hyperkalaemia gives tall, peaked (tented) T waves: the rapid delayed-rectifier potassium channel (IKr) works better, so repolarisation starts sooner and is steeper.
Explanation

Paradoxically, high extracellular potassium increases the conductance of IKr, so phase 3 is faster and the T wave becomes tall, narrow and tent-shaped. As potassium climbs further: about 8 mmol/L → long PR interval and depressed ST segment; about 9 → loss of P waves and a wide QRS merging into the T wave; about 10 → ventricular fibrillation.

  • Flat T waves with U waves are the signs of hypokalaemia, the opposite problem.
  • ST elevation with Q waves indicates myocardial infarction, not an electrolyte disturbance.
Slides (2)
L80Learning
Why does hyperkalaemia widen the QRS complex?
  1. A. Resting potential more negative → cells further from threshold → each cell takes longer to fire
  2. B. Resting potential less negative → more sodium channels inactivated → slower upstroke and slower spread through the ventricle
  3. C. Potassium blocks the L-type calcium channels → the plateau lengthens → depolarisation lasts longer
AnswerB. Resting potential less negative → more sodium channels inactivated → slower upstroke and slower spread through the ventricle
WhyHigh extracellular K+ makes the resting potential less negative, which inactivates sodium channels; fewer channels give a slower upstroke and slower conduction, so the QRS widens.
Explanation

Raising extracellular potassium lowers the potassium gradient, so the resting potential moves closer to threshold: the cells are more excitable. But a partly depolarised membrane keeps many fast sodium channels inactivated, so phase 0 rises more slowly and less high, and the impulse spreads more slowly through the ventricle. The paradox: more excitable, yet slower conduction (long PR, wide QRS).

  • More negative resting potential is what hypokalaemia does, not hyperkalaemia.
  • Calcium-channel block and a longer plateau would lengthen the ST segment and QT, not the QRS; in hyperkalaemia repolarisation is actually faster.
Slides (3)
L81Learning
Which EKG pattern goes with hypokalaemia?
  1. A. Flat T waves, prominent U waves and a long QT interval
  2. B. Tall peaked T waves, a wide QRS and a long PR interval
  3. C. ST-segment elevation with an otherwise normal tracing
AnswerA. Flat T waves, prominent U waves and a long QT interval
WhyLow potassium impairs repolarisation: the T wave flattens, the QT interval lengthens and a prominent U wave appears.
Explanation

With less extracellular potassium, the repolarising potassium currents (such as IKr) work less well, so phase 3 is delayed. As potassium falls toward 3 mmol/L the T wave flattens, a U wave appears and the QT lengthens; by about 2.5 mmol/L the ST segment is depressed as well. Delayed repolarisation favours ventricular arrhythmias, and hypokalaemia also increases digoxin toxicity.

  • Tall peaked T, wide QRS, long PR is the pattern of hyperkalaemia.
  • ST elevation is the sign of acute myocardial infarction.
Slides (3)

PHYS-L22 Cardiac muscle contraction

45 learning questions · of 96
Learning questions 45

Cardiac muscle cells

L1Learning
How are cardiac muscle cells shaped and joined?
  1. A. Long and unbranched, joined side by side by tight junctions
  2. B. Long and multinucleate, joined end to end by tendons
  3. C. Short and branched, joined end to end by intercalated discs
AnswerC. Short and branched, joined end to end by intercalated discs
WhyCardiac myocytes are short, branched cells with one or two central nuclei, joined end to end at intercalated discs.
Explanation

An intercalated disc is the stepped junction where two cardiac cells meet end to end. It carries three junctions: the fascia adherens (anchors the actin of the last sarcomere), desmosomes (hold the cells together) and gap junctions (let current pass). Because the cells branch and are electrically coupled, the whole network contracts as a functional syncytium.

  • Long, unbranched, joined by tight junctions: tight junctions seal epithelia; they are not part of the disc.
  • Long, multinucleate, joined by tendons describes skeletal muscle fibres, each fired by its own nerve ending.
Slides (3)
L2LearningHigh yield
Which current holds up the plateau (phase 2) of the ventricular action potential, and why does it matter for contraction?
  1. A. Inward T-type Ca2+ current (ICa-T), which supplies the trigger calcium
  2. B. Inward L-type Ca2+ current (ICa-L), which supplies the trigger calcium
  3. C. Outward K+ current (IK1), which refills the calcium store
AnswerB. Inward L-type Ca2+ current (ICa-L), which supplies the trigger calcium
WhyPhase 2 balances inward L-type Ca2+ current against outward IKs; the Ca2+ that enters is the trigger for calcium-induced calcium release.
Explanation

The ventricular action potential rests at about −96 mV, peaks near +52 mV and lasts about 200 ms:

  • phase 0: fast Na+ in (INa); phase 1: transient K+/Cl− out (Ito);
  • phase 2: Ca2+ in (ICa-L, “L” for long-lasting) balanced by K+ out (IKs);
  • phase 3: K+ out (IKs, IKr, IK1); phase 4: IK1.

The plateau calcium both prolongs the action potential and triggers SR release. T-type channels open briefly at more negative voltages and matter in pacemaker cells, not the ventricular plateau. IK1 carries K+ out and sets the resting potential; it moves no calcium.

Slides (3)

Excitation-contraction coupling and relaxation

L3LearningHigh yield
What is the sequence of cardiac excitation-contraction coupling?
  1. A. Action potential → Ca2+ enters during the plateau → calcium-induced calcium release from the SR → Ca2+ binds tropomyosin → cross-bridge cycling → tension
  2. B. Action potential → Ca2+ enters during the plateau → calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) → Ca2+ binds troponin C → cross-bridge cycling → tension
  3. C. Action potential → Na+ enters during the plateau → sodium-induced calcium release from the SR → Ca2+ binds troponin C → cross-bridge cycling → tension
AnswerB. Action potential → Ca2+ enters during the plateau → calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) → Ca2+ binds troponin C → cross-bridge cycling → tension
WhyAction potential → plateau Ca2+ entry → calcium-induced calcium release from the SR → Ca2+ binds troponin C → cross-bridges cycle → tension.
Explanation

Excitation-contraction coupling is the chain that turns an electrical event into force. The action potential spreads down the T tubules; during the plateau a small amount of Ca2+ enters through L-type channels; that trigger opens ryanodine receptors and the SR floods the cytoplasm with Ca2+; Ca2+ binds troponin C, tropomyosin moves off the myosin-binding sites on actin, and cross-bridges cycle. Relaxation follows when SERCA and the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger clear the Ca2+.

  • Ca2+ binds tropomyosin: tropomyosin binds no calcium; it is the strand that gets moved.
  • Sodium-induced calcium release does not exist here; the plateau current and the trigger are calcium.
Slides (3)
L4LearningHigh yield
The L-type Ca2+ channel in the T-tubule membrane is also called what?
  1. A. The dihydropyridine receptor
  2. B. The ryanodine receptor
  3. C. The IP3 receptor
AnswerA. The dihydropyridine receptor
WhyThe L-type Ca2+ channel is the dihydropyridine receptor, named for the drug class that binds and blocks it; the SR release channel is the ryanodine receptor.
Explanation

The pair to remember: dihydropyridine receptor on the T tubule (lets trigger Ca2+ in from the extracellular fluid) → ryanodine receptor on the SR (releases the stored Ca2+). Each is named after a compound that binds it: dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine, and the plant alkaloid ryanodine.

  • The ryanodine receptor is the SR release channel, opened by the trigger calcium, not the sarcolemmal channel.
  • The IP3 receptor releases Ca2+ from internal stores in Gq signalling (for example smooth muscle); it is not the cardiac trigger channel.
Slides (1)
L5LearningHigh yield
Is the Ca2+ that enters during the plateau enough on its own to contract the cell?
  1. A. Yes: it binds troponin directly and drives the whole contraction
  2. B. Yes: the SR store is used only by skeletal muscle
  3. C. No: its job is to trigger release of a much larger store from the SR
AnswerC. No: its job is to trigger release of a much larger store from the SR
WhyThe plateau Ca2+ is only a trigger; most of the Ca2+ that reaches troponin comes from the SR through ryanodine receptors.
Explanation

Calcium amplifies calcium: a small influx through L-type channels opens the ryanodine receptors, and the SR releases many times that amount. This is why the extra Ca2+ that “initiates contraction” comes from the SR, not from the extracellular fluid.

  • Binds troponin directly and drives the whole contraction: the influx alone is far too small to saturate troponin C.
  • SR store used only by skeletal muscle: both muscles release SR calcium; they differ in how release is triggered (mechanical coupling in skeletal muscle, a Ca2+ trigger in cardiac muscle).
Slides (2)
L6LearningHigh yield
What does the force of a cardiac beat track?
  1. A. How much Ca2+ reaches troponin C
  2. B. How much Na+ enters during the upstroke
  3. C. How much ATP the cell holds
AnswerA. How much Ca2+ reaches troponin C
WhyTension is proportional to the intracellular Ca2+ available to bind troponin C; every inotropic change works by changing it.
Explanation

Unlike skeletal muscle, which grades force by recruiting fibres and summing twitches, every cardiac cell contracts on every beat, so force can only be graded inside each cell, by how much Ca2+ reaches troponin C. More Ca2+ (sympathetic stimulation, digoxin, a faster rate) = positive inotropy; less = negative inotropy.

  • Na+ entry during the upstroke fires the action potential but is the same on every beat; it does not set force.
  • ATP is needed for cross-bridge cycling and Ca2+ pumping, but at normal levels it is not what grades tension.
Slides (2)
L7Learning
Which two sources together set how much Ca2+ reaches troponin C on a beat?
  1. A. Inward Ca2+ current during the plateau + Ca2+ stored in the mitochondria
  2. B. Inward Ca2+ current during the plateau + Ca2+ already stored in the SR
  3. C. Inward Na+ current during the upstroke + Ca2+ already stored in the SR
AnswerB. Inward Ca2+ current during the plateau + Ca2+ already stored in the SR
WhyTension depends on the plateau Ca2+ current (the trigger) and the Ca2+ previously stored in the SR (what the trigger releases).
Explanation

This pair explains every way contractility can be raised. More trigger: sympathetic phosphorylation of L-type channels. A fuller SR store: phosphorylated phospholamban speeding SERCA, a faster heart rate (staircase), the extra Ca2+ of an extrasystole, or digoxin leaving more Ca2+ in the cell.

  • Mitochondria can buffer Ca2+, but they are not the beat-to-beat source for contraction.
  • The Na+ current of the upstroke carries no calcium; it only depolarises the membrane.
Slides (2)
L8Learning
Which drugs act on the L-type Ca2+ channels of the trigger step, and how?
  1. A. Calcium channel blockers open them further
    β agonists block them
  2. B. Calcium channel blockers block them
    β agonists open them further
  3. C. Calcium channel blockers block them
    β blockers open them further
AnswerB. Calcium channel blockers block them
β agonists open them further
WhyCalcium channel blockers cut the trigger Ca2+ (weaker contraction); β agonists, through protein kinase A, let more Ca2+ in (stronger contraction).
Explanation

The L-type channel is the gate for trigger calcium, so drugs acting on it change contractility directly. Blocking it means less trigger, less SR release and a weaker beat; in vascular smooth muscle the same block relaxes arterioles, which is why these drugs lower blood pressure. β1 stimulation raises cAMP, and protein kinase A phosphorylates the channel so more Ca2+ enters.

  • The swapped pair reverses both effects.
  • β blockers do not open the channels; by removing β1-driven phosphorylation they reduce Ca2+ entry and lower contractility.
Slides (2)
L9LearningHigh yield
What clears Ca2+ from the cytoplasm after a beat?
  1. A. Ryanodine receptor: pumps it into the SR
    Na+/Ca2+ exchanger: moves it out of the cell
  2. B. SERCA (SR Ca2+-ATPase): pumps it into the SR
    Na+/Ca2+ exchanger: moves it out of the cell
  3. C. SERCA (SR Ca2+-ATPase): moves it out of the cell
    Na+/Ca2+ exchanger: pumps it into the SR
AnswerB. SERCA (SR Ca2+-ATPase): pumps it into the SR
Na+/Ca2+ exchanger: moves it out of the cell
WhySERCA pumps most Ca2+ back into the SR (stored for the next beat); the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger expels the rest across the cell membrane.
Explanation

SERCA is an ATP-driven pump in the SR membrane, controlled by phospholamban. The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger in the sarcolemma uses the inward Na+ gradient to push Ca2+ out (secondary active transport); the Na+/K+-ATPase keeps that gradient steep. Over a steady state, the exchanger removes exactly as much Ca2+ as entered as trigger.

  • The ryanodine receptor is a release channel, not a pump; Ca2+ only flows out of the SR through it.
  • The swapped locations put each transporter in the wrong membrane.

This is the link digoxin exploits: blunt the Na+ gradient and the exchanger removes less Ca2+.

Slides (3)
L10Learning
Is cardiac relaxation passive or active?
  1. A. Active: it uses ATP
  2. B. Passive: elastic recoil alone
  3. C. Passive: Ca2+ diffuses back into the SR by itself
AnswerA. Active: it uses ATP
WhyRelaxation is active: SERCA is an ATPase, the exchanger runs on a gradient the Na+/K+-ATPase builds, and myosin needs ATP to let go of actin.
Explanation

Ca2+ has to be moved against a steep gradient, into the SR and out of the cell, and that costs energy: directly through SERCA, indirectly through the Na+/K+-ATPase. Myosin heads also need a new ATP to detach. This is why ischaemia impairs relaxation (stiff ventricle, diastolic dysfunction) as well as contraction.

  • Elastic recoil alone cannot lower cytoplasmic Ca2+; without Ca2+ removal the muscle stays contracted.
  • Ca2+ diffusing back by itself: the SR holds far more Ca2+ than the cytoplasm, so diffusion would carry it the wrong way.
Slides (1)
L11Learning
How long is the cardiac muscle refractory period, and why does that matter?
  1. A. About 25 ms, much shorter than the contraction, so the cell can be re-excited while it is contracting
  2. B. About 250 ms, nearly as long as the contraction, so the cell cannot be re-excited until it is relaxing
  3. C. About 250 ms, but it ends at peak tension, so beats can summate into tetanus
AnswerB. About 250 ms, nearly as long as the contraction, so the cell cannot be re-excited until it is relaxing
WhyThe refractory period (about 250 ms) lasts almost as long as the twitch, so a new beat cannot start until the muscle is relaxing: the heart cannot be tetanised.
Explanation

On the time-course figure the action potential and the refractory period span 0 to about 250 ms, while tension rises, peaks and is mostly gone by then. Because the long plateau keeps the cell refractory through nearly all of contraction, beats cannot fuse into a sustained (tetanic) contraction, and the ventricle always gets a relaxation phase in which to fill.

  • About 25 ms is the order of a skeletal-muscle or nerve refractory period; that brevity is what lets skeletal muscle tetanise.
  • Ending at peak tension would allow summation; the cardiac refractory period runs on into relaxation.
Slides (3)

Autonomic control of contractility

L12LearningHigh yield
What is the sympathetic signalling chain that raises contractility?
  1. A. Norepinephrine/epinephrine → α1 → Gq → phospholipase C → IP3 → protein kinase C (PKC)
  2. B. Norepinephrine/epinephrine → β1 → Gi → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A (PKA)
  3. C. Norepinephrine/epinephrine → β1 → Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A (PKA)
AnswerC. Norepinephrine/epinephrine → β1 → Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A (PKA)
WhyCardiac sympathetic effects run through β1 → Gs → adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP → protein kinase A, which phosphorylates the Ca2+-handling proteins.
Explanation

β1 receptors on ventricular muscle are coupled to the stimulatory G protein Gs. Its α subunit activates adenylyl cyclase, cAMP rises and frees protein kinase A, which phosphorylates the L-type channel, the ryanodine receptor, phospholamban and troponin I. The result is a positive inotropic effect. Agonists such as dobutamine use this chain; β blockers such as metoprolol interrupt it.

  • α1 → Gq → IP3 is the vascular smooth-muscle pathway (vasoconstriction), not the cardiac inotropic one.
  • β1 → Gi mixes up the G protein: Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase and belongs to the M2 receptor.
Slides (3)
L13LearningHigh yield
Which four targets does protein kinase A phosphorylate in cardiac muscle?
  1. A. L-type Ca2+ channels
    Na+/Ca2+ exchanger
    Phospholamban
    Myosin heavy chain
  2. B. L-type Ca2+ channels
    Ryanodine receptors
    Phospholamban
    Tropomyosin
  3. C. L-type Ca2+ channels
    Ryanodine receptors
    Phospholamban
    Troponin I
AnswerC. L-type Ca2+ channels
Ryanodine receptors
Phospholamban
Troponin I
WhyProtein kinase A phosphorylates the L-type channel and ryanodine receptor (more Ca2+ in and out of the SR), phospholamban and troponin I (faster relaxation).
Explanation

Two targets make the beat stronger, two make it shorter:

  • L-type channel → more trigger Ca2+; ryanodine receptor → more SR release.
  • Phospholamban → SERCA released from its brake (faster reuptake, fuller store); troponin I → troponin lets go of Ca2+ sooner.

The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger and myosin heavy chain and tropomyosin are not on the lecture diagram's list; tropomyosin in particular is moved by troponin, not phosphorylated by PKA.

Slides (3)
L14LearningHigh yield
What does phosphorylating phospholamban achieve?
  1. A. Removes the brake on ryanodine receptors → more SR Ca2+ release (stronger beat) + slower relaxation
  2. B. Strengthens the brake on SERCA → slower SR Ca2+ reuptake (slower relaxation) + less stored (weaker next beat)
  3. C. Removes the brake on SERCA → faster SR Ca2+ reuptake (quicker relaxation) + more stored (stronger next beat)
AnswerC. Removes the brake on SERCA → faster SR Ca2+ reuptake (quicker relaxation) + more stored (stronger next beat)
WhyPhosphorylated phospholamban releases SERCA: Ca2+ is pumped back faster (quicker relaxation) and more is stored for the next beat.
Explanation

This one change does two jobs. Faster reuptake ends each contraction sooner, preserving filling time. A fuller SR store means more Ca2+ is released on the following beat, adding to the inotropic effect. It is the classic exam answer for “an effect of sympathetic stimulation”: phosphorylation of phospholamban and increased Ca2+ pumped into the SR.

  • Phospholamban acts on SERCA, not the ryanodine receptor, and sympathetic stimulation speeds relaxation rather than slowing it.
  • Strengthening the brake is what dephosphorylated phospholamban does; it is the opposite of the sympathetic effect.
Slides (2)
L15LearningHigh yield
What three changes in the contraction result from sympathetic stimulation?
  1. A. Faster rate of tension development
    Higher peak tension
    Faster rate of relaxation
  2. B. Faster rate of tension development
    Higher peak tension
    Slower rate of relaxation
  3. C. Slower rate of tension development
    Higher peak tension
    Faster rate of relaxation
AnswerA. Faster rate of tension development
Higher peak tension
Faster rate of relaxation
WhySympathetic stimulation raises the rate of tension development, the peak tension and the rate of relaxation: a stronger, briefer beat.
Explanation

The lecture's three “increases” map onto the protein kinase A targets: more trigger Ca2+ and more SR release → faster rise and higher peak; phosphorylated phospholamban and troponin I → faster relaxation.

  • Slower relaxation is a favourite false statement; the sympathetic system speeds Ca2+ reuptake.
  • Slower tension development contradicts the larger, quicker Ca2+ rise.

Parasympathetic stimulation of the atria does the reverse for the first two (slower rate, lower peak).

Slides (3)
L16LearningHigh yield
What is the parasympathetic signalling chain that lowers contractility?
  1. A. Acetylcholine → M2 → Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase → less cAMP
  2. B. Acetylcholine → M3 → Gq activates phospholipase C → more IP3
  3. C. Norepinephrine → α2 → Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase → less cAMP
AnswerA. Acetylcholine → M2 → Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase → less cAMP
WhyVagal acetylcholine acts on M2 receptors coupled to Gi, which inhibits adenylyl cyclase and lowers cAMP.
Explanation

M2 is the heart's muscarinic receptor. Gi opposes the sympathetic Gs chain: less cAMP, less protein kinase A, less phosphorylation of the Ca2+-handling proteins. Its βγ subunits also open IK-ACh channels.

  • M3 → Gq is the muscarinic receptor of glands and smooth muscle, not the heart.
  • Norepinephrine on α2 is a presynaptic sympathetic receptor; it is not the parasympathetic path to the myocardium.

Hook: Gs for stimulate, Gi for inhibit.

Slides (3)
L17LearningHigh yield
What is the parasympathetic effect on contractility, and where?
  1. A. Negative inotropy in the atria: slower tension development, lower peak tension
  2. B. Negative inotropy in the ventricles: slower tension development, lower peak tension
  3. C. Positive inotropy in the atria: faster tension development, higher peak tension
AnswerA. Negative inotropy in the atria: slower tension development, lower peak tension
WhyAcetylcholine causes negative inotropy in the atria: slower rate of tension development and lower peak tension. The ventricles are barely affected.
Explanation

The lecture table puts it plainly: parasympathetic = “negative inotropic effect in atria”, decreasing the rate and the peak of tension. The vagus also slows heart rate (SA node) and AV conduction, but its direct effect on ventricular force is minimal.

  • Ventricles: they get little vagal innervation, so a direct ventricular negative inotropic effect is the classic wrong answer.
  • Positive inotropy is the sympathetic effect.

Indirectly, more vagal tone usually means less sympathetic tone, which does weaken the ventricles.

Slides (3)
L18Learning
How does acetylcholine lower atrial contractility at the cell membrane?
  1. A. ↑ Inward Ca2+ current in the plateau + ↓ IK-ACh, which lengthens the action potential
  2. B. ↓ Inward Ca2+ current in the plateau + ↑ IK-ACh, which shortens the action potential
  3. C. ↓ Inward Na+ current in the upstroke + ↑ If, which shortens the action potential
AnswerB. ↓ Inward Ca2+ current in the plateau + ↑ IK-ACh, which shortens the action potential
WhyAcetylcholine cuts the plateau Ca2+ current and opens IK-ACh; the shorter action potential lets even less Ca2+ in, so less trigger and less SR release.
Explanation

Two routes, one result. Directly, less cAMP means less L-type Ca2+ current. Indirectly, the extra K+ conductance (IK-ACh) repolarises the atrial cell sooner, cutting the time the L-type channels stay open. Less Ca2+ enters, less is released, and peak tension falls.

  • The reversed pair (more Ca2+ current, less IK-ACh) would be positive inotropy.
  • Na+ current and If: the funny current is a pacemaker (SA node) current, and acetylcholine reduces it there, slowing heart rate.
Slides (2)

Heart rate and contractility

L19LearningHigh yield
Why does a faster heart beat more strongly?
  1. A. More beats/min → more Ca2+ enters per minute → SR stores more → more to release each beat
  2. B. More beats/min → less Ca2+ enters per minute → SR releases it faster each beat
  3. C. More beats/min → more Na+ enters per minute → stronger upstroke each beat
AnswerA. More beats/min → more Ca2+ enters per minute → SR stores more → more to release each beat
WhyMore action potentials per minute → more plateau Ca2+ entry → more Ca2+ stored in the SR → more released on each beat.
Explanation

Every plateau brings in some Ca2+. With more plateaus per minute, more Ca2+ accumulates in the cell and the SR, until a maximum storage level is reached. The action potentials are not longer, just more frequent.

  • Less Ca2+ per minute gets the arithmetic backwards.
  • Na+ and a stronger upstroke: the upstroke does not set force; Ca2+ does.
Slides (2)
L20Learning
Why is the beat after an extrasystole stronger?
  1. A. The extra beat brings in extra Ca2+ that the SR stores
  2. B. The extra beat empties the SR, so less Ca2+ is buffered
  3. C. The extra beat triggers a burst of sympathetic norepinephrine
AnswerA. The extra beat brings in extra Ca2+ that the SR stores
WhyThe extrasystole adds an extra plateau of Ca2+ entry; the SR stores it and releases more on the next beat.
Explanation

It is the staircase mechanism in miniature: one additional action potential = one additional dose of trigger Ca2+ loaded into the SR, available for the next normal beat.

  • Emptying the SR would make the next beat weaker, not stronger.
  • A sympathetic burst is not needed; the effect occurs in isolated muscle with no nerves at all.
Slides (2)
L21LearningHigh yield
An EKG shows ventricular extrasystoles. On the extrasystolic beat itself, what happens to pulse pressure, and why?
  1. A. It rises, because the early beat has increased contractility
  2. B. It rises, because the momentary heart rate is faster
  3. C. It falls, because the early beat has little filling time and a small stroke volume
AnswerC. It falls, because the early beat has little filling time and a small stroke volume
WhyThe extrasystole fires before the ventricle has filled: less end-diastolic volume → smaller stroke volume → smaller pulse pressure.
Explanation

Pulse pressure (systolic minus diastolic) tracks stroke volume. The premature beat “beats too soon”, so it ejects little and the arterial pressure rise is small. The next normal beat is the opposite: extra stored Ca2+ raises contractility (and the pause before it adds filling), so its pulse pressure is larger.

  • Increased contractility belongs to the post-extrasystolic beat, not the extrasystole.
  • A faster momentary rate does not raise the pulse pressure of a single poorly filled beat.
Slides (1)

Digoxin

L22LearningHigh yield
How does digoxin raise contractility?
  1. A. Pump blocked → intracellular Na+ high → Na+/Ca2+ exchanger stalls → intracellular Ca2+ high → stronger contraction
  2. B. Exchanger blocked → intracellular Na+ high → Na+/K+-ATPase stalls → intracellular Ca2+ high → stronger contraction
  3. C. Pump blocked → intracellular Na+ low → Na+/Ca2+ exchanger speeds up → intracellular Ca2+ high → stronger contraction
AnswerA. Pump blocked → intracellular Na+ high → Na+/Ca2+ exchanger stalls → intracellular Ca2+ high → stronger contraction
WhyNa+/K+-ATPase blocked → ↑intracellular Na+ → smaller Na+ gradient → exchanger removes less Ca2+ → ↑intracellular Ca2+ → ↑contractility.
Explanation

Four links, in order: (1) the pump is inhibited; (2) Na+ builds up inside; (3) the inward Na+ gradient that powers Ca2+ extrusion shrinks, so the exchanger removes less Ca2+; (4) more Ca2+ stays in the cell and is loaded into the SR, so more is released onto troponin C each beat. Any digoxin question is a question about one of these links.

  • The exchanger is not the primary target; it slows as a consequence of the pump block.
  • Intracellular Na+ low, exchanger faster would lower intracellular Ca2+; that is the direction of pump stimulation.
Slides (3)
L23LearningHigh yield
What are the uses of digoxin?
  1. A. Slowing the rate in rapid atrial arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation, flutter, supraventricular tachycardia)
    Heart failure still symptomatic after an ACE inhibitor, β blocker and spironolactone
  2. B. Speeding the rate in bradycardias (sinus bradycardia, heart block, sick sinus)
    Heart failure as first-line therapy before an ACE inhibitor or β blocker
  3. C. Slowing the rate in rapid atrial arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation, flutter, supraventricular tachycardia)
    Acute angina unresponsive to nitrates, β blocker and aspirin
AnswerA. Slowing the rate in rapid atrial arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation, flutter, supraventricular tachycardia)
Heart failure still symptomatic after an ACE inhibitor, β blocker and spironolactone
WhyDigoxin slows the ventricular rate in rapid atrial arrhythmias and adds contractility in heart failure still symptomatic after an ACE inhibitor, β blocker and spironolactone.
Explanation

Rate control: digoxin increases vagal effects at the AV node, slowing AV conduction and lengthening the AV nodal refractory period, so fewer atrial impulses reach the ventricles in atrial fibrillation, flutter or supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). Heart failure: it is an add-on (ACE = angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor), not first line; it improves symptoms and hospitalisations, not survival.

  • Speeding the rate in bradycardias: digoxin slows conduction and can cause heart block.
  • Acute angina: raising contractility raises O2 demand; digoxin is not an anti-anginal drug.
Slides (1)
L24LearningHigh yield
What are the toxic effects of digoxin?
  1. A. Arrhythmias
    Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea
    Seizures
    Visual disturbances
  2. B. Hypotension
    Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea
    Tinnitus
    Hypokalaemia
  3. C. Bradycardia only
    Constipation
    Hearing loss
    Hyperglycaemia
AnswerA. Arrhythmias
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea
Seizures
Visual disturbances
WhyDigoxin is “loaded with toxicity”: arrhythmias, nausea/vomiting/diarrhoea, seizures and visual disturbances.
Explanation

The therapeutic window is narrow. Ca2+ overload and a partly depolarised membrane make myocytes irritable, so almost any arrhythmia can occur (digoxin can both treat and cause arrhythmias). Gastrointestinal upset and blurred or yellow-tinted vision are the classic early warning signs.

  • Tinnitus belongs to salicylate or quinine toxicity, and digoxin toxicity raises plasma K+, it does not lower it.
  • Bradycardia only understates it, and constipation, hearing loss and hyperglycaemia are not its effects.
Slides (2)
L25LearningHigh yield
Why does low potassium make digoxin toxicity more likely?
  1. A. Digoxin binds the pump at its K+ site; less K+ competing → more digoxin binds
  2. B. Digoxin binds the pump at its K+ site; less K+ competing → less digoxin binds
  3. C. Digoxin binds the pump at its Na+ site; less K+ → more Na+ competing → more digoxin binds
AnswerA. Digoxin binds the pump at its K+ site; less K+ competing → more digoxin binds
WhyDigoxin and K+ compete for the same extracellular site on the Na+/K+-ATPase; with hypokalaemia more digoxin binds, so pump inhibition and toxicity increase.
Explanation

This is why patients on digoxin plus a K+-wasting diuretic need their potassium checked: low plasma K+ leaves more pump sites free for digoxin. The lecture states it as “low potassium LEADS to toxicity”.

  • Less digoxin binds gets the competition backwards: removing the competitor increases binding.
  • The Na+ site: digoxin binds the outward-facing K+ site, not the inner Na+ site.

Contrast the next question: low K+ causes toxicity, toxicity causes high K+.

Slides (2)
L26LearningHigh yield
Why does digoxin toxicity cause high plasma potassium?
  1. A. Exchanger blocked → K+ not swapped for Ca2+ → builds up in plasma
  2. B. Kidneys blocked → K+ not excreted in urine → builds up in plasma
  3. C. Pump blocked → K+ not pumped back into cells → builds up in plasma
AnswerC. Pump blocked → K+ not pumped back into cells → builds up in plasma
WhyThe Na+/K+-ATPase is what moves K+ into cells; block enough of it and K+ stays outside: hyperkalaemia.
Explanation

Every cell in the body uses the same pump, so a toxic dose of digoxin stops K+ being taken back up after it leaks out. Plasma K+ rises and intracellular K+ falls. The lecture: “toxicity LEADS to hyperkalemia”.

  • The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger moves Na+ and Ca2+; it carries no K+.
  • Kidney block is not the mechanism; the shift is a cellular redistribution.
Slides (2)

Preload, afterload and contractility

L27LearningHigh yield
What three things determine stroke volume?
  1. A. Preload
    Afterload
    Contractility
  2. B. Preload
    Afterload
    Heart rate
  3. C. Preload
    Compliance
    Contractility
AnswerA. Preload
Afterload
Contractility
WhyStroke volume is set by preload (filling), afterload (the pressure ejected against) and contractility (strength at a given filling).
Explanation

Every drug and disease in this block acts on one of these three; expect to be given a change and asked which one moved and which way stroke volume goes:

  • ↑ preload → ↑ SV (Frank-Starling);
  • ↑ afterload → ↓ SV;
  • ↑ contractility → ↑ SV.

Heart rate is the other factor in cardiac output (CO = SV × HR), not a determinant of stroke volume. Compliance affects how easily the ventricle fills, but it acts through preload.

Slides (2)
L28LearningHigh yield
What does a higher afterload do to ejection?
  1. A. The harder the ventricle has to push, the less it ejects: stroke volume falls
  2. B. The harder the ventricle has to push, the more it ejects: stroke volume rises
  3. C. The harder the ventricle has to push, the less it fills: end-diastolic volume falls
AnswerA. The harder the ventricle has to push, the less it ejects: stroke volume falls
WhyRaising afterload means more of each contraction is spent building pressure, so the ventricle shortens less and stroke volume falls (end-systolic volume rises).
Explanation

The ventricle must first raise its pressure above aortic pressure before the aortic valve opens; the higher that pressure, the later ejection starts and the earlier it stops. Less shortening means a bigger end-systolic volume and a smaller stroke volume. Lowering afterload (arteriolar dilation) is therefore a way to raise stroke volume in heart failure.

  • Ejects more reverses the relation.
  • Fills less / EDV falls mixes up the phases: afterload acts during ejection, not filling; if anything, the extra blood left behind raises the next end-diastolic volume.
Slides (3)
L29LearningHigh yield
At what afterload does cardiac muscle shorten fastest?
  1. A. Maximal afterload
  2. B. An afterload equal to the preload
  3. C. Zero afterload
AnswerC. Zero afterload
WhyThe force-velocity relation is inverse: the lighter the load, the faster the shortening; extrapolated to zero afterload it gives the maximal velocity (Vmax).
Explanation

Like any muscle, the heart can shorten quickly against a light load and only slowly against a heavy one. At zero afterload (in theory, zero aortic pressure) velocity is maximal; as afterload rises velocity falls, until at maximal afterload the muscle develops force without shortening at all (isometric). A positive inotrope raises velocity at every afterload.

  • Maximal afterload gives zero velocity, the opposite end of the curve.
  • Afterload equal to preload has no special meaning on the force-velocity curve.
Slides (2)
L30Learning
What happens to a ventricle that faces high afterload for a long time, and what are two causes?
  1. A. It thickens
    Causes: severe hypotension, leaky mitral valve
  2. B. It thickens
    Causes: severe hypertension, tight (stenotic) aortic valve
  3. C. It dilates
    Causes: severe hypertension, tight (stenotic) aortic valve
AnswerB. It thickens
Causes: severe hypertension, tight (stenotic) aortic valve
WhyChronic pressure overload (hypertension, aortic stenosis) makes the ventricle wall thicken (concentric hypertrophy) to generate the higher pressure.
Explanation

Wall thickening spreads the extra load over more muscle and keeps wall stress down (law of Laplace), at the price of a stiffer ventricle that fills less easily and needs more O2.

  • Hypotension and a leaky mitral valve lower the pressure load (a leaky mitral valve gives the ventricle an extra low-pressure exit); they cause volume, not pressure, problems.
  • Dilation is the response to chronic volume overload (for example a leaking valve), not pressure overload.
Slides (2)

Length-tension and the Frank-Starling mechanism

L31LearningHigh yield
At what sarcomere length is tension greatest?
  1. A. About 1.6 µm (best actin-myosin overlap)
  2. B. About 3.0 µm (best actin-myosin overlap)
  3. C. About 2.2 µm (best actin-myosin overlap)
AnswerC. About 2.2 µm (best actin-myosin overlap)
WhyCardiac muscle develops maximal tension at a sarcomere length of about 2.2 µm (Lmax), where actin and myosin overlap best.
Explanation

On the length-tension curve, tension climbs as the muscle is stretched toward 2.2 µm and falls beyond it. At Lmax every myosin head can reach an actin site without thin filaments from opposite ends colliding.

  • 1.6 µm is on the ascending limb: thin filaments overlap one another and thick filaments butt against the Z lines.
  • 3.0 µm is on the descending limb: too few cross-bridges can form.
Slides (1)
L32Learning
What is the passive (diastolic) ventricular pressure-volume curve?
  1. A. The pressure in the aorta during diastole while the valve stays shut
  2. B. The pressure produced just by stretching the relaxed ventricle as it fills
  3. C. The pressure produced by atrial contraction as the ventricle empties
AnswerB. The pressure produced just by stretching the relaxed ventricle as it fills
WhyThe passive curve is the pressure of the relaxed ventricle at each filling volume; it rises steeply (exponentially) as the wall is stretched.
Explanation

In the left-ventricular graph, end-diastolic volume is on the x axis. Along the passive (diastolic) curve no contraction occurs: the pressure comes only from the elastic stretch of the wall, low at first and then rising sharply as the muscle approaches its limit. That curve defines the ventricle's compliance and where end-diastolic pressure ends up.

  • Aortic pressure in diastole is a different vessel and a different trace.
  • Atrial contraction helps fill the ventricle; it does not empty it.
Slides (2)
L33LearningHigh yield
What is the Frank-Starling mechanism?
  1. A. The more the ventricle fills, the harder it contracts: bigger end-diastolic volume → bigger stroke volume
  2. B. The more the ventricle fills, the weaker it contracts: bigger end-diastolic volume → smaller stroke volume
  3. C. The higher the aortic pressure, the harder it contracts: bigger afterload → bigger stroke volume
AnswerA. The more the ventricle fills, the harder it contracts: bigger end-diastolic volume → bigger stroke volume
WhyFrank-Starling: within limits, a ventricle stretched by more filling contracts more forcefully, so stroke volume rises with end-diastolic volume.
Explanation

More filling stretches the sarcomeres toward their optimal length (and raises Ca2+ sensitivity), so the next beat is stronger. It is built into the muscle: no nerves or hormones are involved, and it works in a transplanted heart.

  • More filling → weaker only happens on the overstretched descending limb, not in the normal working range.
  • More afterload → more SV: higher afterload lowers stroke volume.
Slides (3)
L34LearningHigh yield
Where does the normal ventricle work relative to the optimal sarcomere length, and so what does extra filling do?
  1. A. Above it: extra filling stretches sarcomeres further from 2.2 µm → weaker next beat
  2. B. Below it: extra filling stretches sarcomeres toward 2.2 µm → stronger next beat
  3. C. Below it: extra filling shortens sarcomeres away from 2.2 µm → weaker next beat
AnswerB. Below it: extra filling stretches sarcomeres toward 2.2 µm → stronger next beat
WhyThe heart normally works on the ascending limb, below the optimal length, so extra filling moves sarcomeres toward 2.2 µm and strengthens the beat.
Explanation

In the Frank-Starling figure the normal resting length sits on the rising part of the curve, with the optimal length further right. That spare capacity is what lets the ventricle respond to more venous return with a bigger stroke volume.

  • Above the optimum is the overstretched, dysfunctional ventricle at the far right of the curve.
  • Filling shortens sarcomeres: filling lengthens them.
Slides (3)
L35LearningHigh yield
Why is the Frank-Starling mechanism so useful?
  1. A. It keeps arterial pressure constant whatever the venous return
  2. B. It keeps the outputs of the two sides of the heart matched automatically
  3. C. It lets sympathetic nerves raise contractility without extra filling
AnswerB. It keeps the outputs of the two sides of the heart matched automatically
WhyBecause each ventricle pumps out what it receives, Frank-Starling keeps right and left outputs matched beat by beat, so blood does not back up in either circuit.
Explanation

If the right ventricle briefly ejects more, more blood returns to the left heart a few beats later, stretching it further, so it ejects more too. Without this, a small mismatch would shift blood into the lungs (pulmonary oedema) or the systemic veins.

  • Constant arterial pressure is the job of the baroreceptor reflex, not Frank-Starling.
  • Sympathetic contractility without extra filling is a change in contractility, which is exactly what Frank-Starling is not.
Slides (1)

Frank-Starling curves: filling versus inotropy

L36LearningHigh yield
What is the difference between preload and contractility?
  1. A. Preload: what the muscle pushes against
    Contractility: how stretched the muscle is
  2. B. Preload: how forcefully it contracts at that stretch
    Contractility: how stretched the muscle is
  3. C. Preload: how stretched the muscle is
    Contractility: how forcefully it contracts at that stretch
AnswerC. Preload: how stretched the muscle is
Contractility: how forcefully it contracts at that stretch
WhyPreload is the starting stretch; contractility is the strength at any given stretch. Frank-Starling is a preload effect, not a change in contractility.
Explanation

Both raise stroke volume, but by different routes. More preload moves the heart along its Frank-Starling curve; more contractility moves it onto a higher curve, so the same end-diastolic volume gives a bigger stroke volume.

  • What the muscle pushes against is afterload.
  • The swapped option gives each term the other's definition.
Slides (2)
L37LearningHigh yield
A positive inotrope raises stroke volume while end-diastolic volume stays the same. What else must have changed?
  1. A. End-systolic volume rose, so ejection fraction rose
  2. B. End-systolic volume fell, so ejection fraction fell
  3. C. End-systolic volume fell, so ejection fraction rose
AnswerC. End-systolic volume fell, so ejection fraction rose
WhySV = EDV − ESV. With EDV fixed, a bigger stroke volume means a smaller end-systolic volume and a higher ejection fraction (SV/EDV).
Explanation

A stronger contraction empties the ventricle further; it does not change how full the ventricle was to start with. So a positive inotrope lowers ESV, raises SV and raises EF, with EDV unchanged (or slightly lower). The same logic answers “if ejection fraction rises, what falls?”: end-systolic volume.

  • ESV rose would shrink stroke volume, the opposite of the stem.
  • EF fell: a larger SV over the same EDV must raise EF.
Slides (1)
L38LearningHigh yield
What shifts the Frank-Starling curve up?
  1. A. Intravenous fluids
    Venoconstriction
    Raised venous return
  2. B. Dobutamine
    Digoxin
    Sympathetic stimulation
  3. C. Dobutamine
    Verapamil
    Parasympathetic stimulation
AnswerB. Dobutamine
Digoxin
Sympathetic stimulation
WhyPositive inotropes shift the curve up: dobutamine (β1 agonist), digoxin (Na+/K+-ATPase inhibitor) and sympathetic stimulation.
Explanation

All three raise the Ca2+ reaching troponin C, so the ventricle ejects more at every end-diastolic volume. The lecture graph labels the upper curve “Digoxin, Dobutamine”.

  • Fluids, venoconstriction and more venous return raise preload: they move the heart along the curve, not up.
  • Verapamil (a calcium channel blocker) and parasympathetic stimulation are negative inotropes; only dobutamine in that list shifts the curve up.
Slides (3)
L39LearningHigh yield
What shifts the Frank-Starling curve down?
  1. A. Systolic dysfunction (the weak ventricle of congestive heart failure)
  2. B. Sympathetic stimulation (the strong ventricle of exercise)
  3. C. Digoxin (the stimulated ventricle of congestive heart failure)
AnswerA. Systolic dysfunction (the weak ventricle of congestive heart failure)
WhySystolic dysfunction, the weak ventricle of congestive heart failure (CHF), lowers contractility and shifts the curve down: less stroke volume at every filling.
Explanation

A failing ventricle (after myocardial infarctions, for example) ejects less for the same end-diastolic volume, so it has to run at a higher filling volume and pressure to keep up, which backs blood up into the lungs. Negative inotropes such as β blockers also shift the curve down, and on a stroke-volume plot so does a rise in afterload.

  • Sympathetic stimulation shifts the curve up.
  • Digoxin is given to raise the curve in heart failure.
Slides (2)

Stroke volume, ejection fraction and cardiac output

L40LearningHigh yield
What is the normal ejection fraction?
  1. A. About 80–95%
  2. B. About 35–45%
  3. C. About 55–70%
AnswerC. About 55–70%
WhyA normal left-ventricular ejection fraction is about 55–70% (roughly 60%; the lecture example is 58%).
Explanation

A healthy ventricle ejects a little over half of what it holds; the rest (end-systolic volume) is a reserve that a stronger contraction can tap. An EF clearly below 55% means systolic dysfunction; around 40% or less is the typical range of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

  • 80–95% would leave almost nothing in the ventricle; it is higher than even a strongly stimulated heart reaches at rest.
  • 35–45% is reduced, as in heart failure.
Slides (1)
L41LearningHigh yield
End-diastolic volume is 170 mL, end-systolic volume 100 mL and heart rate 72 beats/min. What are the cardiac output and ejection fraction?
  1. A. CO ≈ 5.0 L/min; EF ≈ 59%
  2. B. CO ≈ 5.0 L/min; EF ≈ 41%
  3. C. CO ≈ 12.2 L/min; EF ≈ 41%
AnswerB. CO ≈ 5.0 L/min; EF ≈ 41%
WhySV = 170 − 100 = 70 mL; CO = 70 × 72 = 5040 mL/min ≈ 5.0 L/min; EF = 70 ÷ 170 ≈ 41% (reduced).
Explanation

Work in order: stroke volume first, then multiply by heart rate for cardiac output, then divide stroke volume by end-diastolic volume for ejection fraction. Note that a normal cardiac output can hide a low EF: this dilated ventricle holds a lot, so even a weak beat ejects 70 mL.

  • EF 59% is ESV ÷ EDV (100 ÷ 170), the fraction left behind.
  • CO 12.2 L/min multiplies EDV, not SV, by heart rate.
Slides (2)
L42LearningHigh yield
A patient has an ejection fraction of 0.5, a heart rate of 80 beats/min and a cardiac output of 4.0 L/min. What is the end-diastolic volume?
  1. A. 100 mL
  2. B. 50 mL
  3. C. 25 mL
AnswerA. 100 mL
WhySV = CO ÷ HR = 4000 ÷ 80 = 50 mL; EDV = SV ÷ EF = 50 ÷ 0.5 = 100 mL.
Explanation

Two rearrangements: CO = SV × HR gives SV; EF = SV ÷ EDV gives EDV = SV ÷ EF. Keep cardiac output in mL/min so the units come out in mL.

  • 50 mL is the stroke volume; the question stops one step early.
  • 25 mL multiplies SV by EF instead of dividing.
Slides (3)
L43Learning
What sets heart rate?
  1. A. Autonomic nerves, hormones and end-systolic volume
  2. B. Venous return, filling time and afterload
  3. C. Autonomic nerves, hormones and the atrial reflex
AnswerC. Autonomic nerves, hormones and the atrial reflex
WhyIn the lecture summary, heart rate is set by autonomic innervation, hormones (epinephrine) and the atrial reflex.
Explanation

The atrial (Bainbridge) reflex links the two halves of the diagram: increased venous return stretches the atria and speeds the heart, so a rise in venous return can raise heart rate as well as preload.

  • End-systolic volume is an output of the stroke-volume side (set by preload, contractility and afterload); it does not feed heart rate.
  • Venous return, filling time, afterload are stroke-volume factors.
Slides (2)
L44Learning
What sets end-diastolic volume (EDV)?
  1. A. Sympathetic drive and Ca2+ handling (contractility)
  2. B. Arterial pressure and vascular tone (afterload)
  3. C. Venous return and filling time (preload)
AnswerC. Venous return and filling time (preload)
WhyEnd-diastolic volume is the preload, fed by venous return and the filling time available in diastole.
Explanation

More venous return or a longer diastole fills the ventricle further; a very fast heart rate, which cuts diastole short, lowers it.

  • Contractility acts on how much is ejected, so it changes end-systolic volume.
  • Afterload also acts on ejection and end-systolic volume.
Slides (2)
L45Learning
What sets end-systolic volume (ESV)?
  1. A. Venous return and filling time alone
  2. B. Heart rate and the atrial reflex alone
  3. C. Contractility and afterload, starting from the preload
AnswerC. Contractility and afterload, starting from the preload
WhyESV is what is left after ejection: stronger contraction lowers it, higher afterload raises it, and a bigger starting volume (preload) feeds into it too.
Explanation

In the lecture's summary diagram, contractility, afterload and preload all feed end-systolic volume, while only preload feeds end-diastolic volume. Then SV = EDV − ESV and CO = HR × SV.

  • Venous return and filling time set end-diastolic volume.
  • Heart rate and the atrial reflex belong to the heart-rate side of the diagram.
Slides (2)

PHYS-L23 Pressure–volume loops

53 learning questions · of 115
Learning questions 53

Reading the loop

L1Learning
Which way does time run around a pressure–volume loop?
  1. A. Clockwise: filling runs right → left along the bottom, ejection left → right along the top
  2. B. Clockwise: filling runs left → right along the top, ejection right → left along the bottom
  3. C. Anticlockwise: filling runs left → right along the bottom, ejection right → left along the top
AnswerC. Anticlockwise: filling runs left → right along the bottom, ejection right → left along the top
WhyThe loop runs anticlockwise: volume rises along the bottom (filling), pressure climbs the right side, volume falls along the top (ejection), pressure drops down the left side.
Explanation

Follow volume and pressure through the beat:

  • Filling: volume rises at low pressure (bottom edge, moving right).
  • Isovolumetric contraction: pressure climbs at fixed volume (right edge, moving up).
  • Ejection: volume falls at high pressure (top edge, moving left).
  • Isovolumetric relaxation: pressure drops at fixed volume (left edge, moving down).

Right, up, left, down is anticlockwise. Filling right → left would mean volume falling while the ventricle fills; filling along the top would mean filling at systolic pressures, whereas filling happens at only a few mmHg.

Slides (2)
L2LearningHigh yield
Name the four phases of the pressure–volume loop in order, starting with filling.
  1. A. Filling → isovolumetric relaxation → ejection → isovolumetric contraction
  2. B. Filling → ejection → isovolumetric contraction → isovolumetric relaxation
  3. C. Filling → isovolumetric contraction → ejection → isovolumetric relaxation
AnswerC. Filling → isovolumetric contraction → ejection → isovolumetric relaxation
WhyAfter filling the ventricle builds pressure with both valves shut (isovolumetric contraction), ejects, then drops pressure with both valves shut (isovolumetric relaxation).
Explanation

Each corner of the loop is a valve event that switches phase:

  • Bottom-right: mitral valve closes → isovolumetric contraction.
  • Top-right: aortic valve opens → ejection.
  • Top-left: aortic valve closes → isovolumetric relaxation.
  • Bottom-left: mitral valve opens → filling.

Putting relaxation before ejection has the ventricle relax before it has pumped. Putting ejection before isovolumetric contraction skips the pressure build-up: blood cannot leave until ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure.

Slides (3)
L3Learning
Which four things can be read directly off a single pressure–volume loop?
  1. A. Preload
    Afterload
    Contractility
    Heart rate
  2. B. Preload
    Afterload
    Contractility
    Stroke volume
  3. C. Preload
    Afterload
    Contractility
    Cardiac output
AnswerB. Preload
Afterload
Contractility
Stroke volume
WhyEnd-diastolic volume shows preload, the ejection pressures show afterload, the end-systolic line's slope shows contractility, and the width is stroke volume.
Explanation

One beat contains all four:

  • Preload = end-diastolic volume, the bottom-right corner.
  • Afterload = the pressure the ventricle must reach to open the aortic valve and eject against (the height of the top).
  • Contractility = the slope of the end-systolic pressure–volume line through the top-left corner.
  • Stroke volume = the width.

Heart rate is not on the loop: a loop is one beat with no time axis. For the same reason cardiac output (stroke volume × heart rate) cannot be read from it.

Slides (2)
L4LearningHigh yield
On the standard numbered loop (point 1 = bottom-right corner, numbered anticlockwise), which segments make up ventricular systole?
  1. A. 2 → 3 only (ejection)
  2. B. 1 → 2 and 2 → 3 (isovolumetric contraction and ejection)
  3. C. 2 → 3 and 3 → 4 (ejection and isovolumetric relaxation)
AnswerB. 1 → 2 and 2 → 3 (isovolumetric contraction and ejection)
WhyVentricular systole runs from mitral valve closure (point 1) to aortic valve closure (point 3): isovolumetric contraction plus ejection.
Explanation

Systole is the period of ventricular contraction. It starts at end-diastole, when the ventricle begins to squeeze and closes the mitral valve (S1), and lasts until ejection ends and the aortic valve closes (S2). Diastole is 3 → 4 (isovolumetric relaxation) plus 4 → 1 (filling).

  • Ejection only leaves out isovolumetric contraction, which is already contraction: the muscle is squeezing even though no blood is leaving yet.
  • Ejection + isovolumetric relaxation counts the relaxing ventricle as systole; relaxation is the first part of diastole.

One lecture diagram labels the top-right corner 'beginning of systole'; that corner is really the beginning of ejection.

Slides (3)

Valve events around the loop

L5LearningHigh yield
What ends isovolumetric contraction, and at about what pressure on the lecture's loop?
  1. A. Left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure (about 120 mmHg) → aortic valve opens
  2. B. Aortic pressure exceeds left ventricular pressure (about 80 mmHg) → aortic valve closes
  3. C. Left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure (about 80 mmHg) → aortic valve opens
AnswerC. Left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure (about 80 mmHg) → aortic valve opens
WhyThe aortic valve opens when left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, which at that moment is the aortic diastolic pressure, about 80 mmHg.
Explanation

Valves move passively on pressure gradients. Just before ejection the aorta has been draining into the arteries all through diastole, so its pressure is at its lowest, about 80 mmHg. Once the contracting ventricle passes that pressure, the aortic valve is pushed open and ejection begins (top-right corner).

  • 120 mmHg is the systolic peak, reached during ejection, not where ejection starts.
  • Aortic pressure exceeding ventricular pressure closes the valve at the end of ejection.
Slides (3)
L6Learning
During which phase of the cardiac cycle is left ventricular pressure highest?
  1. A. Ventricular ejection
  2. B. Isovolumetric contraction
  3. C. Atrial systole
AnswerA. Ventricular ejection
WhyLeft ventricular pressure peaks (about 120 mmHg) during ejection: the ventricle keeps contracting after the aortic valve opens.
Explanation

Isovolumetric contraction raises pressure only as far as aortic diastolic pressure (~80 mmHg), because the aortic valve opens there. Contraction continues, so pressure climbs further to the systolic peak during rapid ejection. That peak is the top of the loop.

  • Isovolumetric contraction ends at about 80 mmHg, well below the peak.
  • Atrial systole adds only a few mmHg to a relaxed ventricle.
Slides (2)
L7Learning
On an unfamiliar pressure–volume loop, what do the two vertical sides tell you?
  1. A. Both valves are open
  2. B. Only the mitral valve is open
  3. C. Both valves are closed
AnswerC. Both valves are closed
WhyVolume can change only through an open valve, so a vertical (constant-volume) segment means both the mitral and aortic valves are shut.
Explanation

The right side is isovolumetric contraction and the left side isovolumetric relaxation. This is the quickest way to orient yourself on any loop: find the vertical sides, and the corners at their ends are the four valve events.

  • Both valves open never happens in a normal heart; blood would run straight from atrium to aorta.
  • Mitral valve open means filling, and volume would be rising.

A leaking valve removes the matching vertical side (see the valve-lesion questions).

Slides (1)
L8Learning
A loop's aortic valve opens at 70 mmHg and its top peaks at 120 mmHg; ventricular pressure during filling is about 10 mmHg. Estimate the arterial blood pressure.
  1. A. About 120/10 mmHg (pulse pressure 110)
  2. B. About 120/70 mmHg (pulse pressure 50)
  3. C. About 70/10 mmHg (pulse pressure 60)
AnswerB. About 120/70 mmHg (pulse pressure 50)
WhyWhile the aortic valve is open, ventricle and aorta share pressure: the loop's peak ≈ systolic, and the pressure at aortic opening ≈ diastolic aortic pressure.
Explanation

The aortic valve opens when ventricular pressure first exceeds aortic pressure, and at that moment aortic pressure is at its lowest: the diastolic pressure (70). During ejection the two pressures move together, so the loop's peak (120) is the systolic pressure. Pulse pressure = 120 − 70 = 50 mmHg.

  • 120/10 takes the ventricle's filling pressure as the diastolic blood pressure. During filling the aortic valve is shut and the aorta keeps its own, much higher pressure.
  • 70/10 mistakes the aortic opening pressure for the systolic pressure.
Slides (2)

Volumes, stroke volume and ejection fraction

L9LearningHigh yield
What is the normal left ventricular end-diastolic volume on the lecture's loop?
  1. A. About 120 mL
  2. B. About 70 mL
  3. C. About 50 mL
AnswerA. About 120 mL
WhyThe ventricle fills to an end-diastolic volume of about 120 mL, the lecture's critical value; this volume is the preload.
Explanation

End-diastolic volume is the volume in the ventricle at the end of filling, just as the mitral valve closes: the bottom-right corner. The other two numbers are the other critical values:

  • 70 mL is the stroke volume (120 − 50).
  • 50 mL is the end-systolic volume, left behind after ejection.

The textbook loop uses 140 mL and 70 mL; its stroke volume is the same 70 mL.

Slides (2)
L10LearningHigh yield
Which dimension of the pressure–volume loop is the stroke volume?
  1. A. The height (systolic − diastolic pressure)
  2. B. The width (end-diastolic − end-systolic volume)
  3. C. The left-hand edge (end-systolic volume)
AnswerB. The width (end-diastolic − end-systolic volume)
WhyStroke volume is the volume ejected in one beat, the horizontal width of the loop: end-diastolic minus end-systolic volume.
Explanation

The x-axis is volume, so the distance from the right edge (end-diastolic volume) to the left edge (end-systolic volume) is how much blood left the ventricle. Any change that widens the loop has raised stroke volume, whether by moving the right edge right (more preload) or the left edge left (more contractility, less afterload).

  • The height is a range of pressure, not of volume.
  • The end-systolic volume is only what is left over.
Slides (2)
L11LearningHigh yield
Calculate the ejection fraction for a stroke volume of 70 mL and an end-diastolic volume of 120 mL. What is the normal range?
  1. A. 70 ÷ 120 = 58%
    Normal 35–50%
  2. B. 50 ÷ 120 = 42%
    Normal 55–70%
  3. C. 70 ÷ 120 = 58%
    Normal 55–70%
AnswerC. 70 ÷ 120 = 58%
Normal 55–70%
Why70 ÷ 120 = 58%, inside the normal ejection fraction range of 55–70%.
Explanation

Ejection fraction = stroke volume ÷ end-diastolic volume; the lecture lists 58% (normal 55–70%) as a critical value.

  • Normal 35–50% is wrong: an ejection fraction below about 40% marks a weak, failing ventricle (systolic heart failure).
  • 50 ÷ 120 divides the end-systolic volume, the blood left behind, so it gives the residual fraction (42%), not the ejected fraction.
Slides (2)
L12LearningHigh yield
A patient has an end-diastolic volume of 140 mL, an end-systolic volume of 70 mL and a heart rate of 75/min. What are the stroke volume, cardiac output and ejection fraction?
  1. A. 70 mL
    5.25 L/min
    50%
  2. B. 70 mL
    10.5 L/min
    50%
  3. C. 70 mL
    5.25 L/min
    100%
AnswerA. 70 mL
5.25 L/min
50%
WhyStroke volume 140 − 70 = 70 mL; cardiac output 70 × 75 = 5,250 mL/min; ejection fraction 70 ÷ 140 = 50%.
Explanation

Work through the three formulas in order:

  • Stroke volume = end-diastolic − end-systolic volume = 70 mL.
  • Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 5.25 L/min. 10.5 L/min multiplies the end-diastolic volume (140 × 75) instead.
  • Ejection fraction = stroke volume ÷ end-diastolic volume = 0.5. 100% divides by the end-systolic volume (70 ÷ 70).

An ejection fraction of 50% is a little below the lecture's normal range of 55–70%.

Slides (3)

Preload, afterload and contractility on the loop

L13LearningHigh yield
How does increased afterload change the pressure–volume loop, and why?
  1. A. Shorter and wider: a lower pressure is needed to open the aortic valve → more ejected
  2. B. Taller and narrower: a higher pressure is needed to open the aortic valve → less ejected
  3. C. Taller and wider: a higher pressure is needed to open the aortic valve → more ejected
AnswerB. Taller and narrower: a higher pressure is needed to open the aortic valve → less ejected
WhyWith higher afterload the ventricle must reach a higher pressure before the aortic valve opens, so the loop is taller; ejection stops sooner, so it is narrower.
Explanation

Afterload is the pressure the ventricle ejects against, essentially aortic pressure. More of each contraction goes into building pressure, and ejection ends at a higher end-systolic pressure on the same end-systolic line, which lies at a larger end-systolic volume. Stroke volume and ejection fraction fall: 'more work for less reward'.

  • Shorter and wider describes reduced afterload (e.g. an ACE inhibitor or another arteriolar dilator).
