  • Taller and wider ignores that ejecting against a higher pressure leaves more blood behind.
Slides (3)
L14Learning
After afterload rises and end-systolic volume increases, why does the loop drift to the right over the next few beats?
  1. A. Venous return falls → end-diastolic volume ↓ → stroke volume falls further
  2. B. Normal venous return is added to the larger residual volume → end-diastolic volume ↑ → Frank–Starling restores part of the stroke volume
  3. C. The aortic valve opens earlier → end-systolic volume ↓ → stroke volume rises above normal
AnswerB. Normal venous return is added to the larger residual volume → end-diastolic volume ↑ → Frank–Starling restores part of the stroke volume
WhyThe extra end-systolic volume stays in the ventricle and venous return is added on top, so end-diastolic volume rises and Frank–Starling partly restores stroke volume.
Explanation

This is why the lecture's 'increased aortic pressure' loop sits to the right of the control loop. Higher afterload first narrows the loop at a larger end-systolic volume. The lungs keep delivering the same venous return, so each filling starts from a bigger residual volume and ends at a bigger end-diastolic volume. The stretched fibres contract harder and stroke volume recovers part of the way, at the cost of more work.

  • Venous return falling is not the mechanism; it is unchanged.
  • The aortic valve opening earlier is backwards: with a higher aortic pressure it opens later in contraction.
Slides (1)
L15Learning
Which line on the pressure–volume diagram reflects contractility, and how is it read?
  1. A. End-systolic pressure–volume line through the top-left corner; flatter = stronger ventricle
  2. B. End-diastolic pressure–volume curve along the bottom edge; steeper = stronger ventricle
  3. C. End-systolic pressure–volume line through the top-left corner; steeper = stronger ventricle
AnswerC. End-systolic pressure–volume line through the top-left corner; steeper = stronger ventricle
WhyThe slope of the end-systolic pressure–volume relationship, the line through the top-left corner, measures inotropy: steeper means a stronger ventricle.
Explanation

The end-systolic line joins the end-systolic corners of loops recorded at different loads. A stronger ventricle reaches a higher pressure at any end-systolic volume, so its line is steeper; a weak, failing ventricle has a flatter line.

  • Flatter = stronger reverses the reading.
  • The end-diastolic curve along the bottom is the passive filling curve. Its steepness reflects stiffness (low compliance), as in a hypertrophied ventricle, not contractility.
Slides (2)
L16LearningHigh yield
What is the quick rule for how preload, afterload and contractility change the loop?
  1. A. More filling → wider to the right
    Harder to push against → taller and narrower
    Stronger squeeze → wider to the left
  2. B. More filling → taller and narrower
    Harder to push against → wider to the right
    Stronger squeeze → wider to the left
  3. C. More filling → wider to the right
    Harder to push against → taller and narrower
    Stronger squeeze → wider to the right
AnswerA. More filling → wider to the right
Harder to push against → taller and narrower
Stronger squeeze → wider to the left
WhyPreload widens the loop to the right, afterload makes it taller and narrower, contractility widens it to the left.
Explanation
ChangeEdge that movesStroke volumeEnd-systolic volume
↑ PreloadRight edge → right↑≈
↑ AfterloadTop ↑, left edge → right↓↑
↑ ContractilityLeft edge → left↑↓

The swapped options give afterload's shape to preload, or move the contractility edge to the filling side. Filling only ever moves the right edge; how hard and how far the ventricle squeezes moves the left edge.

Slides (3)
L17LearningHigh yield
Two patients' loops have the same width and the same pressures, but patient 2's loop sits further to the right. Which is greater in patient 2?
  1. A. Stroke work
  2. B. Stroke volume
  3. C. Preload (end-diastolic volume)
AnswerC. Preload (end-diastolic volume)
WhyA loop shifted right with the same width has a larger end-diastolic volume (preload) but the same stroke volume and stroke work.
Explanation

Stroke volume is the width and stroke work is the enclosed area (about stroke volume × pressure); neither changes when the whole loop slides right. What changes is the volume at which the ventricle works: a larger end-diastolic volume, so a larger radius. By Laplace's law the larger radius raises wall tension, so the right-shifted heart spends more O2 for the same work: it is less efficient.

  • Stroke work and stroke volume are equal, because the loops have the same width and height.
Slides (1)

Cardiac work and oxygen cost

L18Learning
How does the lecture define the left ventricle's work per beat (stroke work)?
  1. A. Stroke volume × heart rate
  2. B. Stroke volume × aortic pressure
  3. C. End-diastolic volume × aortic pressure
AnswerB. Stroke volume × aortic pressure
WhyStroke work = stroke volume × aortic pressure: the volume pushed out times the pressure it is pushed against.
Explanation

Work is force × distance; for a pump this becomes pressure × volume moved. So the ventricle does more work if it ejects more blood (volume work) or ejects against a higher pressure (pressure work). Multiplying by heart rate gives the work per minute (cardiac output × aortic pressure).

  • Stroke volume × heart rate is cardiac output, a flow, not work.
  • End-diastolic volume × aortic pressure counts blood that stays in the ventricle; only the ejected volume is moved against aortic pressure.
Slides (2)
L19Learning
Which part of the pressure–volume loop represents the work done on the blood in that beat?
  1. A. The slope of the end-systolic line
  2. B. The area enclosed by the loop
  3. C. The area under the filling curve
AnswerB. The area enclosed by the loop
WhyThe area inside the loop is the stroke work: pressure × volume summed around the beat.
Explanation

Summing pressure over the volume ejected, minus the small amount returned during filling, gives the net work the ventricle does on the blood. Taller loops (more afterload) and wider loops (more stroke volume) both enclose more area.

  • The end-systolic slope measures contractility, not work.
  • The area under the filling curve is the small work the incoming blood does on the relaxed ventricle, not work done by the ventricle.
Slides (1)
L20Learning
Trace the chain from more cardiac work to clinical harm.
  1. A. More work → more myocardial O2 consumption → more hypertrophy → less arrhythmia and death
  2. B. More work → less myocardial O2 consumption → more coronary flow → more arrhythmia and death
  3. C. More work → more myocardial O2 consumption → more ischaemia → more arrhythmia and death
AnswerC. More work → more myocardial O2 consumption → more ischaemia → more arrhythmia and death
WhyExtra work raises myocardial O2 consumption; when supply cannot keep up, ischaemia follows, and ischaemic myocardium triggers arrhythmia and death.
Explanation

The heart extracts most of the O2 from its coronary blood even at rest, so it can meet extra demand only by raising coronary flow. If the coronaries are narrowed, demand outruns supply, causing angina, infarction and arrhythmias. This chain is why the lecture says 'more work kills you'.

  • Hypertrophy → less arrhythmia is wrong: hypertrophy is itself a risk factor for ischaemia and arrhythmia.
  • Less O2 consumption reverses the first link: more work always costs more O2.
Slides (1)
L21Learning
Which costs the heart more O2: pressure work or volume work?
  1. A. Pressure work
  2. B. Volume work
  3. C. They cost the same O2
AnswerA. Pressure work
WhyEjecting against a higher pressure costs far more O2 than ejecting a larger volume at the same pressure.
Explanation

Myocardial O2 use tracks the wall tension the muscle must develop and hold, and tension rises with pressure (Laplace). Raising aortic pressure is therefore the expensive kind of work; raising stroke volume (exercise, volume loading) is comparatively cheap. The lecture's image: a big empty box is less work to carry than a small heavy one.

  • Volume work is the cheaper kind.
  • The same O2 ignores that equal external work can carry very different tension costs.

This is why hypertension and aortic stenosis are so costly for the heart.

Slides (3)
L22Learning
Which drug class lowers afterload and lowers mortality in congestive heart failure?
  1. A. Cardiac glycosides (digoxin)
  2. B. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors
  3. C. β1 agonists (dobutamine)
AnswerB. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors
WhyACE inhibitors block angiotensin II formation, dilating arterioles: they lower afterload and lower mortality in heart failure.
Explanation

Angiotensin II is a potent arteriolar constrictor and also drives aldosterone release and cardiac remodelling. Blocking its production lowers total peripheral resistance, so the ventricle works against a lower pressure and consumes less O2.

  • Digoxin raises contractility but lowers neither afterload nor mortality.
  • Dobutamine is a positive inotrope used short term; it raises O2 demand and does not lower mortality.
Slides (3)

Law of Laplace

L23LearningHigh yield
State the law of Laplace for ventricular wall tension as the lecture writes it.
  1. A. T = P × r
    With wall thickness: T = (P × r) × thickness
  2. B. T = P ÷ r
    With wall thickness: T = (P ÷ r) × thickness
  3. C. T = P × r
    With wall thickness: T = (P × r) ÷ thickness
AnswerC. T = P × r
With wall thickness: T = (P × r) ÷ thickness
WhyWall tension = pressure × radius, divided by wall thickness: big, thin-walled, high-pressure ventricles carry the most tension.
Explanation

T is the tension in the wall, P the pressure inside the chamber, r its radius. A larger radius or a higher pressure loads each part of the wall more; a thicker wall shares the load among more muscle, so tension per unit of wall falls.

  • × thickness would make hypertrophy raise tension, the opposite of why ventricles thicken.
  • P ÷ r inverts the radius effect: dilated hearts carry more tension, not less.
Slides (3)
L24LearningHigh yield
Why does a ventricle that pumps against high pressure hypertrophy?
  1. A. A thicker wall lowers wall tension
  2. B. A thicker wall raises wall tension
  3. C. A thicker wall enlarges the radius
AnswerA. A thicker wall lowers wall tension
WhyBy T = P × r ÷ thickness, thickening the wall lowers wall tension, restoring it toward normal despite the higher pressure: 'a wall thickens to decrease wall tension'.
Explanation

Hypertension and aortic stenosis raise the pressure the left ventricle must generate; pulmonary hypertension does the same for the right ventricle. The muscle adds sarcomeres in parallel, thickening the wall around a normal or smaller cavity (concentric hypertrophy), which lets it generate the higher pressure at normal tension.

  • Raising tension inverts the role of thickness in Laplace's law.
  • Enlarging the radius would raise tension; concentric hypertrophy narrows the cavity instead.
Slides (3)
L25Learning
Which change increases myocardial O2 consumption?
  1. A. Enlargement (dilation) of the heart
  2. B. A fall in aortic pressure
  3. C. A fall in heart rate
AnswerA. Enlargement (dilation) of the heart
WhyA dilated heart has a larger radius, so (T = P × r) it must develop more wall tension for the same pressure, and tension drives O2 use.
Explanation

Myocardial O2 consumption rises with the tension the muscle develops, with heart rate (more tension-developing beats per minute) and with contractility. Wall tension rises with pressure and with radius, so a big, dilated ventricle is expensive to run even at a normal output.

  • A fall in aortic pressure lowers afterload and tension, so O2 use falls.
  • A fall in heart rate means fewer beats per minute, so O2 use falls.
Slides (2)
L26LearningHigh yield
In which valve disorder does left ventricular hypertrophy typically develop?
  1. A. Mitral stenosis
  2. B. Aortic stenosis
  3. C. Tricuspid stenosis
AnswerB. Aortic stenosis
WhyIn aortic stenosis the left ventricle must generate very high pressures to push blood through the narrowed valve, so it thickens its wall to keep tension down.
Explanation

Aortic stenosis is a pure pressure (afterload) load on the left ventricle, the same stimulus as long-standing systemic hypertension. The result is concentric hypertrophy: a thick wall around a normal or small cavity.

  • Mitral stenosis obstructs inflow: the left atrium faces the high pressure and enlarges, while the left ventricle is underfilled.
  • Tricuspid stenosis loads the right atrium.

Rule: the chamber upstream of a stenotic valve takes the load.

Slides (1)

Fick principle and O2 content

L27LearningHigh yield
State the Fick principle for cardiac output.
  1. A. Cardiac output = O2 consumption ÷ ([O2]pulmonary vein − [O2]pulmonary artery)
  2. B. Cardiac output = O2 consumption ÷ ([O2]pulmonary artery − [O2]pulmonary vein)
  3. C. Cardiac output = ([O2]pulmonary vein − [O2]pulmonary artery) ÷ O2 consumption
AnswerA. Cardiac output = O2 consumption ÷ ([O2]pulmonary vein − [O2]pulmonary artery)
WhyFick: cardiac output = O2 consumption ÷ the O2 each mL of blood picks up in the lungs (pulmonary vein minus pulmonary artery content).
Explanation

It is mass balance. In a steady state the O2 the lungs add to the blood equals the O2 the body consumes. The O2 added per mL of blood is the pulmonary vein content minus the pulmonary artery content. Dividing total O2 uptake by the O2 each mL picks up gives mL of blood per minute: the cardiac output.

  • Artery minus vein (pulmonary) is negative, because the pulmonary artery carries the deoxygenated blood.
  • The inverted fraction has the wrong units; it is not a flow.
Slides (3)
L28Learning
In the Fick calculation, which blood has the lowest O2 saturation, and why?
  1. A. Pulmonary vein blood: it has just left the lungs
  2. B. Left atrial blood: it receives the bronchial veins
  3. C. Pulmonary artery blood: it is mixed venous blood returning from the whole body
AnswerC. Pulmonary artery blood: it is mixed venous blood returning from the whole body
WhyPulmonary artery blood is mixed venous blood, the pooled return from every organ, before it reaches the lungs: the lowest saturation in the Fick equation.
Explanation

The right ventricle pumps the mixed return of the venae cavae and coronary sinus into the pulmonary artery, so this one sample reflects the whole body's O2 extraction (about 75% saturated at rest).

  • Pulmonary vein blood has just been oxygenated: it has the highest saturation.
  • Left atrial blood gets only a trace of bronchial venous blood, which barely lowers its saturation; it is still essentially arterial.
Slides (2)
L29Learning
Which blood has even lower O2 content than pulmonary artery blood?
  1. A. Superior vena cava blood (drains the brain)
  2. B. Coronary sinus blood (drains the heart muscle)
  3. C. Aortic blood (leaves the left ventricle)
AnswerB. Coronary sinus blood (drains the heart muscle)
WhyCoronary sinus blood drains the myocardium, which extracts about 70–75% of its O2 even at rest: the most deoxygenated venous blood in the body.
Explanation

The heart's O2 extraction is near maximal at rest, so coronary venous blood leaves with very little O2 (about 25–30% saturated). This is also why the heart meets extra demand mainly by raising coronary flow, not extraction.

  • Superior vena cava blood comes from the brain and upper body, which extract less; it is close to mixed venous blood.
  • Aortic blood is arterial: fully oxygenated.
Slides (2)
L30Learning
A woman with heavy menstrual losses has a haemoglobin of 7.5 g/dL with a normal arterial PO2 and normal saturation. Which value is reduced?
  1. A. Arterial O2 content (about 10 mL per 100 mL)
  2. B. Arterial O2 saturation (about 50%)
  3. C. Arterial PO2 (about 50 mmHg)
AnswerA. Arterial O2 content (about 10 mL per 100 mL)
WhyO2 content ≈ 1.34 × haemoglobin × saturation, so halving haemoglobin halves content (to about 10 mL per 100 mL) while saturation and PO2 stay normal.
Explanation

PO2 depends on the lungs and saturation on PO2; neither depends on how much haemoglobin there is. Content, the total mL of O2 per 100 mL, is the only one that does: 1.34 × 7.5 ≈ 10 mL instead of 20. Delivery to the tissues falls, which explains fatigue in anaemia.

  • Saturation is the percentage of available sites filled; it stays ~98% because each remaining haemoglobin is fully loaded.
  • PO2 reflects dissolved O2 set by alveolar gas exchange, which is normal.
Slides (1)
L31LearningHigh yield
Calculate cardiac output: O2 consumption 250 mL/min, arterial O2 0.20 and venous O2 0.15 mL O2 per mL of blood.
  1. A. 250 ÷ (0.20 − 0.15) = 500 mL/min
  2. B. 250 × (0.20 − 0.15) = 12.5 mL/min
  3. C. 250 ÷ (0.20 − 0.15) = 5,000 mL/min
AnswerC. 250 ÷ (0.20 − 0.15) = 5,000 mL/min
WhyEach mL of blood picks up 0.05 mL O2, so 250 mL O2/min needs 250 ÷ 0.05 = 5,000 mL/min of blood.
Explanation

The lecture's worked example: you measure the 250 mL O2 consumed per minute and the 0.05 mL/mL arteriovenous difference, then divide. The answer, 5 L/min, matches the normal resting cardiac output.

  • 500 mL/min is a decimal slip: dividing by 0.05 multiplies by 20.
  • Multiplying instead of dividing gives 12.5 in units of mL O2/min × mL O2/mL blood, which is not a flow of blood.
Slides (3)
L32Learning
In practice, which sample can replace pulmonary vein blood in the Fick equation?
  1. A. Blood from any systemic artery (for example the brachial artery)
  2. B. Blood from the coronary sinus
  3. C. Blood from the superior vena cava
AnswerA. Blood from any systemic artery (for example the brachial artery)
WhyBlood leaving the lungs is the blood the left ventricle ejects, so any systemic artery has the same O2 content as pulmonary vein blood.
Explanation

Arteries do not exchange O2, so a peripheral arterial sample (radial, brachial) equals pulmonary vein content. The other term needs truly mixed venous blood, sampled from the pulmonary artery with a catheter, because each organ's venous blood differs.

  • Coronary sinus blood is the most deoxygenated venous blood in the body, the opposite end of the scale.
  • Superior vena cava blood is venous (upper-body return), close to the pulmonary artery side, not the pulmonary vein side.
Slides (1)

The cardiac cycle on the Wiggers diagram

L33Learning
On the Wiggers diagram, what do you use as the clock?
  1. A. The venous pulse: a wave (ventricles contract) → v wave (atria contract)
  2. B. The ECG: P wave (atria depolarise) → QRS (ventricles depolarise)
  3. C. The aortic trace: dicrotic notch (atria contract) → upstroke (ventricles contract)
AnswerB. The ECG: P wave (atria depolarise) → QRS (ventricles depolarise)
WhyThe ECG is the reference: the P wave triggers atrial systole, and the QRS triggers ventricular contraction.
Explanation

Electrical events precede mechanical ones, so the ECG waves mark the start of each phase: P wave → atrial systole; QRS → isovolumetric contraction; T wave → end of ejection; after T → isovolumetric relaxation.

  • The venous pulse is mislabelled: the a wave is atrial contraction and the v wave atrial filling.
  • The dicrotic notch is aortic valve closure, not atrial contraction.
Slides (2)
L34Learning
List the seven phases of the cardiac cycle in order.
  1. A. Atrial systole → isovolumetric contraction → rapid ejection → reduced ejection → rapid filling → isovolumetric relaxation → reduced filling (diastasis)
  2. B. Atrial systole → rapid ejection → isovolumetric contraction → reduced ejection → isovolumetric relaxation → rapid filling → reduced filling (diastasis)
  3. C. Atrial systole → isovolumetric contraction → rapid ejection → reduced ejection → isovolumetric relaxation → rapid filling → reduced filling (diastasis)
AnswerC. Atrial systole → isovolumetric contraction → rapid ejection → reduced ejection → isovolumetric relaxation → rapid filling → reduced filling (diastasis)
WhyAtrial systole, isovolumetric contraction, rapid and reduced ejection, isovolumetric relaxation, then rapid filling and diastasis.
Explanation
PhaseValves / soundsMarkers
Atrial systoleS4 if stiff ventricleAfter P; a wave
Isovolumetric contractionAtrioventricular valves close: S1With QRS; c wave
Rapid, reduced ejectionAortic valve openVolume falls; T wave in reduced
Isovolumetric relaxationSemilunar valves close: S2After T; dicrotic notch
Rapid fillingMitral opens; S3Just after v wave peak
DiastasisNoneLongest; shortens first

The wrong orders put filling before relaxation, or ejection before isovolumetric contraction.

Slides (3)
L35LearningHigh yield
Isovolumetric contraction: which valves close, which heart sound, and which markers?
  1. A. Atrioventricular valves close → S1; begins with the QRS; c wave
  2. B. Atrioventricular valves open → S1; begins with the P wave; a wave
  3. C. Semilunar valves close → S2; begins after the T wave; v wave
AnswerA. Atrioventricular valves close → S1; begins with the QRS; c wave
WhyVentricular contraction after the QRS closes the atrioventricular (mitral, tricuspid) valves, producing S1; the bulging tricuspid valve makes the c wave.
Explanation

Ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure and the atrioventricular valves slam shut (S1), but pressure has not yet reached aortic pressure, so the semilunar valves stay shut: volume is constant. The c wave starts as the tricuspid valve bulges back into the right atrium; on the textbook figure it peaks just as ejection begins.

  • Valves opening with the P wave describes nothing real; atrial systole happens with the atrioventricular valves already open.
  • Semilunar closure, S2, after T is isovolumetric relaxation.
Slides (3)
L36Learning
On the figure that overlays the ventricular action potential on the cardiac cycle, which mechanical phase coincides with the Ca2+ plateau?
  1. A. Ventricular ejection (high ventricular pressure)
  2. B. Ventricular filling (low ventricular pressure)
  3. C. Atrial systole (before the QRS)
AnswerA. Ventricular ejection (high ventricular pressure)
WhyThe plateau (Ca2+ entry) keeps ventricular cells contracting, so it spans ejection; repolarisation (K+ efflux, T wave) comes as ejection ends.
Explanation

Na+ entry produces the upstroke (QRS); L-type Ca2+ entry holds the plateau and triggers Ca2+ release, so contraction lasts as long as the action potential does; K+ efflux repolarises the cell (T wave) and the ventricle relaxes. The long plateau also keeps the muscle refractory through the contraction, so it cannot be tetanised.

  • Filling happens after repolarisation, when the cells are at rest.
  • Atrial systole comes before the ventricular action potential starts.
Slides (1)
L37LearningHigh yield
Isovolumetric relaxation: which valves close, which heart sound, and which aortic pressure marker?
  1. A. Semilunar valves open → S2; dicrotic notch on the aortic trace (with the P wave)
  2. B. Atrioventricular valves close → S1; dicrotic notch on the aortic trace (before the QRS)
  3. C. Semilunar valves close → S2; dicrotic notch on the aortic trace (after the T wave)
AnswerC. Semilunar valves close → S2; dicrotic notch on the aortic trace (after the T wave)
WhyIsovolumetric relaxation begins when the aortic and pulmonic valves close (S2), which notches the aortic trace (dicrotic notch) just after the T wave.
Explanation

As the repolarised ventricle relaxes, its pressure falls below aortic pressure; blood briefly flows backward, snapping the aortic valve shut. Pressure then falls steeply with both valves shut until it drops below atrial pressure.

  • The semilunar valves open at the start of ejection, silently; S2 is their closure.
  • Atrioventricular closure and S1 mark the start of systole, with the QRS.
Slides (3)
L38LearningHigh yield
Which phase of the cardiac cycle is the longest, and the first to shorten when heart rate rises?
  1. A. Rapid ejection
  2. B. Reduced filling (diastasis)
  3. C. Isovolumetric contraction
AnswerB. Reduced filling (diastasis)
WhyDiastasis (reduced filling) is the longest phase at rest, and it is the first to be cut when heart rate rises.
Explanation

As heart rate rises the cycle shortens mainly at the expense of diastole, and diastasis, the slow late-filling period, goes first. Little filling is lost at first, because most filling happens in the rapid phase; only at very high rates does filling time limit stroke volume (and coronary flow, which happens mainly in diastole).

  • Rapid ejection is short and changes little with heart rate.
  • Isovolumetric contraction is one of the shortest phases (about 0.05 s).
Slides (2)

Heart sounds and the venous pulse

L39Learning
Why is the second heart sound normally split during inspiration?
  1. A. Pulmonic closure is delayed: more right-heart filling prolongs right ventricular ejection
  2. B. Aortic closure is delayed: more left-heart filling prolongs left ventricular ejection
  3. C. Mitral closure is delayed: more left-heart filling prolongs atrial systole
AnswerA. Pulmonic closure is delayed: more right-heart filling prolongs right ventricular ejection
WhyInspiration draws more venous blood into the right heart, so right ventricular ejection lasts longer and the pulmonic valve closes later than the aortic valve.
Explanation

Falling intrathoracic pressure on inspiration increases venous return to the right side. The right ventricle takes longer to eject the extra volume, delaying the pulmonic component (P2); the aortic component (A2) still comes first, so S2 splits into A2–P2.

  • Aortic delay is wrong: during inspiration left-heart filling falls slightly, so A2 if anything comes earlier.
  • Mitral closure belongs to S1, not S2.
Slides (2)
L40LearningHigh yield
What does S3 represent, and what does it mean in an adult?
  1. A. Rapid ventricular filling; a pathological sign of congestive heart failure
  2. B. Atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle; a sign of hypertrophy
  3. C. Rapid ventricular ejection; a sign of aortic stenosis
AnswerA. Rapid ventricular filling; a pathological sign of congestive heart failure
WhyS3 is heard in rapid ventricular filling, early in diastole; in an adult it is a pathological sign of heart failure that usually needs more treatment.
Explanation

Blood rushing from the atrium into a dilated, overfull ventricle is suddenly decelerated, setting up a low-pitched vibration just after S2. In children and young athletes it can be normal; in an adult it signals volume overload or systolic failure (lecture: 'pathologic sign of CHF, usually needs more treatment').

  • Atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle is S4.
  • Ejection is in systole; S3 is a diastolic sound.
Slides (2)
L41LearningHigh yield
What does S4 represent?
  1. A. Rapid passive filling of a dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle
  2. B. Atrial systole pushing blood into a stiff, non-compliant ventricle
  3. C. Closure of the atrioventricular valves at the start of systole
AnswerB. Atrial systole pushing blood into a stiff, non-compliant ventricle
WhyS4 is atrial systole forcing blood into a stiff, non-compliant ventricle, heard late in diastole just before S1.
Explanation

A hypertrophied ventricle resists filling, so it depends on the atrial kick; the atrium contracts hard against the stiff wall and the sudden tensing makes S4. It coincides with the a wave, just after the P wave, and is absent if the atria are not contracting (atrial fibrillation).

  • Rapid passive filling of a dilated ventricle is S3.
  • Atrioventricular valve closure is S1.
Slides (2)
L42Learning
Which venous-pulse wave reflects atrial filling while the atrioventricular valves are shut during ventricular systole?
  1. A. a wave
  2. B. c wave
  3. C. v wave
AnswerC. v wave
WhyThe v wave is the rise in atrial pressure as venous blood fills the atrium against a closed tricuspid valve during ventricular systole; it peaks just before the valve opens.
Explanation

The three positive venous waves:

  • a wave: atrial contraction, after the P wave.
  • c wave: tricuspid valve bulging back into the atrium as the ventricle starts to contract.
  • v wave: venous filling of the atrium during systole; it falls once the valve opens and rapid filling starts.

Regurgitation through the atrioventricular valve (tricuspid on the right, mitral on the left) adds ventricular blood to the atrium in systole and makes the v wave tall.

Slides (2)

Valve lesions on the loop

L43LearningHigh yield
How does aortic stenosis change the pressure–volume loop, and why?
  1. A. Taller and narrower: very high pressure is needed to eject through the narrowed valve
  2. B. Wider and shifted right: extra volume returns through a leaking valve
  3. C. Shorter and wider: lower pressure is needed to eject through the narrowed valve
AnswerA. Taller and narrower: very high pressure is needed to eject through the narrowed valve
WhyAortic stenosis is a pure afterload problem: the ventricle must reach very high pressures to eject, so the loop is tall and narrow.
Explanation

The narrowed orifice resists outflow, so left ventricular pressure must rise far above aortic pressure (to ~200 mmHg on the lecture loop) and ejection ends early, leaving a larger end-systolic volume. Stroke volume falls, pressure work and O2 use climb (angina), and over time the wall hypertrophies.

  • Wide and shifted right is aortic regurgitation, where extra volume returns in diastole.
  • Shorter and wider describes reduced afterload.
Slides (3)
L44LearningHigh yield
How does aortic regurgitation change the pressure–volume loop?
  1. A. Small and shifted left: small end-diastolic volume, small stroke volume
  2. B. Tall and narrow: high peak pressure, small stroke volume
  3. C. Wide and shifted right: large end-diastolic volume, large stroke volume
AnswerC. Wide and shifted right: large end-diastolic volume, large stroke volume
WhyBlood leaks back from the aorta in diastole on top of normal filling, so the ventricle reaches a very large end-diastolic volume and ejects a very large stroke volume: wide and shifted right.
Explanation

The ventricle receives blood from two sources during diastole: the left atrium and the leaking aorta. Frank–Starling turns the large end-diastolic volume into a large total stroke volume, part of which leaks straight back. Cardiac output from the ventricle rises; the extra volume is the 'volume work' that eventually dilates the ventricle.

  • Small and shifted left is mitral stenosis, with under-filling.
  • Tall and narrow is aortic stenosis.
Slides (2)
L45LearningHigh yield
How does chronic aortic regurgitation change arterial blood pressure?
  1. A. Systolic ↑, diastolic ↓ → wide pulse pressure
  2. B. Systolic ↓, diastolic ↓ → narrow pulse pressure
  3. C. Systolic ↑, diastolic ↑ → unchanged pulse pressure
AnswerA. Systolic ↑, diastolic ↓ → wide pulse pressure
WhyThe large stroke volume raises systolic pressure, and backflow into the ventricle drains the aorta in diastole, lowering diastolic pressure: a wide pulse pressure.
Explanation

Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic. In aortic regurgitation both changes widen it, which gives the bounding, rapid-upstroke-and-collapse pulse of this lesion.

  • Systolic ↓ with a narrow pulse pressure is aortic stenosis: a small stroke volume enters the aorta slowly.
  • Diastolic ↑ is wrong: the leaking valve cannot hold aortic pressure up in diastole.
Slides (2)
L46LearningHigh yield
How does mitral stenosis change the pressure–volume loop?
  1. A. Small and shifted right: increased preload, reduced stroke volume
  2. B. Tall and narrower: increased afterload, reduced stroke volume
  3. C. Small and shifted left: reduced preload, reduced stroke volume
AnswerC. Small and shifted left: reduced preload, reduced stroke volume
WhyA narrowed mitral valve obstructs filling, so end-diastolic volume (preload) falls and, by Frank–Starling, stroke volume falls: a small loop shifted left.
Explanation

Blood backs up into the left atrium, whose pressure rises; this pressure is passed back to the pulmonary capillaries, so exertion (faster heart rate, shorter filling time) can bring on pulmonary oedema. The ventricle itself is underfilled and works normally; outflow is unobstructed.

  • Shifted right would mean more filling, the opposite of an inflow obstruction.
  • Tall and narrower is aortic stenosis, an outflow obstruction.
Slides (2)
L47Learning
How does acute mitral regurgitation change the end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes?
  1. A. End-diastolic volume ↓, end-systolic volume ↑ → narrower loop
  2. B. End-diastolic volume ↑, end-systolic volume ↓ → wider loop
  3. C. End-diastolic volume ↑, end-systolic volume ↑ → same width, shifted right
AnswerB. End-diastolic volume ↑, end-systolic volume ↓ → wider loop
WhyRegurgitated blood returns from the atrium in diastole (end-diastolic volume ↑), and the low-pressure escape route lowers afterload (end-systolic volume ↓): a wider loop.
Explanation

The ventricle ejects into two outlets: the aorta and, at low pressure, the left atrium. Emptying is easier, so the ventricle ends systole smaller. The high left atrial pressure then refills it more. Total stroke volume is large, but forward stroke volume into the aorta is reduced, because part goes backward.

  • End-diastolic ↓, end-systolic ↑ describes a weak, underfilled ventricle, not a regurgitant one.
  • Both ↑ with no change in width ignores the reduced afterload.
Slides (2)
L48LearningHigh yield
A pressure–volume loop has lost its vertical contraction side. Which valve is incompetent?
  1. A. Mitral valve
  2. B. Aortic valve
  3. C. Pulmonic valve
AnswerA. Mitral valve
WhyThe contraction side is vertical only while the mitral valve holds; if it leaks, contraction pushes blood back into the atrium and volume falls at once: mitral regurgitation.
Explanation

Match each vertical side to the valve that must seal it:

  • Isovolumetric contraction (right side) depends on a competent mitral valve, because ventricular pressure is rising above atrial pressure.
  • Isovolumetric relaxation (left side) depends on a competent aortic valve, because aortic pressure is above ventricular pressure.

The pulmonic valve belongs to the right ventricle and does not shape the left ventricular loop.

Slides (1)
L49Learning
Which valve lesion produces a systolic murmur?
  1. A. Mitral regurgitation
  2. B. Mitral stenosis
  3. C. Aortic regurgitation
AnswerA. Mitral regurgitation
WhyIn systole blood is forced backward through a leaking mitral valve, making a systolic murmur; aortic stenosis and tricuspid regurgitation are the other classic systolic murmurs.
Explanation

Ask what the valve should be doing in systole: atrioventricular valves should be shut (a leak = regurgitation murmur) and semilunar valves should be open (a narrowing = stenosis murmur). So systolic murmurs are mitral/tricuspid regurgitation and aortic/pulmonic stenosis.

  • Mitral stenosis obstructs flow in diastole, when the mitral valve should be open.
  • Aortic regurgitation leaks in diastole, when the aortic valve should be shut.
Slides (2)
L50Learning
What determines where a heart murmur radiates?
  1. A. The direction of the abnormal blood flow (jet)
  2. B. The position of the cardiac apex
  3. C. The route of the conduction system
AnswerA. The direction of the abnormal blood flow (jet)
WhyA murmur's radiation follows the direction of blood flow: the sound travels with the turbulent jet, e.g. aortic stenosis toward the carotids, mitral regurgitation toward the axilla.
Explanation

A murmur is the sound of turbulent flow, and the vibrations travel along the path of that jet. So the direction the blood is driven sets where the murmur is also heard: aortic stenosis is carried up the ascending aorta into the carotids; mitral regurgitation squirts back and outward into the left atrium and is carried toward the left axilla.

  • The cardiac apex is just one auscultation point (where mitral murmurs are loudest); it does not decide radiation.
  • The conduction system carries electrical activity, not sound; it has nothing to do with murmurs.
Slides (2)

Heart failure on the loop

L51Learning
Systolic heart failure (reduced contractility): how do the loop's volumes change?
  1. A. End-systolic volume ↓, end-diastolic volume ↑, stroke volume and ejection fraction ↑
  2. B. End-systolic volume unchanged, end-diastolic volume ↓, ejection fraction preserved
  3. C. End-systolic volume ↑, end-diastolic volume ↑, stroke volume and ejection fraction ↓
AnswerC. End-systolic volume ↑, end-diastolic volume ↑, stroke volume and ejection fraction ↓
WhyA weak ventricle cannot empty: end-systolic volume rises; venous return is added to that residue, so end-diastolic volume rises too, but less, so stroke volume and ejection fraction fall.
Explanation

The end-systolic line flattens, so ejection ends at a larger volume. The heart leans on Frank–Starling (bigger end-diastolic volume) to hold stroke volume up, but the dilated ventricle has higher wall tension (Laplace) and higher filling pressures, which back up into the left atrium and lungs.

  • End-systolic volume ↓ with ejection fraction ↑ is increased contractility.
  • Normal end-systolic volume, low end-diastolic volume, preserved ejection fraction is diastolic failure.
Slides (3)
L52Learning
A hypertensive man has left ventricular hypertrophy and impaired diastolic filling. What directly impairs the filling?
  1. A. Decreased ventricular contractility
  2. B. Increased ventricular compliance (a floppy, thin wall)
  3. C. Decreased ventricular compliance (a stiff, thick wall)
AnswerC. Decreased ventricular compliance (a stiff, thick wall)
WhyThe hypertrophied wall is stiff (low compliance), so it resists stretch in diastole: filling pressure rises while end-diastolic volume falls.
Explanation

Compliance = change in volume ÷ change in pressure. A thick, stiff ventricle gains little volume for a large rise in pressure: the filling curve along the bottom of the loop is steep. The result is diastolic heart failure: lower end-diastolic volume and stroke volume, a preserved ejection fraction, high left atrial pressure, and often an S4 from the atrium pushing against the stiff wall.

  • Decreased contractility is systolic failure, a problem of emptying, not filling.
  • Increased compliance would make filling easier, not harder.
Slides (3)
L53Learning
Why do aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation both cause dyspnoea?
  1. A. Raised right ventricular pressure backs up into the systemic veins → ↑ peripheral capillary hydrostatic pressure
  2. B. Low plasma oncotic pressure lets fluid leak into the alveoli → ↓ pulmonary capillary oncotic pressure
  3. C. Raised left ventricular filling pressure backs up into the left atrium → ↑ pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure
AnswerC. Raised left ventricular filling pressure backs up into the left atrium → ↑ pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure
WhyBoth lesions load the left ventricle; its high diastolic pressure is passed back to the left atrium and pulmonary capillaries, pushing fluid into the lungs.
Explanation

The pulmonary veins and capillaries drain into the left atrium, so whatever raises left atrial pressure raises pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure. Fluid filters into the interstitium and alveoli (crackles, breathlessness). The same mechanism operates in any failing or overfilled left ventricle.

  • Systemic venous congestion is right-sided failure: leg oedema and raised jugular pressure, not primarily dyspnoea.
  • Low oncotic pressure is a protein problem (liver disease, nephrotic syndrome), not a valve problem.
Slides (1)

PHYS-L24 Cardiac output & venous return (+ clinical cases)

31 learning questions · of 68
Learning questions 31

Venous return equals cardiac output

L1LearningHigh yield
In the steady state, how does venous return compare with cardiac output?
  1. A. Cardiac output is slightly larger than venous return
  2. B. They are equal
  3. C. Venous return is slightly larger than cardiac output
AnswerB. They are equal
WhyThe circulation is one closed loop: the heart can only eject what comes back to it, so in the steady state venous return = cardiac output.
Explanation

Venous return is the blood flowing back into the right atrium per minute; cardiac output is the blood the left ventricle ejects per minute. Because the two pumps and the vessels form one loop, these flows must match once things settle.

  • If cardiac output stayed larger, the heart would pump the veins and atria dry within minutes.
  • If venous return stayed larger, blood would pile up in the veins and atria.

Brief mismatches do happen (for a few beats after standing up), but the Frank–Starling mechanism corrects them: the heart pumps out whatever fills it.

Slides (3)
L2Learning
Trace the lecture's chain from venous return to cardiac output.
  1. A. Venous return → right atrial pressure → left ventricular filling (end-diastolic volume) → stroke volume → × heart rate = cardiac output
  2. B. Venous return → left ventricular filling (end-diastolic volume) → right atrial pressure → stroke volume → × heart rate = cardiac output
  3. C. Venous return → right atrial pressure → stroke volume → left ventricular filling (end-diastolic volume) → × heart rate = cardiac output
AnswerA. Venous return → right atrial pressure → left ventricular filling (end-diastolic volume) → stroke volume → × heart rate = cardiac output
WhyReturning blood raises right atrial pressure, which fills the ventricle (end-diastolic volume); filling sets stroke volume, and stroke volume × heart rate = cardiac output.
Explanation

Each link causes the next:

  • Blood returning from the body raises right atrial pressure, the filling pressure of the heart.
  • That pressure fills the ventricles; what reaches the left ventricle after the lungs is the left ventricular end-diastolic volume (preload). The lecture's motto: you can't empty what you haven't filled.
  • By Frank–Starling, a fuller ventricle ejects a larger stroke volume; × heart rate = cardiac output.

The wrong chains put ventricular filling before the atrial pressure that produces it, or stroke volume before the filling that sets it.

Slides (2)
L3LearningHigh yield
Which of these increases venous return?
  1. A. A Valsalva manoeuvre (straining against a closed glottis)
  2. B. Contraction of the skeletal muscles in the limbs
  3. C. A rise in intrathoracic pressure, as in coughing
AnswerB. Contraction of the skeletal muscles in the limbs
WhyContracting limb muscles squeeze the deep veins, and their one-way valves send the blood towards the heart: the skeletal muscle pump raises venous return.
Explanation

The deep veins of the limbs run between muscles. Each contraction compresses them; the venous valves let blood move only towards the heart, so walking or leg exercise keeps pumping blood back and stops it pooling.

  • A Valsalva manoeuvre raises intrathoracic pressure, which compresses the thoracic veins and the right atrium, so venous return falls.
  • Coughing works the same way: a sharp rise in intrathoracic pressure briefly impedes return.

The opposite, a fall in intrathoracic pressure during inspiration, helps venous return (the respiratory pump).

Slides (1)

The cardiac function curve

L4LearningHigh yield
What does the cardiac function curve show?
  1. A. Higher right atrial pressure (more filling) → higher cardiac output: Frank–Starling as a graph
  2. B. Higher right atrial pressure (more filling) → lower cardiac output: overstretch as a graph
  3. C. Higher right atrial pressure (more back-pressure) → lower venous return: the return curve as a graph
AnswerA. Higher right atrial pressure (more filling) → higher cardiac output: Frank–Starling as a graph
WhyThe cardiac function curve plots left ventricular output against right atrial pressure: more filling stretches the muscle and raises output (Frank–Starling) until it plateaus.
Explanation

The x-axis is right atrial pressure (the filling pressure, a stand-in for end-diastolic volume); the y-axis is cardiac output of the left ventricle. The curve rises steeply because a fuller ventricle starts its contraction from a better sarcomere length, then flattens at about 4 mmHg and 9 L/min.

  • Higher filling → lower output describes a descending limb from overstretch; the lecture's curve does not fall, it plateaus.
  • Higher right atrial pressure → lower venous return is the vascular function curve, the other curve on the same graph.
Slides (3)
L5Learning
At about what right atrial pressure does the cardiac function curve level off, and at what maximum output?
  1. A. About 0 mmHg; about 5 L/min
  2. B. About 7 mmHg; about 5 L/min
  3. C. About 4 mmHg; about 9 L/min
AnswerC. About 4 mmHg; about 9 L/min
WhyIn the lecture the cardiac function curve peaks at a right atrial pressure of about 4 mmHg and a cardiac output of about 9 L/min.
Explanation

Below the plateau, each rise in right atrial pressure fills the ventricle more and raises output. At about 4 mmHg the ventricle is as full as it usefully gets, and output tops out near 9 L/min.

  • 0 mmHg and 5 L/min mixes the left end of the venous return plateau with the normal resting output.
  • 7 mmHg is the mean systemic filling pressure, the x-axis intercept of the vascular curve, and 5 L/min is the normal operating point (right atrial pressure about 2 mmHg).

The textbook figure shows the plateau starting slightly further right (about 5 mmHg); the lecture's numbers are the ones tested.

Slides (2)
L6Learning
A failing heart sits at a high preload with congestion. A positive inotrope is given. Where does the heart move on the stroke volume–preload graph?
  1. A. Further right along the same flat curve: more preload, same stroke volume
  2. B. Up onto a higher curve: more stroke volume at a lower preload
  3. C. Down onto a lower curve: less stroke volume at a higher preload
AnswerB. Up onto a higher curve: more stroke volume at a lower preload
WhyA positive inotrope (or sympathetic stimulation) lifts the heart onto a higher Frank–Starling curve, so it ejects more at a lower preload, relieving congestion.
Explanation

Two different movements:

  • More filling (higher end-diastolic volume) moves the heart along its own curve. On the flat curve of a failing heart this adds congestion but almost no stroke volume.
  • More contractility moves the heart onto another curve. The stronger beat empties the ventricle better, so stroke volume rises while end-diastolic volume and filling pressures fall, which is the arrow on the lecture's graph pointing up and to the left.

A lower curve is what a negative inotrope or worsening failure does.

Slides (2)

The vascular function curve and mean systemic filling pressure

L7LearningHigh yield
What does the vascular function curve show, and which way does it slope?
  1. A. Higher right atrial pressure → more venous return; it slopes upward
  2. B. Higher mean arterial pressure → less venous return; it slopes downward
  3. C. Higher right atrial pressure → less venous return; it slopes downward
AnswerC. Higher right atrial pressure → less venous return; it slopes downward
WhyThe vascular function curve plots venous return against right atrial pressure: a higher atrial pressure leaves a smaller gradient to drive blood back, so it slopes down.
Explanation

Blood returns to the heart down a pressure gradient: from the mean systemic filling pressure in the veins to the right atrial pressure. Raise right atrial pressure and the gradient narrows, so venous return falls; lower it and return rises (the lecture: decreased right atrial pressure increases venous return).

  • Sloping upward describes the cardiac function curve, where higher atrial pressure means more output.
  • Mean arterial pressure is not on the x-axis; both curves share right atrial pressure.
Slides (3)
L8Learning
Why does the vascular function curve go flat at its left end?
  1. A. Right atrial pressure below zero → the arterioles constrict → no further gain in return
  2. B. Right atrial pressure below zero → the great veins collapse → no further gain in return
  3. C. Right atrial pressure equals mean systemic filling pressure → flow stops
AnswerB. Right atrial pressure below zero → the great veins collapse → no further gain in return
WhyWhen right atrial pressure falls below about 0 mmHg, the thin-walled veins entering the chest collapse, so lowering atrial pressure further adds no venous return.
Explanation

On the left side of the graph, right atrial pressure is negative. Lowering it more should widen the gradient, but the veins near the heart are thin-walled and collapse under the negative pressure, which limits flow. Venous return therefore levels off (about 7 L/min in the textbook figure).

  • Arteriolar constriction is not triggered by a low atrial pressure and is not what limits return here.
  • Right atrial pressure equal to mean systemic filling pressure is the right end of the curve, the x-axis intercept, where venous return is zero.
Slides (1)
L9Learning
Where is the mean systemic filling pressure on the vascular function curve?
  1. A. The x-axis intercept
  2. B. The left-hand plateau
  3. C. The y-axis intercept
AnswerA. The x-axis intercept
WhyWhere venous return falls to zero, right atrial pressure has risen to equal mean systemic filling pressure: that point is the x-axis intercept (about 7 mmHg).
Explanation

Venous return stops when there is no gradient left, which is when right atrial pressure equals the mean systemic filling pressure. That is the same situation as a stopped heart, so the x-intercept is the mean systemic filling pressure.

  • The left-hand plateau is where the great veins collapse at negative atrial pressures.
  • The y-axis intercept is venous return at a right atrial pressure of 0 mmHg, a flow, not a pressure.

Tip: a parallel shift of the curve moves the intercept (a change in filling pressure); a rotation keeps it fixed (a change in resistance).

Slides (3)
L10LearningHigh yield
What are the only two things that change mean systemic filling pressure?
  1. A. Blood volume
    Arteriolar resistance (how tightly the arterioles constrict)
  2. B. Heart rate
    Contractility (how hard the ventricle squeezes)
  3. C. Blood volume
    Venous tone (how tightly the veins hold the blood)
AnswerC. Blood volume
Venous tone (how tightly the veins hold the blood)
WhyMean systemic filling pressure depends on how much blood there is (blood volume) and how much of it is stressed, which venous tone (compliance) decides.
Explanation

Mean systemic filling pressure = stressed volume ÷ compliance of the vessels. So it rises when you add blood (transfusion, fluid retention) or when the veins constrict and push unstressed blood into the stressed pool, and it falls with haemorrhage or venodilation.

  • Arteriolar resistance (total peripheral resistance) changes the slope of the vascular curve, not its x-intercept.
  • Heart rate and contractility belong to the pump; they move the cardiac function curve, not the filling pressure.
Slides (3)

Putting the two curves together

L11Learning
Which variable do the cardiac function curve and the vascular function curve share on their x-axis?
  1. A. Mean arterial pressure (effectively the heart's afterload)
  2. B. Total peripheral resistance (effectively the heart's afterload)
  3. C. Right atrial pressure (effectively the heart's filling pressure)
AnswerC. Right atrial pressure (effectively the heart's filling pressure)
WhyBoth curves are drawn against right atrial pressure: for the heart it is the filling pressure that sets output; for the vessels it is the back-pressure that limits return.
Explanation

Because they share the x-axis (and both plot a flow in L/min on the y-axis), the two curves can be drawn on one graph. Right atrial pressure plays opposite roles: a higher value raises cardiac output (more filling) but lowers venous return (less gradient).

  • Mean arterial pressure is the afterload side of the circulation and appears on neither axis.
  • Total peripheral resistance is not an axis at all; changing it moves both curves.
Slides (2)
L12LearningHigh yield
What does the crossing point of the cardiac and vascular function curves represent?
  1. A. The point at which right atrial pressure is zero and flow is maximal
  2. B. The operating point: the heart pumps exactly what the vessels return
  3. C. The mean systemic filling pressure: the pressure with the heart stopped
AnswerB. The operating point: the heart pumps exactly what the vessels return
WhyThe curves cross at the steady-state operating point, the one right atrial pressure at which cardiac output = venous return (normally about 5 L/min at about 2 mmHg).
Explanation

Each curve alone allows many combinations. Only at the intersection do the heart and the vessels agree: the flow the heart pumps out equals the flow the veins bring back, at the same right atrial pressure. Any drug or disease is analysed by asking which curve moves and where the new crossing point lies.

  • Right atrial pressure of zero sits near the vascular curve's plateau, not at the intersection (about +2 mmHg).
  • Mean systemic filling pressure is the vascular curve's x-intercept, where venous return is zero.
Slides (3)

Stressed and unstressed volume

L13Learning
What proportion of the blood volume do the veins hold?
  1. A. About 60%
  2. B. About 15%
  3. C. About 85%
AnswerA. About 60%
WhyThe veins hold about 60% of the blood volume: they are the body's blood reservoir (capacitance vessels).
Explanation

Veins have thin walls and high compliance, so they take up large volumes at low pressure. That makes them the reservoir that venoconstriction can squeeze and venodilators can expand, which is why venous tone matters so much for venous return.

  • About 15% is closer to the share held in the arteries.
  • About 85% overstates it: the heart, lungs, arteries and capillaries together hold the remaining ~40%.

Some textbooks give about 65%; the lecture's figure is 60%.

Slides (2)
L14Learning
Which component holds the largest share of the total blood volume?
  1. A. The stressed volume, which produces blood pressure
  2. B. The unstressed volume, which produces no pressure
  3. C. The capillaries, which have the largest cross-sectional area
AnswerB. The unstressed volume, which produces no pressure
WhyMost of the blood (about 4 of 5 L) is unstressed volume, held at low pressure in the compliant veins.
Explanation

Veins are easily distended and stay distended, so they hold the largest volume at little pressure. That blood is the unstressed volume.

  • The stressed volume sits mainly in the stiffer, elastic arteries. It is small (about 1 L) but makes the blood pressure.
  • The capillaries have the largest total cross-sectional area, but they are short and many are closed at rest, so they hold only about 5–7% of the blood. Area and volume are a classic swap.
Slides (2)
L15LearningHigh yield
How does venoconstriction raise blood pressure?
  1. A. Raises venous compliance → shifts blood into the unstressed volume
  2. B. Raises arteriolar resistance → shifts blood into the unstressed volume
  3. C. Lowers venous compliance → shifts blood into the stressed volume
AnswerC. Lowers venous compliance → shifts blood into the stressed volume
WhyConstricted veins are less compliant, so they hold less blood: blood moves from the unstressed to the stressed volume, and more stressed volume means higher blood pressure.
Explanation

The lecture's chain: venous constriction → decreased compliance → shift of blood to the 'stressed' volume → higher blood pressure. The same shift raises mean systemic filling pressure and venous return, which is how sympathetic venoconstriction supports blood pressure on standing or after a bleed.

  • Raising venous compliance is what a venodilator does; it moves blood the other way and lowers pressure.
  • Arteriolar resistance is set by arterioles, not veins, and it does not move blood into the unstressed pool.
Slides (2)

Inotropes move the cardiac curve

L16LearningHigh yield
More contractility (e.g. a positive inotrope or sympathetic drive): what happens to the curves and the new operating point?
  1. A. Cardiac curve shifts up → higher cardiac output, lower right atrial pressure
  2. B. Cardiac curve shifts up → higher cardiac output, higher right atrial pressure
  3. C. Vascular curve shifts right → higher cardiac output, higher right atrial pressure
AnswerA. Cardiac curve shifts up → higher cardiac output, lower right atrial pressure
WhyA stronger heart ejects more and empties the atrium better: the cardiac curve shifts up, so the new operating point has higher output and lower right atrial pressure.
Explanation

The lecture: positive inotropes increase contractility, stroke volume and cardiac output, 'all leading to decreased right atrial pressure'. On the graph, the raised cardiac curve meets the unchanged vascular curve further up and to the left, and the lower atrial pressure itself widens the gradient for venous return.

  • Higher right atrial pressure would mean the atrium is fuller, which is the opposite of what a stronger pump does.
  • A rightward vascular shift gives higher output and higher atrial pressure, but that is a volume or venous-tone change, not inotropy.
Slides (3)
L17LearningHigh yield
Heart failure or a negative inotrope: what happens to the curves and the new operating point?
  1. A. Cardiac curve shifts down → lower cardiac output, lower right atrial pressure
  2. B. Vascular curve shifts left → lower cardiac output, lower right atrial pressure
  3. C. Cardiac curve shifts down → lower cardiac output, higher right atrial pressure
AnswerC. Cardiac curve shifts down → lower cardiac output, higher right atrial pressure
WhyA weaker heart ejects less and leaves blood behind: the cardiac curve drops, so the operating point has lower output and higher right atrial pressure.
Explanation

The lecture: negative inotropes decrease contractility, stroke volume and cardiac output, 'all leading to increased right atrial pressure'. The lowered cardiac curve crosses the unchanged vascular curve down and to the right. The raised atrial pressure is the back-pressure that causes venous congestion in heart failure.

  • Lower right atrial pressure with a weaker heart would require the atrium to empty better, which it cannot.
  • A leftward vascular shift (lower output and lower atrial pressure) is a haemorrhage or venodilation pattern.

Examples: β-blockers acutely, calcium-channel blockers, myocardial infarction, myocarditis.

Slides (3)

Blood volume and venous tone move the vascular curve

L18LearningHigh yield
More blood volume or venoconstriction: what is the new operating point?
  1. A. Higher cardiac output and higher right atrial pressure
  2. B. Lower cardiac output and higher right atrial pressure
  3. C. Higher cardiac output and lower right atrial pressure
AnswerA. Higher cardiac output and higher right atrial pressure
WhyThe vascular curve shifts right and meets the unchanged cardiac curve further up and to the right: higher cardiac output and higher right atrial pressure.
Explanation

The lecture: increased blood volume → more stressed volume → increase in cardiac output and increase in right atrial pressure; decreased venous compliance does the same. The heart gets more filling and responds by Frank–Starling, so output rises at the cost of a higher filling pressure.

  • Lower output with higher atrial pressure is the heart-failure (negative inotrope) pattern.
  • Higher output with lower atrial pressure is the positive-inotrope pattern.

Hook: on these graphs, cardiac output and right atrial pressure move together when the vascular curve shifts, and in opposite directions when the cardiac curve shifts.

Slides (3)
L19Learning
In heart failure, contractility falls and the kidneys then retain fluid to compensate. How do the curves and the operating point change?
  1. A. Cardiac curve down, vascular curve right → output partly restored, right atrial pressure rises steeply
  2. B. Cardiac curve up, vascular curve left → output rises, right atrial pressure falls
  3. C. Cardiac curve down, vascular curve left → output falls, right atrial pressure falls
AnswerA. Cardiac curve down, vascular curve right → output partly restored, right atrial pressure rises steeply
WhyWeaker pump (cardiac curve down) plus fluid retention (vascular curve right): output is propped up but right atrial pressure rises steeply.
Explanation

The fall in contractility lowers output; the kidneys sense the low output and retain Na+ and water (renin–angiotensin–aldosterone), raising blood volume and mean systemic filling pressure. The rightward vascular shift claws back some output via Frank–Starling, but only at a much higher filling pressure: distended neck veins, an enlarged liver, leg and pulmonary oedema.

  • Cardiac curve up describes treatment with an inotrope, not the disease.
  • Vascular curve left would mean volume loss (a diuretic or a bleed), not retention.
Slides (1)

Total peripheral resistance moves both curves

L20Learning
Which variable moves both the cardiac and the vascular function curves, and what mainly sets it?
  1. A. Contractility; set mainly by sympathetic β1 stimulation
  2. B. Mean systemic filling pressure; set mainly by the veins
  3. C. Total peripheral resistance; set mainly by the arterioles
AnswerC. Total peripheral resistance; set mainly by the arterioles
WhyTotal peripheral resistance, set mainly by the arterioles, moves both curves: as afterload it lowers the cardiac curve; as resistance to flow it rotates the vascular curve.
Explanation

Arterioles are the main resistance vessels, so their tone sets total peripheral resistance. Changing it acts on both sides of the graph at once:

  • On the cardiac side it is afterload: higher resistance → lower curve.
  • On the vascular side it is resistance to flow: higher resistance → the curve rotates down about a fixed x-intercept.

Contractility moves only the cardiac curve. Mean systemic filling pressure moves only the vascular curve (a parallel shift).

Slides (3)
L21Learning
How does a higher total peripheral resistance affect the vascular function curve?
  1. A. Rotates it up about an unchanged x-axis intercept (mean systemic filling pressure)
  2. B. Shifts it right in parallel, raising the x-axis intercept (mean systemic filling pressure)
  3. C. Rotates it down about an unchanged x-axis intercept (mean systemic filling pressure)
AnswerC. Rotates it down about an unchanged x-axis intercept (mean systemic filling pressure)
WhyResistance changes the slope, not the intercept: higher total peripheral resistance rotates the vascular curve down, while mean systemic filling pressure stays the same.
Explanation

Mean systemic filling pressure depends only on blood volume and venous compliance, so arteriolar tone cannot move the x-intercept. What it changes is how much flow a given gradient produces: more resistance, less venous return at every right atrial pressure. The line pivots downward about the same intercept.

  • Rotating up is what a fall in resistance does.
  • A parallel rightward shift is a rise in mean systemic filling pressure (blood volume or venoconstriction), not a resistance change.
Slides (3)
L22Learning
What does a lower total peripheral resistance do to the curves and to cardiac output?
  1. A. Both curves move down → lower cardiac output
  2. B. Both curves move up → higher cardiac output
  3. C. Only the vascular curve moves up → unchanged cardiac output
AnswerB. Both curves move up → higher cardiac output
WhyLower resistance lowers afterload (cardiac curve up) and eases return (vascular curve rotates up), so the crossing point has a higher cardiac output.
Explanation

Both effects push output the same way, so cardiac output and venous return rise, while right atrial pressure stays about the same (the two curves move up together). Examples: exercise (muscle arteriolar dilation), arteriolar vasodilators, an arteriovenous fistula, ACE inhibitors.

  • Both curves down is the pattern for raised resistance.
  • Only the vascular curve up ignores the afterload effect on the heart, and even that alone would raise output, not leave it unchanged.
Slides (2)

Venodilators and venous pooling

L23Learning
Which list matches the lecture's venodilators?
  1. A. Nitrates (nitroglycerin, amyl nitrite)
    Morphine
    Furosemide
    Sildenafil
    Phenylephrine
  2. B. Nitrates (nitroglycerin, amyl nitrite)
    Morphine
    Hydralazine
    Sildenafil
    Prostacyclin
  3. C. Nitrates (nitroglycerin, amyl nitrite)
    Morphine
    Furosemide
    Sildenafil
    Prostacyclin
AnswerC. Nitrates (nitroglycerin, amyl nitrite)
Morphine
Furosemide
Sildenafil
Prostacyclin
WhyThe lecture's venodilators: nitrates (nitroglycerin, amyl nitrite), morphine, furosemide, sildenafil (nitric oxide pathway) and prostacyclin.
Explanation

All of them raise venous compliance, so blood pools in the veins as unstressed volume and preload falls. Nitrates and sildenafil both work through nitric oxide and cGMP; morphine and intravenous furosemide venodilate within minutes, before any diuresis, which is why they are used in acute pulmonary oedema.

  • Phenylephrine is an α1 agonist: it constricts veins and arterioles.
  • Hydralazine dilates arterioles, not veins; it lowers afterload, not unstressed volume.
Slides (1)
L24Learning
Sublingual nitroglycerin relieves exertional angina within minutes. What is its main mechanism?
  1. A. Positive inotropy → stronger contraction → more coronary flow
  2. B. Venodilation → lower preload → lower myocardial O2 demand
  3. C. Platelet inhibition → the coronary clot dissolves → flow is restored
AnswerB. Venodilation → lower preload → lower myocardial O2 demand
WhyNitroglycerin is mainly a venodilator: blood pools in the veins, preload falls, the ventricle is smaller and its wall tension and O2 demand drop.
Explanation

Exertional angina is a supply–demand mismatch across a fixed narrowing. By raising unstressed volume, nitroglycerin lowers end-diastolic volume; by Laplace's law a smaller ventricle has less wall tension, so it needs less O2. (At higher doses it also dilates arterioles and large coronary arteries, but the preload effect dominates.)

  • Nitroglycerin is not an inotrope; a stronger contraction would raise O2 demand.
  • It has no meaningful antiplatelet or clot-dissolving action; that is aspirin and thrombolytics.
Slides (2)
L25Learning
Which set of findings fits acute pulmonary oedema?
  1. A. Sudden breathlessness
    Rales
    Oedema
    S3 gallop
  2. B. Sudden chest pain
    Rales
    Cyanosis
    Pericardial rub
  3. C. Sudden breathlessness
    Wheeze
    Clubbing
    S4 gallop
AnswerA. Sudden breathlessness
Rales
Oedema
S3 gallop
WhyAcute pulmonary oedema: sudden shortness of breath, rales (crackles), oedema and an S3 gallop; the patient needs volume removed from the lungs fast.
Explanation

A failing left ventricle cannot clear the pulmonary venous return, so left atrial and pulmonary capillary pressures rise and fluid floods the alveoli. Rales are the crackles of fluid-filled alveoli; the S3 is rapid filling of an overfull, dilated ventricle; orthopnoea and peripheral oedema often accompany it.

  • Pericardial rub points to pericarditis, and sudden chest pain to ischaemia or pericarditis rather than to the oedema itself.
  • Clubbing takes months to develop and wheeze is airway narrowing; an S4 is atrial kick into a stiff ventricle.
Slides (1)
L26Learning
In acute pulmonary oedema, what do a venodilator and a diuretic each do with the excess volume?
  1. A. Venodilator moves it into the stressed volume; diuretic adds to it
  2. B. Venodilator parks it in the unstressed volume; diuretic removes it from the body
  3. C. Venodilator removes it from the body; diuretic parks it in the unstressed volume
AnswerB. Venodilator parks it in the unstressed volume; diuretic removes it from the body
WhyA venodilator moves blood into the compliant veins (↑ unstressed volume) within minutes; a diuretic then removes volume through the kidneys.
Explanation

The goal is to get volume out of the lungs fast. Venodilation shifts the vascular curve left: venous return, right atrial pressure and pulmonary pressures fall, though the blood is still in the body, just parked. A diuretic actually lowers total blood volume, which takes longer (furosemide also venodilates early).

  • Moving blood into the stressed volume would raise venous return and worsen congestion.
  • The third choice swaps the two roles.
Slides (2)
L27LearningHigh yield
A recruit stands motionless at attention for over an hour and becomes lightheaded and tachycardic. What is the mechanism?
  1. A. No leg-muscle pump → arterioles in the legs dilate → total peripheral resistance falls → reflex bradycardia
  2. B. No leg-muscle pump → blood pools in the leg veins → venous return and output fall → reflex tachycardia
  3. C. Leg muscles contract continuously → venous return rises → output rises → reflex tachycardia
AnswerB. No leg-muscle pump → blood pools in the leg veins → venous return and output fall → reflex tachycardia
WhyStanding still removes the muscle pump: blood fills the leg veins (↑ venous capacitance) → ↓ venous return and output → ↓ blood pressure → baroreceptor-driven tachycardia.
Explanation

Gravity plus motionless legs let blood accumulate in the veins as unstressed volume. Less blood returns, so by Frank–Starling cardiac output falls, blood pressure and cerebral perfusion drop (lightheadedness), and the carotid baroreceptors fire less, triggering sympathetic tachycardia. The same mechanism causes orthostatic syncope on standing up quickly.

  • Arteriolar dilation is not the cause, and the reflex response is tachycardia, not bradycardia.
  • Continuously contracting leg muscles would help venous return, not reduce it.
Slides (3)

Drugs on the curves

L28LearningHigh yield
On the lecture's combined-curve graph, a diuretic is given. What happens to the curves and the operating point?
  1. A. Less blood volume → vascular curve shifts right → higher output, higher right atrial pressure
  2. B. Less blood volume → vascular curve shifts left → lower output, lower right atrial pressure
  3. C. Less blood volume → cardiac curve drops → lower output, higher right atrial pressure
AnswerB. Less blood volume → vascular curve shifts left → lower output, lower right atrial pressure
WhyA diuretic lowers blood volume and mean systemic filling pressure: the vascular curve shifts left, giving lower output and lower right atrial pressure.
Explanation

On the lecture's drill (start at point C), the diuretic answer is point B: the crossing of the same cardiac curve with the next vascular curve to the left, down and to the left of C. The red arrow on the drill graph marks that intersection.

  • A rightward shift is what adding volume does.
  • A drop of the cardiac curve needs a loss of contractility; a diuretic does not weaken the heart.
DrugCurvePoint from C
DiureticVascular leftB
ACE inhibitor, ARBTotal peripheral resistance ↓D
Digoxin, dobutamineCardiac upE
Slides (2)
L29LearningHigh yield
In congestive heart failure, why can the β1-blocker metoprolol raise cardiac output even though it slows the heart?
  1. A. A larger stroke volume more than offsets the slower rate
  2. B. A smaller stroke volume lowers the oxygen cost of each beat
  3. C. A faster heart rate more than offsets the smaller stroke volume
AnswerA. A larger stroke volume more than offsets the slower rate
WhyCardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate; in heart failure metoprolol lets the ventricle fill and eject better, so the larger stroke volume outweighs the lower rate.
Explanation

A slower heart has longer diastoles, so the ventricle fills more (Frank–Starling) and the coronaries perfuse longer. Over weeks, blocking chronic sympathetic overdrive also lets the failing myocardium recover and remodel less. Stroke volume rises enough that cardiac output goes up despite the lower rate.

  • A smaller stroke volume with a slower rate could only lower output.
  • Metoprolol slows the heart; a faster rate is the opposite of its action.

In a normal heart, a β-blocker lowers cardiac output; the paradox is specific to chronic heart failure.

Slides (1)

Measuring cardiac output (Fick)

L30Learning
By the Fick principle, how is cardiac output calculated from oxygen?
  1. A. Cardiac output = O2 consumption per minute × arteriovenous O2 content difference
  2. B. Cardiac output = arteriovenous O2 content difference ÷ O2 consumption per minute
  3. C. Cardiac output = O2 consumption per minute ÷ arteriovenous O2 content difference
AnswerC. Cardiac output = O2 consumption per minute ÷ arteriovenous O2 content difference
WhyAll the O2 the body uses must be delivered by blood, so cardiac output = O2 consumption ÷ (arterial − mixed venous O2 content).
Explanation

Conservation of mass: each litre of blood gives up (arterial − venous) mL of O2 to the tissues. Dividing the total O2 consumed per minute by what each litre gives up gives the litres that must have flowed per minute. Arterial content is measured in pulmonary vein (or any systemic arterial) blood; mixed venous content in pulmonary artery blood.

  • Multiplying gives meaningless units (mL O2/min × mL O2/mL blood), not a flow in mL blood/min.
  • The inverted ratio gives the reciprocal of flow: it would fall as output rises.
Slides (3)
L31Learning
At a fixed O2 consumption, what does a wide arteriovenous O2 difference indicate?
  1. A. High cardiac output
  2. B. Low O2 consumption
  3. C. Low cardiac output
AnswerC. Low cardiac output
WhyIf the tissues take more O2 out of each litre while using the same total, fewer litres must be flowing: a wide arteriovenous difference means low cardiac output.
Explanation

Rearranged Fick: arteriovenous difference = O2 consumption ÷ cardiac output. When output falls (heart failure, shock), blood moves slowly through the tissues, each litre gives up more O2, and mixed venous O2 content drops. A falling mixed venous saturation is therefore a bedside warning of low output.

  • High cardiac output narrows the difference: blood passes quickly and gives up less.
  • Low O2 consumption would also narrow it, and the stem holds consumption fixed.
Slides (1)

PHYS-L25 Regulation of arterial pressure

36 learning questions · of 77
Learning questions 36

Mean arterial pressure and its two controllers

L1LearningHigh yield
Give the equation for mean arterial pressure in terms of cardiac output and resistance.
  1. A. MAP = cardiac output (CO) × total peripheral resistance (TPR)
  2. B. MAP = cardiac output (CO) ÷ total peripheral resistance (TPR)
  3. C. MAP = stroke volume (SV) × total peripheral resistance (TPR)
AnswerA. MAP = cardiac output (CO) × total peripheral resistance (TPR)
WhyPressure = flow × resistance, so MAP = CO × TPR: every pressure reflex works by changing cardiac output, resistance, or both.
Explanation

This is Ohm's law (ΔP = Q × R) applied to the whole systemic circulation: the pressure drop from aorta to right atrium (≈ MAP, since right atrial pressure is near zero) equals cardiac output times total peripheral resistance. It tells you the only two levers the body has: raise CO (heart rate, contractility, venous return) or raise TPR (arteriolar constriction).

  • CO ÷ TPR inverts the relation: more resistance would then lower pressure, which is the opposite of what arteriolar constriction does.
  • SV × TPR drops heart rate: flow per minute is SV × heart rate, so stroke volume alone is not the flow term.
Slides (3)
L2LearningHigh yield
Give the equation for mean arterial pressure from systolic and diastolic pressure.
  1. A. MAP = diastolic + ½ pulse pressure (systolic − diastolic)
  2. B. MAP = systolic − ⅓ pulse pressure (systolic − diastolic)
  3. C. MAP = diastolic + ⅓ pulse pressure (systolic − diastolic)
AnswerC. MAP = diastolic + ⅓ pulse pressure (systolic − diastolic)
WhyAt rest the heart spends about two-thirds of each cycle in diastole, so MAP sits closer to diastolic: diastolic + ⅓ pulse pressure.
Explanation

Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic pressure, the rise produced by each ejection. Because diastole lasts about twice as long as systole at resting heart rates, the time-weighted average lies one-third of the way up from diastolic, not halfway.

  • Diastolic + ½ pulse pressure is the simple arithmetic mean of systolic and diastolic; it would only be right if systole and diastole lasted equally long.
  • Systolic − ⅓ pulse pressure puts MAP two-thirds of the way up, too close to systolic.

At fast heart rates diastole shortens, so the true MAP drifts toward the arithmetic mean.

Slides (3)
L3LearningHigh yield
Why does doubling cardiac output not double mean arterial pressure?
  1. A. Heart rate falls whenever CO rises, so CO can never truly double
  2. B. CO and TPR are independent: TPR is fixed by vessel anatomy and cannot change
  3. C. CO and TPR are not independent: when one changes, the other tends to move the opposite way
AnswerC. CO and TPR are not independent: when one changes, the other tends to move the opposite way
WhyCO and TPR are linked: when one rises, the other tends to fall, so MAP = CO × TPR changes far less than either factor alone.
Explanation

The equation MAP = CO × TPR looks as if doubling one factor must double MAP, but the two factors are not independent variables. When cardiac output rises, the higher pressure loads the baroreceptors, which withdraw sympathetic tone, so arterioles dilate and TPR falls (in exercise, metabolic vasodilation in muscle lowers TPR further); when TPR rises, venous return and cardiac output tend to fall. The result: 2 × CO ≠ 2 × MAP and 2 × TPR ≠ 2 × MAP.

  • Heart rate falls whenever CO rises is wrong: in exercise both rise together, and CO can more than double.
  • TPR is fixed by anatomy is wrong: arteriolar tone changes TPR minute to minute; it is the most adjustable term in the equation.
Slides (2)
L4LearningHigh yield
What are the body's fast and slow systems for holding blood pressure steady?
  1. A. Fast: baroreceptor reflex (hours)
    Slow: renin-angiotensin-aldosterone (weeks to months)
  2. B. Fast: baroreceptor reflex (seconds)
    Slow: renin-angiotensin-aldosterone (hours to days)
  3. C. Fast: renin-angiotensin-aldosterone (seconds)
    Slow: baroreceptor reflex (hours to days)
AnswerB. Fast: baroreceptor reflex (seconds)
Slow: renin-angiotensin-aldosterone (hours to days)
WhyThe baroreceptor reflex is neural and acts within seconds; the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) is hormonal and acts over hours to days.
Explanation

The baroreceptor reflex is a nerve arc (stretch receptors → cranial nerves IX and X → medulla → autonomic nerves to heart and vessels), so it corrects a pressure change within a beat or two. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is a hormone cascade: renin must be released, angiotensin II formed, aldosterone synthesised and the kidney must retain salt and water, so its full effect takes hours to days.

  • Baroreflex in hours, RAAS in weeks stretches both timescales: a nerve reflex is not slow, and aldosterone acts within days.
  • RAAS fast, baroreflex slow swaps the two systems.
Slides (2)
L5LearningHigh yield
By what main lever does each system correct arterial pressure?
  1. A. Baroreceptor reflex: heart rate, contractility and vessel tone
    RAAS: mainly blood volume
  2. B. Baroreceptor reflex: blood volume
    RAAS: heart rate and vessel tone
  3. C. Baroreceptor reflex: blood volume
