    RAAS: blood volume as well
AnswerA. Baroreceptor reflex: heart rate, contractility and vessel tone
RAAS: mainly blood volume
WhyThe baroreflex changes heart rate, contractility and vessel tone; the RAAS works mainly by changing blood volume (salt and water retention).
Explanation

The baroreflex acts on the two terms of MAP = CO × TPR directly: heart rate and contractility (cardiac output) and arteriolar and venous tone (resistance and venous return). The RAAS has one fast effect (angiotensin II vasoconstriction) but its main, lasting effect is on extracellular fluid volume: angiotensin II and aldosterone make the kidney retain Na+, water follows, and blood volume rises.

  • Baroreflex → volume is wrong: nerves cannot add or remove fluid within seconds.
  • Both → volume ignores that the baroreflex works through the autonomic nerves to heart and vessels.
Slides (2)

Baroreceptors: where they are and what they sense

L6LearningHigh yield
Where are the arterial baroreceptors?
  1. A. Carotid body
    Aortic body
  2. B. Carotid sinus
    Aortic arch
  3. C. Carotid sinus
    Right atrium
AnswerB. Carotid sinus
Aortic arch
WhyThe arterial baroreceptors sit in the walls of the carotid sinus and the aortic arch, guarding the pressure that reaches the brain.
Explanation

Baroreceptors are stretch-sensitive nerve endings in the walls of two high-pressure sites: the carotid sinus (a bulge at the start of the internal carotid artery, at the bifurcation of the common carotid) and the aortic arch.

  • Carotid body and aortic body are the peripheral chemoreceptors: small nodules of glomus cells that sense O2, CO2 and pH, sitting near the baroreceptor sites but not in the vessel wall.
  • Right atrium holds low-pressure (cardiopulmonary) stretch receptors that sense filling volume, not arterial pressure.
Slides (2)
L7LearningHigh yield
How does baroreceptor firing change with arterial pressure?
  1. A. Pressure ↑ → more stretch → less firing
    Pressure ↓ → more firing
  2. B. Pressure ↑ → less stretch → more firing
    Pressure ↓ → less firing
  3. C. Pressure ↑ → more stretch → more firing
    Pressure ↓ → less firing
AnswerC. Pressure ↑ → more stretch → more firing
Pressure ↓ → less firing
WhyMore pressure stretches the wall more, so baroreceptors fire faster; a fall in pressure slows their firing.
Explanation

Baroreceptors fire continuously (they are tonically active) at normal pressure. Their firing rate follows an S-shaped curve against mean arterial pressure, steepest around the normal value of about 100 mmHg, which is where they are most sensitive. A rise in pressure increases firing; a fall decreases it, and the brain reads both directions.

  • Pressure ↑ → less firing reverses the relation; it is the most common slip on reflex questions (on standing, firing slows).
  • Pressure ↑ → less stretch is physically wrong: higher pressure always distends the wall more.
Slides (1)
L8Learning
Two pressure rises reach the same peak, one quickly and one slowly. Which makes the carotid sinus fire more?
  1. A. The one that rises slowly
  2. B. The one that rises quickly
  3. C. Neither: firing depends only on the peak pressure
AnswerB. The one that rises quickly
WhyBaroreceptors sense both the absolute pressure and its rate of change: a faster rise gives more firing.
Explanation

Baroreceptor endings respond to the level of stretch and, more strongly, to how fast the stretch changes. A rapid rise in pressure produces a burst of firing larger than the same rise reached slowly. This makes the reflex good at catching sudden changes, such as standing up or a sudden bleed.

  • The slow rise gives less firing, not more; slow changes allow the endings partly to adapt.
  • Only the peak matters ignores the rate-of-change sensitivity.

The same property explains why baroreceptors adapt to a sustained high pressure and reset in chronic hypertension.

Slides (3)
L9LearningHigh yield
Which arterial pressure changes do the carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors mainly respond to?
  1. A. Carotid sinus: increases and decreases
    Aortic arch: mainly increases
  2. B. Carotid sinus: mainly increases
    Aortic arch: increases and decreases
  3. C. Carotid sinus: mainly decreases
    Aortic arch: mainly increases
AnswerA. Carotid sinus: increases and decreases
Aortic arch: mainly increases
WhyThe carotid sinus reports pressure changes in both directions; the aortic arch responds mainly to rises in pressure.
Explanation

Carotid sinus receptors fire at normal pressure, so they can signal a fall (less firing) as well as a rise (more firing). Aortic arch receptors have a higher threshold and respond chiefly to increases. This is why the carotid sinus is the main sensor for a sudden fall, as on standing or in haemorrhage.

  • Carotid mainly increases, aortic both swaps the two sites.
  • Carotid mainly decreases is wrong: a rise in carotid pressure clearly increases firing (that is how carotid massage works).
Slides (1)
L10LearningHigh yield
What happens to the baroreceptors in chronic hypertension?
  1. A. They degenerate and stop firing altogether
  2. B. They reset to defend the new, higher pressure
  3. C. They reset to defend a new, lower pressure
AnswerB. They reset to defend the new, higher pressure
WhyOver days the baroreceptors reset to the higher pressure and become less sensitive, so the reflex then defends the hypertension instead of correcting it.
Explanation

The baroreflex corrects an acute rise within seconds, but if pressure stays high, the receptors adapt: within a day or two their operating range shifts so that the new pressure reads as "normal", and the brainstem set point effectively rises with it. Their sensitivity to changes around the old set point is also reduced. The reflex therefore cannot be the long-term controller of pressure; that job falls to the kidney and the RAAS.

  • They stop firing is wrong: they keep firing and still buffer short-term swings, just around the new level.
  • Reset lower is the wrong direction: resetting follows the sustained pressure upward.
Slides (2)

The reflex pathway: nerves and medullary centres

L11LearningHigh yield
Which nerves carry carotid sinus baroreceptor signals to the medulla?
  1. A. Carotid sinus nerve (Hering's nerve) → glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
  2. B. Carotid sinus nerve (Hering's nerve) → vagus nerve (CN X)
  3. C. Carotid sinus nerve (Hering's nerve) → hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
AnswerA. Carotid sinus nerve (Hering's nerve) → glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
WhyCarotid sinus afferents run in Hering's nerve, a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), to the medulla. Carotid = nine.
Explanation

The carotid sinus nerve (Hering's nerve) leaves the sinus wall and joins the glossopharyngeal nerve, which enters the medulla and ends in the nucleus tractus solitarius.

  • Vagus (CN X) carries the aortic arch baroreceptors, not the carotid ones; mixing up IX and X is the most-tested slip.
  • Hypoglossal (CN XII) crosses near the carotid bifurcation but is purely motor to the tongue.

Hook: the carotid sinus is higher up in the neck, the aorta is lower; IX comes before X.

Slides (2)
L12LearningHigh yield
Which medullary nucleus receives baroreceptor input?
  1. A. Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
  2. B. Rostral ventrolateral medulla
  3. C. Nucleus of the solitary tract (nucleus tractus solitarius)
AnswerC. Nucleus of the solitary tract (nucleus tractus solitarius)
WhyBoth CN IX and CN X baroreceptor fibres end in the nucleus tractus solitarius, the medulla's main input station for visceral sensation.
Explanation

The nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) is the sensory relay in the dorsal medulla. It reads the baroreceptor firing rate and then excites the parasympathetic (cardiac decelerator) neurons and inhibits the sympathetic (cardiac accelerator and vasoconstrictor) neurons.

  • Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus is an output nucleus: it sends parasympathetic fibres out, it does not receive the afferent input.
  • Rostral ventrolateral medulla is the sympathetic vasoconstrictor (C1) area, which the NTS inhibits; it is downstream, not the first stop.
Slides (2)
L13Learning
Name the three medullary centres of the baroreceptor reflex and their outflow.
  1. A. Cardiac decelerator (cardioinhibitory) → sympathetic
    Cardiac accelerator → vagus to heart
    Vasoconstrictor (C1) → sympathetic
  2. B. Cardiac decelerator (cardioinhibitory) → vagus to heart
    Cardiac accelerator → sympathetic
    Vasoconstrictor (C1) → vagus to vessels
  3. C. Cardiac decelerator (cardioinhibitory) → vagus to heart
    Cardiac accelerator → sympathetic
    Vasoconstrictor (C1) → sympathetic
AnswerC. Cardiac decelerator (cardioinhibitory) → vagus to heart
Cardiac accelerator → sympathetic
Vasoconstrictor (C1) → sympathetic
WhyCardiac decelerator = parasympathetic (vagus); cardiac accelerator and vasoconstrictor (C1) = sympathetic. The nucleus tractus solitarius excites the decelerator and inhibits the other two.
Explanation

The vasomotor area of the medulla has three functional centres:

  • Cardiac decelerator (cardioinhibitory): vagal output to the SA node, slowing the heart.
  • Cardiac accelerator: sympathetic output to the SA node and myocardium (β1), raising heart rate and contractility.
  • Vasoconstrictor (C1 area): sympathetic output to arterioles and veins (α1).

The wrong choices swap the outflows: the accelerator is never vagal, and the vagus does not supply vessel smooth muscle (blood vessels receive sympathetic fibres only).

Slides (2)

Reflex responses: pressure falls, pressure rises

L14LearningHigh yield
Name the four effector responses to a fall in arterial pressure, with their receptors.
  1. A. Heart rate ↑ (β1)
    Contractility ↑ (β1)
    Arterioles and veins constrict (α1)
    Renin ↑ (β1)
  2. B. Heart rate ↑ (β1)
    Contractility ↑ (α1)
    Arterioles and veins constrict (β2)
    Renin ↑ (α1)
  3. C. Heart rate ↑ (β2)
    Contractility ↑ (β1)
    Arterioles and veins constrict (α2)
    Renin ↑ (β1)
AnswerA. Heart rate ↑ (β1)
Contractility ↑ (β1)
Arterioles and veins constrict (α1)
Renin ↑ (β1)
WhySympathetic norepinephrine raises heart rate, contractility and renin via β1 and constricts arterioles and veins via α1.
Explanation

When pressure falls, the sympathetic surge acts on four targets:

  • SA node (β1): faster heart rate.
  • Ventricular muscle (β1): stronger contraction.
  • Arterioles (α1): constriction, ↑ TPR; veins (α1): constriction, ↓ unstressed volume, ↑ venous return.
  • Juxtaglomerular cells (β1): renin release, starting the slow RAAS arm.

The wrong choices move single receptors: β2 dilates vessels, α2 is mainly presynaptic, and α1 does not drive contractility or renin. Hook: "β1 = heart and kidney, α1 = vessels".

Slides (3)
L15LearningHigh yield
What does the baroreceptor reflex do when arterial pressure rises?
  1. A. Receptors fire more → ↓ vagal, ↑ sympathetic → heart rate and contractility ↑; arterioles and veins constrict
  2. B. Receptors fire less → ↑ vagal, ↓ sympathetic → heart rate and contractility ↓; arterioles and veins dilate
  3. C. Receptors fire more → ↑ vagal, ↓ sympathetic → heart rate and contractility ↓; arterioles and veins dilate
AnswerC. Receptors fire more → ↑ vagal, ↓ sympathetic → heart rate and contractility ↓; arterioles and veins dilate
WhyHigh pressure → more firing → ↑ vagal (ACh), ↓ sympathetic → slower, weaker heart and dilated arterioles and veins → ↓ CO and ↓ TPR.
Explanation

The sequence: more stretch of the carotid sinus and aortic arch → more firing up CN IX and X → nucleus tractus solitarius → cardiac decelerator excited, cardiac accelerator and vasoconstrictor centres inhibited. Result: heart rate and contractility fall (↓ cardiac output), arterioles dilate (↓ TPR) and veins dilate (more blood held in the veins, ↓ venous return). Pressure falls back toward the set point.

  • ↓ Vagal, ↑ sympathetic is the response to a fall in pressure.
  • Receptors fire less gets the sensing step wrong: a pressure rise always increases firing.
Slides (2)
L16LearningHigh yield
When arterial pressure rises, what mainly lowers ventricular contractility?
  1. A. More vagal (acetylcholine) drive to the ventricles
  2. B. Less sympathetic (β1) drive to the ventricles
  3. C. Less vagal drive to the ventricles
AnswerB. Less sympathetic (β1) drive to the ventricles
WhyVentricular contractility is set by sympathetic β1 tone; the reflex lowers it by withdrawing sympathetic drive. The vagus mainly slows the SA node.
Explanation

Vagal fibres end chiefly on the SA node, the AV node and the atria; the ventricles receive very little parasympathetic innervation. So the two limbs divide the work: more vagal tone slows heart rate, while less sympathetic tone weakens ventricular contraction (less β1 → less cAMP → less Ca2+ entry). Together they lower cardiac output.

  • More vagal drive to the ventricles overstates the vagal role: acetylcholine reduces atrial contractility only.
  • Less vagal drive is the direction for a pressure fall.
Slides (2)

The baroreflex in action: posture, bleeding, drugs

L17LearningHigh yield
Why does standing up not normally make you faint?
  1. A. Blood pools in the legs → venous return and pressure dip → baroreceptors fire less → sympathetic response within seconds
  2. B. Blood shifts to the chest → venous return and pressure dip → chemoreceptors fire → sympathetic response within minutes
  3. C. Blood pools in the legs → venous return and pressure dip → renin-angiotensin-aldosterone restores pressure within seconds
AnswerA. Blood pools in the legs → venous return and pressure dip → baroreceptors fire less → sympathetic response within seconds
WhyOn standing, about half a litre pools in the legs; the dip in pressure unloads the baroreceptors, and the sympathetic response restores pressure within seconds.
Explanation

Gravity pools blood in the leg veins → venous return, stroke volume and arterial pressure fall → carotid sinus stretch and firing decrease → sympathetic outflow rises and vagal tone falls → heart rate, contractility, arteriolar and venous constriction all increase → pressure recovers before the brain is underperfused.

  • Blood shifts to the chest is the supine direction, and chemoreceptors are not the posture sensors.
  • RAAS within seconds is too fast for a hormone cascade; renin does rise on standing, but it supports pressure only later.
Slides (3)
L18LearningHigh yield
In an experiment, the common carotid artery is partly tied off below the carotid sinus. Which set of changes follows?
  1. A. Sympathetic activity ↑, renal blood flow ↑, TPR ↑
  2. B. Sympathetic activity ↑, renal blood flow ↓, TPR ↑
  3. C. Sympathetic activity ↓, renal blood flow ↑, TPR ↓
AnswerB. Sympathetic activity ↑, renal blood flow ↓, TPR ↑
WhyLower pressure at the sinus reads as hypotension → sympathetic ↑ → renal and other arterioles constrict → renal flow ↓, TPR ↑.
Explanation

The baroreceptors only know the pressure in their own wall. Tightening the carotid artery upstream lowers the pressure reaching the sinus, so firing falls even though systemic pressure is normal. The medulla responds as if there were a haemorrhage: sympathetic activity rises, arterioles constrict throughout the body (including the kidney), TPR rises and systemic pressure goes up.

  • Renal blood flow ↑ is wrong: sympathetic α1 constriction of renal arterioles reduces renal flow.
  • Sympathetic ↓ is the response to more stretch, as in carotid massage.
Slides (1)
L19Learning
What causes orthostatic hypotension?
  1. A. An overactive baroreflex arc: excess sympathetic tone, or a drug boosting the vessels' ability to respond
  2. B. An overactive renin-angiotensin arc: excess renin, or a drug boosting angiotensin II formation
  3. C. A broken baroreflex arc: autonomic neuropathy, or a drug blocking the vessels' ability to respond
AnswerC. A broken baroreflex arc: autonomic neuropathy, or a drug blocking the vessels' ability to respond
WhyOrthostatic hypotension means the baroreflex arc fails: damaged autonomic nerves (diabetes, sympathectomy) or drugs such as α1 blockers stop the sympathetic response to standing.
Explanation

On standing, pressure dips in everyone; it normally recovers within seconds because the baroreflex raises sympathetic outflow. If any part of the arc is broken, the dip persists and the person becomes light-headed or faints. Causes:

  • Sensor/nerve damage: diabetic or age-related autonomic neuropathy, surgical sympathectomy.
  • Effector blockade: α1 blockers, venodilators, some antihypertensives.
  • Low blood volume (dehydration, bleeding) also contributes.

The wrong choices describe overactive pressor systems (sympathetic or renin-angiotensin), which would raise, not drop, pressure on standing.

Slides (2)
L20LearningHigh yield
During a phenylephrine (α1 agonist) infusion, blood pressure rises and the heart rate falls. What causes the fall in heart rate?
  1. A. Baroreceptor reflex → increased vagal tone to the SA node
  2. B. Direct α1 inhibition of the SA node
  3. C. Direct β1 blockade by phenylephrine
AnswerA. Baroreceptor reflex → increased vagal tone to the SA node
WhyPhenylephrine constricts arterioles → ↑ MAP → more baroreceptor firing → ↑ vagal, ↓ sympathetic outflow → reflex bradycardia.
Explanation

Phenylephrine acts on vascular α1 receptors only. The rise in TPR raises pressure, the carotid sinus and aortic arch fire faster, and the medulla increases acetylcholine release at the SA node. The slowing is entirely reflex: if the vagus is blocked with atropine, the bradycardia disappears.

  • Direct α1 action on the SA node: the pacemaker is driven by β1 and M2 receptors, not α1.
  • β1 blockade: phenylephrine is not a β antagonist.

Rule: whatever a drug does to mean pressure, the baroreflex pushes heart rate the other way unless the arc is blocked.

Slides (2)

Valsalva manoeuvre and carotid sinus massage

L21LearningHigh yield
Trace the Valsalva manoeuvre from intrathoracic pressure to heart rate.
  1. A. ↑ Intrathoracic pressure → great veins compressed → venous return ↓ → cardiac output and arterial pressure ↑ → carotid baroreceptors → tachycardia
  2. B. ↑ Intrathoracic pressure → great veins compressed → venous return ↓ → cardiac output and arterial pressure ↓ → carotid baroreceptors → tachycardia
  3. C. ↓ Intrathoracic pressure → great veins compressed → venous return ↓ → cardiac output and arterial pressure ↓ → carotid baroreceptors → bradycardia
AnswerB. ↑ Intrathoracic pressure → great veins compressed → venous return ↓ → cardiac output and arterial pressure ↓ → carotid baroreceptors → tachycardia
WhyValsalva: ↑ chest pressure → ↓ venous return → ↓ CO and BP → carotid baroreceptors fire less → sympathetic tachycardia.
Explanation

The full chain during the strain: forced expiration against a closed glottis raises intrathoracic pressure → venae cavae compressed → venous return and preload fall → stroke volume and cardiac output fall → arterial pressure falls → carotid sinus firing falls (signal up CN IX) → medulla raises sympathetic and lowers vagal outflow → heart rate rises and vessels constrict.

  • Arterial pressure ↑ is wrong once venous return has fallen; less blood in means less pressure out.
  • ↓ Intrathoracic pressure describes inspiration, not straining, and bradycardia is the response to a pressure rise.

The manoeuvre is a bedside test of the whole baroreflex arc.

Slides (3)
L22Learning
When the Valsalva strain is released, what happens to heart rate?
  1. A. It slows, as rebounding venous return overshoots pressure in the still-constricted vessels
  2. B. It rises further as venous return falls again
  3. C. It stays high until the next strain
AnswerA. It slows, as rebounding venous return overshoots pressure in the still-constricted vessels
WhyOn release, venous return rushes back into a still-constricted circulation; pressure overshoots, the baroreceptors fire hard and a reflex bradycardia follows.
Explanation

During the strain the sympathetic system raised heart rate and constricted arterioles. When the glottis opens, intrathoracic pressure falls, the dammed-up venous blood returns, stroke volume jumps and is ejected into vessels that are still narrowed, so arterial pressure briefly rises above baseline. More stretch of the carotid sinus → more vagal outflow → heart rate slows below baseline, then everything settles.

  • Rises further gets the venous return direction wrong: release restores it.
  • Stays high ignores the reflex response to the overshoot.

A normal response (tachycardia during strain, bradycardia after release) shows an intact baroreflex arc.

Slides (1)
L23Learning
What does the Valsalva manoeuvre do to most heart murmurs?
  1. A. Makes them quieter (less blood moving through the heart)
  2. B. Makes them louder (more blood moving through the heart)
  3. C. Makes them louder (higher intrathoracic pressure)
AnswerA. Makes them quieter (less blood moving through the heart)
WhyValsalva cuts venous return, so less blood flows across the valves and most murmurs soften.
Explanation

Murmurs are produced by turbulent flow; less flow means less turbulence. During the strain, preload falls and fewer millilitres cross each valve, so most murmurs (aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation, flow murmurs) become quieter.

  • Louder from more flow is the response to squatting or leg raising, which increase venous return.
  • Louder from chest pressure confuses the cause: pressure does not make a murmur louder; flow does.

The two exceptions that get louder with Valsalva are hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (a smaller ventricle narrows the outflow tract) and mitral valve prolapse (the click and murmur come earlier).

Slides (2)
L24LearningHigh yield
How does carotid sinus massage slow the heart?
  1. A. Stretches the sinus (mimics a pressure rise) → ↑ CN IX firing → reflex vagal slowing
  2. B. Stretches the sinus (mimics a pressure rise) → ↑ CN X firing → reflex sympathetic slowing
  3. C. Compresses the sinus (mimics a pressure fall) → ↓ CN IX firing → reflex vagal slowing
AnswerA. Stretches the sinus (mimics a pressure rise) → ↑ CN IX firing → reflex vagal slowing
WhyMassage deforms the sinus wall like a pressure rise → more firing up CN IX → nucleus tractus solitarius → ↑ vagal outflow to the SA and AV nodes.
Explanation

The baroreceptors cannot tell external pressure from internal distension: rubbing the carotid sinus stretches the endings and they fire as if arterial pressure had jumped. The medulla responds with more vagal (acetylcholine) output, which slows the SA node and lengthens AV nodal conduction, and with less sympathetic output, so TPR and venous tone also fall.

  • CN X with sympathetic slowing has the wrong afferent nerve for the carotid sinus, and sympathetic nerves never slow the heart.
  • Mimics a pressure fall would speed the heart up, the opposite effect.
Slides (2)
L25LearningHigh yield
Carotid sinus massage is a first treatment for which arrhythmia?
  1. A. Supraventricular tachycardia
  2. B. Ventricular fibrillation
  3. C. Ventricular tachycardia
AnswerA. Supraventricular tachycardia
WhyIn supraventricular tachycardia the circuit runs through the AV node, so the vagal slowing of AV conduction from carotid massage (via CN IX) can break it.
Explanation

Most supraventricular tachycardias are re-entry circuits that use the AV node. Vagal manoeuvres (carotid sinus massage, a modified Valsalva) increase acetylcholine at the AV node, slowing conduction and lengthening its refractory period, which can terminate the circuit. The reflex mechanism is stimulation of the glossopharyngeal afferents (CN IX) from the stretched sinus; the vagus is the efferent limb.

  • Ventricular tachycardia arises below the AV node, so vagal tone does not reach its circuit.
  • Ventricular fibrillation is pulseless and needs immediate defibrillation.
Slides (1)

Renin: triggers and the cascade

L26LearningHigh yield
What are the three triggers for renin release?
  1. A. Low renal perfusion (less afferent arteriole stretch)
    High Na+ reaching the macula densa
    β1 sympathetic stimulation
  2. B. High renal perfusion (more afferent arteriole stretch)
    Low Na+ reaching the macula densa
    β1 sympathetic stimulation
  3. C. Low renal perfusion (less afferent arteriole stretch)
    Low Na+ reaching the macula densa
    β1 sympathetic stimulation
AnswerC. Low renal perfusion (less afferent arteriole stretch)
Low Na+ reaching the macula densa
β1 sympathetic stimulation
WhyRenin rises with low blood pressure (less afferent arteriole stretch), low Na+ delivery to the macula densa, and β1 sympathetic stimulation.
Explanation

All three triggers signal "volume or pressure is low":

  • Low renal perfusion pressure: the juxtaglomerular cells are themselves stretch sensors (an intrarenal baroreceptor); less stretch → more renin.
  • Low NaCl at the macula densa: less filtered salt reaching the distal tubule means low volume.
  • β1 stimulation: sympathetic nerves (for example from the baroreflex) act directly on the juxtaglomerular cells.

The wrong choices flip one trigger: high perfusion and high Na+ both suppress renin. Dehydration and bleeding raise renin, and through it aldosterone.

Slides (3)
L27LearningHigh yield
Put the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone cascade in order, from low pressure to restored pressure.
  1. A. ↓ Renal perfusion → renin: angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → (ACE) angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone → Na+ and water retained → ↑ volume → ↑ pressure
  2. B. ↓ Renal perfusion → ACE: angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → (renin) angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone → Na+ and water retained → ↑ volume → ↑ pressure
  3. C. ↓ Renal perfusion → renin: angiotensin I → angiotensinogen → (ACE) angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone → Na+ and water retained → ↑ volume → ↑ pressure
AnswerA. ↓ Renal perfusion → renin: angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → (ACE) angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone → Na+ and water retained → ↑ volume → ↑ pressure
WhyRenin makes angiotensin I from angiotensinogen; ACE makes angiotensin II, which constricts arterioles and releases aldosterone → Na+ and water retention → ↑ volume.
Explanation

The full loop: ↓ arterial pressure → ↓ renal perfusion → juxtaglomerular cells release renin → angiotensinogen (liver) → angiotensin I → ACE (lungs) → angiotensin II. Angiotensin II then raises pressure two ways: fast, by arteriolar vasoconstriction (↑ TPR), and slowly, by expanding extracellular volume (aldosterone, direct proximal tubule Na+ reabsorption, ADH, thirst).

  • The chain with ACE acting on angiotensinogen swaps renin and ACE.
  • The chain running angiotensin I → angiotensinogen reverses the precursor and product: angiotensinogen comes first.
Slides (3)
L28LearningHigh yield
A hypertensive man has high plasma renin and aldosterone. Right renal vein renin is high; left renal vein renin is low. What is the most likely cause?
  1. A. Right renal artery stenosis
  2. B. Left renal artery stenosis
  3. C. An aldosterone-secreting adrenal tumour
AnswerA. Right renal artery stenosis
WhyThe under-perfused right kidney pours out renin; the left kidney, seeing high pressure, suppresses its own renin. Diagnosis: right renal artery stenosis.
Explanation

A narrowed renal artery lowers perfusion pressure beyond the narrowing. That kidney's juxtaglomerular cells read the low pressure as hypotension and release renin → angiotensin II → aldosterone → salt and water retention and vasoconstriction → systemic hypertension (renovascular hypertension). The healthy kidney is exposed to the high pressure, so its renin output falls.

  • Left renal artery stenosis would give the opposite pattern: high renin from the left vein.
  • An aldosterone-secreting tumour (primary hyperaldosteronism) raises aldosterone while suppressing renin from both kidneys.
Slides (1)

Angiotensin II and aldosterone

L29LearningHigh yield
Name the five actions of angiotensin II, plus its growth effect.
  1. A. Arteriolar vasodilatation
    Aldosterone release (adrenal cortex)
    ↑ Na+ reabsorption in proximal tubule
    Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release from pituitary
    Thirst
    + Cardiac and vascular hypertrophy
  2. B. Arteriolar vasoconstriction
    Aldosterone release (adrenal medulla)
    ↓ Na+ reabsorption in proximal tubule
    Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) release from heart
    Thirst
    + Cardiac and vascular hypertrophy
  3. C. Arteriolar vasoconstriction
    Aldosterone release (adrenal cortex)
    ↑ Na+ reabsorption in proximal tubule
    Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release from pituitary
    Thirst
    + Cardiac and vascular hypertrophy
AnswerC. Arteriolar vasoconstriction
Aldosterone release (adrenal cortex)
↑ Na+ reabsorption in proximal tubule
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release from pituitary
Thirst
+ Cardiac and vascular hypertrophy
WhyAngiotensin II: vasoconstriction, aldosterone, proximal tubule Na+ reabsorption, ADH, thirst, plus heart and vessel hypertrophy. Every action raises pressure or volume.
Explanation

Angiotensin II acts on AT1 receptors in many tissues:

  • Arterioles: direct constriction, ↑ TPR (fast).
  • Proximal tubule: ↑ Na+/H+ exchange, ↑ Na+ reabsorption (fast).
  • Adrenal cortex (zona glomerulosa): ↑ aldosterone (slow).
  • Posterior pituitary: ↑ ADH; hypothalamus: thirst.
  • Heart and vessels: hypertrophy and remodelling.

The wrong lists insert opposites: vasodilatation, ↓ Na+ reabsorption, ANP (which opposes the RAAS) and the adrenal medulla (which makes catecholamines, not aldosterone).

Slides (3)
L30Learning
In the proximal tubule, what happens to the H+ secreted by the Na+/H+ exchanger?
  1. A. H+ + filtered HCO3− → CO2 + water → CO2 exhaled → H+ + HCO3− → HCO3− into urine
  2. B. H+ + filtered HCO3− → CO2 + water → CO2 enters cell → H+ + HCO3− → HCO3− into blood
  3. C. H+ + filtered Cl− → HCl → excreted in urine → Cl− lost → HCO3− into blood
AnswerB. H+ + filtered HCO3− → CO2 + water → CO2 enters cell → H+ + HCO3− → HCO3− into blood
WhySecreted H+ turns filtered HCO3− into CO2, which enters the cell and is rebuilt into HCO3− that returns to the blood.
Explanation

This is how the proximal tubule reclaims filtered bicarbonate:

  • In the lumen: H+ + HCO3− → H2CO3 → CO2 + H2O (carbonic anhydrase on the brush border).
  • CO2 diffuses into the cell; inside, carbonic anhydrase re-forms H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3−.
  • H+ is recycled out by the exchanger; HCO3− crosses the basolateral membrane into the blood.

The wrong chains end with bicarbonate in the urine (the opposite of reclamation) or invent an HCl route that does not exist here.

Slides (2)
L31LearningHigh yield
What is contraction alkalosis, and why does it happen?
  1. A. Low volume → high angiotensin II → bicarbonate retained → metabolic alkalosis
  2. B. Low volume → low angiotensin II → bicarbonate excreted → metabolic acidosis
  3. C. High volume → high angiotensin II → bicarbonate retained → metabolic alkalosis
AnswerA. Low volume → high angiotensin II → bicarbonate retained → metabolic alkalosis
WhyVolume contraction raises angiotensin II, which drives proximal Na+/H+ exchange and HCO3− reabsorption, producing a metabolic alkalosis.
Explanation

When extracellular volume falls (sweating, vomiting, diuretics, dehydration), renin and angiotensin II rise. Angiotensin II increases proximal Na+/H+ exchange to save Na+ and water; each H+ secreted reclaims a bicarbonate, so plasma HCO3− rises. Aldosterone adds distal H+ secretion. The result is a metabolic alkalosis caused by volume loss.

  • Low angiotensin II → acidosis gets the hormone response to low volume backwards.
  • High volume suppresses renin and angiotensin II.
Slides (2)
L32LearningHigh yield
What does aldosterone do, and why is it the slow arm?
  1. A. Kidney retains K+ and therefore water; slow because it works through cAMP cascades (minutes)
  2. B. Kidney retains Na+ and therefore water; slow because it works by making new proteins (hours to days)
  3. C. Kidney excretes Na+ and therefore water; slow because it must travel to the brain first (hours to days)
AnswerB. Kidney retains Na+ and therefore water; slow because it works by making new proteins (hours to days)
WhyAldosterone makes the distal nephron retain Na+ (water follows); it acts through gene transcription and new protein synthesis, so it takes hours to days.
Explanation

Aldosterone, from the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex, is a steroid. It enters principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct, binds a cytoplasmic mineralocorticoid receptor, and the complex switches on genes for epithelial Na+ channels and Na+/K+-ATPase pumps. More Na+ is reabsorbed (and more K+ and H+ secreted); water follows the Na+, so volume rises. Building those proteins takes hours.

  • Retains K+ is wrong: aldosterone secretes K+, and acts via nuclear receptors, not cAMP.
  • Excretes Na+ reverses its action; it acts on the kidney directly, not via the brain.
Slides (2)

Drugs on the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone cascade

L33LearningHigh yield
Where in the cascade do ACE inhibitors act?
  1. A. Block binding of angiotensin II → AT1 receptor
  2. B. Block conversion of angiotensinogen → angiotensin I
  3. C. Block conversion of angiotensin I → angiotensin II
AnswerC. Block conversion of angiotensin I → angiotensin II
WhyACE inhibitors (captopril, lisinopril, the "-prils") block angiotensin-converting enzyme, so angiotensin I is not converted to angiotensin II.
Explanation

With ACE blocked, angiotensin II falls, so its vasoconstriction, aldosterone release, proximal Na+ reabsorption, ADH and thirst effects all diminish: TPR and volume fall and pressure drops. Because ACE also breaks down bradykinin, bradykinin accumulates (cough, angioedema).

  • Blocking angiotensin II at its receptor is the ARB mechanism ("-sartans").
  • Blocking angiotensinogen → angiotensin I is the renin step, blocked by aliskiren.
Slides (2)
L34LearningHigh yield
A man with essential hypertension starts an ACE inhibitor. What happens to plasma renin, total peripheral resistance and renal Na+ excretion?
  1. A. Renin ↑, TPR ↓, Na+ excretion ↑
  2. B. Renin ↓, TPR ↓, Na+ excretion ↑
  3. C. Renin ↑, TPR ↑, Na+ excretion ↓
AnswerA. Renin ↑, TPR ↓, Na+ excretion ↑
WhyLess angiotensin II removes its negative feedback on renin (renin ↑), removes vasoconstriction (TPR ↓) and removes Na+ retention (excretion ↑).
Explanation

Angiotensin II normally inhibits renin release by the juxtaglomerular cells. When an ACE inhibitor cuts angiotensin II, that brake is lost and renin (and angiotensin I) rise. Meanwhile, without angiotensin II, arterioles relax (↓ TPR), aldosterone and proximal tubule Na+ reabsorption fall, and the kidney excretes more Na+ and water.

  • Renin ↓ forgets the lost feedback; renin release falls with β blockers, not with ACE inhibitors.
  • TPR ↑ and Na+ excretion ↓ are the effects of more angiotensin II.
Slides (1)
L35Learning
A patient starts metoprolol, a β1 blocker. What happens to renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone?
  1. A. Renin ↑, angiotensin II ↑, aldosterone ↑
  2. B. Renin ↑, angiotensin II ↓, aldosterone ↓
  3. C. Renin ↓, angiotensin II ↓, aldosterone ↓
AnswerC. Renin ↓, angiotensin II ↓, aldosterone ↓
Whyβ1 receptors on juxtaglomerular cells drive renin release; blocking them lowers renin, so angiotensin I, angiotensin II and aldosterone all fall.
Explanation

β blockers lower blood pressure partly by this renal action: less renin → less angiotensin I → less angiotensin II → less aldosterone, along with less vasoconstriction and less salt retention. Every step downstream of renin falls together because renin is the rate-limiting enzyme.

  • All ↑ is the response to β1 stimulation (or to hypotension).
  • Renin ↑, angiotensin II ↓ is the ACE inhibitor pattern, where the block is downstream of renin.
Slides (1)
L36Learning
Inhibiting which step of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system has NOT been proven to lower mortality in congestive heart failure?
  1. A. Angiotensin I → angiotensin II (ACE inhibitors)
  2. B. Aldosterone at its receptor (spironolactone, eplerenone)
  3. C. Angiotensinogen → angiotensin I (renin inhibition)
AnswerC. Angiotensinogen → angiotensin I (renin inhibition)
WhyACE inhibitors, ARBs and aldosterone blockers all lower mortality in heart failure; renin inhibition (aliskiren) has not been shown to.
Explanation

Large trials showed lower mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction for ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, which is why they are standard therapy. Aliskiren lowers blood pressure, but trials in heart failure did not show a mortality benefit, and adding it to an ACE inhibitor increased adverse effects (hyperkalaemia, low pressure, kidney injury).

  • ACE inhibition and aldosterone receptor blockade are both proven, life-prolonging steps.
Slides (1)

PHYS-L26 Chemoreceptors & microcirculation (+ clinical cases)

40 learning questions · of 89
Learning questions 40

Exchange across the capillary wall

L1LearningHigh yield
Why are capillaries built so well for exchange?
  1. A. Wall one cell thick; largest total cross-sectional area → slowest blood velocity
  2. B. Wall one cell thick; smallest total cross-sectional area → fastest blood velocity
  3. C. Wall wrapped in smooth muscle; largest total cross-sectional area → slowest blood velocity
AnswerA. Wall one cell thick; largest total cross-sectional area → slowest blood velocity
WhyA wall of a single endothelial layer plus the largest total cross-sectional area gives a huge exchange surface and the slowest flow, so there is time to exchange.
Explanation

Capillaries are the site where nutrients, gases and wastes actually move between blood and tissue. Three features make them good at it:

  • the wall is only endothelium on a basement membrane, so the diffusion distance is tiny;
  • there are billions of them, so their combined cross-sectional area is the largest in the circulation;
  • because velocity = flow ÷ area, the same cardiac output moving through that huge area travels slowest here, which gives time for exchange.

Smallest area, fastest velocity describes the aorta, not capillaries. Smooth muscle sits in arterioles and precapillary sphincters; the capillary wall itself has none.

Slides (3)
L2Learning
Which property of a substance decides the route it takes across the capillary wall?
  1. A. Whether it carries an electrical charge
  2. B. Whether it binds plasma proteins
  3. C. Whether it dissolves in lipid
AnswerC. Whether it dissolves in lipid
WhyLipid-soluble substances pass straight through the endothelial cell membranes; water-soluble ones must go between the cells through water-filled clefts.
Explanation

The endothelial cell membrane is a lipid bilayer. A substance that dissolves in lipid (O2, CO2) can diffuse through the whole surface of every cell. A substance that does not (water, ions, glucose, amino acids) is restricted to the narrow water-filled clefts between neighbouring cells, so it crosses more slowly.

  • Charge is not the deciding feature: glucose carries no charge yet still has to use the clefts, because it is water-soluble.
  • Binding to plasma proteins keeps a substance in the blood rather than choosing its route; protein itself barely crosses at all.
Slides (2)
L3Learning
What two factors set how fast O2 and CO2 diffuse across the capillaries of a tissue?
  1. A. Capillary hydrostatic pressure
    Surface area of open capillaries
  2. B. Size of the intercellular clefts
    Plasma protein concentration
  3. C. Partial-pressure difference
    Surface area of open capillaries
AnswerC. Partial-pressure difference
Surface area of open capillaries
WhyGas diffusion depends on the partial-pressure gradient across the wall and the surface area available, which rises when more capillaries are open.
Explanation

For a lipid-soluble gas, the driving force is the difference in partial pressure between blood and tissue (for O2, high in the capillary, low in active tissue). The more capillaries are open, the more surface is available and the shorter the distance to each cell, so diffusion rises.

  • Capillary hydrostatic pressure drives bulk filtration of fluid (Starling forces), not diffusion of gases.
  • Cleft size matters only for water-soluble substances, and plasma protein concentration sets oncotic pressure; gases go through the cells and ignore both.
Slides (2)
L4Learning
What do precapillary sphincters do in the microcirculation?
  1. A. Open and close the entrances of capillaries, switching flow into parts of the bed
  2. B. Close the venous ends of capillaries, holding blood back for reabsorption
  3. C. Stop backflow from capillaries into arterioles, acting as one-way valves
AnswerA. Open and close the entrances of capillaries, switching flow into parts of the bed
WhyPrecapillary sphincters are rings of smooth muscle at capillary entrances; relaxing or contracting them sets how many capillaries are open and so the exchange surface.
Explanation

Capillaries have no smooth muscle of their own. Flow into a given capillary is controlled upstream by the arteriole and by a band of smooth muscle at the capillary entrance, the precapillary sphincter. In active tissue, local metabolites relax the sphincters, more capillaries open, and the surface area for diffusion rises while the distance to each cell falls.

  • They sit at the arterial (entrance) end, not at the venous end.
  • They are muscular gates that open and close; they are not one-way valves. Valves are found in veins and lymphatics.
Slides (2)

The four Starling pressures

L5Learning
How many pressures govern fluid movement across the capillary wall, and how do they split?
  1. A. Two: one favours filtration, one favours reabsorption
  2. B. Four: three favour filtration, one favours reabsorption
  3. C. Four: two favour filtration, two favour reabsorption
AnswerC. Four: two favour filtration, two favour reabsorption
WhyFluid movement is set by four Starling pressures: a hydrostatic and an oncotic pressure on each side of the wall, two pushing fluid out and two pulling it in.
Explanation

Each side of the capillary wall has two pressures:

  • hydrostatic pressure, the fluid pressure that pushes water away from its own side (Pc inside, Pi outside);
  • oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure, the pull of proteins that draws water toward their own side (πc inside, πi outside).

Pc and πi favour filtration (out); πc and Pi favour reabsorption (in). Two pressures is the slide's simplified picture (blood pressure out, plasma oncotic in), but the full balance has four. Three out, one in wrongly counts interstitial hydrostatic pressure as an outward force.

Slides (2)
L6Learning
What happens to fluid at the venular end of a typical capillary, and why?
  1. A. Mostly filtered out: hydrostatic pressure has risen, oncotic pressure has fallen
  2. B. Mostly reabsorbed: oncotic pressure has fallen, hydrostatic pressure has not
  3. C. Mostly reabsorbed: hydrostatic pressure has fallen, oncotic pressure has not
AnswerC. Mostly reabsorbed: hydrostatic pressure has fallen, oncotic pressure has not
WhyHydrostatic pressure falls along the capillary to ~15 mmHg, while plasma oncotic pressure stays ~25 mmHg, so at the venular end fluid is reabsorbed.
Explanation

Friction along the capillary uses up hydrostatic pressure: it drops from about 35 to about 15 mmHg. Plasma proteins do not leave, so oncotic pressure stays near 25 mmHg along the whole length. Near the venule the inward pull now exceeds the outward push and most of the filtered fluid comes back in. The small remainder is collected by lymphatics.

  • Hydrostatic pressure rising along the capillary is backwards: it falls from the arteriolar to the venular end.
  • Oncotic pressure falling is also backwards: it is roughly constant (if anything, it rises slightly as protein-free fluid filters out).
Slides (2)

The Starling equation and calculations

L7LearningHigh yield
Which is the Starling equation for fluid movement across a capillary?
  1. A. Jv = Kf [(Pc + Pi) − (πc + πi)]
  2. B. Jv = Kf [(Pc − Pi) − (πc − πi)]
  3. C. Jv = Kf [(Pc − Pi) + (πc − πi)]
AnswerB. Jv = Kf [(Pc − Pi) − (πc − πi)]
WhyJv = Kf [(Pc − Pi) − (πc − πi)]: the hydrostatic difference minus the oncotic difference, times the filtration coefficient.
Explanation

Terms: Jv = fluid movement (mL/min); Kf = filtration coefficient (hydraulic conductance, mL/min per mmHg); Pc and Pi = capillary and interstitial hydrostatic pressure; πc and πi = capillary and interstitial oncotic pressure.

Each bracket is "inside minus outside". The hydrostatic difference pushes fluid out; the oncotic difference pulls it in, so it is subtracted.

  • Adding Pc + Pi treats the interstitial pressure as if it pushed fluid out; it pushes fluid in.
  • Adding the oncotic difference would make plasma proteins push fluid out; they pull it in, so the oncotic bracket is subtracted.
Slides (2)
L8Learning
In the Starling equation, what is Kf?
  1. A. Filtration coefficient (hydraulic conductance): how permeable the wall is to water
  2. B. Reflection coefficient: how completely the wall holds back protein
  3. C. Filtration fraction: the share of plasma that filters out
AnswerA. Filtration coefficient (hydraulic conductance): how permeable the wall is to water
WhyKf is the filtration coefficient (hydraulic conductance): how easily water crosses the wall, so it scales the net pressure into a flow.
Explanation

Kf depends on how leaky the wall is and how much wall surface there is. Its units are mL/min per mmHg: multiply it by the net Starling pressure and you get mL/min of fluid moved. With the same driving pressure, a leakier capillary (higher Kf, for example after a burn or histamine release in inflammation) filters more.

  • The reflection coefficient is σ, a separate term that applies to the oncotic difference.
  • Filtration fraction is a kidney term (GFR ÷ renal plasma flow), not part of the capillary equation.
Slides (2)
L9Learning
In the Starling equation, what are πc and πi?
  1. A. Capillary (plasma) and interstitial crystalloid osmotic pressure
  2. B. Capillary and interstitial hydrostatic pressure
  3. C. Capillary (plasma) and interstitial oncotic pressure
AnswerC. Capillary (plasma) and interstitial oncotic pressure
WhyThe π terms are oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressures from proteins: πc in plasma pulls fluid in, πi in tissue fluid pulls it out.
Explanation

Oncotic pressure is the osmotic pressure made by molecules too big to cross the capillary wall, mainly albumin. Only these count, because only substances that cannot cross can hold water on their side.

  • Crystalloid osmotic pressure (from small solutes such as Na+ and glucose) is huge in absolute terms, but these solutes cross the capillary clefts freely, so they are equal on both sides and do not move fluid across a capillary.
  • Hydrostatic pressures are the P terms.
Slides (2)
L10Learning
Which is the net driving force (NDF) form of the Starling equation that includes the reflection coefficient σ?
  1. A. NDF = σ(Pc − Pi) − (πc − πi)
  2. B. NDF = (Pc − Pi) − σ(πc − πi)
  3. C. NDF = (Pc − Pi) + σ(πc − πi)
AnswerB. NDF = (Pc − Pi) − σ(πc − πi)
WhyThe reflection coefficient multiplies only the oncotic difference: NDF = (Pc − Pi) − σ(πc − πi).
Explanation

σ says how much of the oncotic difference is actually felt. Protein can only pull water if the wall holds the protein back; if some protein leaks through, its pull is weaker. So σ scales the oncotic term only. Hydrostatic pressure pushes water regardless of protein permeability, so it is not multiplied by σ.

  • σ on the hydrostatic term puts it on the wrong bracket.
  • Adding the oncotic term would make plasma proteins push fluid out; they pull it in, so the term is subtracted.

When σ = 1 this form is the ordinary Starling equation.

Slides (2)
L11Learning
Which capillaries have the highest filtration coefficient (Kf)?
  1. A. Brain capillaries
  2. B. Renal glomerular capillaries
  3. C. Skeletal muscle capillaries
AnswerB. Renal glomerular capillaries
WhyGlomerular capillaries are fenestrated and built to filter, so their Kf is the highest; brain capillaries, sealed by tight junctions, have the lowest.
Explanation

Kf is not the same in every tissue: it depends on how many and how wide the water pathways in the wall are.

  • Glomerular capillaries have large fenestrations and filter about 180 L/day, so their Kf is far higher than anywhere else.
  • Brain capillaries are continuous with tight junctions (the blood–brain barrier): almost no clefts, so they have the lowest permeability.
  • Skeletal muscle capillaries are ordinary continuous capillaries with clefts: intermediate.
Slides (1)
L12LearningHigh yield
In a capillary, Pc = 30, Pi = −2, πc = 25 and πi = 2 mmHg. What is the net driving force and direction?
  1. A. +5 mmHg → filtration
  2. B. +9 mmHg → filtration
  3. C. −9 mmHg → reabsorption
AnswerB. +9 mmHg → filtration
WhyPc − Pi = 30 − (−2) = 32; πc − πi = 23; 32 − 23 = +9 mmHg, so filtration.
Explanation

The trap is the negative interstitial pressure. Subtracting a negative number adds it:

  • Hydrostatic: 30 − (−2) = 32 mmHg.
  • Oncotic: 25 − 2 = 23 mmHg.
  • Net = 32 − 23 = +9 mmHg → filtration.

A negative Pi means the tissue is slightly sucking fluid out, so it adds to filtration.

  • +5 mmHg comes from treating −2 as +2 (30 − 2 = 28; 28 − 23 = 5).
  • −9, reabsorption has the right size but the sign reversed: outward forces win here.
Slides (1)

What sets capillary hydrostatic pressure

L13Learning
On the lecture's idealised profile (hydrostatic 35 → 15 mmHg, oncotic 25 mmHg throughout), what is the net fluid change?
  1. A. Net filtration: loss from plasma exceeds gain back
  2. B. None: loss from plasma equals gain back to plasma
  3. C. Net reabsorption: gain to plasma exceeds loss from plasma
AnswerB. None: loss from plasma equals gain back to plasma
WhyOn the idealised graph the filtration triangle (35 down to 25) equals the reabsorption triangle (25 down to 15): loss from plasma = gain to plasma, no net change.
Explanation

Hydrostatic pressure falls linearly from 35 to 15 mmHg, crossing the 25 mmHg oncotic line exactly halfway. The outward excess in the first half (up to 10 mmHg) mirrors the inward excess in the second half, so the two shaded areas are equal and the slide labels it "no net change".

Textbook caveat: real capillaries filter slightly more than they reabsorb (a few litres a day in total), and that surplus returns to the blood as lymph. The exam follows the slide for this graph; remember the lymph for questions about oedema.

  • Net filtration is the real-life picture, not what this graph shows.
  • Net reabsorption would need the crossover point to sit nearer the arteriolar end.
Slides (2)
L14Learning
Which of these changes lowers the tendency to form oedema?
  1. A. Arteriolar constriction
  2. B. Venous constriction
  3. C. Rise in venous pressure
AnswerA. Arteriolar constriction
WhyArteriolar constriction raises resistance upstream of the capillary, lowers capillary hydrostatic pressure and so reduces filtration.
Explanation

Where the resistance sits decides what happens to capillary pressure:

  • Upstream (arteriolar) constriction drops more pressure before the capillary: Pc falls, filtration falls, oedema is less likely.
  • Venous constriction adds resistance downstream: blood backs up, Pc rises and filtration increases.
  • A rise in venous pressure (heart failure, a venous clot, standing) is transmitted straight back into the capillary: Pc rises and oedema is more likely.
Slides (1)
L15LearningHigh yield
Capillary hydrostatic pressure is more affected by changes in which pressure, and why?
  1. A. Arterial pressure: the resistance between artery and capillary is low, so changes pass straight through
  2. B. Venous pressure: the resistance between capillary and vein is low, so changes pass straight back
  3. C. Neither: capillary hydrostatic pressure is set by plasma protein concentration
AnswerB. Venous pressure: the resistance between capillary and vein is low, so changes pass straight back
WhyPostcapillary resistance is low and precapillary (arteriolar) resistance is high, so a change in venous pressure reaches the capillary almost fully.
Explanation

The capillary sits between a large resistance (the arteriole) and a small one (venule and vein). A rise in arterial pressure is mostly absorbed by the arteriole before it reaches the capillary. A rise in venous pressure meets little resistance and is transmitted back into the capillary almost one-for-one. That is why heart failure, venous thrombosis and standing still cause oedema: they raise venous pressure and therefore Pc.

  • The artery-to-capillary resistance (the arteriole) is the largest in the circuit, not low.
  • Plasma protein sets oncotic pressure, not hydrostatic pressure.
Slides (2)

Lymphatics

L16Learning
What happens to the small fluid surplus left in the tissue after filtration and reabsorption?
  1. A. Lymphatics collect it → return it to the circulation
  2. B. Veins collect it directly from the tissue → return it to the heart
  3. C. It stays in the tissue → reabsorbed by the next capillary pass
AnswerA. Lymphatics collect it → return it to the circulation
WhyFiltration slightly exceeds reabsorption; lymphatic capillaries collect the surplus fluid and any leaked protein and return them to the blood.
Explanation

Across the whole body, capillaries filter a little more than they reabsorb, and a small amount of protein leaks out too. Lymphatic capillaries in the interstitium take up this fluid and protein (now called lymph) and carry it through lymph vessels and nodes back to the large veins. Lymph flow therefore matches the net filtration: anything that increases filtration increases lymph flow, until the lymphatics are overwhelmed and oedema appears.

  • Veins do not take up tissue fluid directly; reabsorption into the blood happens only at the capillary and venule level, driven by Starling forces.
  • If the surplus simply stayed in the tissue, it would accumulate every pass: that accumulation is oedema.
Slides (2)
L17Learning
What do the one-way flap valves of lymphatic capillaries let in?
  1. A. Interstitial fluid and protein: in, but not back out
  2. B. Interstitial fluid only: protein is kept out
  3. C. Interstitial fluid and protein: in and back out freely
AnswerA. Interstitial fluid and protein: in, but not back out
WhyThe overlapping endothelial edges act as one-way flap valves: interstitial fluid and protein can enter the lymphatic but cannot flow back out.
Explanation

When interstitial pressure rises, the flaps are pushed inward and fluid with its protein enters the lymphatic capillary. When pressure inside the lymphatic rises, the flaps close, so the lymph cannot leak back. This is how the lymphatics remove the protein that has leaked from blood capillaries: no other route returns it to the blood.

  • Keeping protein out would leave leaked protein trapped in the tissue, raising interstitial oncotic pressure and causing oedema.
  • Flow back out is exactly what the flaps prevent.
Slides (2)
L18Learning
What propels lymph along the lymphatic vessels?
  1. A. Capillary hydrostatic pressure alone
    Arterial pulsation alone
  2. B. The heart pumping it directly
    Gravity draining it downward
  3. C. The vessels' own smooth muscle contracting
    Surrounding skeletal muscle squeezing them
AnswerC. The vessels' own smooth muscle contracting
Surrounding skeletal muscle squeezing them
WhyLymph is pushed by rhythmic contraction of smooth muscle in the lymph vessel walls and by skeletal muscle compression, with one-way valves keeping flow forward.
Explanation

The lymphatic system has no pump of its own like the heart. Larger lymph vessels contain smooth muscle that contracts rhythmically, and the surrounding skeletal muscles squeeze them during movement. Valves inside the vessels make every squeeze push lymph forward toward the thoracic duct. This is why immobility and prolonged standing reduce lymph flow and favour leg oedema.

  • Capillary pressure and arterial pulsation help a little at most; they are not the main drivers.
  • The heart does not pump lymph, and much of the lymph from the legs must travel upward, against gravity.
Slides (2)

Oedema: mechanisms and clinical cases

L19Learning
What are the four mechanisms of oedema?
  1. A. Capillary hydrostatic pressure too high
    Plasma oncotic pressure too low
    Capillary too leaky
    Lymphatics blocked
  2. B. Capillary hydrostatic pressure too low
    Plasma oncotic pressure too high
    Capillary too leaky
    Lymphatics blocked
  3. C. Capillary hydrostatic pressure too high
    Plasma oncotic pressure too high
    Capillary too tight
    Lymphatics overactive
AnswerA. Capillary hydrostatic pressure too high
Plasma oncotic pressure too low
Capillary too leaky
Lymphatics blocked
WhyOedema comes from ↑ Pc, ↓ πc, ↑ Kf (leaky wall) or impaired lymphatic drainage.
Explanation

Each mechanism is one term of the Starling balance pushed toward filtration, or the drain that removes the surplus:

  • ↑ Pc: more outward push (heart failure, venous obstruction, arteriolar dilation).
  • ↓ πc: less inward pull (low albumin: liver failure, nephrotic syndrome, malnutrition).
  • ↑ Kf: leakier wall (burns, inflammation).
  • Blocked lymphatics: the surplus is not removed (node removal, filariasis).

The wrong lists reverse the directions: low Pc, high πc and a tighter wall all reduce filtration. Every oedema question asks which of these four is at work.

Slides (3)
L20LearningHigh yield
Which causes of oedema work by raising capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc)?
  1. A. Heart failure
    Venous constriction
    Arteriolar constriction
    Extracellular fluid volume depletion
    Lying flat
  2. B. Liver failure
    Nephrotic syndrome
    Arteriolar dilation
    Malnutrition
    Standing
  3. C. Heart failure
    Venous constriction
    Arteriolar dilation
    Extracellular fluid volume expansion
    Standing
AnswerC. Heart failure
Venous constriction
Arteriolar dilation
Extracellular fluid volume expansion
Standing
WhyPc rises when more pressure reaches the capillary (arteriolar dilation), when blood backs up from the veins (heart failure, venous constriction, standing), or with volume expansion.
Explanation
  • Heart failure: the failing ventricle cannot clear venous return, venous pressure rises and is transmitted back into the capillaries.
  • Venous constriction or obstruction: added resistance downstream backs blood up.
  • Arteriolar dilation: less pressure is lost upstream.
  • Extracellular fluid volume expansion: more blood volume, higher venous and capillary pressures.
  • Standing: gravity raises venous and capillary pressure in the feet.

The list with arteriolar constriction, volume depletion and lying flat has three items reversed: these all lower Pc. The list with liver failure, nephrotic syndrome and malnutrition mixes in three conditions that cause oedema by lowering plasma oncotic pressure.

Slides (2)
L21LearningHigh yield
Which causes of oedema work by lowering plasma oncotic pressure (πc)?
  1. A. Liver failure
    Heart failure
    Dehydration
  2. B. Liver failure
    Nephrotic syndrome
    Protein malnutrition
  3. C. Heart failure
    Venous obstruction
    Standing
AnswerB. Liver failure
Nephrotic syndrome
Protein malnutrition
WhyPlasma oncotic pressure falls when albumin falls: not made (liver failure), lost in urine (nephrotic syndrome), or not supplied (protein malnutrition).
Explanation

Albumin provides most of plasma oncotic pressure. Each of these lowers it by a different route:

  • Liver failure (cirrhosis): the liver synthesises albumin, so less is made.
  • Nephrotic syndrome: damaged glomeruli lose more than 3.5 g of protein a day in the urine.
  • Protein malnutrition (kwashiorkor): too little dietary protein to make albumin.

With less inward pull, less fluid is reabsorbed at the venular end. Heart failure, venous obstruction and standing act through raised capillary hydrostatic pressure instead. Dehydration does the opposite: it concentrates plasma protein and raises πc.

Slides (2)
L22LearningHigh yield
How do burns and inflammation cause oedema?
  1. A. Capillary wall made leaky (↑ Kf) → fluid and protein escape into the tissue
  2. B. Plasma oncotic pressure lowered → albumin lost in the urine
  3. C. Lymphatics blocked → interstitial fluid and protein cannot drain
AnswerA. Capillary wall made leaky (↑ Kf) → fluid and protein escape into the tissue
WhyBurns and inflammation (histamine, cytokines) increase capillary permeability (↑ Kf), so fluid and protein pour out into the tissue.
Explanation

Inflammatory mediators such as histamine and cytokines open gaps between endothelial cells, and burns damage the wall directly. A leakier wall raises Kf, so the same pressures move more fluid. Protein escapes too, which lowers the reflection coefficient and raises interstitial oncotic pressure: several Starling terms shift toward filtration at once. Inflammation also dilates arterioles, raising Pc.

  • Albumin lost in urine is nephrotic syndrome (↓ πc).
  • Blocked lymphatics is the mechanism of lymphoedema after node removal or filariasis.
Slides (2)
L23Learning
How does lymphatic obstruction lead to oedema?
  1. A. Lymph backs up into the veins → capillary hydrostatic pressure rises
  2. B. Filtered fluid and leaked protein are not removed → they build up, raising interstitial oncotic pressure
  3. C. Albumin is lost into the blocked lymph → plasma oncotic pressure falls
AnswerB. Filtered fluid and leaked protein are not removed → they build up, raising interstitial oncotic pressure
WhyWith the drain blocked, the normal filtration surplus and leaked protein stay in the tissue; the trapped protein raises πi, which pulls out still more fluid.
Explanation

Normal capillaries leave a small excess of fluid and some protein in the interstitium every day, and only the lymphatics can remove them. When lymphatics are blocked, the fluid accumulates, and the protein that can no longer be cleared raises interstitial oncotic pressure. That favours filtration further, so lymphoedema is typically protein-rich and firm.

  • Lymph does not back up into the veins and raise capillary pressure; the blood-side Starling pressures are not the primary problem.
  • The protein is trapped in the tissue, not lost from the body, so plasma oncotic pressure is not the cause.
Slides (2)
L24LearningHigh yield
After a myocardial infarction, a papillary muscle of the mitral valve ruptures and the patient develops breathlessness with lung crackles. What causes the lung finding?
  1. A. ↑ Right atrial pressure → ↑ systemic capillary hydrostatic pressure → pulmonary oedema
  2. B. ↓ Plasma oncotic pressure → less reabsorption in the pulmonary capillaries → pulmonary oedema
  3. C. ↑ Left atrial pressure → ↑ pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure → pulmonary oedema
AnswerC. ↑ Left atrial pressure → ↑ pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure → pulmonary oedema
WhyAcute mitral regurgitation sends blood back into the left atrium; the pressure backs up through the pulmonary veins and raises pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure, flooding the lungs.
Explanation

When the papillary muscle tears, the mitral valve can no longer close, and every systole forces blood back into the left atrium. Left atrial pressure rises sharply and is transmitted backward through the pulmonary veins into the pulmonary capillaries. The raised hydrostatic pressure filters fluid into the lung interstitium and alveoli, which is heard as crackles (rales). It is the left-heart counterpart of ankle oedema in right heart failure.

  • Right atrial pressure backs up into the systemic veins and gives peripheral oedema, not lung crackles.
  • Nothing here lowers plasma albumin.
Slides (2)

Peripheral chemoreceptors

L25Learning
What role do chemoreceptors play in the control of blood pressure?
  1. A. Backup system that drives a strong sympathetic response when pressure falls low enough to starve tissue of O2
  2. B. Long-term setting of blood pressure through the kidney
  3. C. Detection of atrial stretch and blood volume
AnswerA. Backup system that drives a strong sympathetic response when pressure falls low enough to starve tissue of O2
WhyChemoreceptors are a backup to the baroreceptors: they matter little in everyday pressure control but fire hard when low pressure leaves tissue short of O2.
Explanation

The baroreceptor reflex handles moment-to-moment pressure. Chemoreceptors sense blood chemistry (O2, CO2, pH). When blood pressure falls far enough that blood flow through the carotid and aortic bodies becomes inadequate, they detect the resulting hypoxia and acidosis and drive a powerful sympathetic vasoconstriction that props pressure up.

  • Long-term setting through the kidney is the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.
  • Atrial stretch and volume are sensed by the cardiopulmonary (low-pressure) baroreceptors.
Slides (1)
L26Learning
Along which nerves do peripheral chemoreceptor signals travel, and to where?
  1. A. Cranial nerves IX and X → nucleus tractus solitarius (medulla)
  2. B. Cranial nerves X and XI → dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (medulla)
  3. C. Cranial nerves V and VII → nucleus ambiguus (medulla)
AnswerA. Cranial nerves IX and X → nucleus tractus solitarius (medulla)
WhyCarotid body afferents run in the glossopharyngeal (IX) nerve and aortic body afferents in the vagus (X), to the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla: the baroreceptor route.
Explanation

The lecture's summary: same sites, same nerves (IX and X), same tract (solitary nucleus), same target (medulla) as the baroreceptors. The carotid body signal travels in the carotid sinus nerve, a branch of IX; the aortic bodies use X. The slide adds "travels with VII", meaning the nucleus tractus solitarius also receives facial-nerve (taste) input; the chemoreceptor fibres themselves run in IX and X.

  • The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus and nucleus ambiguus are output (efferent) nuclei to the heart, not the sensory relay.
  • Cranial nerves XI and V carry no chemoreceptor input.
Slides (2)
L27Learning
What three responses follow hypoxia sensed by the peripheral chemoreceptors?
  1. A. Arteriolar vasoconstriction
    Transient fall in heart rate
    Hyperventilation
  2. B. Arteriolar vasodilation
    Transient rise in heart rate
    Hypoventilation
  3. C. Arteriolar vasoconstriction
    Sustained fall in heart rate
    Hypoventilation
AnswerA. Arteriolar vasoconstriction
Transient fall in heart rate
Hyperventilation
WhyHypoxia sensed peripherally causes arteriolar vasoconstriction, a transient fall in heart rate and hyperventilation.
Explanation
  • Vasoconstriction: sympathetic outflow to arterioles rises, raising total peripheral resistance and blood pressure.
  • Transient bradycardia: the direct reflex effect on the heart is vagal slowing, but it is short-lived because the extra breathing soon reverses it.
  • Hyperventilation: the respiratory centre is driven to breathe more and raise PO2. This is why hypoxaemia lowers arterial PCO2.

Vasodilation, tachycardia and hypoventilation reverses all three. A sustained bradycardia with hypoventilation is also wrong: the slowing is brief and hypoxia stimulates breathing.

Slides (2)
L28LearningHigh yield
A patient with COPD has pH 7.22, PCO2 70 mmHg and PO2 55 mmHg. Given 100% O2, he gets worse. Why?
  1. A. Respiratory alkalosis from the extra O2
  2. B. Loss of hypoxic drive → breathing falls off
  3. C. Sudden drop in PCO2 → central drive lost
AnswerB. Loss of hypoxic drive → breathing falls off
WhyWith chronic CO2 retention his breathing depends on hypoxic drive from the peripheral chemoreceptors; high-flow O2 removes that drive and breathing falls.
Explanation

In chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with chronic CO2 retention, the central response to CO2 is blunted, so the low PO2 acting on the carotid and aortic bodies keeps him breathing. 100% O2 abolishes that stimulus, ventilation falls, and PCO2 climbs further (worse acidosis, drowsiness).

  • Respiratory alkalosis is the opposite of what happens: he already has acidosis and it worsens.
  • PCO2 rises, not drops, when ventilation falls.

Note: the lecture key is loss of hypoxic drive. Current clinical evidence attributes much of the CO2 rise to worsening ventilation–perfusion matching and the Haldane effect, which is why such patients are given controlled O2 (target saturation 88–92%).

Slides (1)

Central chemoreceptors and the Cushing reflex

L29LearningHigh yield
Which pairing of chemoreceptor, location and main stimulus is correct?
  1. A. Peripheral: medulla; mainly high PCO2 and low pH
  2. B. Peripheral: carotid and aortic bodies; mainly low PO2
  3. C. Central: medulla; mainly low PO2
AnswerB. Peripheral: carotid and aortic bodies; mainly low PO2
WhyPeripheral = carotid and aortic bodies, mainly hypoxia. Central = medulla, mainly high PCO2 and low pH, little response to hypoxia.
Explanation
PeripheralCentral
SiteCarotid bodies, aortic bodiesMedulla
Main stimulus↓ PO2 (sensitised by ↑ PCO2, ↓ pH)↑ PCO2, ↓ pH
HypoxiaMain stimulusLittle effect

Peripheral in the medulla, sensing CO2/pH gives the peripheral receptors the central site and stimulus. Central sensing low PO2 gives the central receptors the peripheral stimulus.

Slides (1)
L30LearningHigh yield
When the brain is short of blood, how do the central chemoreceptors respond?
  1. A. Local CO2 rises → big sympathetic discharge + peripheral vasoconstriction → blood shunted to the brain
  2. B. Local CO2 falls → sympathetic withdrawal + peripheral vasodilation → blood pressure falls
  3. C. Local CO2 rises → big vagal discharge + peripheral vasodilation → blood shunted to the limbs
AnswerA. Local CO2 rises → big sympathetic discharge + peripheral vasoconstriction → blood shunted to the brain
WhyBrain ischaemia lets CO2 and H+ build up locally; the central chemoreceptors trigger a massive sympathetic discharge that constricts peripheral vessels and shunts blood to the brain.
Explanation

This is the central nervous system ischaemic response, one of the most powerful pressor responses in the body. When medullary blood flow falls, CO2 produced by brain tissue is not removed, the local pH drops and the central chemoreceptors fire intensely. Sympathetic outflow surges, peripheral arterioles constrict, arterial pressure rises and blood is diverted to the central nervous system.

  • Inadequate flow makes local CO2 rise, not fall.
  • The response is sympathetic vasoconstriction, not vagal vasodilation; it protects the brain, not the limbs.
Slides (2)
L31LearningHigh yield
What is the Cushing reflex?
  1. A. Raised intracranial pressure → hypotension with tachycardia
  2. B. Raised intracranial pressure → hypertension with bradycardia
  3. C. Lowered intracranial pressure → hypertension with tachycardia
AnswerB. Raised intracranial pressure → hypertension with bradycardia
WhyIn the Cushing reflex, raised intracranial pressure produces hypertension with bradycardia (often with irregular breathing).
Explanation

When intracranial pressure rises (bleeding, tumour, cerebral oedema), it compresses the cerebral arteries. The brainstem becomes ischaemic, the central chemoreceptors trigger the CNS ischaemic response, and arterial pressure rises until it can once again push blood into the brain. The heart rate falls as a reflex response to the very high pressure. Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration form Cushing's triad, a warning sign of impending brain herniation.

  • Hypotension with tachycardia is the picture of haemorrhagic or septic shock.
  • Lowered intracranial pressure does not trigger this reflex.
Slides (2)

ADH (vasopressin)

L32Learning
From where is antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) released into the blood?
  1. A. Anterior pituitary
  2. B. Posterior pituitary
  3. C. Adrenal cortex
AnswerB. Posterior pituitary
WhyADH is made by hypothalamic neurons (supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei) and released from their endings in the posterior pituitary.
Explanation

ADH is a peptide synthesised in the cell bodies of hypothalamic neurons. It travels down their axons and is stored in nerve endings in the posterior pituitary, from where it is released into the blood when osmolality rises or blood pressure/volume falls. The lecture notes that volume detectors lower ADH by inhibiting the hypothalamus.

  • The anterior pituitary is glandular tissue that makes its own hormones (for example ACTH, growth hormone); it does not release ADH.
  • The adrenal cortex makes aldosterone, the other volume-regulating hormone.
Slides (2)
L33Learning
What are the two triggers for ADH release?
  1. A. Osmolality rises
    Pressure or volume rises
  2. B. Osmolality falls
    Pressure or volume rises
  3. C. Osmolality rises
    Pressure or volume falls
AnswerC. Osmolality rises
Pressure or volume falls
WhyADH is released when plasma osmolality rises (too little water) or when blood pressure or volume falls.
Explanation

Both triggers mean the body needs to hold on to water. A rise in osmolality is sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors; a fall in pressure or volume is sensed by the arterial and cardiopulmonary baroreceptors, whose reduced firing releases the hypothalamus from inhibition. ADH then conserves water through the kidney (V2) and constricts arterioles (V1).

  • A rise in pressure or volume inhibits ADH release (stretch of the low-pressure receptors lowers ADH).
  • A fall in osmolality (dilute plasma) also switches ADH off, so the kidney can excrete the extra water.
Slides (2)
L34LearningHigh yield
How much must plasma osmolality rise to release ADH, and which receptor and effect follow?
  1. A. ~10% → V2 in the kidney: water reabsorption
  2. B. ~1% → V2 in the kidney: water reabsorption
  3. C. ~1% → V1 in the kidney: sodium reabsorption
AnswerB. ~1% → V2 in the kidney: water reabsorption
WhyA 1% rise in osmolality releases ADH, which acts on V2 receptors in the kidney collecting ducts to reabsorb water.
Explanation

The osmolality signal is very sensitive: about a 1% rise is enough. ADH then binds V2 receptors on the collecting-duct cells, which insert water channels and reabsorb water, concentrating the urine and diluting the plasma back toward normal.

TriggerChangeReceptor, effect
Osmolality ↑~1%V2 (kidney): water reabsorption
Pressure/volume ↓~10%V1 (vascular smooth muscle): vasoconstriction
  • 10% is the threshold for the pressure/volume trigger.
  • V1 receptors are on vascular smooth muscle, and ADH reabsorbs water, not sodium.
Slides (3)
L35Learning
Through which second-messenger pathway do V1 receptors constrict vascular smooth muscle?
  1. A. Gs → cAMP → ↑ intracellular Ca2+ → contraction
  2. B. Gq → IP3 → ↑ intracellular Ca2+ → contraction
  3. C. Gi → ↓ cAMP → ↑ intracellular Ca2+ → contraction
AnswerB. Gq → IP3 → ↑ intracellular Ca2+ → contraction
WhyV1 receptors couple to Gq: phospholipase C makes IP3, which releases Ca2+ and contracts vascular smooth muscle.
Explanation

V1 works like the α1-adrenergic receptor on arterioles: Gq activates phospholipase C, which splits a membrane lipid into IP3 and diacylglycerol. IP3 releases Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and the smooth muscle contracts, raising total peripheral resistance.

  • Gs → cAMP is the V2 pathway in the kidney collecting duct; in vascular smooth muscle, cAMP causes relaxation (as with β2).
  • Gi is wrong: some review answers give V1 as Gi, but it is Gq.
Slides (2)
L36Learning
A patient in septic shock stays hypotensive despite several litres of normal saline. Which drug will help most immediately?
  1. A. Albumin infusion
  2. B. Intravenous antibiotics
  3. C. Vasopressin
AnswerC. Vasopressin
WhyVasopressin acts on V1 receptors to constrict arterioles directly, raising total peripheral resistance and blood pressure within minutes.
Explanation

Septic shock is a distributive shock: inflammatory mediators dilate arterioles and total peripheral resistance collapses. Once volume has been replaced and pressure is still low, a vasoconstrictor is needed. Vasopressin (V1) constricts vascular smooth muscle through a pathway separate from the adrenergic receptors, so it works even when catecholamines are failing.

  • Albumin (or dextran) adds more volume; volume has already failed to fix the problem because the vessels are dilated.
  • Antibiotics and blood cultures are essential but treat the infection over hours to days; they do not raise pressure immediately.
Slides (2)

Low-pressure baroreceptors, ANP and BNP

L37LearningHigh yield
What do the cardiopulmonary (low-pressure) baroreceptors sense?
  1. A. Fullness of the venous side (volume), not arterial pressure
  2. B. Arterial pressure, not volume
  3. C. Arterial O2 and CO2 levels
AnswerA. Fullness of the venous side (volume), not arterial pressure
WhyThe cardiopulmonary baroreceptors are venous-side volume detectors: they sense fullness (stretch) of the veins, atria and pulmonary artery.
Explanation

Because they sit in compliant, low-pressure structures that hold most of the blood, their stretch reflects blood volume. When volume rises they stretch more and trigger responses that get rid of fluid: ↑ ANP, ↓ ADH, renal vasodilation and ↑ heart rate (Bainbridge reflex).

  • Arterial pressure is sensed by the high-pressure baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch.
  • Blood gases are sensed by the chemoreceptors.
Slides (2)
L38LearningHigh yield
What are the four responses of the low-pressure baroreceptors to a rise in blood volume?
  1. A. ↑ Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)
    ↑ ADH (hypothalamus stimulated)
    Renal vasodilation → kidney excretes the extra volume
    ↓ Heart rate (Bainbridge reflex)
  2. B. ↑ Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)
    ↓ ADH (hypothalamus inhibited)
    Renal vasodilation → kidney excretes the extra volume
    ↑ Heart rate (Bainbridge reflex)
  3. C. ↑ Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)
    ↓ ADH (hypothalamus inhibited)
    Renal vasoconstriction → kidney retains the extra volume
    ↑ Heart rate (Cushing reflex)
AnswerB. ↑ Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)
↓ ADH (hypothalamus inhibited)
Renal vasodilation → kidney excretes the extra volume
↑ Heart rate (Bainbridge reflex)
WhyExtra volume stretches the atria: ↑ ANP, ↓ ADH, renal vasodilation to excrete salt and water, and ↑ heart rate (Bainbridge) to pass the volume forward.
Explanation

Every response unloads volume:

  • ANP from stretched atrial cells: vasodilation and renal salt and water loss.
  • Less ADH: the kidney excretes more water.
  • Renal vasodilation (less renal sympathetic tone): more filtration and excretion.
  • Bainbridge reflex: faster heart rate moves the extra venous blood into the arterial side.

A list with ↑ ADH and ↓ heart rate reverses two responses. A list with renal vasoconstriction makes the kidney retain volume and misnames the heart-rate reflex: the Cushing reflex is the response to raised intracranial pressure.

Slides (2)
L39Learning
How does heart rate respond to a rise in firing of the arterial (high-pressure) receptors compared with the venous (low-pressure) receptors?
  1. A. Arterial receptors → heart rate ↑
    Venous receptors → heart rate ↓
  2. B. Arterial receptors → heart rate ↓
    Venous receptors → heart rate ↓
  3. C. Arterial receptors → heart rate ↓
    Venous receptors → heart rate ↑
AnswerC. Arterial receptors → heart rate ↓
Venous receptors → heart rate ↑
