WhyHigh arterial pressure slows the heart (baroreceptor reflex); high venous filling speeds it (Bainbridge reflex).
Explanation

The two reflexes have different goals. The arterial baroreceptor reflex defends arterial pressure: if pressure rises, it lowers heart rate and resistance to bring pressure down. The Bainbridge reflex prevents blood piling up on the venous side: if the atria are overfilled, the heart speeds up to pump the extra volume forward.

  • Arterial ↑, venous ↓ swaps the two reflexes.
  • Both ↓ ignores the Bainbridge reflex, the classic exception where stretch raises heart rate.
Slides (2)
L40Learning
What is BNP?
  1. A. Atrial natriuretic peptide, released mainly by stretched atria
  2. B. B-type natriuretic peptide, released mainly by stretched ventricles
  3. C. Brain natriuretic peptide, released mainly by the hypothalamus
AnswerB. B-type natriuretic peptide, released mainly by stretched ventricles
WhyBNP is B-type natriuretic peptide, a relative of ANP released mainly by stretched ventricular muscle, so it rises in heart failure.
Explanation

BNP was first found in pig brain, hence the old name "brain natriuretic peptide", but in humans it comes mainly from the ventricles when they are stretched by high filling pressure. Its actions resemble ANP's (vasodilation, natriuresis). A blood BNP level is used clinically to tell whether breathlessness is due to congestive heart failure.

  • Atrial natriuretic peptide is ANP, a different peptide from the atria. The lecture's question slide labels BNP "atrial natriuretic peptide"; that label is wrong.
  • Despite its old name, BNP is not a hypothalamic hormone.
Slides (2)

PHYS-L27 Special circulations

27 learning questions · of 56
Learning questions 27

Lecture 27 · Cardiac output shares and autoregulation

L1LearningHigh yield
At rest, roughly what share of the cardiac output goes to the brain, the heart and the skin?
  1. A. Brain ~25%
    Heart ~5%
    Skin ~15%
  2. B. Brain ~15%
    Heart ~5%
    Skin ~5%
  3. C. Brain ~5%
    Heart ~15%
    Skin ~5%
AnswerB. Brain ~15%
Heart ~5%
Skin ~5%
WhyThe brain takes about 15% of the resting cardiac output; the heart and the skin about 5% each.
Explanation

These three beds complete the lecture's table (muscle, gut and kidney 25% each). The brain, only ~2% of body weight, gets 15% because neurons cannot store fuel. The heart gets only 5% of the output it pumps, yet it extracts so much oxygen from that small flow that coronary sinus blood is the most desaturated in the body.

  • Heart ~15%, brain ~5% swaps the two.
  • Brain ~25%, skin ~15% overstates both; skin flow is small at rest and rises only when heat must be lost.
Slides (2)
L2Learning
Which structures receive all of the cardiac output every minute?
  1. A. The right heart chambers only
  2. B. Each heart chamber and the lungs
  3. C. The left ventricle and the brain
AnswerB. Each heart chamber and the lungs
WhyThe whole cardiac output passes through every heart chamber and through the lungs each minute, because the two circuits are in series.
Explanation

The systemic organs sit in parallel, so each takes only a fraction of the output. The pulmonary circuit is in series with the systemic one: every drop that returns to the right atrium must go through the right ventricle, the lungs, the left atrium and the left ventricle before it reaches any organ.

  • Right heart chambers only forgets that the same volume then passes through the left heart.
  • Left ventricle and brain: the brain is a parallel systemic bed that gets only ~15%.
Slides (2)
L3Learning
From which two directions is an organ's blood flow controlled?
  1. A. Local: sympathetic nerves act on its arterioles
    Neural and hormonal: tissue metabolites + circulating vasoactive substances
  2. B. Local: tissue metabolites act on its arterioles
    Neural and hormonal: sympathetic nerves + circulating vasoactive substances
  3. C. Local: endothelial shear stress only
    Neural and hormonal: parasympathetic nerves + circulating vasoactive substances
AnswerB. Local: tissue metabolites act on its arterioles
Neural and hormonal: sympathetic nerves + circulating vasoactive substances
WhyLocal control comes from the organ's own metabolites acting on its arterioles; neural/hormonal control comes from outside: sympathetic nerves and circulating vasoactive substances.
Explanation

Local (intrinsic) control matches flow to the tissue's own metabolic need: products of metabolism change the resistance of the organ's arterioles. Extrinsic control is imposed from outside the organ, by the sympathetic nervous system and by circulating vasoactive substances (histamine, bradykinin, serotonin, prostaglandins, catecholamines).

  • Putting sympathetic nerves under local control swaps the two categories: nerves come from outside the organ.
  • Parasympathetic nerves have almost no role in arteriolar tone, and shear stress is not the main local signal.
Slides (2)
L4LearningHigh yield
What is autoregulation?
  1. A. The brainstem keeping arterial pressure nearly constant despite changing organ flow, via sympathetic nerves
  2. B. An organ keeping its own perfusion pressure nearly constant despite changing flow, by adjusting its venules
  3. C. An organ keeping its own blood flow nearly constant despite changing arterial pressure, by adjusting its arterioles
AnswerC. An organ keeping its own blood flow nearly constant despite changing arterial pressure, by adjusting its arterioles
WhyAutoregulation is an organ holding its blood flow nearly constant when arterial pressure changes, by changing the resistance of its own arterioles.
Explanation

Flow = pressure ÷ resistance. If perfusion pressure rises, the organ's arterioles constrict so resistance rises in proportion and flow barely changes; if pressure falls, they dilate. It is intrinsic: it works in a denervated, isolated organ. Two mechanisms explain it: myogenic and metabolic.

  • Constant pressure despite changing flow inverts what is held constant, and venules are not the resistance vessels.
  • Brainstem control of arterial pressure is the baroreceptor reflex, an extrinsic neural reflex.

The slide words it as flow constant 'with changing arterial flow'; it means changing arterial pressure.

Slides (3)
L5LearningHigh yield
Where is autoregulation strongest, and where weakest?
  1. A. Strongest: skin, skeletal muscle
    Weakest: brain, kidney
  2. B. Strongest: heart, brain, kidney
    Weakest: skin, bone
  3. C. Strongest: skin, bone
    Weakest: heart, brain, kidney
AnswerB. Strongest: heart, brain, kidney
Weakest: skin, bone
WhyThe vital organs, heart, brain and kidney, autoregulate most; uncritical tissues such as skin and bone autoregulate least.
Explanation

The lecture's rule: important organs are 'independent' and protect their own flow whatever the arterial pressure does; less important tissues are left to central (sympathetic) control so their flow can be sacrificed. That is why the skin goes pale in haemorrhage while cerebral and coronary flow are defended.

  • Skin and muscle strongest is wrong: skin is the classic sympathetically controlled bed, and resting muscle is under central control too.
  • Skin and bone strongest reverses the ranking completely.

Hook: the autoregulating trio are the organs you cannot live without for even minutes: heart, brain, kidney.

Slides (2)
L6LearningHigh yield
How does the law of Laplace explain the myogenic response to a rise in pressure?
  1. A. Pressure ↑ → arteriole widens → wall tension falls; the lower resistance holds flow constant
  2. B. Pressure ↑ → venule narrows → wall tension steady; the extra capacitance holds flow constant
  3. C. Pressure ↑ → arteriole narrows → wall tension steady; the extra resistance holds flow constant
AnswerC. Pressure ↑ → arteriole narrows → wall tension steady; the extra resistance holds flow constant
WhyWith T = P × r, a rise in pressure is offset by a fall in radius: tension stays steady and the higher resistance holds flow constant.
Explanation

If perfusion pressure rises, the stretched smooth muscle contracts and the radius falls, so the product P × r (the tension) stays about the same. Because resistance varies with 1/r4, a small narrowing raises resistance enough to balance the higher pressure, and flow (ΔP ÷ R) barely changes. When pressure falls, the arteriole widens.

  • Arteriole widens would add more flow on top of a higher pressure, the reverse of autoregulation.
  • Venules are capacitance vessels; they do not set organ flow.
Slides (3)
L7LearningHigh yield
What is the metabolic mechanism of autoregulation?
  1. A. Local waste products (adenosine, CO2, K+) dilate arterioles when flow falls short of need
  2. B. Local waste products (adenosine, CO2, K+) constrict arterioles when flow falls short of need
  3. C. Local waste products (angiotensin II, O2, Na+) dilate arterioles when flow falls short of need
AnswerA. Local waste products (adenosine, CO2, K+) dilate arterioles when flow falls short of need
WhyIn the metabolic mechanism, vasodilator metabolites build up when flow is too low for the tissue's need and dilate its arterioles.
Explanation

Oxygen delivery is matched to oxygen use. If flow falls (or metabolism rises), CO2, H+, K+, lactate and adenosine accumulate and O2 falls; these dilate the arterioles and restore flow. If flow is excessive, the metabolites are washed out and the arterioles constrict back. The same mechanism explains active and reactive hyperaemia.

  • Metabolites constricting is backwards: in systemic beds they are vasodilators.
  • Angiotensin II, O2 and Na+ are not tissue waste products; angiotensin II is a circulating constrictor and O2 falls, rather than rises, in working tissue.
Slides (3)

Lecture 27 · Hyperaemia and metabolites

L8LearningHigh yield
Which pairing of organ and type of hyperaemia is correct?
  1. A. Heart (after each systole): reactive
    Exercising muscle: active
  2. B. Heart (after each systole): myogenic
    Exercising muscle: reactive
  3. C. Heart (after each systole): active
    Exercising muscle: reactive
AnswerA. Heart (after each systole): reactive
Exercising muscle: active
WhyThe heart is the classic example of reactive hyperaemia (flow repays the debt after systolic compression); exercising muscle shows active hyperaemia.
Explanation

During systole the contracting myocardium squeezes its own vessels, so coronary flow nearly stops and an oxygen debt builds; in diastole flow surges to repay it, which is reactive hyperaemia. Exercising skeletal muscle dilates while the demand is rising, through lactate, K+ and adenosine, which is active hyperaemia.

  • Heart active, muscle reactive swaps the two.
  • Myogenic is an autoregulation mechanism responding to pressure, not a type of hyperaemia, and exercising muscle is not reactive.
Slides (3)
L9LearningHigh yield
Which set lists the dilating metabolites produced by working tissue?
  1. A. Lactate, H+, CO2, K+, angiotensin II, endothelin
  2. B. Lactate, H+, O2, Na+, adenosine, inorganic phosphate
  3. C. Lactate, H+, CO2, K+, adenosine, inorganic phosphate
AnswerC. Lactate, H+, CO2, K+, adenosine, inorganic phosphate
WhyWork makes tissue hypoxic and produces lactate, H+, CO2, K+, adenosine and phosphate; all of them dilate most vascular beds.
Explanation

The lecture builds the list from what work does to a tissue: work → hypoxia; hypoxia → lactate and acid (H+); work → CO2 and potassium (K+ leaks out of contracting cells); work → adenosine and phosphate (from ATP breakdown). These metabolites cause both active and reactive hyperaemia. The lung is the exception, where hypoxia constricts.

  • O2 and Na+ do not accumulate in working tissue; O2 falls, and sodium is not a vasodilator.
  • Angiotensin II and endothelin are vasoconstrictors, not tissue metabolites.
Slides (2)
L10Learning
Why does a small rise in ATP turnover cause a large proportional rise in adenosine?
  1. A. Cells hold ~1000× more adenosine than ATP
  2. B. Cells hold ~10× more ATP than adenosine
  3. C. Cells hold ~1000× more ATP than adenosine
AnswerC. Cells hold ~1000× more ATP than adenosine
WhyThe normal ATP : adenosine ratio is about 1000 : 1, so breaking down even a tiny fraction of ATP multiplies the adenosine level.
Explanation

Because adenosine starts from such a low baseline, converting even 0.1% of the ATP pool doubles it. This makes adenosine a sensitive signal of energy imbalance: a modest rise in work or a brief shortfall of oxygen produces a big relative rise in adenosine and strong dilation, especially in the coronary bed.

  • ~10× would blunt the amplification a hundredfold.
  • More adenosine than ATP is backwards: ATP is the abundant energy currency.
Slides (2)
L11Learning
How does a raised extracellular K+ dilate vessels?
  1. A. Depolarizes vascular smooth muscle → opens Ca2+ channels → contracts
  2. B. Hyperpolarizes vascular smooth muscle → it cannot depolarize to contract → relaxes
  3. C. Depolarizes vascular smooth muscle → inactivates Na+ channels → relaxes
AnswerB. Hyperpolarizes vascular smooth muscle → it cannot depolarize to contract → relaxes
WhyK+ released by contracting muscle hyperpolarizes vascular smooth muscle, so it cannot depolarize to contract: the vessel relaxes and dilates.
Explanation

Each contraction lets K+ leak out of skeletal muscle fibres, raising interstitial K+. A modest rise in K+ increases the conductance of inward-rectifier K+ channels and stimulates the Na+/K+ pump in arteriolar smooth muscle, which hyperpolarizes it. Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels then stay shut, Ca2+ entry falls and the muscle relaxes.

  • Depolarization → Ca2+ entry → contraction is what happens with very high K+ (as in cardioplegia), not the local metabolic effect.
  • Na+ channel inactivation is not how vascular smooth muscle tone is set.
Slides (2)

Lecture 27 · Coronary and cerebral beds

L12LearningHigh yield
Which are the strongest coronary vasodilators?
  1. A. Lactate
    Histamine
  2. B. Hypoxia
    Potassium
  3. C. Hypoxia
    Adenosine
AnswerC. Hypoxia
Adenosine
WhyHypoxia dilates the coronaries the most, and adenosine does too: the coronary bed's two key metabolites.
Explanation

The heart extracts most of the oxygen it receives, so any rise in work makes it hypoxic at once. Hypoxia acts directly on the arterioles and also speeds ATP breakdown, releasing adenosine. Both dilate the coronary arterioles and raise flow. This is why adenosine is used to stress the coronary bed in patients who cannot exercise.

  • Potassium belongs with lactate as a skeletal-muscle dilator.
  • Lactate is the skeletal-muscle metabolite; histamine is an inflammatory mediator, not a coronary regulator.
Slides (2)
L13Learning
Why can the heart get more oxygen only by getting more flow?
  1. A. It already extracts about three quarters of the delivered O2 at rest, near the maximum
  2. B. Its haemoglobin cannot unload O2 in the coronary capillaries
  3. C. It extracts only about a quarter of the delivered O2 at rest, leaving a large reserve
AnswerA. It already extracts about three quarters of the delivered O2 at rest, near the maximum
WhyThe coronary bed works at near-maximal oxygen extraction even at rest, so more flow is the only way to deliver more oxygen.
Explanation

Most tissues extract about 25% of the oxygen offered and can raise extraction when demand rises. The myocardium already removes ~70–80% at rest, which is why coronary sinus blood is the most desaturated in the body and why the heart has the widest arteriovenous O2 difference. With little extraction reserve left, a rise in demand must be met by coronary vasodilation.

  • A quarter is the typical value for the body as a whole, not the heart.
  • Haemoglobin cannot unload is false: coronary blood unloads more O2 than any other bed.
Slides (3)
L14LearningHigh yield
When does the left coronary artery fill, and why?
  1. A. Equally through the cycle: coronary flow is not affected by contraction
  2. B. Mainly in diastole: in systole the contracting muscle squeezes its own vessels shut
  3. C. Mainly in systole: in diastole the relaxed muscle collapses its own vessels
AnswerB. Mainly in diastole: in systole the contracting muscle squeezes its own vessels shut
WhyLeft coronary flow happens mainly in diastole: in systole the contracting left ventricle compresses its own intramural vessels.
Explanation

During systole left ventricular wall pressure exceeds the pressure inside the vessels that run through it, especially in the subendocardium, so flow nearly stops (the lecture: 'no flow in systole'). When the muscle relaxes, flow surges, which is the reactive hyperaemia that repays the systolic oxygen debt. Tachycardia shortens diastole and so cuts the time for coronary filling.

  • Mainly in systole reverses it: relaxed muscle opens the vessels.
  • Equal through the cycle ignores the mechanical compression shown in the special-circulation table.

The thinner-walled right ventricle compresses its vessels less, so right coronary flow continues in systole too.

Slides (3)
L15LearningHigh yield
What is cerebral blood flow most sensitive to?
  1. A. Interstitial K+ (plus tight autoregulation)
  2. B. Arterial O2 (plus tight autoregulation)
  3. C. Arterial CO2 (plus tight autoregulation)
AnswerC. Arterial CO2 (plus tight autoregulation)
WhyCO2 is the main local regulator of cerebral blood flow (H+ acts the same way); the brain also autoregulates tightly against pressure changes.
Explanation

The special-circulation table lists CO2 and H+ as the cerebral vasoactive metabolites. CO2 crosses the blood–brain barrier freely and lowers the pH around the cerebral arterioles, which dilates them; low CO2 constricts them.

  • O2 has little effect on cerebral vessels until it falls very low; hypoxia is the coronary signal.
  • K+ is a skeletal-muscle dilator.

Hook: the brain wants to get rid of CO2; the heart wants to get more O2.

Slides (3)
L16Learning
Why does rising intracranial pressure reduce cerebral blood flow?
  1. A. In a rigid skull, intracranial pressure opposes the arterial pressure driving blood in
  2. B. In a compliant skull, rising pressure stretches the vessels and lowers their resistance
  3. C. Rising pressure triggers a sympathetic reflex that constricts the cerebral arterioles
AnswerA. In a rigid skull, intracranial pressure opposes the arterial pressure driving blood in
WhyIn the rigid skull, a rise in intracranial pressure compresses the cerebral vessels; the effective driving pressure (arterial minus intracranial) falls, so flow falls.
Explanation

Cerebral perfusion pressure ≈ mean arterial pressure − intracranial pressure. A haematoma, oedema or tumour raises intracranial pressure because the skull cannot expand, and that pressure squeezes the thin-walled vessels. The special-circulation table lists this as the cerebral mechanical effect.

  • The adult skull is not compliant, and compression raises resistance rather than lowering it.
  • Cerebral vessels have little sympathetic control; the reflex response to high intracranial pressure (the Cushing reflex) raises systemic arterial pressure to push blood in.
Slides (1)
L17LearningHigh yield
An epidural haematoma is herniating the brain; one pupil is dilated. Why is the patient intubated and hyperventilated before drainage?
  1. A. Low CO2 constricts cerebral vessels → intracranial pressure falls quickly
  2. B. High CO2 dilates cerebral vessels → brain perfusion rises quickly
  3. C. Low O2 constricts cerebral vessels → intracranial pressure falls quickly
AnswerA. Low CO2 constricts cerebral vessels → intracranial pressure falls quickly
WhyHyperventilation lowers arterial CO2, which constricts cerebral arterioles, shrinks cerebral blood volume and rapidly lowers intracranial pressure.
Explanation

A herniating brain needs its pressure lowered within minutes. Blowing off CO2 constricts the cerebral arterioles; less blood inside the skull means lower intracranial pressure. It is a short-term holding measure until the haematoma is drained, because sustained constriction would itself starve the brain of flow.

  • Low O2 is not what hyperventilation produces (it raises O2), and O2 is not the cerebral signal.
  • Raising CO2 would dilate the vessels, increase cerebral blood volume and worsen herniation.
Slides (2)

Lecture 27 · Lung, skin, muscle, kidney

L18LearningHigh yield
How do pulmonary vessels respond to low alveolar oxygen?
  1. A. They constrict (hypoxia dilates systemic beds)
  2. B. They dilate (hypoxia constricts systemic beds)
  3. C. They constrict (hypoxia constricts systemic beds too)
AnswerA. They constrict (hypoxia dilates systemic beds)
WhyIn the lung, hypoxia constricts the arterioles: the 'biggest exception', since hypoxia dilates every systemic bed.
Explanation

Low alveolar PO2 constricts the small pulmonary arteries supplying that alveolar region (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction). In systemic beds such as the heart, low O2 is a vasodilator signal that raises delivery. The lung behaves the other way because blood goes there to pick up oxygen, not to deliver it.

  • Dilation is the systemic (e.g. coronary) response, not the pulmonary one.
  • Systemic beds constrict with hypoxia is false: the coronary bed dilates most strongly of all.

This exception is the most frequently tested fact in the lecture.

Slides (2)
L19LearningHigh yield
A man with long-standing emphysema has right ventricular hypertrophy. What is the mechanism?
  1. A. Hypoxic vasodilation → excess pulmonary flow → right ventricular volume overload
  2. B. Hypoxic vasoconstriction → pulmonary hypertension → raised right ventricular afterload
  3. C. Adenosine-induced vasodilation → low pulmonary pressure → reflex right ventricular growth
AnswerB. Hypoxic vasoconstriction → pulmonary hypertension → raised right ventricular afterload
WhyChronic alveolar hypoxia causes widespread hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction; the resulting pulmonary hypertension forces the right ventricle to hypertrophy.
Explanation

The right ventricle must generate a higher pressure to push its output through a constricted pulmonary bed. Like any ventricle facing a chronic pressure load, it thickens its wall (concentric hypertrophy), which by Laplace's law lowers the wall stress each fibre bears. Right ventricular hypertrophy from lung disease is called cor pulmonale.

  • Hypoxic vasodilation is the systemic response; the lung constricts.
  • Adenosine-induced dilation is the coronary story and would lower, not raise, the load on the right ventricle.
Slides (2)
L20Learning
What is skin blood flow mainly controlled for?
  1. A. Body temperature, not the skin's own needs: the body's radiator
  2. B. Arterial pressure, not temperature: the body's blood reservoir
  3. C. The skin's oxygen supply, not temperature: local metabolic control
AnswerA. Body temperature, not the skin's own needs: the body's radiator
WhySkin flow is controlled for temperature regulation, far beyond the skin's own needs; it is set mainly by sympathetic nerves.
Explanation

The skin's own metabolism is tiny, so its flow is free to serve the whole body. Blood is sent to the surface to lose heat (sympathetic withdrawal → dilation) and kept away to conserve heat (sympathetic alpha-1 constriction), so skin flow swings over a very wide range. Local metabolic control is the least important skin mechanism.

  • Oxygen supply: skin needs little, and metabolites matter least here.
  • Arterial pressure: skin is clamped when pressure falls, but that is a by-product of its sympathetic control; its main job is heat exchange.
Slides (2)
L21LearningHigh yield
What mainly controls skeletal-muscle blood flow while running?
  1. A. Central sympathetic tone: noradrenaline on alpha-1 receptors
  2. B. Parasympathetic tone: acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors
  3. C. Local metabolites (lactate, K+, adenosine) + epinephrine on beta-2
AnswerC. Local metabolites (lactate, K+, adenosine) + epinephrine on beta-2
WhyDuring exercise muscle switches to autoregulation: lactate, K+ and adenosine dilate its arterioles, aided by circulating epinephrine on beta-2 receptors.
Explanation

Running makes muscle important, and important things autoregulate. Working fibres release vasodilator metabolites that override sympathetic alpha-1 tone in the active muscle (active hyperaemia), so muscle flow can rise many-fold. Adrenal epinephrine adds beta-2 dilation.

  • Sympathetic alpha-1 constriction is the resting control; in exercise it still constricts gut, kidney and inactive muscle, but local metabolites dominate in working muscle.
  • Parasympathetic nerves do not supply skeletal-muscle arterioles.
Slides (2)
L22LearningHigh yield
How is renal blood flow autoregulated?
  1. A. Myogenic response + sympathetic baroreflex
  2. B. Myogenic response + tubuloglomerular feedback
  3. C. Metabolic dilators + hypoxic vasoconstriction
AnswerB. Myogenic response + tubuloglomerular feedback
WhyThe kidney autoregulates its flow by the myogenic response of the afferent arteriole and by tubuloglomerular feedback.
Explanation

A rise in renal perfusion pressure stretches the afferent arterioles, which constrict (myogenic). It also raises the filtered load reaching the macula densa, which signals the afferent arteriole to constrict (tubuloglomerular feedback). Both raise afferent resistance so renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate stay nearly constant. A fall in pressure produces the opposite: afferent dilation.

  • Hypoxic vasoconstriction is the pulmonary mechanism, and metabolites are not the renal regulators.
  • The sympathetic baroreflex is extrinsic, not autoregulation; renal autoregulation persists in a denervated (e.g. transplanted) kidney.
Slides (2)

Lecture 27 · Neural and chemical control

L23LearningHigh yield
Which vascular beds have dense sympathetic supply, and which have very little?
  1. A. Dense: coronary, cerebral
    Very little: skin, skeletal muscle
  2. B. Dense: skin, pulmonary
    Very little: coronary, skeletal muscle
  3. C. Dense: skin, skeletal muscle
    Very little: coronary, pulmonary, cerebral
AnswerC. Dense: skin, skeletal muscle
Very little: coronary, pulmonary, cerebral
WhySkin and skeletal muscle are richly supplied with sympathetic fibres; the coronary, pulmonary and cerebral beds have very few and little neural control.
Explanation

The pattern fits the lecture's theme: the vital beds (heart, brain, and the lung, which must take the whole output) are controlled locally, so a sympathetic discharge cannot starve them. Skin and muscle are the beds the sympathetic system uses to set total peripheral resistance and to redistribute flow.

  • Dense: coronary, cerebral swaps the two groups.
  • Dense: skin, pulmonary puts the pulmonary bed with skin (the lung's arterioles respond to alveolar O2, not to nerves) and wrongly puts skeletal muscle among the sparsely supplied beds.
Slides (1)
L24LearningHigh yield
What is the major vascular difference between epinephrine and norepinephrine?
  1. A. Beta-1: epinephrine dilates skin vessels via beta-1; norepinephrine constricts via alpha-2
  2. B. Beta-2: norepinephrine dilates muscle vessels via beta-2; epinephrine (little beta-2) constricts via alpha-1
  3. C. Beta-2: epinephrine dilates muscle vessels via beta-2; norepinephrine (little beta-2) constricts via alpha-1
AnswerC. Beta-2: epinephrine dilates muscle vessels via beta-2; norepinephrine (little beta-2) constricts via alpha-1
WhyThe key difference is beta-2: epinephrine stimulates it and dilates skeletal-muscle vessels; norepinephrine has little beta-2 effect and constricts through alpha-1.
Explanation

Both catecholamines stimulate alpha-1 and beta-1 receptors, but only epinephrine has strong beta-2 activity. Beta-2 receptors on skeletal-muscle arterioles act through Gs → cAMP, which inhibits myosin light-chain kinase and relaxes the smooth muscle. So epinephrine (especially at low doses) dilates muscle beds and can lower diastolic pressure, while norepinephrine constricts nearly everywhere and raises total peripheral resistance.

  • The second choice gives the beta-2 action to the wrong hormone.
  • Beta-1 receptors are cardiac (rate and contractility); they do not dilate skin vessels.
Slides (3)
L25LearningHigh yield
Where are epinephrine and norepinephrine made?
  1. A. Epinephrine: only the adrenal cortex
    Norepinephrine: adrenal cortex, sympathetic nerve endings, brain
  2. B. Norepinephrine: only the adrenal medulla
    Epinephrine: adrenal medulla, sympathetic nerve endings, brain
  3. C. Epinephrine: only the adrenal medulla
    Norepinephrine: adrenal medulla, sympathetic nerve endings, brain
AnswerC. Epinephrine: only the adrenal medulla
Norepinephrine: adrenal medulla, sympathetic nerve endings, brain
WhyEpinephrine is made only in the adrenal medulla; norepinephrine is made there and by postganglionic sympathetic nerve endings and the CNS.
Explanation

Only adrenal chromaffin cells have much phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase, the enzyme that converts norepinephrine to epinephrine; cortisol flowing from the adrenal cortex through the medulla induces it. So circulating epinephrine is a hormone of the adrenal medulla, while norepinephrine is the transmitter released at sympathetic nerve endings (and in the brain).

  • The second choice swaps the two catecholamines.
  • The adrenal cortex makes steroids (cortisol, aldosterone, androgens), not catecholamines.
Slides (1)
L26LearningHigh yield
What do histamine and bradykinin do to the microcirculation?
  1. A. Dilate arterioles, constrict venules → capillary pressure ↑ → fluid leaks out
  2. B. Constrict arterioles, dilate venules → capillary pressure ↓ → fluid is reabsorbed
  3. C. Constrict arterioles and venules → capillary pressure ↑ → fluid leaks out
AnswerA. Dilate arterioles, constrict venules → capillary pressure ↑ → fluid leaks out
WhyHistamine and bradykinin dilate arterioles and constrict venules: capillary hydrostatic pressure rises and fluid filters out, causing local oedema.
Explanation

Capillary pressure depends on the balance between upstream (arteriolar) and downstream (venular) resistance. Opening the arterioles lets more arterial pressure through; narrowing the venules dams blood in the capillaries. Both raise capillary hydrostatic pressure. Both mediators also increase capillary permeability, so the inflamed area swells.

  • The second choice is the exact reverse and would draw fluid back into the capillaries.
  • Arteriolar constriction would lower, not raise, the pressure reaching the capillaries.
Slides (3)
L27Learning
What is the overall vascular effect of the prostaglandins?
  1. A. Variable, but mostly vasoconstrictor
  2. B. Variable, but mostly vasodilator
  3. C. No direct effect on vessels
AnswerB. Variable, but mostly vasodilator
WhyProstaglandins have variable effects, but most of them dilate vessels.
Explanation

Prostaglandins are made from arachidonic acid by cyclooxygenase in many tissues. Prostacyclin (PGI2) and PGE2 are vasodilators; thromboxane A2 and PGF2α are vasoconstrictors. On balance the family is described as mostly dilatory.

  • Mostly vasoconstrictor describes serotonin or thromboxane A2, not the family as a whole.
  • No direct effect is false: they act on vascular smooth muscle receptors directly.
Slides (2)

PHYS-L28 Temperature regulation & exercise

24 learning questions · of 49
Learning questions 24

Lecture 28 · Normal temperature and the thermostat

L1Learning
When in the day is body temperature lowest and highest?
  1. A. Lowest about 6 pm
    Highest about 6 am
  2. B. Lowest about 6 am
    Highest about 6 pm
  3. C. Lowest about midnight
    Highest about noon
AnswerB. Lowest about 6 am
Highest about 6 pm
WhyCore temperature follows a circadian rhythm: lowest around 6 am and highest around 6 pm.
Explanation

Body temperature swings by roughly 0.5–1 °C over 24 hours under hypothalamic circadian control. It bottoms out in the early morning, at the end of sleep, and peaks in the late afternoon or early evening.

  • Midnight/noon shifts both points about six hours too early.
  • 6 pm low, 6 am high is the rhythm exactly reversed.

Clinical consequence: a 37.8 °C reading at 6 am is more worrying than the same reading at 6 pm.

Slides (2)
L2Learning
How does body temperature change around ovulation?
  1. A. Warmer before ovulation, cooler after
  2. B. Unchanged across the menstrual cycle
  3. C. Cooler before ovulation, warmer after
AnswerC. Cooler before ovulation, warmer after
WhyTemperature is lower before ovulation and higher after it, because the corpus luteum's progesterone is thermogenic.
Explanation

After ovulation the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, which raises the hypothalamic set point by about 0.3–0.5 °C for the rest of the luteal phase. The follicular (pre-ovulation) phase is therefore the cooler half of the cycle. This is the basis of basal-body-temperature charting for fertility.

  • Warmer before, cooler after reverses the progesterone effect.
  • Unchanged ignores a shift large enough to chart at home.
Slides (2)
L3Learning
Where is the body's thermostat, and what kind of control does it use?
  1. A. Hypothalamus; negative feedback
  2. B. Hypothalamus; positive feedback
  3. C. Anterior pituitary; negative feedback
AnswerA. Hypothalamus; negative feedback
WhyThe hypothalamus compares core temperature with a set point and drives responses that oppose any deviation: negative feedback.
Explanation

Thermoreceptors in the skin and in the hypothalamus itself report temperature to hypothalamic centres. If core temperature is above the set point, the hypothalamus turns on heat loss (skin vasodilation, sweating); if below, it turns on heat gain (skin vasoconstriction, shivering, sympathetic and thyroid thermogenesis). Each response pushes temperature back towards the set point, which is the definition of negative feedback. Fever is the same thermostat with the set point raised.

  • Positive feedback would amplify a rise in temperature, a runaway seen only when regulation fails (heat stroke).
  • The anterior pituitary releases thyroid-stimulating hormone, one effector of heat gain, but it does not sense temperature or hold the set point.
Slides (2)
L4Learning
How are heat loss and heat gain divided within the hypothalamus?
  1. A. Lateral hypothalamus: heat loss
    Posterior hypothalamus: heat gain
  2. B. Anterior hypothalamus: heat loss
    Posterior hypothalamus: heat gain
  3. C. Anterior hypothalamus: heat gain
    Posterior hypothalamus: heat loss
AnswerB. Anterior hypothalamus: heat loss
Posterior hypothalamus: heat gain
WhyThe anterior hypothalamus runs heat loss (skin vasodilation, sweating); the posterior hypothalamus runs heat gain (vasoconstriction, shivering).
Explanation

The anterior hypothalamus (preoptic area) responds to warming: it cuts sympathetic tone to skin arterioles and drives sympathetic cholinergic sweating. The posterior hypothalamus responds to cold: it raises sympathetic outflow to skin vessels and brown fat and activates the alpha and gamma motor neurons that cause shivering.

  • Anterior = heat gain swaps the two centres.
  • The lateral hypothalamus is the feeding (hunger) centre, not a temperature centre.

Hook: Anterior = Air-conditioner; posterior = furnace.

Slides (1)

Lecture 28 · Making and losing heat

L5Learning
What are the three ways the body generates heat?
  1. A. Thyroid hormone
    Sympathetic stimulation
    Shivering
  2. B. Cortisol
    Sympathetic stimulation
    Skin vasodilation
  3. C. Thyroid hormone
    Parasympathetic stimulation
    Shivering
AnswerA. Thyroid hormone
Sympathetic stimulation
Shivering
WhyHeat is generated by thyroid hormone (raised metabolic rate), sympathetic stimulation (brown fat, catecholamines) and shivering (muscle work).
Explanation

All three convert stored chemical energy into heat. Thyroid hormone raises the basal metabolic rate of nearly every cell; sympathetic activity burns brown fat and raises metabolism through catecholamines; shivering makes skeletal muscle contract rhythmically without useful movement, so its energy appears as heat.

  • The parasympathetic system does not generate heat; heat gain is sympathetic.
  • Skin vasodilation loses heat. Cortisol is released by cold, but the lecture's three generators are thyroid, sympathetic and shivering.
Slides (1)
L6LearningHigh yield
How does thyroid hormone generate heat?
  1. A. T4 → T3 (more active) → inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase → ↓ O2 consumption and metabolic rate
  2. B. T4 → T3 (more active) → ↑ Na+/K+-ATPase → ↑ O2 consumption and metabolic rate
  3. C. T3 → T4 (more active) → ↑ Na+/K+-ATPase → ↑ O2 consumption and metabolic rate
AnswerB. T4 → T3 (more active) → ↑ Na+/K+-ATPase → ↑ O2 consumption and metabolic rate
WhyThyroxine (T4) is converted to the more active T3, which induces Na+/K+-ATPase; pumping burns ATP, raising O2 consumption, metabolic rate and heat.
Explanation

The thyroid secretes mostly T4; tissues remove one iodine to make T3, the form that binds nuclear receptors. T3 increases synthesis of Na+/K+-ATPase. More pumps consume more ATP, so mitochondria burn more fuel and O2, and the energy released appears as heat. Thyroid hormone is therefore directly thermogenic, and cold exposure increases its secretion.

  • T3 → T4 reverses the activation step: T4 is the prohormone.
  • Inhibiting the pump would lower metabolic rate and heat, the picture of hypothyroidism.
Slides (1)
L7LearningHigh yield
In the cold, how do catecholamines both make heat and keep it?
  1. A. Beta receptors on brown fat → heat produced
    Alpha-1 receptors on skin vessels → constriction keeps heat in
  2. B. Alpha-1 receptors on brown fat → heat produced
    Beta-2 receptors on skin vessels → dilation keeps heat in
  3. C. Beta receptors on white fat → heat produced
    Alpha-1 receptors on skin vessels → dilation keeps heat in
AnswerA. Beta receptors on brown fat → heat produced
Alpha-1 receptors on skin vessels → constriction keeps heat in
WhyNorepinephrine on brown-fat beta receptors burns fat to make heat; on skin alpha-1 receptors it constricts vessels to keep that heat in the core.
Explanation

Brown fat (interscapular, around the neck and great vessels; abundant in newborns) has many mitochondria containing uncoupling protein-1 (thermogenin). Sympathetic stimulation of its beta receptors releases fatty acids that are burned with the proton gradient 'short-circuited', so the energy appears as heat instead of ATP. The lecture slide names beta-1 receptors on brown fat; most textbooks name beta-3. Exam answers will say 'beta'.

  • Alpha-1 on brown fat / beta-2 dilation keeps heat in swaps the receptors, and dilation would lose heat.
  • White fat stores energy and is not thermogenic, and alpha-1 constricts, it never dilates.
Slides (3)
L8Learning
The lecture says thyroid hormone is 'permissive' for catecholamines in heat production. What does that mean?
  1. A. Catecholamines need thyroid hormone present to give their full heat-producing effect
  2. B. Thyroid hormone blocks catecholamine effects, keeping heat production steady
  3. C. Catecholamines are needed for the thyroid gland to secrete any hormone at all
AnswerA. Catecholamines need thyroid hormone present to give their full heat-producing effect
WhyA permissive hormone does not cause the response itself but must be present for another hormone (here catecholamines) to act fully; thyroid hormone up-regulates the beta-adrenergic machinery.
Explanation

Thyroid hormone increases the number and responsiveness of beta-adrenergic receptors and the enzymes they drive. With normal thyroid levels, sympathetic stimulation of brown fat and other tissues produces its full thermogenic effect; in hypothyroidism the same sympathetic drive makes much less heat. This is why the two systems work together: blocking either one reduces maximal heat production.

  • Thyroid secretion is driven by thyroid-stimulating hormone from the pituitary, not by catecholamines.
  • Blocking is the opposite of permissive; thyroid hormone amplifies, not damps, the catecholamine effect.
Slides (1)
L9LearningHigh yield
Which nerve fibres drive sweating?
  1. A. Sympathetic fibres releasing norepinephrine onto alpha-1 receptors
  2. B. Sympathetic fibres releasing acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors
  3. C. Parasympathetic fibres releasing acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors
AnswerB. Sympathetic fibres releasing acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors
WhyThermoregulatory sweat glands are innervated by sympathetic cholinergic fibres: sympathetic anatomy, but they release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors.
Explanation

This is the classic exception to the rule that sympathetic postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine. The fibres run in sympathetic nerves and are activated by the anterior hypothalamus when the body is warm, but their transmitter is acetylcholine. That is why anticholinergic drugs (atropine) cause hot, dry skin.

  • Norepinephrine / alpha-1 is the transmitter-receptor pair for skin vessels, not eccrine sweat glands.
  • The parasympathetic system has no supply to the skin; only the receptor (muscarinic) is shared.
Slides (3)

Lecture 28 · Fever and heat illness

L10LearningHigh yield
What is the sequence of events that produces fever?
  1. A. Pyrogens → interleukin-1 → hypothalamus → prostaglandin E2 → raised set point
  2. B. Pyrogens → interleukin-1 → pituitary → thromboxane A2 → raised set point
  3. C. Pyrogens → prostaglandin E2 → hypothalamus → interleukin-1 → raised set point
AnswerA. Pyrogens → interleukin-1 → hypothalamus → prostaglandin E2 → raised set point
WhyPyrogens make phagocytes release interleukin-1 (IL-1), which acts on the anterior hypothalamus to produce prostaglandin E2 (PGE2); PGE2 raises the temperature set point.
Explanation

A pyrogen is any substance that causes fever (bacterial endotoxin, other microbial products). It stimulates macrophages and other phagocytes to release IL-1 (along with IL-6 and tumour necrosis factor). IL-1 induces cyclooxygenase in the hypothalamus, and the PGE2 it makes is the internal signal that resets the thermostat upwards. The body then 'feels cold' at 37 °C and generates heat until it reaches the new set point.

  • PGE2 before IL-1 reverses the order: PGE2 is the last, local step.
  • The pituitary and thromboxane A2 play no part; the thermostat is hypothalamic and the mediator is PGE2.
Slides (2)
L11Learning
At the start of a fever the patient shivers and has cold, pale skin even though the core temperature is already 37.5 °C. Why?
  1. A. The set point has risen above core temperature, so heat-gain mechanisms are switched on
  2. B. Pyrogens act directly on muscle and skin vessels, bypassing the hypothalamus
  3. C. The set point has fallen below core temperature, so heat-gain mechanisms are switched on
AnswerA. The set point has risen above core temperature, so heat-gain mechanisms are switched on
WhyProstaglandin E2 resets the thermostat higher; the hypothalamus now reads the body as too cold and drives shivering and skin vasoconstriction (chills) until core temperature reaches the new set point.
Explanation

Fever is regulated hyperthermia: the thermostat still works by negative feedback, only around a higher target. If the set point jumps to 39 °C, a core temperature of 37.5 °C is an error signal of −1.5 °C, so the patient shivers, constricts skin vessels, feels cold and reaches for blankets. Once core temperature matches the new set point, the chills stop.

  • A lowered set point would trigger heat loss (sweating, flushing), not shivering.
  • Pyrogens act through interleukin-1 and hypothalamic PGE2; they do not drive muscles or vessels directly.
Slides (2)
L12LearningHigh yield
How do aspirin, other NSAIDs and acetaminophen lower a fever?
  1. A. Inhibit phospholipase A2 → no arachidonic acid
  2. B. Inhibit lipoxygenase → no leukotriene B4
  3. C. Inhibit cyclooxygenase → no prostaglandin E2
AnswerC. Inhibit cyclooxygenase → no prostaglandin E2
WhyAntipyretics block cyclooxygenase (COX), the enzyme that makes prostaglandins, so the hypothalamus cannot make the PGE2 that raised the set point.
Explanation

Cyclooxygenase converts arachidonic acid into prostaglandins. Aspirin and the other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) inhibit it throughout the body; acetaminophen inhibits it mainly within the central nervous system, so it lowers fever without much anti-inflammatory effect. The lecture calls this blocking the last step of the fever pathway: interleukin-1 is still released, but it can no longer raise the set point.

  • Phospholipase A2 is the step before COX; it is inhibited by glucocorticoids, not NSAIDs.
  • Lipoxygenase makes leukotrienes, which are not the fever mediator.
Slides (2)
L13Learning
Which picture is heat exhaustion?
  1. A. Hot dry skin, temperature above 40 °C, persisting confusion, often a raised creatine kinase
  2. B. Cramping leg and abdominal muscles; normal temperature, creatine kinase and mental status
  3. C. Sweating, nausea, weakness, severe thirst, normal blood pressure; any confusion clears within 30 minutes of cooling
AnswerC. Sweating, nausea, weakness, severe thirst, normal blood pressure; any confusion clears within 30 minutes of cooling
WhyHeat exhaustion = a sweating, thirsty, nauseated, weak patient with normal blood pressure and normal mental status (or mild confusion that clears within 30 minutes of cooling): mild-to-moderate dehydration.
Explanation

The lecture's list: sweating; nausea, vomiting, headache; fatigue, weakness, dizziness; normal BP; fainting with prompt return of normal mental status; severe thirst; signs of mild to moderate dehydration. The key point is that sweating and thermoregulation are still working; the problem is the volume lost through them.

  • Hot dry skin, above 40 °C, persisting confusion is heat stroke: thermoregulation has failed and the brain is affected.
  • Cramps with everything else normal is heat cramps, the mildest disorder.
Slides (2)
L14LearningHigh yield
What are the defining features of heat stroke?
  1. A. Above 40 °C; altered mental status; dry skin; creatine kinase often raised
  2. B. Above 40 °C; normal mental status; heavy sweating; creatine kinase normal
  3. C. Normal temperature; altered mental status; dry skin; creatine kinase normal
AnswerA. Above 40 °C; altered mental status; dry skin; creatine kinase often raised
WhyHeat stroke = core temperature above 40 °C + altered mental status, with dry skin and often a raised creatine kinase from muscle breakdown.
Explanation

In heat stroke thermoregulation fails: sweating stops, heat can no longer be lost, and core temperature climbs past 40 °C. The brain is injured (confusion, delirium, seizures, coma) and muscle breaks down (rhabdomyolysis, raised creatine kinase). The lecture slide writes 'creatinine kinase'; the enzyme is creatine kinase. Dry skin is the classic sign; exertional heat stroke in athletes can still present with some sweating.

  • Normal mental status with heavy sweating describes heat exhaustion.
  • A normal temperature rules heat stroke out by definition.
Slides (2)
L15Learning
How is heat stroke treated?
  1. A. Evaporative cooling + intravenous fluids
  2. B. Antipyretics (acetaminophen) + oral fluids
  3. C. Dantrolene + intravenous fluids
AnswerA. Evaporative cooling + intravenous fluids
WhyHeat stroke is treated by evaporative cooling ('spray them down') plus intravenous fluids.
Explanation

The aim is to lower core temperature fast: strip the patient, spray lukewarm water on the skin and fan it, so evaporation removes heat (ice-water immersion is also used). Intravenous fluids restore the volume lost to sweating and support blood pressure.

  • Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia by blocking calcium release in muscle; it does not help heat stroke.
  • Antipyretics work only when the set point is raised (fever). In heat stroke the set point is normal and the body is overwhelmed, so blocking prostaglandin E2 does nothing; an altered patient also cannot drink safely.
Slides (1)
L16Learning
What is malignant hyperthermia, and what are its findings?
  1. A. Probably inherited reaction to anaesthetics (enflurane, sevoflurane): masseter and general rigidity, high creatine kinase and arterial CO2
  2. B. Probably inherited reaction to local anaesthetics (lidocaine): masseter and general rigidity, low creatine kinase and arterial CO2
  3. C. Infection-triggered reaction to anaesthetics (enflurane, sevoflurane): flaccid paralysis, normal creatine kinase and arterial CO2
AnswerA. Probably inherited reaction to anaesthetics (enflurane, sevoflurane): masseter and general rigidity, high creatine kinase and arterial CO2
WhyMalignant hyperthermia is an idiosyncratic, probably genetic reaction to inhaled anaesthetics: high temperature, masseter and general muscle rigidity, high creatine kinase and high PCO2.
Explanation

In susceptible people (usually a mutation in the skeletal-muscle ryanodine receptor, RYR1) volatile anaesthetics such as enflurane and sevoflurane, and succinylcholine, trigger uncontrolled Ca2+ release in muscle. Sustained contraction produces rigidity (often first in the jaw), massive heat and CO2 production, and muscle breakdown with a high creatine kinase (CK, CPK).

  • Lidocaine (a local anaesthetic) is not a trigger, and CK and CO2 rise, not fall.
  • It is not infection-triggered, and muscles are rigid, not flaccid.
Slides (2)

Lecture 28 · Exercise

L17LearningHigh yield
Where does the cardiovascular drive in exercise begin?
  1. A. Arterial baroreceptors in the carotid sinus, plus central chemoreceptors in the medulla
  2. B. Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid body, plus stretch receptors in the lung
  3. C. Central command from the brain, plus mechanoreceptors and chemoreceptors in working muscle
AnswerC. Central command from the brain, plus mechanoreceptors and chemoreceptors in working muscle
WhyThe exercise response is started by central command (the cerebral motor cortex anticipating and directing exercise) and reinforced by mechano- and chemoreceptors in the working muscles.
Explanation

Even before muscles start working, the motor cortex signals the medullary cardiovascular centres to raise heart rate and blood pressure: this is central command. Once exercise starts, receptors in the muscle sense stretch/tension (mechanoreceptors) and metabolites (chemoreceptors) and add to the drive.

  • Baroreceptors oppose rises in pressure; in exercise they are reset upward rather than starting the response.
  • Peripheral chemoreceptors respond to low arterial O2, but arterial PO2, PCO2 and pH barely change in moderate exercise, so they play little role.
Slides (2)
L18LearningHigh yield
What is the overall cardiovascular response to exercise?
  1. A. Metabolites constrict working muscle; parasympathetic ↑ rate and contractility; venous return ↓; cardiac output ↑ slightly
  2. B. Metabolites dilate working muscle; sympathetic ↓ rate, ↑ contractility; venous return ↓; cardiac output ↑ several-fold
  3. C. Metabolites dilate working muscle; sympathetic ↑ rate and contractility; venous return ↑; cardiac output ↑ several-fold
AnswerC. Metabolites dilate working muscle; sympathetic ↑ rate and contractility; venous return ↑; cardiac output ↑ several-fold
WhyTwo arms act together: local metabolites dilate working muscle (↓ total peripheral resistance), while sympathetic drive raises heart rate, contractility and venous return, so cardiac output rises several-fold.
Explanation

The local arm directs flow: lactate, adenosine and K+ dilate the arterioles of the working muscle. The central arm supplies the flow: sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate and contractility, constricts veins and constricts arterioles in inactive beds. Venous return and cardiac output rise together (in a steady state they must be equal), from about 5 to 15–25 L/min.

  • Sympathetic ↓ rate and ↓ venous return could not support a several-fold rise in output.
  • Metabolites dilate, never constrict, and the parasympathetic system does not raise contractility.
Slides (3)
L19LearningHigh yield
How does venous return keep pace with cardiac output in exercise?
  1. A. Veins dilate, and the muscle pump squeezes them against one-way valves towards the heart
  2. B. Veins constrict, and the muscle pump squeezes them against one-way valves towards the heart
  3. C. Arteries constrict, and the muscle pump squeezes them against two-way valves towards the heart
AnswerB. Veins constrict, and the muscle pump squeezes them against one-way valves towards the heart
WhySympathetic venoconstriction moves blood out of the venous reservoir, and the skeletal-muscle pump squeezes veins whose one-way valves let blood go only towards the heart.
Explanation

Veins hold most of the blood volume (the unstressed volume). Constricting them shifts that blood into the circulating (stressed) volume and raises venous return and preload. Each muscle contraction compresses deep veins; the valves stop backflow, so blood is pumped heartwards. More filling → greater stroke volume by the Frank-Starling mechanism.

  • Veins dilate would increase venous capacity and let blood pool, lowering return.
  • Arteries have no valves, and venous valves are one-way; two-way valves could not pump.
Slides (1)
L20LearningHigh yield
During exercise, in which vascular beds do the arterioles constrict?
  1. A. Skin, coronary, working muscle, kidney
  2. B. Skin, spleen, gut, kidney, inactive muscle
  3. C. Coronary, cerebral, working muscle
AnswerB. Skin, spleen, gut, kidney, inactive muscle
WhySympathetic alpha-1 constriction in the skin, spleen, gut, kidney and inactive muscle diverts flow towards the working muscle and heart.
Explanation

This is 'selective arteriolar constriction'. Beds that can tolerate less flow for a while are turned down, which keeps arterial pressure up and frees cardiac output for the exercising muscle. Skin is a special case: it constricts at first, then dilates as body temperature climbs.

  • Coronary, cerebral and working muscle are the beds that dilate (or are protected), the opposite list.
  • The skin, coronary, working muscle, kidney list mixes constricting beds (skin, kidney) with dilating ones (coronary, working muscle).
Slides (2)
L21LearningHigh yield
During exercise total peripheral resistance (TPR) falls. Why?
  1. A. Local metabolites dilate the arterioles of the large exercising muscle mass
  2. B. Local metabolites dilate the arterioles of the cerebral circulation
  3. C. Sympathetic nerves dilate the arterioles of the splanchnic and renal beds
AnswerA. Local metabolites dilate the arterioles of the large exercising muscle mass
WhyLactate, adenosine and K+ from working muscle dilate its arterioles; skeletal muscle is such a large share of the circulation that whole-body TPR falls despite constriction elsewhere.
Explanation

This is active hyperaemia on a massive scale. Total peripheral resistance (TPR) is the combined resistance of all the parallel beds. Skeletal muscle makes up about 40% of body mass, so opening its arterioles lowers TPR more than sympathetic constriction of the gut, kidney and skin raises it. The metabolites override sympathetic vasoconstriction in the working muscle itself.

  • Sympathetic nerves constrict splanchnic and renal arterioles through alpha-1 receptors; that raises, not lowers, their resistance.
  • Cerebral flow is protected but small; it cannot account for the whole-body fall in TPR.
Slides (2)
L22LearningHigh yield
In exercise, why does mean arterial pressure rise only a little, and what happens to pulse pressure?
  1. A. Small ↑ cardiac output × big ↑ total peripheral resistance = small ↑ mean pressure
    Pulse pressure narrows
  2. B. Big ↑ cardiac output × small ↓ total peripheral resistance = small ↑ mean pressure
    Pulse pressure narrows
  3. C. Big ↑ cardiac output × small ↓ total peripheral resistance = small ↑ mean pressure
    Pulse pressure widens
AnswerC. Big ↑ cardiac output × small ↓ total peripheral resistance = small ↑ mean pressure
Pulse pressure widens
WhyMean arterial pressure = cardiac output × total peripheral resistance (TPR): a big rise in output times a smaller fall in TPR gives a small rise in mean pressure; the larger stroke volume widens pulse pressure.
Explanation

If cardiac output triples while TPR halves, mean pressure rises by half; the fall in TPR stops pressure from rising as much as output does. Pulse pressure (systolic minus diastolic) depends mainly on stroke volume and arterial compliance; exercise raises stroke volume and ejects it faster, so systolic rises clearly, while the low TPR lets diastolic stay the same or fall. The gap widens.

  • Pulse pressure narrows only when stroke volume falls (haemorrhage, heart failure).
  • TPR falls, not rises, in exercise, because working muscle dilates.
Slides (3)
L23LearningHigh yield
In the same exerciser, arterial PO2 stays at 100 mmHg but mixed venous PO2 falls from 40 to 25 mmHg. Why?
  1. A. Blood flow through the working muscle falls during exercise
  2. B. The lungs load less O2 into the blood during exercise
  3. C. Working muscle extracts more O2 from each litre of blood
AnswerC. Working muscle extracts more O2 from each litre of blood
WhyArterial blood is fully loaded (PO2 100), so the fall in venous PO2 means the tissues are extracting more O2: the arteriovenous O2 difference widens.
Explanation

Working muscle consumes O2 fast; its tissue PO2 falls, the gradient for diffusion steepens, and acidity, CO2 and heat shift haemoglobin to unload more O2. Blood leaving the muscle is therefore much more deoxygenated. Total O2 delivery rises from both higher cardiac output and greater extraction. Arterial PO2, PCO2 and pH stay near normal in moderate exercise because ventilation rises in step.

  • Less loading in the lungs would lower arterial PO2, which is unchanged at 100.
  • Muscle blood flow rises in exercise; falling flow is not what happens.
Slides (2)
L24Learning
Why is hard exercise in hot weather especially likely to cause collapse?
  1. A. Sweating thickens the blood so much that flow to the brain stops
  2. B. Working muscle and skin both demand flow, and cardiac output cannot supply both
  3. C. Heat directly depresses the myocardium, so cardiac output falls
AnswerB. Working muscle and skin both demand flow, and cardiac output cannot supply both
WhyIn heat, the skin needs large flows to shed heat while working muscle needs flow for O2; together they lower resistance and pool blood beyond what cardiac output can supply, and arterial pressure falls.
Explanation

Skin vasodilation fills the large cutaneous venous plexus, lowering venous return just when muscle vasodilation has already lowered total peripheral resistance. Sweating removes plasma volume at the same time. Cardiac output has a ceiling, so arterial pressure, and brain perfusion, can fall: the exerciser becomes light-headed or faints, and if sweating then fails, core temperature climbs towards heat stroke.

  • Heat does not depress the myocardium at these temperatures; the heart beats faster in heat.
  • Dehydration raises viscosity only slightly; it does not stop brain flow.
Slides (1)

PHYS-L29 Hemorrhage & posture

20 learning questions · of 40
Learning questions 20

Lecture 29 · Haemorrhage

L1LearningHigh yield
What is the first haemodynamic chain set off by a haemorrhage?
  1. A. Volume ↓ → cardiac output ↓ → venous return ↓ → arterial pressure ↑
  2. B. Volume ↓ → arterial pressure ↓ → venous return ↓ → cardiac output ↓
  3. C. Volume ↓ → venous return ↓ → cardiac output ↓ → arterial pressure ↓
AnswerC. Volume ↓ → venous return ↓ → cardiac output ↓ → arterial pressure ↓
WhyLosing blood lowers venous return and right atrial pressure; less filling means a smaller stroke volume (Frank-Starling), so cardiac output and then arterial pressure fall.
Explanation

Mean arterial pressure = cardiac output × total peripheral resistance. Haemorrhage acts on the first factor: less blood → less venous return → lower end-diastolic volume → lower stroke volume and cardiac output → lower arterial pressure (Pa). Every compensation that follows tries to undo one of these steps.

  • Pressure ↑ at the end is wrong; haemorrhage lowers arterial pressure. Cardiac output also follows venous return, not the reverse.
  • Arterial pressure falls because cardiac output falls; it is the last link, not the second.
Slides (2)
L2LearningHigh yield
What is the immediate reflex response to haemorrhage?
  1. A. Carotid sinus (IX) and aortic arch (X) baroreceptors → hypothalamus: ↓ sympathetic, ↑ parasympathetic → bradycardia, ↓ contractility, arteriolar dilation (↓ TPR), venodilation
  2. B. Carotid sinus (X) and aortic arch (IX) baroreceptors → medulla: ↑ sympathetic, ↓ parasympathetic → tachycardia, ↑ contractility, arteriolar constriction (↑ TPR), venoconstriction
  3. C. Carotid sinus (IX) and aortic arch (X) baroreceptors → medulla: ↑ sympathetic, ↓ parasympathetic → tachycardia, ↑ contractility, arteriolar constriction (↑ TPR), venoconstriction
AnswerC. Carotid sinus (IX) and aortic arch (X) baroreceptors → medulla: ↑ sympathetic, ↓ parasympathetic → tachycardia, ↑ contractility, arteriolar constriction (↑ TPR), venoconstriction
WhyThe baroreceptor reflex: carotid sinus (nerve IX) and aortic arch (nerve X) → medulla → ↑ sympathetic, ↓ parasympathetic → ↑ heart rate, ↑ contractility, ↑ total peripheral resistance (TPR), venoconstriction.
Explanation

Each effector restores a factor in the pressure equation: heart rate and contractility raise cardiac output; arteriolar constriction raises TPR; venoconstriction lowers the unstressed volume and returns more blood to the heart. These are the four compensations on the lecture slide and the most-asked haemorrhage fact.

  • The choice with carotid sinus (X) and aortic arch (IX) swaps the nerves: the carotid sinus nerve joins the glossopharyngeal (IX), the aortic arch nerve joins the vagus (X).
  • The bradycardia and dilation choice describes the response to raised pressure; it would make haemorrhage worse, and the integrating centre is the medulla, not the hypothalamus.
Slides (3)
L3LearningHigh yield
In haemorrhage, which beds are constricted, and why?
  1. A. Skin, gut, kidney and skeletal muscle → to protect the brain and heart
  2. B. Lung and skeletal muscle only → to protect the kidney and gut
  3. C. Brain and heart → to protect the skin, gut and kidney
AnswerA. Skin, gut, kidney and skeletal muscle → to protect the brain and heart
WhySympathetic arteriolar constriction raises resistance in skin, splanchnic, renal and muscle beds while sparing the coronary and cerebral circulations, which autoregulate.
Explanation

The aim is to keep arterial pressure, and flow to the organs that cannot survive without it, adequate. Beds dominated by sympathetic alpha-1 control (skin, gut, kidney, resting muscle) are turned down; the heart and brain are controlled mainly by local metabolites and autoregulation, so they keep their flow. Pale, cool skin and low urine output are visible signs of this redistribution: arterial pressure is protected at the kidney's expense.

  • Constricting the brain and heart would sacrifice the organs the reflex exists to protect.
  • The lung is not a sympathetic-resistance bed, and the kidney and gut are among the beds sacrificed, not protected.
Slides (2)
L4LearningHigh yield
Why does fluid move from the tissues into the blood after a haemorrhage?
  1. A. Constricted venules ↓ capillary hydrostatic pressure → Starling balance tips to filtration
  2. B. Constricted arterioles ↑ capillary hydrostatic pressure → Starling balance tips to filtration
  3. C. Constricted arterioles ↓ capillary hydrostatic pressure → Starling balance tips to reabsorption
AnswerC. Constricted arterioles ↓ capillary hydrostatic pressure → Starling balance tips to reabsorption
WhyArteriolar constriction lets less pressure through to the capillaries; capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) falls, so oncotic pressure wins and fluid is reabsorbed into the blood.
Explanation

Net driving force = (Pc − Pi) − σ(πc − πi). Positive means filtration, negative means reabsorption. Sympathetic and angiotensin II constriction of upstream arterioles lowers Pc; plasma oncotic pressure is unchanged (whole blood was lost), so the balance tips towards reabsorption. This 'autotransfusion' restores plasma volume over hours, and it dilutes the red cells, which is why the haematocrit falls only later.

  • ↑ Pc is what venous (downstream) constriction or pooling does, the cause of oedema on standing.
  • Lower Pc cannot cause filtration; it reduces it.
Slides (2)
L5LearningHigh yield
Why is renin released in haemorrhage?
  1. A. ↓ Renal perfusion and ↓ afferent arteriolar stretch → juxtaglomerular cells release renin
  2. B. ↑ Renal perfusion and ↑ afferent arteriolar stretch → juxtaglomerular cells release renin
  3. C. ↓ Renal perfusion → macula densa cells release renin into the tubule
AnswerA. ↓ Renal perfusion and ↓ afferent arteriolar stretch → juxtaglomerular cells release renin
WhyLow systolic pressure lowers renal perfusion and stretch of the afferent arteriole; the juxtaglomerular cells in its wall sense this and secrete renin into the blood.
Explanation

The juxtaglomerular cells are modified smooth-muscle cells of the afferent arteriole that act as an intrarenal baroreceptor: less stretch → more renin. Sympathetic beta-1 stimulation of the same cells, raised by the baroreceptor reflex, adds to renin release. Renin starts the cascade angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → angiotensin II → aldosterone.

  • More perfusion and stretch suppress renin; that is how high pressure switches the system off.
  • The macula densa senses tubular NaCl and signals the juxtaglomerular cells; it does not secrete renin, and renin goes into the blood, not the tubule.
Slides (2)
L6LearningHigh yield
What does angiotensin II do in haemorrhage?
  1. A. Dilates arterioles
    Stimulates aldosterone → Na+ and water retained
  2. B. Constricts arterioles
    Stimulates aldosterone → Na+ and water retained
  3. C. Constricts arterioles
    Stimulates antidiuretic hormone → Na+ excreted, water retained
AnswerB. Constricts arterioles
Stimulates aldosterone → Na+ and water retained
WhyAngiotensin II constricts arterioles (↑ total peripheral resistance, fast) and stimulates aldosterone, which makes the kidney reabsorb Na+ and water (↑ blood volume, slow).
Explanation

The two actions work on the two factors of arterial pressure. Vasoconstriction raises resistance within minutes. Aldosterone acts on the principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct to reabsorb Na+; water follows, extracellular and blood volume rise over hours to days, and pressure returns towards normal. Angiotensin II also stimulates thirst and some proximal-tubule Na+ reabsorption directly.

  • Angiotensin II does also stimulate antidiuretic hormone release, but Na+ is retained, not excreted, in haemorrhage; excreting it would lose volume.
  • Angiotensin II is one of the most potent constrictors; it never dilates arterioles.
Slides (2)
L7LearningHigh yield
What does antidiuretic hormone (ADH) do in haemorrhage, and through which receptors?
  1. A. V1 receptors → arteriolar constriction
    V2 receptors → water reabsorption in the kidney
  2. B. V1 receptors → arteriolar dilation
    V2 receptors → water excretion by the kidney
  3. C. V2 receptors → arteriolar constriction
    V1 receptors → water reabsorption in the kidney
AnswerA. V1 receptors → arteriolar constriction
V2 receptors → water reabsorption in the kidney
WhyADH (vasopressin) acts on V1 receptors to constrict arterioles and on V2 receptors in the collecting duct to reabsorb water.
Explanation

ADH is normally controlled by osmolarity: a 1% rise in plasma osmolarity releases enough to act on V2 receptors. A ~10% fall in blood volume releases much more, enough to act on vascular V1 receptors as well, so in haemorrhage ADH both retains water and raises total peripheral resistance. V2 receptors insert aquaporin-2 channels into the collecting-duct cells.

  • The swapped choice reverses the receptors: V1 is Vascular, V2 is the kidney.
  • ADH is anti-diuretic: it conserves water and constricts vessels; it never dilates or causes water loss.

Hook: V1 = Vasoconstriction; V2 = 2 kidneys.

Slides (2)
L8Learning
How do chemoreceptors add to the response to haemorrhage?
  1. A. Hypoxia → peripheral chemoreceptors ↑ parasympathetic outflow; cerebral ischaemia → baroreceptors ↑ parasympathetic outflow
  2. B. Hypoxia → peripheral chemoreceptors ↑ sympathetic outflow; cerebral ischaemia → central chemoreceptors ↑ sympathetic outflow
  3. C. Hypoxia → central chemoreceptors ↓ sympathetic outflow; cerebral ischaemia → peripheral chemoreceptors ↓ sympathetic outflow
AnswerB. Hypoxia → peripheral chemoreceptors ↑ sympathetic outflow; cerebral ischaemia → central chemoreceptors ↑ sympathetic outflow
WhySevere blood loss makes the carotid and aortic bodies hypoxic (peripheral chemoreceptors), and brain ischaemia stimulates central receptors; both raise sympathetic outflow, pressure and resistance.
Explanation

The peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies have a very high blood flow; when pressure and flow fall far enough they become hypoxic and fire, adding sympathetic drive to the baroreceptor reflex. If pressure falls so low that the brainstem itself becomes ischaemic, the central response (the central nervous system ischaemic response) produces intense sympathetic vasoconstriction, a last-ditch defence.

  • Both chemoreceptor responses increase, not decrease, sympathetic outflow.
  • Neither raises parasympathetic outflow; that would slow the heart.
Slides (3)
L9LearningHigh yield
What does a haemorrhage do to the vascular function (venous return) curve?
  1. A. Rotates it clockwise, because total peripheral resistance rises
  2. B. Shifts it to the right, because mean systemic filling pressure rises
  3. C. Shifts it to the left, because mean systemic filling pressure falls
AnswerC. Shifts it to the left, because mean systemic filling pressure falls
WhyLosing blood lowers the stressed volume and therefore the mean systemic filling pressure; the vascular function curve shifts in parallel to the left, so cardiac output and right atrial pressure both fall.
Explanation

The vascular function curve plots venous return against right atrial pressure; its x-intercept is the mean systemic filling pressure. Blood volume sets that intercept: a loss of volume moves the whole curve left without changing its slope. Where it crosses the cardiac function curve, both cardiac output and right atrial pressure are lower.

  • Right shift happens with transfusion or venoconstriction (more stressed volume), not haemorrhage.
  • Rotation is caused by changes in total peripheral resistance (a rise rotates the curve counterclockwise, not clockwise), not by a change in blood volume, and the immediate effect of blood loss is a parallel shift.
Slides (1)

Lecture 29 · Standing up and orthostatic hypotension

L10LearningHigh yield
When a person stands up, what property of the circulation allows so much blood to pool in the legs?
  1. A. The low capacitance (compliance) of the veins
  2. B. The high capacitance (compliance) of the veins
  3. C. The high capacitance (compliance) of the arterioles
AnswerB. The high capacitance (compliance) of the veins
WhyVeins are highly compliant capacitance vessels: gravity raises their pressure and they stretch to hold several hundred millilitres more blood in the legs.
Explanation

Compliance = change in volume / change in pressure. Venous walls are thin with little smooth muscle, so a modest rise in venous pressure (the weight of the column of blood when upright) distends them greatly. About 500–800 mL shifts into the leg veins on standing, which lowers venous return and cardiac output.

  • Arterioles are resistance vessels with thick muscular walls and low compliance; they hold little blood.
  • Low venous compliance would prevent pooling; the problem is that veins are so distensible.
Slides (1)
L11Learning
A man jumps out of bed, feels light-headed, then feels better once he starts walking. Why does walking help?
  1. A. Walking constricts the leg arterioles, raising capillary hydrostatic pressure
  2. B. Contracting leg muscles squeeze the veins, pumping pooled blood back to the heart
  3. C. Walking dilates the leg veins, increasing their capacity to hold blood
AnswerB. Contracting leg muscles squeeze the veins, pumping pooled blood back to the heart
WhyThe skeletal-muscle pump: contracting leg muscles compress the deep veins, and the one-way valves send the pooled blood heartwards, restoring venous return and cardiac output.
Explanation

Standing still lets blood pool in the compliant leg veins. Each step squeezes those veins; valves prevent backflow, so blood moves up towards the heart and leg venous pressure falls. Venous return, stroke volume and cardiac output recover, adding to the baroreceptor reflex. Soldiers who faint on parade do so because they stand motionless; clenching the leg muscles helps for the same reason.

  • Walking does not constrict leg arterioles, and raising capillary pressure would cause oedema, not help the circulation.
  • Dilating the veins would let more blood pool, making the light-headedness worse.
Slides (1)
L12LearningHigh yield
A diabetic man becomes light-headed on standing. Supine: 132/78 mmHg, pulse 76. Standing: 96/58 mmHg, pulse 78. Which finding points to a failure of the baroreceptor reflex?
  1. A. The systolic pressure falls by more than 20 mmHg
  2. B. The supine blood pressure is normal
  3. C. The pulse barely rises despite a large fall in pressure
AnswerC. The pulse barely rises despite a large fall in pressure
WhyA healthy reflex answers a large fall in pressure with tachycardia; a pulse that does not rise shows the reflex arc (here autonomic neuropathy) is broken.
Explanation

A 36 mmHg systolic fall proves orthostatic hypotension but not its cause. If the cause were low volume (bleeding, dehydration), the reflex would be intact and the pulse would rise steeply. A pressure fall with an unchanged pulse localises the problem to the reflex itself: damaged autonomic nerves (diabetic autonomic neuropathy), sympathectomy or drugs such as beta-blockers.

  • The systolic fall confirms orthostatic hypotension, but volume loss would produce it too; it does not localise the cause.
  • A normal supine pressure is expected in both causes and tells you nothing about the reflex.
Slides (1)
L13Learning
What defines a positive orthostatic test, and what does it indicate?
  1. A. Pulse ↑ 10, systolic ↓ 20, diastolic ↓ 10 → about 15–20% of blood volume lost
  2. B. Pulse ↑ 10, systolic ↓ 20, diastolic ↓ 10 → about 30–40% of blood volume lost
  3. C. Pulse ↓ 10, systolic ↑ 20, diastolic ↑ 10 → about 15–20% of blood volume lost
AnswerA. Pulse ↑ 10, systolic ↓ 20, diastolic ↓ 10 → about 15–20% of blood volume lost
WhyA 10-point rise in pulse, 20-point fall in systolic or 10-point fall in diastolic pressure on standing indicates about 15–20% volume loss.
Explanation

Orthostatic vital signs unmask a moderate volume loss that the reflex can still hide when the patient lies flat. Lying, the pressure may be normal; standing adds the pooling stress and exposes the deficit. Most guidelines define orthostatic hypotension as a fall of at least 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic; the lecture adds the pulse rise of 10.

  • 30–40% loss usually produces a low pressure or fast pulse even lying down (next question); orthostatics are not needed then.
  • The direction is a pulse rise and pressure fall, not the reverse.
Slides (2)
L14Learning
A man with three black, bloody stools has blood pressure 96/60 mmHg and pulse 115/min. How much blood has he likely lost, and what is the next step?
  1. A. About 30% lost → skip orthostatics; give 1 L normal saline
  2. B. About 15–20% lost → check orthostatics first, then give fluid
  3. C. About 30% lost → give 1 L 5% dextrose in water
AnswerA. About 30% lost → skip orthostatics; give 1 L normal saline
WhyA systolic below 100 or pulse above 100 lying down already signals about 30% volume loss: orthostatics add nothing, so give 1 L normal saline at once.
Explanation

Orthostatic testing is for unmasking a hidden 15–20% loss. When the patient is already hypotensive or tachycardic at rest, the loss is larger and standing him up risks collapse. Fluid comes first; endoscopy and repeat blood counts can follow. (Trauma grading systems place a pulse of 100–120 with normal systolic pressure at 15–30% loss; the lecture uses the simpler 'below 100 / above 100 = 30%' rule.)

  • Checking orthostatics first delays treatment and is unnecessary once resting vitals are abnormal.
  • 5% dextrose does not stay in the circulation (next question).
Slides (1)
L15LearningHigh yield
Why replace blood loss with normal saline rather than 5% dextrose in water?
  1. A. Dextrose water stays in the circulation better but causes hyperglycaemia
  2. B. Dextrose water pulls fluid out of cells into the circulation
  3. C. Dextrose water spreads through all body water instead of staying in the circulation
AnswerC. Dextrose water spreads through all body water instead of staying in the circulation
WhyNormal saline (0.9% NaCl) stays in the extracellular fluid, much of it in the plasma; 5% dextrose becomes free water once the glucose is metabolised and spreads through all body water, so little stays in the vessels.
Explanation

Na+ is held outside cells by the Na+/K+-ATPase, so isotonic saline distributes only in the extracellular fluid: about a quarter to a third of each litre stays intravascular. Dextrose is taken up and burned, leaving water that distributes across intracellular and extracellular fluid in proportion (about two-thirds inside cells), so only roughly a twelfth of a litre stays in the plasma. Half-normal saline falls between the two.

  • Dextrose water is effectively hypotonic; it moves water into cells, not out of them.
  • It stays in the circulation worse, not better.
Slides (1)

Lecture 29 · Swan–Ganz catheter and shock

L16Learning
What does the Swan–Ganz 'wedge' pressure estimate?
  1. A. Pulmonary artery systolic pressure
  2. B. Left atrial pressure
  3. C. Right atrial pressure
AnswerB. Left atrial pressure
WhyWith the balloon wedged in a small pulmonary artery branch, the tip sees a still column of blood continuous with the pulmonary veins, so it reads left atrial pressure.
Explanation

Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is measured by inflating the balloon until it blocks a small pulmonary artery branch. Flow beyond it stops, so there is no pressure drop across that segment, and the pressure at the tip equals the pressure downstream: pulmonary capillaries → pulmonary veins → left atrium (normally about 8–10 mmHg). With the mitral valve open in diastole it also approximates left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, so it is the bedside measure of left-sided preload.

  • Pulmonary artery systolic pressure (about 25 mmHg) is read with the balloon deflated, upstream of the pulmonary resistance.
  • Right atrial pressure is read from the catheter's proximal port, on the other side of the lungs.
Slides (3)
L17Learning
How is systemic vascular resistance (SVR) obtained with a Swan–Ganz catheter?
  1. A. Calculated from the wedge pressure alone
  2. B. Calculated from the cardiac output it measures, with arterial and right atrial pressures
  3. C. Read directly from the right atrial pressure alone
