AnswerB. Calculated from the cardiac output it measures, with arterial and right atrial pressures
WhySVR is calculated: (mean arterial pressure − right atrial pressure) ÷ cardiac output, the output being measured by the catheter's thermodilution sensor.
Explanation

This is Ohm's law for the systemic circulation, R = ΔP/Q. The pressure drop is from the aorta (mean arterial pressure) to the right atrium; the flow is the cardiac output. Low SVR indicates vasodilation (sepsis, anaphylaxis); high SVR indicates reflex vasoconstriction (heart failure, hypovolaemia).

  • Wedge pressure reflects left atrial filling, not systemic resistance.
  • Right atrial pressure is only one term in the calculation; resistance needs flow as well.
Slides (2)
L18LearningHigh yield
Which Swan–Ganz pattern fits hypovolaemia?
  1. A. SVR ↑
    Cardiac output ↓
    Wedge ↓
  2. B. SVR ↑
    Cardiac output ↓
    Wedge ↑
  3. C. SVR ↓
    Cardiac output ↑
    Wedge ↓
AnswerA. SVR ↑
Cardiac output ↓
Wedge ↓
WhyToo little blood → low venous return, so filling pressures (wedge) and cardiac output both fall; reflex vasoconstriction raises SVR.
Explanation

The heart is healthy but under-filled. Less venous return reaches the right heart, less passes through the lungs, and left atrial pressure (wedge) falls; by Frank-Starling, output falls too. The baroreceptor reflex and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system constrict arterioles, raising systemic vascular resistance.

SVRCOWedge
Sepsis↓↑↓
Cardiac failure↑↓↑
Hypovolaemia↑↓↓

The wedge separates the two low-output states: high in pump failure, low in hypovolaemia.

Slides (2)
L19Learning
A man with severe heart failure (ejection fraction below 20%) suddenly drops his blood pressure to 70/30 mmHg. Which value is decreased?
  1. A. Central venous pressure
  2. B. Systemic vascular resistance
  3. C. Mixed venous O2 saturation
AnswerC. Mixed venous O2 saturation
WhyWith cardiac output very low, tissues extract more O2 from each litre of blood, so the blood returning to the heart has a low O2 saturation.
Explanation

By the Fick principle, O2 consumption = cardiac output × arteriovenous O2 difference. If output falls while consumption stays the same, the arteriovenous difference must widen, so mixed venous O2 saturation (measured from the pulmonary artery by the Swan–Ganz catheter) falls. It is a marker of inadequate output.

  • Central venous pressure rises in cardiogenic shock: the failing heart cannot move blood forward, so it backs up.
  • Systemic vascular resistance rises from reflex sympathetic vasoconstriction (and angiotensin II and vasopressin).
Slides (2)
L20LearningHigh yield
A man with a gunshot wound to the abdomen still has pulse 140/min and blood pressure 70/40 mmHg after 4 L of normal saline. What is the most useful next step as he is prepared for surgery?
  1. A. Start a vasodilator: nitroglycerin (or nitroprusside)
  2. B. Start a vasopressor: norepinephrine (or dopamine, vasopressin, phenylephrine)
  3. C. Start an inotrope: dobutamine
AnswerB. Start a vasopressor: norepinephrine (or dopamine, vasopressin, phenylephrine)
WhyShock that persists after adequate fluid needs a vasopressor to raise vascular resistance and pressure; norepinephrine is first choice, with dopamine, vasopressin or phenylephrine as alternatives.
Explanation

Four litres of saline should have corrected simple volume loss; continuing shock (here likely septic from faecal contamination of the peritoneum) means the vessels are dilated. Norepinephrine acts on alpha-1 receptors to constrict arterioles and veins (and on beta-1 to support the heart); vasopressin acts on V1 receptors; phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 agonist; dopamine at high doses also acts on alpha-1.

  • Dobutamine raises contractility but its beta-2 action can lower resistance; it suits cardiogenic shock, not vasodilated shock.
  • Nitroglycerin/nitroprusside dilate vessels and would drop the pressure further; they are the least helpful choice.
Slides (1)

PHYS-RX Cardiovascular drug actions / ANS–CV drug workshop

31 learning questions · of 71
Learning questions 31

The rule: BP = CO × TPR

L1LearningHigh yield
A drug can change blood pressure only by changing which two things directly?
  1. A. CO (acting on the arterioles)
    TPR (acting on the heart)
  2. B. Heart rate (acting on the heart)
    Blood volume (acting on the arterioles)
  3. C. CO (acting on the heart or venous return)
    TPR (acting on the arterioles)
AnswerC. CO (acting on the heart or venous return)
TPR (acting on the arterioles)
WhyA drug can only change cardiac output (heart rate, stroke volume, venous return) or total peripheral resistance (arteriolar tone); BP follows.
Explanation

Blood pressure (BP) is never acted on by itself: it is the product of cardiac output (CO) and total peripheral resistance (TPR). CO is set by the heart (rate through β1 and M2, force through β1) and by venous return (venodilators, diuretics). TPR is set by arteriolar smooth muscle (α1 constricts; β2, M3/nitric oxide and α1 blockers dilate).

  • CO acting on the arterioles / TPR acting on the heart swaps the two sites.
  • Blood volume changes pressure only by changing venous return and so CO; it is not a separate lever, and it is not set at the arterioles.
Slides (2)
L2LearningHigh yield
In what order do the events appear on a drug's blood-pressure tracing?
  1. A. Direct effect on CO or TPR → change in BP → baroreceptor reflex
  2. B. Change in BP → direct effect on CO or TPR → baroreceptor reflex
  3. C. Baroreceptor reflex → direct effect on CO or TPR → change in BP
AnswerA. Direct effect on CO or TPR → change in BP → baroreceptor reflex
WhyThe drug first changes CO or TPR directly (1), pressure then follows (2), and only the pressure change triggers the baroreceptor reflex (3).
Explanation

The answer key numbers every tracing this way. For phenylephrine: TPR ↑ (1) → BP ↑ (2) → vagal reflex slows the heart, CO ↓ (3). For a vasodilator: TPR ↓ (1) → BP ↓ (2) → β1 reflex tachycardia, CO ↑ (3).

  • BP first is impossible: pressure can only change because CO or TPR changed.
  • Reflex first is impossible: baroreceptors respond to a change in pressure, so the reflex is always the last step, and it can be absent if the drug blocks its pathway.
Slides (3)

Receptors on the heart and vessels

L3LearningHigh yield
What does β2 receptor activation do to the vessels?
  1. A. Skeletal-muscle arterioles constrict → TPR ↑
  2. B. Skeletal-muscle arterioles dilate → TPR ↓
  3. C. Skin and gut arterioles constrict → TPR ↑
AnswerB. Skeletal-muscle arterioles dilate → TPR ↓
Whyβ2 (Gs, cAMP) relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle, mainly in skeletal muscle, so total peripheral resistance and diastolic pressure fall.
Explanation

β2 receptors raise cAMP in vascular smooth muscle, which inhibits myosin light-chain kinase and relaxes the vessel. Skeletal muscle is a large vascular bed, so its dilation lowers total peripheral resistance (TPR) noticeably. β2 is more sensitive to epinephrine than α1, which is why low doses of epinephrine dilate.

  • Muscle arterioles constrict is the opposite of β2.
  • Skin and gut constriction is α1.

Drugs with β2 action in this lesson: epinephrine, isoproterenol, albuterol, terbutaline.

Slides (2)
L4LearningHigh yield
Atropine is given alone. What happens to resting heart rate?
  1. A. Falls: M2 block removes sympathetic tone at the SA node
  2. B. Rises: atropine stimulates β1 receptors at the SA node
  3. C. Rises: M2 block removes vagal tone at the SA node
AnswerC. Rises: M2 block removes vagal tone at the SA node
WhyAtropine blocks M2; at rest the SA node is held down by vagal tone, so removing it raises heart rate (used for unstable bradycardia).
Explanation

Atropine is a competitive muscarinic antagonist. The resting SA node fires near 100/min intrinsically and is slowed to about 70/min by continuous vagal (M2) tone. Blocking M2 takes that brake off, so heart rate and AV conduction rise. Atropine also abolishes every vagal effect in the workshop: vagal stimulation, the vagal reflex after phenylephrine, and nicotine's vagal dip.

  • Sympathetic tone is carried by norepinephrine on β1, which atropine does not touch; M2 is the parasympathetic receptor.
  • Atropine has no agonist action at β1; the rise comes only from removing the vagal brake.
Slides (2)
L5LearningHigh yield
What does M3 receptor activation do to the vessels?
  1. A. Endothelium releases nitric oxide → vessels constrict
  2. B. Endothelium releases nitric oxide → vessels dilate
  3. C. Endothelium releases endothelin → vessels constrict
AnswerB. Endothelium releases nitric oxide → vessels dilate
WhyEndothelial M3 (Gq) activates nitric oxide synthase; nitric oxide diffuses to the smooth muscle and dilates the vessel.
Explanation

Blood vessels have no parasympathetic innervation, but their endothelium carries M3 receptors. Circulating acetylcholine (or a drug) binds them: Gq → Ca2+ → endothelial nitric oxide synthase → nitric oxide → smooth-muscle cGMP → relaxation. This is how injected acetylcholine lowers blood pressure.

  • Nitric oxide constricts is wrong: nitric oxide is a vasodilator.
  • Endothelin is an endothelial vasoconstrictor, but it is not released by M3.

If the endothelium is damaged, acetylcholine acts on smooth-muscle M3 directly and constricts instead.

Slides (3)
L6LearningHigh yield
What does α2 receptor activation do?
  1. A. Brakes acetylcholine release from the nerve ending; in the brainstem ↑ sympathetic outflow
  2. B. Speeds norepinephrine release from the nerve ending; in the brainstem ↑ sympathetic outflow
  3. C. Brakes norepinephrine release from the nerve ending; in the brainstem ↓ sympathetic outflow
AnswerC. Brakes norepinephrine release from the nerve ending; in the brainstem ↓ sympathetic outflow
Whyα2 (Gi) is an inhibitory receptor: on the nerve ending it brakes norepinephrine release, and in the vasomotor centre it lowers sympathetic outflow.
Explanation

α2 receptors are Gi-coupled (cAMP ↓). Presynaptic α2 autoreceptors give negative feedback on norepinephrine release. Central α2 receptors in the medullary vasomotor centre cut sympathetic outflow to heart and vessels: this is how clonidine lowers blood pressure. Blocking α2 (phentolamine) removes the brake, so more norepinephrine reaches cardiac β1.

  • Acetylcholine release is not the main α2 target here, and central α2 lowers outflow.
  • Speeding release is the opposite of an autoreceptor's job.
Slides (2)

The baroreceptor reflex

L7LearningHigh yield
What reflex follows a drug-induced fall in blood pressure?
  1. A. Sympathetic (β1) reflex → heart slows
  2. B. Vagal (M2) reflex → heart speeds up
  3. C. Sympathetic (β1) reflex → heart speeds up
AnswerC. Sympathetic (β1) reflex → heart speeds up
WhyUnloaded baroreceptors fire less; the medulla raises sympathetic (β1) drive and withdraws vagal tone, giving reflex tachycardia.
Explanation

When pressure falls the baroreceptors fire less, so the medulla increases sympathetic outflow (norepinephrine on SA-node and ventricular β1, plus α1 vasoconstriction where it is not blocked) and decreases vagal outflow. The handout calls this "tachycardia at a reduced blood pressure (Sympathetic Reflex)".

  • β1 slowing is wrong: β1 only speeds the heart.
  • Vagal M2 speeding is wrong: M2 only slows the heart (withdrawing vagal tone helps, but the active arm is β1).
Slides (3)
L8LearningHigh yield
Why does a ganglion blocker abolish every baroreceptor reflex?
  1. A. Both reflex arms end on β1 receptors on the heart
  2. B. Both reflex arms (vagal and sympathetic) relay through autonomic ganglia
  3. C. Both reflex arms relay through the adrenal medulla
AnswerB. Both reflex arms (vagal and sympathetic) relay through autonomic ganglia
WhyVagal and sympathetic efferents both synapse on NN receptors in autonomic ganglia; block the ganglia and no reflex can reach heart or vessels.
Explanation

The reflex's efferent limb is two-neuron in both divisions: preganglionic → ganglion (NN) → postganglionic. A ganglion blocker such as mecamylamine interrupts both, so after it a pressor drug raises pressure with no reflex slowing and a depressor drug lowers it with no reflex speeding. Hook: "All reflex must go through a ganglion."

  • β1 on the heart is the end of the sympathetic arm only; the vagal arm ends on M2.
  • The adrenal medulla contributes circulating epinephrine but is not the route of the vagal reflex.
Slides (2)

Pressors, vasodilators and inotropes

L9LearningHigh yield
What tracing does phenylephrine (pure α1 agonist) produce?
  1. A. TPR ↑ → BP ↑ → vagal reflex slows the heart → CO ↓
  2. B. CO ↑ → BP ↑ → vagal reflex slows the heart → CO ↓
  3. C. TPR ↓ → BP ↓ → sympathetic reflex speeds the heart → CO ↑
AnswerA. TPR ↑ → BP ↑ → vagal reflex slows the heart → CO ↓
WhyPhenylephrine constricts arterioles: TPR ↑ (1) → BP ↑ (2) → vagal reflex bradycardia, CO ↓ (3).
Explanation

Phenylephrine acts only on α1, so it cannot touch the heart directly. Systolic and diastolic pressure both climb; the baroreceptor reflex then slows the heart through vagal M2, so cardiac output falls. The table row reads CO ↓ (3), TPR ↑ (1), BP ↑ (2), reflex yes.

  • CO ↑ first would need β1 action, which phenylephrine lacks.
  • TPR ↓ with reflex tachycardia is the vasodilator (α1 blocker or β2 agonist) tracing.
Slides (3)
L10LearningHigh yield
What tracing does a pure arteriolar vasodilator produce?
  1. A. TPR ↓ → BP ↓ → reflex tachycardia → CO ↑
  2. B. TPR ↑ → BP ↑ → reflex bradycardia → CO ↓
  3. C. CO ↓ → BP ↓ → reflex vasoconstriction → TPR ↑
AnswerA. TPR ↓ → BP ↓ → reflex tachycardia → CO ↑
WhyA vasodilator lowers TPR (1) → BP falls (2) → the β1 sympathetic reflex speeds the heart and CO rises (3).
Explanation

The arteriolar dilator row of the table: CO ↑ (3), TPR ↓ (1), BP ↓ (2), reflex yes, "expect reflexive tachycardia". Diastolic pressure falls most, because it depends most on resistance. The same tracing comes from a β2 agonist or an α1 blocker.

  • TPR ↑ with reflex bradycardia is the phenylephrine (vasoconstrictor) tracing.
  • CO ↓ first describes a venodilator or diuretic (less venous return), not an arteriolar dilator.
Slides (2)
L11LearningHigh yield
A man on several medicines feels faint every time he stands up. Which of his drugs is the most likely cause?
  1. A. Phenylephrine (α1 agonist) nasal decongestant
  2. B. Prazosin (α1 blocker) for blood pressure
  3. C. Albuterol (β2 agonist) inhaler for asthma
AnswerB. Prazosin (α1 blocker) for blood pressure
WhyOn standing, pressure is held up by α1 venous and arteriolar constriction; an α1 blocker removes it, causing orthostatic hypotension, worst after the first dose.
Explanation

Standing pools blood in the legs; the baroreflex answers with sympathetic α1 constriction (and β1 speeding). Prazosin, doxazosin and terazosin block the α1 arm, so pressure falls on standing: dizziness, blurred vision, falls in older patients.

  • Phenylephrine stimulates α1: it raises pressure, the opposite of orthostatic hypotension.
  • Inhaled albuterol may cause tremor or tachycardia but is not a recognised cause of postural hypotension.

β blockers can add to orthostasis by blunting the β1 arm, but the α1 blocker is the classic culprit.

Slides (2)
L12LearningHigh yield
How does raising stroke volume alone (β1 agonist such as dobutamine, cardiotonic use) change the blood-pressure tracing?
  1. A. TPR ↑ → BP ↑: diastolic rises most, pulse pressure narrows
  2. B. TPR ↓ → BP ↓: diastolic falls, pulse pressure widens
  3. C. CO ↑ → BP ↑: systolic rises, pulse pressure widens
AnswerC. CO ↑ → BP ↑: systolic rises, pulse pressure widens
Whyβ1 alone raises stroke volume: CO ↑ (1) → BP ↑ (2), seen mostly as a higher systolic peak and a wider pulse pressure.
Explanation

A bigger stroke volume ejected into the same arterial tree raises systolic pressure more than diastolic, so the swings on the tracing get taller. The key labels it "β1 alone", CO ↑ (1), BP ↑ (2). Dobutamine (and dopamine at moderate doses) is used this way in cardiogenic shock and acute heart failure.

  • Diastolic up most, narrow pulse pressure is the α1 (phenylephrine) pattern.
  • Diastolic down, wide pulse pressure is isoproterenol, which adds β2 vasodilation.
Slides (2)

Phenylephrine after pretreatment

L13LearningHigh yield
What does phenylephrine do after mecamylamine (ganglion blocker)?
  1. A. No rise at all: the α1 response must pass through a ganglion
  2. B. Pressure rises with no reflex at all: every reflex passes through a ganglion
  3. C. Pressure falls with reflex tachycardia: the ganglion blocker reverses the α1 effect
AnswerB. Pressure rises with no reflex at all: every reflex passes through a ganglion
WhyPhenylephrine acts directly on vascular α1, so pressure still rises; mecamylamine blocks both reflex arms at the ganglia, so there is no reflex.
Explanation

The drug's target is on the smooth muscle itself, downstream of any ganglion, so the direct effect is intact. Both the vagal slowing and the sympathetic withdrawal that would buffer the rise relay through NN ganglia, so neither happens: TPR ↑ (1), BP ↑ (2), heart rate unchanged.

  • No rise is wrong: a ganglion blocker does not touch postjunctional α1 receptors.
  • Fall with tachycardia is wrong: nothing reverses α1 stimulation here, and a tachycardic reflex would need intact ganglia.
Slides (2)
L14LearningHigh yield
What does phenylephrine do after physostigmine (anticholinesterase)?
  1. A. Pressure rises with no reflex, because acetylcholine is destroyed faster
  2. B. Pressure rises, then an exaggerated vagal reflex slows the heart sharply
  3. C. Pressure rises, then a potentiated sympathetic reflex speeds the heart
AnswerB. Pressure rises, then an exaggerated vagal reflex slows the heart sharply
WhyPhysostigmine stops acetylcholine breakdown, so the vagal (M2) reflex to the rise in pressure is potentiated: deep, prolonged slowing (CO ↓ 3).
Explanation

The direct effect is normal: TPR ↑ (1), BP ↑ (2). When the baroreflex fires the vagus, the acetylcholine released at the SA node lingers because cholinesterase is inhibited, so the bradycardia is much stronger ("increased cholinergic activity", "potentiated vagal reflex"). The tracing shows long pauses between beats.

  • Acetylcholine destroyed faster is the opposite of what an anticholinesterase does.
  • Sympathetic speeding is wrong: a rise in pressure triggers the vagal reflex, not the sympathetic one.
Slides (3)

Catecholamines: norepinephrine, epinephrine, isoproterenol

L15LearningHigh yield
Which receptors does norepinephrine act on, and what happens to pressure?
  1. A. α1 and β2: TPR ↑ and CO ↓ → BP unchanged
  2. B. α2 and β1: TPR and CO ↓ together → BP falls
  3. C. α1 and β1: TPR and CO ↑ together → BP climbs steeply
AnswerC. α1 and β1: TPR and CO ↑ together → BP climbs steeply
WhyNorepinephrine is α1 + β1 (little β2): it raises TPR and CO at once, so systolic and diastolic pressure both climb.
Explanation

The tracing title reads "Norepinephrine (α-1, β-1)" and the table row is CO ↑ (1), TPR ↑ (1), BP ↑ (2). With both factors of BP = CO × TPR rising, the pressor response is strong. Norepinephrine also stimulates α2 but has little β2 action, which is what separates it from epinephrine.

  • β2 is the receptor norepinephrine largely lacks.
  • α2 with a fall in pressure is the clonidine pattern, not norepinephrine's.
Slides (3)
L16LearningHigh yield
In this course, why does norepinephrine's tracing show no reflex slowing of the heart?
  1. A. No vagal reflex is triggered, because pressure rises too slowly
  2. B. A vagal reflex is triggered, but norepinephrine's direct β1 action covers it
  3. C. The vagal reflex is blocked at the ganglion by norepinephrine
AnswerB. A vagal reflex is triggered, but norepinephrine's direct β1 action covers it
WhyThe pressure rise does fire the vagal (M2) reflex, but norepinephrine's direct β1 push on the heart masks it.
Explanation

The course's answer key marks norepinephrine "reflex: no" for exactly this reason. Many pharmacology texts instead show heart rate falling slightly during a norepinephrine infusion, because the strong α1 pressor effect makes the vagal reflex outweigh the direct β1 effect. For this exam, follow the key. Either way, block the reflex (ganglion blocker, atropine) and the direct β1 tachycardia appears.

  • Pressure rises too slowly: the rise is steep, and baroreceptors respond to it.
  • Blocked at the ganglion: norepinephrine does not block NN receptors.
Slides (2)
L17LearningHigh yield
Why does diastolic pressure rise less with epinephrine than with norepinephrine?
  1. A. β1 stimulation shortens diastole and lowers filling pressure
  2. B. β2 dilation of muscle arterioles opposes the α1 constriction
  3. C. α2 constriction of muscle arterioles opposes the β2 dilation
AnswerB. β2 dilation of muscle arterioles opposes the α1 constriction
WhyDiastolic pressure tracks TPR; epinephrine's β2 dilation in skeletal muscle offsets part of its α1 constriction, so TPR rises less.
Explanation

During diastole the aorta runs off through the arterioles, so diastolic pressure depends mainly on resistance. Norepinephrine (little β2) raises resistance unopposed; epinephrine's β2 pulls the other way ("β2 vs α1 compromises diastolic BP"). Its β1 action raises stroke volume, so systolic still climbs and pulse pressure widens.

  • Shorter diastole leaves less time for run-off, which would raise diastolic pressure, not blunt it; filling pressure is a ventricular, not an arterial, pressure.
  • α2 opposing β2 reverses the logic: it is β2 that opposes the constriction.
Slides (1)
L18LearningHigh yield
Which receptors does isoproterenol act on, and what happens to pressure?
  1. A. β2 only (no β1): TPR ↓ → mean and diastolic ↓; CO ↓, pulse pressure narrows
  2. B. β1 and β2 (no α): TPR ↑ → mean and diastolic ↑; CO ↓, pulse pressure widens
  3. C. β1 and β2 (no α): TPR ↓ → mean and diastolic ↓; CO ↑, pulse pressure widens
AnswerC. β1 and β2 (no α): TPR ↓ → mean and diastolic ↓; CO ↑, pulse pressure widens
WhyIsoproterenol is a pure β1 + β2 agonist: β2 lowers TPR so mean and diastolic fall; β1 raises CO so pulse pressure widens.
Explanation

Table row: CO ↑ (1), TPR ↓ (1), BP ↓ (2), reflex no, "direct β1 agonist action hides any sympathetic reflex". The tracing shows a brief systolic rise (β1) then a fall in diastolic and mean pressure (β2), with tall, wide swings. It has no α action at all.

  • β2 only with CO ↓ ignores isoproterenol's strong direct β1 stimulation.
  • TPR ↑ is wrong: without α1, nothing in isoproterenol can constrict arterioles.
Slides (3)

Agonists after α and β blockers

L19Learning
What does norepinephrine do after phentolamine (α blocker)?
  1. A. Only β1 is left: pressure still rises, on output alone
  2. B. Only β2 is left: pressure falls (reversal)
  3. C. Nothing is left: the response is abolished
AnswerA. Only β1 is left: pressure still rises, on output alone
WhyWith α blocked, norepinephrine still has β1: CO ↑ (1) → BP ↑ (2), a smaller rise than before.
Explanation

Phentolamine removes the α1 constriction, so TPR no longer rises. Norepinephrine's β1 action on the heart is untouched, so cardiac output rises and pressure still goes up, less steeply. Because norepinephrine has little β2, nothing is left to dilate, so there is no reversal.

  • Reversal needs a strong β2 agonist, which is epinephrine, not norepinephrine.
  • Abolished would need both α and β1 blocked.
Slides (2)
L20LearningHigh yield
What does epinephrine do after phentolamine (α blocker)?
  1. A. α1 constriction wins → TPR ↑ → BP rises more steeply
  2. B. β2 dilation wins → TPR ↓ → BP falls (epinephrine reversal)
  3. C. All its receptors are blocked → BP unchanged
AnswerB. β2 dilation wins → TPR ↓ → BP falls (epinephrine reversal)
WhyWith α1 blocked, epinephrine's β2 vasodilation is unopposed: TPR ↓ (1) → BP ↓ (2), with β1 tachycardia. This is Dale's vasomotor reversal.
Explanation

Normally epinephrine's α1 constriction outweighs its β2 dilation and pressure rises. Take α1 away and only β1 (heart) and β2 (vessels) remain: the vessels dilate, TPR falls, and pressure falls even though the heart is beating faster and harder. The tracing labels the two curves "α-1, β-1, β-2" (rise) and "β-1, β-2" (fall).

  • Steeper rise is what a β blocker does to epinephrine (α1 left unopposed).
  • Unchanged is wrong: phentolamine blocks α only; both β receptors still work.
Slides (3)
L21LearningHigh yield
A woman taking propranolol (β1 + β2 blocker) is given epinephrine for anaphylaxis. What blood-pressure response should be expected?
  1. A. A fall: β2 dilation is now unopposed by α1
  2. B. A marked rise: α1 constriction is now unopposed by β2
  3. C. No change: all of epinephrine's receptors are blocked
AnswerB. A marked rise: α1 constriction is now unopposed by β2
WhyWith both β receptors blocked, epinephrine is left with α1 only: unopposed vasoconstriction gives hypertension, often with reflex bradycardia.
Explanation

Normally β2 dilation in muscle beds blunts epinephrine's pressor effect and β1 drives the heart. Propranolol removes both, so epinephrine behaves like phenylephrine: TPR ↑ → BP ↑, and the vagal reflex can slow the heart. The same logic explains why epinephrine reliably constricts vessels in a patient on nadolol.

  • A fall is epinephrine reversal, which needs an α blocker, not a β blocker.
  • No change is wrong: propranolol does not block α1.
Slides (2)
L22LearningHigh yield
What does isoproterenol do after metoprolol (β1-selective blocker)?
  1. A. β2 lowers TPR, but a β1 reflex tachycardia restores BP to baseline
  2. B. β2 still lowers TPR and BP, with no direct CO rise and no β1 reflex
  3. C. The response is abolished, because metoprolol blocks β2 as well
AnswerB. β2 still lowers TPR and BP, with no direct CO rise and no β1 reflex
WhyMetoprolol blocks β1 only, so isoproterenol's β2 dilation remains: TPR ↓ (1) → BP ↓ (2), and "no direct ↑ CO, no β1 reflex".
Explanation

Without metoprolol, isoproterenol's β1 action raises cardiac output and partly offsets the fall in resistance. With β1 blocked, the heart cannot respond, either directly or by reflex, so the pressure fall is unbuffered and hypotension results.

  • Reflex restores BP: the reflex tachycardia needs β1, which is blocked.
  • Abolished: metoprolol is β1-selective at usual doses; abolition needs a non-selective blocker.
Slides (2)

Vagal and carotid reflex demonstrations

L23Learning
What happens during and after prolonged vagal stimulation?
  1. A. The heart escapes and beats again (β1 drive helping); when stimulation stops, the sympathetic reflex (α1, β1) leaves pressure above baseline
  2. B. The heart stays stopped until stimulation ends; when stimulation stops, pressure returns exactly to baseline with no overshoot
  3. C. The heart escapes and beats again (α1 drive helping); when stimulation stops, pressure stays at the low level reached during stimulation
AnswerA. The heart escapes and beats again (β1 drive helping); when stimulation stops, the sympathetic reflex (α1, β1) leaves pressure above baseline
WhyVagal escape: the heart resumes beating despite continued stimulation (β1); when stimulation ends, the built-up sympathetic reflex overshoots pressure above baseline.
Explanation

The slide is titled "Vagus (M2), Vagal Escape (β-1) and SANS Reflex (α-1, β-1)". The fall in pressure unloads the baroreceptors, which drives sympathetic β1 output to the heart and α1 output to vessels; beats return during stimulation, and after "finish stimulus" pressure sits above the control level. Physiology texts add that escape also reflects latent pacemakers below the SA node; this course attributes it to β1.

  • No escape, no overshoot: the tracing shows both.
  • α1 drive restarting the heart: α1 acts on vessels, not pacemaker cells.
Slides (2)
L24Learning
What does bilateral carotid occlusion do to the tracing?
  1. A. Carotid-sinus pressure falls → baroreceptors signal a fall → sympathetic (α1, β1) pressor rise, limited by the vagal (M2) reflex
  2. B. Carotid-sinus pressure falls → baroreceptors signal a rise → sympathetic (α1, β1) pressor rise, limited by an M3 reflex
  3. C. Carotid-sinus pressure rises → baroreceptors signal a rise → vagal (M2) fall in pressure, limited by the β1 reflex
AnswerA. Carotid-sinus pressure falls → baroreceptors signal a fall → sympathetic (α1, β1) pressor rise, limited by the vagal (M2) reflex
WhyClamping below the carotid sinus unloads it; the brain reads a fall and fires a sympathetic α1/β1 pressor response, trimmed by a vagal (M2) reflex.
Explanation

The carotid sinus lies above the clamp, so its baroreceptors are unloaded even though systemic pressure is normal. The medulla responds as if pressure had fallen: sympathetic constriction (α1) and cardiac stimulation (β1) raise pressure. The aortic baroreceptors, still exposed to the rising pressure, drive a vagal M2 reflex that limits it. When the clamp is released ("finish") pressure returns.

  • "Signal a rise": unloaded receptors fire less, which the brain reads as a fall.
  • Sinus pressure rises: the clamp is below the sinus, so pressure there falls.
Slides (3)

Acetylcholine, nicotine and the ganglia

L25Learning
What tracing does nicotine (NN agonist) produce?
  1. A. A small vagal dip, then a larger sympathetic pressor rise
  2. B. A large sympathetic rise, then a small vagal dip
  3. C. A sustained rise with no dip: it stimulates sympathetic ganglia only
AnswerA. A small vagal dip, then a larger sympathetic pressor rise
WhyNicotine stimulates NN in every ganglion: phase I, a brief vagal dip; phase II, a larger sympathetic (plus adrenal epinephrine) rise.
Explanation

The tracing is marked "Phase I" (a small fall: parasympathetic ganglia fire and M2 slows the heart) and "II, Sym" (a bigger rise: sympathetic ganglia and the adrenal medulla release norepinephrine and epinephrine onto α1 and β1). Which phase shows depends on the pretreatment.

  • Rise first reverses the order on the tracing.
  • Sympathetic ganglia only: NN receptors are in parasympathetic ganglia too.
Slides (2)
L26LearningHigh yield
A drug lowers mean pressure by 30 mmHg in controls, by 50 mmHg after mecamylamine, and not at all after atropine. What kind of drug is it?
  1. A. An α1 blocker, like prazosin
  2. B. A direct muscarinic (M3) agonist, like acetylcholine
  3. C. A ganglion blocker, like mecamylamine
AnswerB. A direct muscarinic (M3) agonist, like acetylcholine
WhyAtropine abolishes it, so the fall is muscarinic; mecamylamine enlarges it, because the reflex that normally buffers the fall is gone: a direct M3 agonist.
Explanation

Work from the pretreatments. A response blocked by atropine acts at muscarinic receptors (endothelial M3 → nitric oxide). A response made larger by a ganglion blocker was being opposed by a baroreflex. Acetylcholine-like direct agonists (acetylcholine, bethanechol) fit.

  • α1 blocker: atropine would not prevent an adrenergic blocker from lowering pressure.
  • Ganglion blocker: adding a second ganglion blocker after mecamylamine would add little, and atropine would not abolish its effect.
Slides (1)

Sympatholytics and antihypertensives: the no-reflex drugs

L27Learning
Why do drugs that remove sympathetic tone lower pressure with no reflex tachycardia?
  1. A. They reset the baroreceptors to a lower set point
  2. B. They remove the sympathetic pathway the reflex would use
  3. C. They also block cardiac M2 receptors
AnswerB. They remove the sympathetic pathway the reflex would use
WhyReflex tachycardia is delivered by sympathetic nerves onto β1; drugs that silence that pathway leave the reflex nothing to work with.
Explanation

Clonidine cuts outflow at the vasomotor centre, mecamylamine blocks the ganglia, metyrosine stops catecholamine synthesis, reserpine empties the vesicles, atenolol and labetalol block β1. In each case the baroreceptors still sense the fall, but the signal cannot reach the heart. Compare prazosin or a direct arteriolar dilator, which lower TPR but leave the pathway intact, so reflex tachycardia appears.

  • Baroreceptor resetting is a slow adaptation to chronic hypertension, not how these drugs act.
  • M2 block would raise heart rate, the opposite of what is seen.
Slides (2)
L28LearningHigh yield
How does mecamylamine lower blood pressure, and why is there no reflex?
  1. A. It stimulates NN receptors in all autonomic ganglia: vagal output slows the heart
  2. B. It blocks NN receptors in all autonomic ganglia: sympathetic tone and every reflex are cut
  3. C. It blocks NM receptors at the neuromuscular junction: muscle pumping of venous return stops
AnswerB. It blocks NN receptors in all autonomic ganglia: sympathetic tone and every reflex are cut
WhyMecamylamine is a ganglion blocker: loss of sympathetic vascular tone gives TPR ↓ (1) → BP ↓ (2), and "reflex not possible, ganglia are blocked".
Explanation

Table row: CO blank, TPR ↓ (1), BP ↓ (2), reflex no. Each organ loses its dominant tone: vessels (sympathetic) dilate, and the heart (vagal tone dominant at rest) tends to speed slightly, while standing pressure cannot be defended, so postural hypotension is marked.

  • Stimulating NN is what nicotine does.
  • NM block is a neuromuscular blocker; mecamylamine does not paralyse skeletal muscle at usual doses.
Slides (2)
L29LearningHigh yield
How does reserpine lower blood pressure?
  1. A. It stops norepinephrine and epinephrine being made (synthesis block)
  2. B. It stimulates central α2 receptors (outflow brake)
  3. C. It empties sympathetic nerve endings of norepinephrine (vesicular transporter block)
AnswerC. It empties sympathetic nerve endings of norepinephrine (vesicular transporter block)
WhyReserpine blocks the vesicular monoamine transporter, so nerve endings cannot store norepinephrine and are depleted: "no norepinephrine", BP ↓, no reflex.
Explanation

Table row: CO ↓ (1), TPR ↓ (1), BP ↓ (2), reflex no. Norepinephrine left in the cytoplasm is destroyed by monoamine oxidase, so each impulse releases little transmitter. Overdose gives sympathetic failure: hypotension, bradycardia; a direct-acting pressor such as norepinephrine still works, while indirect drugs that need stored transmitter do not.

  • Synthesis block is metyrosine.
  • Central α2 agonism is clonidine.
Slides (2)
L30LearningHigh yield
A patient has headache and palpitations with a blood pressure of 200/110 and a heart rate of 120/min. Which single drug best controls both the pressure and the rate?
  1. A. Labetalol (α1 + β blocker)
  2. B. Atenolol (β1 blocker)
  3. C. Prazosin (α1 blocker)
AnswerA. Labetalol (α1 + β blocker)
WhyThe pressure comes from α1 constriction and the rate from β1; labetalol blocks both, lowering TPR and CO without reflex tachycardia.
Explanation

One drug has to lower resistance and slow the heart. Labetalol's α1 block lowers TPR; its β block lowers rate and contractility and prevents the baroreflex from speeding the heart as pressure falls.

  • Atenolol slows the heart but leaves α1 constriction untouched, so pressure stays high.
  • Prazosin lowers pressure but provokes a reflex tachycardia, making the rate worse.

In a confirmed pheochromocytoma the standard is α blockade first, then a β blocker.

Slides (1)
L31LearningHigh yield
How do venodilators and diuretics lower blood pressure?
  1. A. ↓ Venous return → CO and BP ↓; no reflex at all, heart rate unchanged
  2. B. ↓ Arteriolar tone → TPR ↓ and BP ↓; reflex ↑ heart rate raises output
  3. C. ↓ Venous return → CO and BP ↓; reflex ↑ heart rate, but output stays low
AnswerC. ↓ Venous return → CO and BP ↓; reflex ↑ heart rate, but output stays low
WhyBoth cut venous return (venodilators pool blood, diuretics shrink volume): CO ↓ (1) → BP ↓ (2); the reflex speeds the heart, but output stays low.
Explanation

Table rows: CO ↓ (1), TPR blank, BP ↓ (2), reflex yes, "reflex is ↑ HR". The key's note: "Low venous return = low cardiac output and low BP. When BP is low, may see reflexive increase in heart rate with low output." A faster heart cannot pump blood that is not returning to it.

  • No reflex: these drugs do not touch the reflex pathway, so the baroreflex works.
  • Arteriolar tone ↓ with output rising is the arteriolar dilator row.
Slides (2)
